snippets.transliteration:
mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñchid asti dhanañjaya
mayi sarvam idaṁ protaṁ sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva

raso ’ham apsu kaunteya prabhāsmi śhaśhi-sūryayoḥ
praṇavaḥ sarva-vedeṣhu śhabdaḥ khe pauruṣhaṁ nṛiṣhu

puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛithivyāṁ cha tejaśh chāsmi vibhāvasau
jīvanaṁ sarva-bhūteṣhu tapaśh chāsmi tapasviṣhu
verseTranslations: O Arjuna! There is nothing higher than Me; all is strung upon Me as rows of pearls upon a thread.
O Arjuna! I am the Fluidity in water, the Light in the sun and in the moon. I am the mystic syllable Om in the Vedic scriptures, the Sound in ether, the Virility in man.
I am the Fragrance of earth, the Brilliance of fire. I am the Life Force in all beings, and I am the Austerity of the ascetics.
snippets.commentary:
Krishna has revealed his two natures: the lower, consisting of the eight material elements, and the higher, the life-force that sustains everything. He has declared himself the origin and dissolution of the entire universe. Now he takes the teaching from cosmic architecture to intimate, personal experience. He is about to show Arjuna how to see the Divine not in distant heavens but in a glass of water.

Verse 7.7: *Mattaḥ parataraṁ nānyat kiñchid asti dhanañjaya, mayi sarvam idaṁ protaṁ sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva.* There is nothing whatsoever higher than Me, O Arjuna. All this is strung upon Me as rows of pearls upon a thread.

The first statement is absolute: *mattaḥ parataraṁ na anyat kiñchit asti*. There is nothing, nothing at all, higher than Me. Not in the physical world, not in the subtlest realms, not in the most abstract reaches of philosophical thought. Krishna is the ceiling. There is no further beyond.

The image that follows is one of the most famous in the Gita: *sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva*, like gems strung on a thread. Picture a pearl necklace. Each pearl is distinct, beautiful in its own right, apparently separate from the others. But running through every pearl, invisible from the outside, is a single thread that holds them all in place. Without the thread, the pearls scatter. They lose their arrangement, their pattern, their coherence as a necklace. The thread gives them unity.

Krishna is that thread. Every being, every object, every experience, every moment is a pearl. They appear separate. They appear independent. But running through all of them, invisible to ordinary perception, is a single connecting principle that holds everything together. Remove that principle, and the universe falls apart into disconnected fragments.

This image reframes the way we look at reality. Normally we see the pearls. We see individual objects, individual people, individual events. We navigate among them, choosing some, avoiding others, comparing them to each other. What we almost never notice is the thread. The unifying presence that makes all of this a coherent whole rather than random chaos.

This image has practical consequences for how we navigate conflict and division. When two people are in disagreement, they see only the separateness of their positions. My view here, your view there, a gap between us. But if both are pearls on the same thread, then the separation is only at the surface. At a deeper level, they are connected by the same sustaining principle. A manager mediating a dispute between two team members, a parent navigating sibling rivalry, a diplomat seeking resolution between nations: in each case, the path forward involves looking past the apparent separateness of the pearls to find the thread that connects them. Krishna is not offering a sentimental platitude about unity. He is describing the actual structure of reality.

The metaphor also illuminates the nature of loss. When someone we love dies, we experience their absence as a disappearance, a pearl removed from the necklace. But if the thread is what gives each pearl its place, and if the thread is eternal and unbroken, then what we call death is a change in the arrangement of pearls, not a break in the thread. The animating principle that made the person alive, the consciousness that looked out through their eyes, the love that flowed through their actions: these belong to the thread, not to the pearl. And the thread, Krishna says, is himself.

Verse 7.8: *Raso 'ham apsu kaunteya prabhāsmi śhaśhi-sūryayoḥ, praṇavaḥ sarva-vedeṣhu śhabdaḥ khe pauruṣhaṁ nṛiṣhu.* I am the taste in water, O son of Kunti. I am the light of the sun and moon. I am the sacred syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in ether, and the ability in human beings.

Krishna does not say, "I am water." He says, "I am the taste in water." This distinction matters enormously. He is not identifying with the material substance. He is identifying with the essential quality that makes the substance what it is. Water without taste is not truly water as we experience it. The sun without light is not the sun. Om without its sacred resonance is just a sound. It is the essential quality, the characteristic that defines the thing, that Krishna claims as himself.

What does this mean in practice? It means that every time you drink water and notice its taste, you are encountering the Divine. Not metaphorically. Not as a nice spiritual thought. Actually. The quality of taste itself, the capacity of water to quench and refresh, is a direct expression of Krishna's nature.

Pause and consider what this means for the structure of your ordinary day. You wake in the morning and feel the warmth of sunlight through the window: that is an encounter with the Divine. You step outside and feel a breeze against your skin: the movement of air is *vayu*, one expression of the lower nature, and the sensation of feeling it is the higher nature at work in you. You eat breakfast, and the taste of each bite is Krishna declaring his presence. These are not poetic metaphors designed to make the mundane seem sacred. They are descriptions of what is actually happening at every moment. The Divine is not absent from daily life, waiting to be found in some special moment of meditation. The Divine is the daily life, expressing itself through every quality, every sensation, every experience.

Every time you see sunlight warming the world, every time moonlight turns an ordinary terrain into something luminous, you are seeing Krishna. The light is not a created thing separate from its creator. The light is the creator's own quality, expressed through sun and moon.

*Praṇavaḥ sarva-vedeṣhu*: Om in all the Vedas. Om is considered the primordial sound, the vibration from which all other sounds and all of creation emerged. Krishna identifies himself with this original vibration. Before there were words, before there were ideas, before there were objects, there was this single sound, and that sound is Krishna.

*Śhabdaḥ khe*: the capacity of sound to travel through space. Space itself is the medium, but the fact that sound can exist within it, that vibration can carry meaning across distance, this capacity is divine.

*Pauruṣhaṁ nṛiṣhu*: the ability in human beings. Some translators render this as "virility" or "prowess," but the deeper meaning is the essential capacity that makes humans capable of doing what they do. The power to think, to create, to act, to love. That power is not self-generated. It flows from the same source as the taste in water and the light in the sun.

Verse 7.9: *Puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛithivyāṁ cha tejaśh chāsmi vibhāvasau, jīvanaṁ sarva-bhūteṣhu tapaśh chāsmi tapasviṣhu.* I am the pure fragrance of earth, the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings, and the austerity of the ascetics.

*Puṇyo gandhaḥ pṛithivyāṁ*: the sacred fragrance of earth. After rain falls on dry soil, there is a smell that rises, clean and ancient. That fragrance is not manufactured. It is the earth expressing its nature. And that nature, Krishna says, is his.

*Tejaḥ vibhāvasau*: the brilliance in fire. Not the logs that burn or the smoke that rises, but the sheer radiance, the transformative power of fire to turn one thing into another. That transforming energy is divine.

There is a parallel between fire's transformative quality and the transformative power of genuine self-inquiry. Fire takes raw material, wood, coal, food, and converts it into something else entirely: heat, light, energy, nourishment. In the same way, the fire of spiritual practice takes raw experience, the confusion, the suffering, the questions, and transforms it into wisdom. The cooking fire that turns raw grain into nourishing food is, in this reading, a visible symbol of the inner fire that turns raw life into understanding. Every kitchen stove, every campfire, every candle flame is a small altar where the transformative nature of the Divine is on display.

*Jīvanaṁ sarva-bhūteṣhu*: the life in all beings. This is the most direct statement yet. Whatever it is that makes a living being alive, that animates the body, that distinguishes a person from a corpse, that is Krishna. The difference between alive and not alive is the presence or absence of the Divine.

*Tapaḥ tapasviṣhu*: the austerity in the austere. When a person practices self-discipline, when they voluntarily undergo difficulty for the sake of growth, the capacity to do that, the inner fire that sustains the effort, is not merely human willpower. It is a manifestation of the Divine.

Taken together, these three verses offer a complete spiritual practice for everyday life. You do not need to retreat to a monastery to encounter the Divine. You do not need special rituals or elaborate ceremonies. You need only pay attention. The next glass of water you drink, notice the taste. That is Krishna. The next time you step outside and feel the sun, notice the warmth. That is Krishna. The next time you smell the earth after rain, the next time a fire crackles and glows, the next time you observe the simple fact that you are alive and aware, you are in the presence of the Divine.

This teaching democratizes spirituality. It removes every barrier of wealth, education, caste, or circumstance. A farmer working the soil and smelling the earth is as close to the Divine as any priest in any temple. A mother watching the light play on her child's face is in the presence of God. Krishna is not hidden. He is everywhere, in everything, expressing himself through every quality that makes the world what it is.

The challenge is not access. The challenge is attention. We have been walking through a gallery of divine art our entire lives, and we have been too busy checking our phones to look at the paintings.

In the next reading, Krishna will continue this theme, declaring himself the eternal seed of all beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the strength of the strong. And he will introduce a surprising distinction: all things come from him, but he is not in them.
snippets.reflection:
"There is nothing higher than Me; all is strung upon Me as rows of pearls upon a thread." This image of the pearl necklace offers a powerful contemplation for today. We see individual beads and think they are separate, but an invisible thread holds them together as one necklace. What is the common thread connecting you to your family, your colleagues, even strangers you pass on the street? Krishna says it is the Self, the "I am" that each being experiences. Today, when someone speaks to you, try to sense that same thread of consciousness animating both of you.

Krishna then gives specific examples: "I am the fluidity in water, the light in sun and moon, the sacred syllable Om, the sound in ether, the virility in man, the fragrance of earth, the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings." These verses teach us to see the Divine not in abstract theology but in immediate experience. What makes water, water? Its wetness, its fluidity. What makes fire, fire? Its heat and brilliance. That essential quality, that dharma, which makes each thing what it is, is the Divine presence.

Today, practice this recognition exercise: For each element you encounter, ask "What is its essential quality?" and recognize that quality as a direct expression of the Divine. The sweetness in your morning fruit, the warmth of sunlight on your skin, the stability of the ground beneath your feet. Can you move through an entire day holding this awareness?
snippets.shortReflection: Krishna describes Himself as the essential quality in everything: the fluidity in water, the light in sun and moon, the strength in the strong. Today's practice: for everything you encounter, identify its dharma, its essential nature, and recognize that quality as Divine presence. The sweetness in fruit. The solidarity of earth. The spaciousness of sky.

snippets.title: Day 99: The Deluded
snippets.sanskrit:
बीजं मां सर्वभूतानां विद्धि पार्थ सनातनम् |
बुद्धिर्बुद्धिमतामस्मि तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम् ||

बलं बलवतां चाहं कामरागविवर्जितम् |
धर्माविरुद्धो भूतेषु कामोऽस्मि भरतर्षभ ||

ये चैव सात्त्विका भावा राजसास्तामसाश्च ये |
मत्त एवेति तान्विद्धि नत्वहं तेषु ते मयि ||
snippets.transliteration:
bījaṁ māṁ sarva-bhūtānāṁ viddhi pārtha sanātanam
buddhir buddhimatām asmi tejas tejasvinām aham

balaṁ balavatāṁ chāhaṁ kāma-rāga-vivarjitam
dharmāviruddho bhūteṣhu kāmo ’smi bharatarṣhabha

ye chaiva sāttvikā bhāvā rājasās tāmasāśh cha ye
matta eveti tān viddhi na tvahaṁ teṣhu te mayi
verseTranslations: Know, O Arjuna, that I am the eternal Seed of being; I am the Intelligence of the intelligent, the Splendour of the resplendent.
I am the Strength of the strong, of them who are free from attachment and desire; and, O Arjuna, I am the Desire for righteousness.
Whatever be the nature of their life, whether it be pure or passionate or ignorant, they are all derived from Me. They are in Me, but I am not in them.
snippets.commentary:
Krishna has been showing Arjuna how to find the Divine in everyday experience: the taste in water, the light of the sun, the fragrance of earth, the life in every living being. Now, in these three verses, he goes deeper. He moves from the qualities of things to the very source of things, and then draws a line that will reshape how Arjuna understands the relationship between God and creation.

Verse 7.10: *Bījaṁ māṁ sarva-bhūtānāṁ viddhi pārtha sanātanam, buddhir buddhimatām asmi tejas tejasvinām aham.* Know Me, O Partha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid.

The word *bījam* means seed. Not a temporary cause, not a one-time creator who sets things in motion and steps away. An eternal seed, *sanātanam*, that remains present in every being for as long as that being exists. A tree grows from a seed, but in ordinary nature the original seed is consumed in the process. Krishna's seed is different. It is never consumed. It remains within every being at every moment, sustaining existence from the inside.

Then two specific manifestations. *Buddhir buddhimatām*: the intelligence in the intelligent. When you encounter someone whose mind cuts through confusion with unusual clarity, that clarity is not self-generated. It flows from the same source as the life in all beings and the taste in water. The brilliant doctor making a diagnosis, the engineer solving an impossible problem, the child who grasps a concept in a flash of insight: in each case, the intelligence at work is a manifestation of the eternal seed.

This has an interesting consequence for how we hold our own intelligence. If your sharpest thinking is a manifestation of the Divine, then intellectual pride becomes absurd. You did not create your intelligence any more than a lightbulb creates electricity. The bulb shapes and directs the light, but the power comes from elsewhere. Recognizing this does not diminish your achievements. It places them in their proper context. You are an instrument through which intelligence expresses itself.

The same reframing applies to the experience of creative flow. Artists, writers, musicians, and scientists often describe their best work as something that came through them rather than from them. The novelist who says 'the characters wrote themselves.' The mathematician who describes a proof as something they discovered, not invented. The musician who feels that the melody was already there, waiting to be heard. These are not modest deflections. They are accurate descriptions of what it feels like when *buddhi* flows without the obstruction of ego. Krishna is naming the source of that flow. When the instrument is clear, when ego and attachment step aside, intelligence moves freely, and the results can be extraordinary.

*Tejas tejasvinām*: the splendor of the splendid. *Tejas* is a rich word. It means brilliance, radiance, vital power, the quality that makes a person or thing shine. When someone walks into a room and their presence changes the atmosphere, when a performer steps on stage and every eye is drawn to them, when a leader speaks and people feel energized, that quality of radiance is what Krishna is claiming.

Every community has known people like this. The elder whose presence calms a room. The teacher whose enthusiasm makes difficult subjects feel accessible. The friend who, without saying anything particularly profound, somehow makes you feel more alive and more yourself when you are around them. This *tejas* is not manufactured through technique or cultivated through self-promotion. It radiates from a quality of being that is rooted in alignment with something larger than the individual personality. When a person lives in harmony with their deeper nature, that harmony becomes visible as a kind of inner luminosity.

Verse 7.11: *Balaṁ balavatāṁ chāhaṁ kāma-rāga-vivarjitam, dharmāviruddho bhūteṣhu kāmo 'smi bharatarṣhabha.* I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and attachment. And I am desire in all beings that is not contrary to dharma, O best of the Bharatas.

The first half makes an important qualification. Krishna is the strength in the strong, but *kāma-rāga-vivarjitam*, strength that is free from desire and attachment. Pure strength, exercised not for domination or personal gain but as a natural expression of capacity. When a parent lifts a child out of danger, the strength they use in that moment is selfless, instinctive, free from calculation. That is the kind of strength Krishna identifies with.

Strength corrupted by desire is something else entirely. The dictator who uses power to crush dissent, the bully who uses physical advantage to intimidate, the corporation that uses market dominance to exploit: these are strength entangled with *kāma* and *rāga*, with craving and attachment. Krishna draws a clear line. He is the strength itself, not the corruption of strength.

This distinction matters enormously in practical life. A leader who exercises authority from a place of service, making difficult decisions for the welfare of the whole, is channeling divine strength. A leader who exercises the same authority from a place of ego, making decisions to consolidate power and silence dissent, is corrupting that strength with personal agenda. Outwardly, the two may look identical. Both give orders, both make decisions, both wield influence. The difference is interior: one is free from desire and attachment; the other is saturated with both. Krishna's teaching trains us to examine not just what we do with our strength but the quality of consciousness from which we exercise it.

The second half is equally significant: *dharmāviruddho bhūteṣhu kāmo 'smi*. I am desire in beings that does not contradict dharma. This is a remarkable statement, because much of spiritual teaching seems to categorically condemn desire. Krishna does not. He says desire that is aligned with duty and righteousness is a manifestation of the Divine.

The desire to protect your family is dharmic. The desire to heal the sick is dharmic. The desire to learn, to create, to contribute, to grow: all dharmic. Even the desire for food, rest, and companionship, when held in proper proportion and not allowed to override one's duties, is natural and legitimate. Krishna is not asking anyone to become desireless in the sense of becoming an empty shell. He is asking them to align their desires with their dharma.

This alignment is itself a lifelong practice. It requires honest self-examination at every stage. The desire that was dharmic at twenty may become a subtle form of attachment at forty. The ambition that once served a genuine purpose may, over time, become an end in itself. Staying aligned means checking in regularly with yourself: is this desire still in service of something larger than my personal comfort? Am I pursuing this because it contributes to the well-being of others, or because I cannot bear to let it go? The answers will shift as you grow, and the willingness to keep asking is itself a form of yoga.

Verse 7.12: *Ye chaiva sāttvikā bhāvā rājasās tāmasāśh cha ye, matta eveti tān viddhi na tvahaṁ teṣhu te mayi.* Know that all states of being, whether *sattvic*, *rajasic*, or *tamasic*, proceed from Me alone. They are in Me, but I am not in them.

The first part is straightforward. Every quality of nature, whether it is clarity and goodness (*sattva*), passion and restlessness (*rajas*), or ignorance and inertia (*tamas*), originates from Krishna. There is no separate source of darkness or evil in this cosmology. The three gunas, with all their infinite combinations, all flow from the single divine source.

But the second part introduces one of the Gita's most subtle teachings: *na tvahaṁ teṣhu te mayi*. They are in Me, but I am not in them. The gunas exist within Krishna. Krishna does not exist within the gunas. He is not conditioned by them, not limited by them, not affected by them.

Picture a movie projector. The images on screen, the heroes, villains, terrains, storms, everything comes from the projector. The entire movie exists within the light emanating from that single source. But the projector is not inside the movie. No character in the film can find the projector by searching within the narrative. The projector is of a fundamentally different order than the images it produces.

Krishna is making the same distinction about his relationship to creation. Everything in the manifest world, every quality, every being, every experience, exists within him. But he is not contained by or limited to any of it. He is the source, the container, the ground, but he is never the content. The content changes, appears, disappears. He remains.

This resolves a problem that haunts many spiritual seekers. If God is in everything, is God also in evil? Is God in cruelty, in suffering, in ignorance? Krishna's answer: all qualities proceed from me, but I am not defined by them. The tamasic and rajasic qualities exist within the divine framework, but they do not touch the divine nature. The projector is not harmed by the villains in the film.

For the seeker, this teaching offers a way to relate to one's own negative qualities. Your moments of laziness, anger, and confusion are natural phenomena, products of the gunas operating within prakriti. They are not signs of spiritual failure. They are movements of nature within the larger field of the Divine. Seeing them this way creates space. Instead of identifying with your worst qualities and thinking "this is who I am," you can observe them as passing states, temporary configurations of the gunas, arising from the source and eventually returning to it.

But this verse also carries a warning. If the three gunas proceed from Krishna yet he transcends them, then seeking God exclusively within the world of the gunas will never succeed. You cannot find the projector by examining the movie more closely. At some point, you must look beyond the screen.

In the next reading, Krishna will explain exactly why most people fail to look beyond the screen. He will describe the power of his divine *Maya*, the three gunas working together as an almost impenetrable veil, and name the four types of people who never seek him. The teaching will grow both more challenging and more compassionate.
snippets.reflection:
"I am the eternal Seed of being; I am the Intelligence of the intelligent, the Splendour of the resplendent." When you feel proud of your intelligence or accomplishments, pause and consider: where does that intelligence come from? Krishna gently reminds us that the intellect and the intellectual both belong to Him. This is not meant to diminish your efforts but to shift your identification. The next time you solve a problem or have a creative insight, try thinking: "That intelligence flowing through me is the Divine expressing itself."

Krishna makes a crucial distinction about strength and desire: "I am the Strength of the strong, of them who are free from attachment and desire; and I am the Desire for righteousness." Notice that divine strength is without the craving to misuse it. Today, examine your own strengths and talents. Are you using them in alignment with your dharma, or are they mixed with selfish desire? The desire to care for your children, to excel at your profession, to serve your community, these are dharma-aviruddha, desires not contrary to righteousness. But the same strength twisted by ego becomes bondage.

The teaching that Sattvic, Rajasic, and Tamasic qualities all come from the Lord, yet He is not in them, is paradoxical but liberating. You are not your moods, your qualities, your changing states. Today, when you notice yourself becoming agitated (rajas) or dull (tamas), remember: these states arise and pass, but the witness of these states, that unchanging awareness, is your true nature. Can you rest in that witness position even briefly?
snippets.shortReflection: "I am the strength in the strong, free from desire and attachment." Examine your own strengths today. Are you using them to serve your dharma, or to feed your ego? The same intelligence that could solve real problems gets wasted on proving you're smarter than others. Where is your strength leaking into ego?

snippets.title: Day 100: The Veil of Three Gunas
snippets.sanskrit:
त्रिभिर्गुणमयैर्भावैरेभिः सर्वमिदं जगत् |
मोहितं नाभिजानाति मामेभ्यः परमव्ययम् ||

दैवी ह्येषा गुणमयी मम माया दुरत्यया |
मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते मायामेतां तरन्ति ते ||

न मां दुष्कृतिनो मूढाः प्रपद्यन्ते नराधमाः |
माययापहृतज्ञाना आसुरं भावमाश्रिताः ||
snippets.transliteration:
tribhir guṇa-mayair bhāvair ebhiḥ sarvam idaṁ jagat
mohitaṁ nābhijānāti māmebhyaḥ param avyayam

daivī hyeṣhā guṇa-mayī mama māyā duratyayā
mām eva ye prapadyante māyām etāṁ taranti te

na māṁ duṣhkṛitino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ
māyayāpahṛita-jñānā āsuraṁ bhāvam āśhritāḥ
verseTranslations: The inhabitants of the world, misled by those natures which the Qualities have engendered, know not that I am higher than them all, and that I do not change.
Verily, this Divine Illusion of Phenomenon manifesting itself in the Qualities is difficult to surmount. Only they who devote themselves to Me and to Me alone can accomplish it.
The sinner, the ignorant, the vile, deprived of spiritual perception by the glamour of Illusion, and he who pursues a godless life - none of them shall find Me.
snippets.commentary:
Krishna has established that all three qualities of nature, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, originate from him, yet he transcends them entirely. They exist within him; he does not exist within them. This creates an obvious question: if the Divine is the source of everything, why do most people never recognize this? Why do we walk through a world that is, in every detail, an expression of the Divine, and see only mundane objects and ordinary events?

Verse 7.13 answers: *Tribhir guṇa-mayair bhāvair ebhiḥ sarvam idaṁ jagat, mohitaṁ nābhijānāti māmebhyaḥ param avyayam.* Deluded by these three qualities of nature, the whole world does not recognize Me, who am above them and imperishable.

The word *mohitam* is devastating in its simplicity. Deluded. The entire world, *sarvam idam jagat*, is in a state of delusion. Not ignorant in the sense of lacking information. Deluded in the sense of being actively misled by appearances. The three gunas create such a convincing display that people take the display for reality and never look for the source behind it.

Think about how completely a well-made film draws you in. Two hours into a great movie, you have forgotten you are sitting in a theater. The emotions feel real. The characters feel like people you know. The story has absorbed your attention so thoroughly that the screen, the projector, and the theater itself have vanished from your awareness. You are living inside the film.

This is what the three gunas do to human consciousness. They create such an absorbing display of sensory experience, emotion, thought, and drama that we forget there is a reality beyond the display. We are so busy navigating the movie of our lives that we never think to ask: who is the projectionist?

The completeness of the absorption is what makes it so effective. It is not that we see the world and choose to ignore the Divine behind it. We do not see the Divine at all. The gunas create a seamless, self-consistent experience that accounts for everything within its own terms. Physics explains motion. Chemistry explains substance. Psychology explains thought. Biology explains life. Each field of knowledge operates entirely within the domain of the gunas, offering explanations that are internally valid but that never point beyond themselves. A person can earn a doctorate in every scientific discipline and still never encounter the question that Krishna is raising: what lies behind the entire system of explanation?

This is not an argument against science or learning. Knowledge of the gunas, of how the material world operates, has immense practical value. The point is that such knowledge, however extensive, addresses the content of the movie, not the existence of the projector. You can understand every frame of the film in perfect detail and still have no idea that a projector exists. Breaking through the delusion requires a different kind of knowing, the kind Krishna has been describing: not more analysis of the display, but a turning of attention toward the source.

Krishna says *māmebhyaḥ param avyayam*: they do not know Me, who am beyond these three gunas and imperishable. The word *avyayam*, imperishable, is key. Everything within the field of the gunas changes. Sattva rises and falls. Rajas surges and subsides. Tamas thickens and thins. Moods shift, circumstances evolve, bodies age, civilizations rise and collapse. All of this is the play of the gunas. But behind it all, unchanging and unaffected, is the reality that Krishna points to. It is the one thing in the universe that does not come and go.

Verse 7.14 explains why this delusion is so hard to penetrate: *Daivī hyeṣhā guṇa-mayī mama māyā duratyayā, mām eva ye prapadyante māyām etāṁ taranti te.* This divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the three gunas, is very difficult to overcome. But those who surrender to Me alone cross beyond it.

The word *daivī* means divine. Krishna is calling his own Maya divine. It is not an accident, a flaw, or a mistake. It is a feature of the cosmic design. The veil exists because the Divine willed it into existence. Why would God create an illusion that hides God? This is one of the deepest questions in the Gita, and Krishna does not answer it fully here. But the implication is that the play of appearance and reality, the game of seeking and finding, the drama of forgetting and remembering, is itself part of the purpose of existence.

*Duratyayā*: very difficult to cross over. Krishna does not sugarcoat this. If you are planning to reason your way past Maya using your intellect alone, you will be disappointed. The intellect is itself a product of the gunas. Using the intellect to see beyond the gunas is like using a flashlight to look at the sun. The tool is not adequate to the task.

But then the escape clause: *mām eva ye prapadyante māyām etāṁ taranti te*. Those who surrender to Me cross beyond this Maya. The word *prapadyante* means to take refuge, to surrender, to approach with complete trust. It is not an intellectual operation. It is not a technique. It is a turning of the whole being toward the Divine.

The nature of this surrender is often misunderstood. It is not passivity. It is not the abandonment of effort. It is the recognition that a certain kind of effort, the effort of the ego to solve its own predicament using its own tools, has reached its limit. A drowning person who thrashes wildly uses enormous energy but goes nowhere. The same person who relaxes and floats is carried by the water. Surrender is learning to float. It is not giving up; it is giving over. You stop fighting the current and allow yourself to be carried by something larger and wiser than your individual will.

In practical terms, surrender often begins with a moment of exhaustion. You have tried everything you know how to try. You have read, studied, practiced, analyzed. And still, the deepest questions remain unanswered. Still, the restlessness persists. Still, the sense that something essential is missing refuses to go away. It is in this moment of honest exhaustion, when the ego finally admits that it cannot solve this particular puzzle, that surrender becomes possible. Not as a strategy, not as a technique, but as the natural response of a mind that has reached the end of its own resources and is willing, at last, to ask for help.

This is the great pivot of Chapter 7. After all the descriptions of matter and spirit, of lower and higher nature, of the thread running through the pearls, Krishna says: the way through is not understanding. It is surrender. You cannot figure out the magician's trick by staring harder at the illusion. You cross the illusion by turning toward the magician and saying, "I give up trying to solve this on my own. Show me."

Verse 7.15 then describes four types of people who fail to make this turn: *Na māṁ duṣhkṛitino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ, māyayāpahṛita-jñānā āsuraṁ bhāvam āśhritāḥ.* The wicked, the deluded, the lowest among people, and those whose knowledge has been stolen by illusion, who have embraced a demonic nature: they do not surrender to Me.

Four categories, each representing a different failure mode.

*Duṣhkṛitinaḥ*: those who actively do wrong. People whose lives are directed toward exploitation, cruelty, or dishonesty. They do not surrender because surrender requires humility, and their way of life depends on the opposite.

*Mūḍhāḥ*: the deluded, those who are so completely absorbed in the sensory world that they have no capacity for reflection. They are not evil. They are simply asleep. The alarm clock rings and they hit snooze, lifetime after lifetime.

*Narādhamāḥ*: the lowest among people. This is traditionally interpreted as those who had the capacity for spiritual life but deliberately chose to ignore it. They were given the opportunity, the intelligence, the circumstances, and they squandered all of it on trivial pursuits.

*Māyayāpahṛita-jñānāḥ*: those whose knowledge has been stolen by Maya. These are perhaps the most tragic. They are not ignorant. They have some knowledge, some education, some understanding. But Maya has corrupted their knowledge so that it serves delusion rather than liberation. The scientist who uses knowledge to build weapons of mass destruction. The priest who uses scripture to justify oppression. The philosopher who uses reason to deny the existence of anything beyond reason. Their knowledge is real, but it has been hijacked.

This category deserves particular attention in the modern context. We live in an age of unprecedented access to information, yet this abundance of knowledge does not automatically produce wisdom. A person can accumulate vast stores of factual knowledge and use them to construct elaborate justifications for selfishness, exploitation, or cruelty. The corporate executive who uses sophisticated economic theory to defend practices that harm communities. The political strategist who uses psychological research to manipulate public opinion. The religious authority who uses scriptural knowledge to maintain personal power. In each case, genuine knowledge exists, but it has been captured by *Maya* and redirected away from truth and toward delusion.

*Āsuraṁ bhāvam āśhritāḥ*: those who have embraced a demonic disposition. This is the overarching quality that enables the other three. The *āsura* bhāva is the orientation that says: I am the center. I am the measure of all things. There is no reality greater than my desires. Whenever this attitude takes hold, surrender becomes impossible, because surrender requires acknowledging something greater than yourself.

This verse is not a condemnation. It is a diagnosis. Krishna is not cursing these four types. He is explaining why they remain trapped in Maya. The cure for each is the same: *prapadyante*, surrender. The wicked must humble themselves. The deluded must wake up. The negligent must choose to engage. Those with stolen knowledge must allow their understanding to be purified. And in every case, the first step is the same: turn toward the Divine and let go.

These three verses together complete the first movement of Chapter 7. Krishna has revealed his two natures, shown how everything is strung upon him like pearls, identified himself in the essential qualities of water, fire, earth, and all beings, explained that the three gunas both emerge from and conceal him, and named the obstacles that keep people from seeing through the veil.

In the readings ahead, Krishna will describe the four types of people who do seek him, the nature of true devotion, and why the one who knows him as he truly is stands at the summit of all spiritual attainment. The journey from knowledge of the self to knowledge of the Divine is gaining momentum.
snippets.reflection:
"The entire world is deluded by the three qualities (gunas) and does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable." This verse explains why spiritual realization seems so elusive. Like watching a captivating movie, we become so absorbed in the play of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas that we forget we are the witness, not the movie. Today, notice how your moods shift throughout the day: clarity and peace (sattva), restlessness and ambition (rajas), heaviness and confusion (tamas). Can you observe these shifting states without being completely identified with them?

Krishna offers both a warning and a promise. The warning: "This divine Maya of Mine, consisting of the three gunas, is difficult to cross." The promise: "Those who take refuge in Me alone shall cross over this illusion." The key word is "alone" (eva). Half-hearted seeking, divided attention, keeping one foot in spiritual practice and both hands grasping worldly security, this approach will not work. The magician's tricks cannot be understood from the audience; you must become his disciple. Today, honestly assess: how much of your day is spent genuinely seeking truth versus being entertained by the magic show of Maya?

The verse about those who do not seek the Divine describes them as "deprived of spiritual perception by the glamour of Illusion." This is not a judgment but a diagnosis. The cure is Bhajanti, which means invoking the Self. Every action requires invoking some self: myself, yourself, itself. Today, consciously invoke the higher Self before important activities. Before a meeting, a difficult conversation, or creative work, pause and remember: "May the Divine intelligence work through me."
snippets.shortReflection: You're deluded not because you're stupid but because Maya is extraordinarily convincing. Like a movie so immersive you forget it's a screen, the three gunas create a world that captures your total attention. The escape hatch isn't figuring out the trick intellectually; it's taking refuge in the Self. Are you trying to solve the puzzle, or surrender to its source?

priyo hi jñānino ’tyartham ahaṁ sa cha mama priyaḥ

udārāḥ sarva evaite jñānī tvātmaiva me matam
āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā mām evānuttamāṁ gatim
verseTranslations: O Arjuna! The righteous who worship Me are grouped by stages: first, they who suffer, next they who desire knowledge, then they who thirst after truth, and lastly they who attain wisdom.

Of all of these, he who has gained wisdom, who meditates on Me without ceasing, devoting himself only to Me, he is the best; for by the wise man I am exceedingly beloved and the wise man, too, is beloved by Me.
Noble-minded are they all, but the wise man I hold as my own Self; for he, remaining always at peace with Me, makes me his final goal.
snippets.commentary:
In Chapter 7, he is teaching us what to meditate upon. In Chapter 6, we learned how to identify with the Supreme Self and detach ourselves from the limited *self* that I consider myself. In Chapter 7, Bhagavan is giving us the indications of how to think about the Supreme Being. We have seen his lower and higher nature.

The lower nature is what I can see, perceive, think in this world -- this is the lower *Prakriti*. So Bhagavan said, he is all-pervading, and anything which I see, I should see his presence in it. Anything which I consider conducive or not conducive is still manifestation of the same underlying reality. This Prakriti has three Gunas: *Sattva*, Rajas, *Tamas*. Whatever there is which is Sattvik, Rajasik or Tamasik, consider that all come from me, the supreme reality.

It is actually my mind which divides this world into three different categories. The world I see as Sattvik, the world I see as Rajasic, the world I see as Tamasic. That makes me think about positive emotions: where I feel happy, I feel that's a Sattvic world. The world which makes me agitated, I consider Rajasic. The world which confuses me is Tamasic for me. But no matter what world you are identifying with, that is your world and you are in the center of it.

But consider that comes from me. All sense objects in this world, whether they give you Sattvic experience, rajasic experience or Tamasic experience, they all come from me. But I am not in them, they are in me. In other words, there is no indication of supreme reality in them. I cannot find its presence in them in those sense objects. But note that all sense objects are in me.

In other words, without that supreme reality, without my *consciousness*, I will not be able to detect any of those sense objects. Therefore, all the sense objects in this world are actually in my consciousness. Consider that they are all present because of my presence as your own *consciousness*. Then Bhagawan explains why we cannot realize that. Because all people, all beings in this world are confused by this Maya. As we have discussed, *Maya* is that which is not, but appears to be.

The world of sense objects is actually created by my own mind. The impression I have of them is actually my impression only. I will never know what the reality is. When I look up into the sky, I see stars and moon and sun. What I see is my world -- the impression I see is the representation of this world in my mind.

I will never know what the reality is. So Bhagawan said, consider all that to be me. But you will never be able to cross this *illusion* that you have created about your world. This *knowledge* about the underlying reality is lost to me because I'm under the spell of *Maya*. I do not see the unity in the diversity of sense objects around me, because I consider myself an island by myself.

I am so unique that I'm different than this world. This notion about my uniqueness creates this duality about I and the world. Because that's the my *illusion* that the Maya's *illusion*. Even knowing, through intellectual appreciation, that my body, my mind, my intellect are part of this *Prakriti* -- this body is nothing but food modified.

But I never see my body as food modified. I always see my body as something very unique. Bhagwan said, that's the confusion created by *Maya*. Tribhir gunamayair bhavair ebhih sarvam idam jagat mohitam -- the entire Jagat, all beings, are confused by the three *Gunas*. But those who have some inkling about this underlying reality will pursue it.

That's basically I'm worshipping. I'm trying to find out and identify with the supreme *self*. I have inkling that there is something higher than me and that I am pursuing. So Bhagavan now tells us which types of people will try to identify with the supreme self. In the last verse we discussed, he said: who will not be aware of something greater than his own *self*? Na mam dushkritino mudhah prapadyante naradhamah, mayaya apahrita jnana, asuram bhavam ashritah. Those who are under the complete spell of *Maya* will only identify with the ignorance they have.

This ignorance that "I am by myself and the world is a completely different entity." Duskritina, Mudha -- people who are not yet evolved to the point of identifying with something higher than their limited *self*. They will not be able to understand this, and therefore they take refuge in their own ignorance: "I am who I am; the world is out there to get me."

In contrast, Bhagavan said there are people who have evolved from identifying with their limited *self* and have recognized an underlying unity in all sense objects. They see that everything is strung into the same reality.

Physics tells us the same thing -- that in this world there is one underlying energy. And in this world nothing is lost. No matter what incident or phenomenon is happening, we know that energy in this world remains constant. If you take a gallon of water and boil it until it all evaporates, that does not mean that the water is lost. The same amount of energy which was in the water -- the mass -- is now converted into something else. When you add all that up, it will come to exactly the same amount.

That's what we learned in high school physics. The Bhagawan said that you in this world there is nothing is really lost or gained. It just changes appearances. And those who have come to the realization that there is an underlying reality, they will pursue identification with that reality. And those people: Chaturvidha bhajante mam janah sukritino Arjuna. Contrast this with the last verse.

The wrongdoers, in essence, are acting in this world with the wrong notion that their own *self* is the only reality. Charvaka darshan: Bhasmi bhutasya dehasya punaragamanam kutah -- when this body is burnt, there is no coming back. So this life is the only life; enjoy as best as you can, no matter what you have to do. Rinam kritva ghritam pibet.

Those are Duskritina because they have a very narrow view about who they are, and therefore their actions are driven by that paradigm -- "I am by myself and have to make the most out of this life." Bhagavan calls them *Maya* Apahrita Jnana: their knowledge about the *self* and their connection with the higher self is lost because of the confusion created by *Maya*.

Chaturvidha bhajanti mam janah sukritina Arjuna. In contrast, the people of good deeds pursue me.

They try to identify with me in four different ways. Or you can say there are four different types of people who identify with me. This can also be one person in four different states of pursuing the supreme reality: Artah, Jijnasu, Artharthi, Gnani -- O Bharatarshabha, best of the Bharat clan. There are four types. The first is Artah, the one who is in distress and looking for help.

But there is a slight distinction people have made in understanding this verse. Bhagavan has called them Sukritina. Also, in the next two verses, he will attach the word Udara to them -- the noble people who are trying to understand why things are the way they are. We have seen that for people who are working only for themselves, all actions are binding. Any *action* which binds me is Dushkrita.

Any *action* which liberates me is Sukrita. So in the last verse, the wrongdoers -- all their actions were binding, getting more and more deeply into the *bondage* of their egos. In contrast, these people are Sukritina. All their actions are towards *liberation* from their false identification.

So this Artah may not be an average person in distress seeking Bhagavan's help -- "I'm in trouble, help me; I have back pain, please help me." He's trying to understand why there is distress in this world, why people are suffering, and he's seeking the Lord's guidance on how to alleviate that suffering. During the pandemic, a person may have been very safe in his house, in a location where he's not going to get infected.

But just watching people suffer, you may think, "Oh Lord, why are you not removing all this suffering and helping those in this pandemic?" Bhagavan said, that's the Artah -- a Bhakta who is pursuing me, disturbed by distress, seeking understanding.

The next is the Jijnasu. He wants to know how this world works, why there is suffering. It may be at a personal level -- when I'm in distress, I'm trying to find out why there is sorrow in my life.

What is it that I'm not doing right which makes me sorrowful? But at a greater level, the Bhakta is trying to understand why people are suffering and trying to find the answer. Bhagavan Buddha was not upset about his own situation. He was well protected in the palace, but he saw the suffering outside. He said, "I need to find the cause for this suffering." Bhagawan said, that's a Jijnasu.

Then the third type, Bhagawan said, is the Artharthi -- one who is seeking wealth. We all fall into that category. We do Lakshmi Puja on Diwali because we want to make sure the next year will be as good or better than the last. But this Artharthi is not seeking just for himself. These people are seeking wealth so that they can help others.

They want to create wealth for the betterment of society so that sorrows can be eliminated. And the last one is the Gnani, who has truly understood the relationship between his limited *self* and the Supreme Self. Bhagavan in the next verse says he is the best: Sa cha mama priyah. Out of these four, they are all selfless workers. They have gone through the first six chapters of Bhagavad Gita and learned the art of *Karma* *Yoga*.

They're working in this world for the greater good, but they still have questions: why is there suffering, where does it come from, what can I do to alleviate it? "Oh Lord, give enough so everyone can eat and nobody goes hungry."

But the Gnani understands that his own limited *self* is none other than the Supreme Self. They are one and the same, connected with each other, only separated by conditioning. Nitya Yukta -- constantly establishing their knowledge. No matter what I see outside, the *Self* is pervading all throughout this world. Whether people are suffering or enjoying, it is the same reality expressing itself. Eka Bhakti Vishishyate -- single-pointedly identified with that, because there is nothing else to identify with, once he has realized that his self is not different from the Supreme *Self*.
snippets.reflection:
Krishna identifies four types of devotees who turn to the Divine: the distressed (arta), the curious seeker of knowledge (jijnasu), the seeker of wealth (artharthi), and the wise one (jnani). Today, honestly identify which category best describes your current spiritual motivation. There is no shame in any of these; Krishna calls all of them "sukritina" (people of good deeds) and "noble." The distressed person who cries out to God in a hospital bed is on the same path as the philosopher seeking ultimate truth. The key is that all four are turning toward the Divine rather than away from it.

Yet Krishna makes clear that the jnani, the one who truly knows, is dearest to Him: "For the wise man I am exceedingly beloved and the wise man, too, is beloved by Me." This is not favoritism but natural law. The closer you come to understanding someone, the deeper your love becomes. The jnani has removed the veil of separateness and sees that "Vasudevah sarvam," Vasudeva is everything. This recognition creates single-pointed devotion (eka-bhakti) naturally, not through effort.

Reflect on your own journey: Have you moved through these stages? Perhaps you first came to spirituality during a crisis (arta), then developed curiosity about how life works (jijnasu), then sought divine help for worldly goals (artharthi). Each stage is valid and necessary. The invitation today is to ask: "What would it mean to move toward jnana, toward actually knowing rather than just believing?" One practice: Choose one teaching from the Gita and contemplate it deeply throughout the day, not just intellectually accepting it, but testing it against your actual experience.
snippets.shortReflection: Which one are you right now? The person reaching out from crisis, the curious seeker, the one wanting something specific, or someone who just knows? Your answer matters less than your honesty about it.

snippets.title: Day 102: Vasudeva Is Everything
snippets.sanskrit:
बहूनां जन्मनामन्ते ज्ञानवान्मां प्रपद्यते |
वासुदेवः सर्वमिति स महात्मा सुदुर्लभः ||

कामैस्तैस्तैर्हृतज्ञानाः प्रपद्यन्तेऽन्यदेवताः |
तं तं नियममास्थाय प्रकृत्या नियताः स्वया ||

यो यो यां यां तनुं भक्तः श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति |
तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहम् ||
snippets.transliteration:
bahūnāṁ janmanām ante jñānavān māṁ prapadyate
vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti sa mahātmā su-durlabhaḥ

kāmais tais tair hṛita-jñānāḥ prapadyante ’nya-devatāḥ
taṁ taṁ niyamam āsthāya prakṛityā niyatāḥ svayā

yo yo yāṁ yāṁ tanuṁ bhaktaḥ śhraddhayārchitum ichchhati
tasya tasyāchalāṁ śhraddhāṁ tām eva vidadhāmyaham
verseTranslations: After many lives, at last the wise man realises Me as I am. A man so enlightened that he sees God everywhere is very difficult to find.
They in whom wisdom is obscured by one desire or the other, worship the lesser Powers, practising many rites which vary according to their temperaments.
But whatever the form of worship, if the devotee have faith, then upon his faith in that worship do I set My own seal.
snippets.commentary:
In Chapter 2, Sankhya *Yoga*, we learned that our self is immortal, imperishable -- though we consider ourselves to be mortal. So that was the path of knowledge revealing the nature of the self. Then from Chapters 3 to 5 we learned Karma Yoga, the Path of Action -- how we can transform our day-to-day actions into selfless activities and purify our mind and intellect. So Karma Yoga is to develop *equanimity* and purification of the mind.

That's the Path of *Action*. And in Chapter 6, Bhagavan taught us Dhyana Yoga, the Yoga of Meditation -- how we can shift our mind from identifying with this limited self (this body, this mind, this intellect that I consider to be my own self). In Chapter 2, we learned that the all-pervading, omniscient, ever-existing Self, which is of the nature of Sat-Chit-Ananda, is nothing but my own self as the universal *Self*. What I consider "myself" right now is conditioned consciousness -- the same consciousness conditioned by what I call body, mind, and intellect. So we learned how to shift this identification from the limited self to the higher Self through Dhyana Yoga by focusing the mind on the supreme *Self*.

At the end of Chapter 6, Bhagavan declared that the Yogi -- one who has tuned his mind to the Supreme *Self*, who has shifted identification from the limited self to the higher Self -- is greater than the Tapasvi (one practicing austerities), greater than the Jnani (one who has acquired *knowledge* through study of scriptures), and greater than the Karmi (one who acts in this world thinking that doing good is good enough). Bhagavan clarified that doing good is not good enough. You have to have the clear understanding that "myself" is not this limited self, but the limited self is nothing but the expression of the Supreme *Self*.

The three paths which are described in our system -- *Karma* Yoga, Gnana Yoga and Bhakti Yoga -- need to be practiced serially. Therefore, the Gita starts with Karma Yoga. Now in Chapter 7, Bhagavan is instructing us how to practice the Path of *Bhakti*, the path of devotion. But before I can start practicing Bhakti Yoga, I have to develop that identification with the supreme Self. Without knowing that supreme Self, I will not be able to focus my limited mind, which is right now fully identified with this limited self, onto that supreme *self* which is limitless.

So Bhagavan in the opening of this chapter gives Arjuna assurance: I will teach you. I will tell you how to do that. Bhagavan opens the chapter by saying Yogam yunjan mat ashrayah -- tune your mind to me. My mind right now is fully tuned with this body, identified with the limited *self*. That mind has to now identify with the Supreme *Self*.

He said, once you do that, you will come to know me. And he assured us that he will teach both the *knowledge* and its application -- Gnanam, the *Knowledge*, and Vignana, Vishishta Gnanam, its application in your life -- without leaving anything behind. Having known that, you will not have to know anything else. In other words, having known myself in its true nature, there will be no need to achieve, accomplish, or acquire anything to find that ultimate happiness -- the happiness which has no limitation. I do not want to be unhappy at any given time.

If you ask me, "When do you want to be happy?" -- it is not okay to be happy during weekdays but unhappy during weekends. I want to be happy all seven days of the week, 365 days of the year. Bhagwan says, having known that your *self* is not the limited *self*, you shall achieve that ultimate happiness. Why are people not achieving this *knowledge*? He said, Manushyanam -- out of thousands of human beings on this planet, someone will try to achieve this perfection.

We can now say billions of people -- out of billions, very few will try this method of achieving perfect happiness by identifying with the Supreme. And of those who are striving, there are very few. Out of billions, maybe a few hundred or a few dozen are trying this. And he says: Yatatam api siddhanam kashchin mam vetti tattvatah -- even those who are striving sincerely, only very few will achieve this perfection.

So this almost looks like Bhagavan is discouraging us. But Bhagavan is not discouraging us. Bhagavan is saying that it is an equal opportunity goal. Anyone can achieve this goal if they try in an appropriate manner. So Bhagavan then describes the people who are striving to achieve identification with the Supreme *Self*. He calls them my devotees, my *Bhakti*.

And he classifies those devotees into four categories. In general, he divided the entire human race into two categories. One, those who are striving for perfection. Those who are not striving for perfection. Those who are striving for perfection are trying to develop some kind of relationship with the Supreme. Others are simply considering that this world is where I can find my happiness.

"I work outside, I go and acquire things, I go and accomplish things, and that will give me happiness." This group of people is not even trying to develop any relationship with the Supreme. He called them Duskritina -- which does not mean they are evildoers, but they are working towards their happiness in a wrong way that will guarantee their failure. He defines the other group as Sukritina, people of good deeds. He says they are his devotees.

But they fall into four different categories, and therefore not all of them will achieve perfection. The first is Artah -- one who reaches out to the Supreme, developing some relationship with Him due to distress. There is sorrow in his life or her life, or there is sorrow all around. He wants to know how invoking God's grace will alleviate that sorrow.

We only invoke His grace when we feel helpless. "I can solve my own problem." It's only when we feel helpless that we seek help from the higher *Self*. They are my devotees, but they have a limited relationship -- they only seek my help when they feel helpless.

It's like my son when he was in college. He would only call me when he really needed something. Otherwise, he was happy doing whatever he was doing. We'd have to call him and say, "Bhai, you didn't call us all month." But when he needs something, he suddenly remembers, "My parents are there to take care of me. Let me call dad" -- and dad sends more money.

So that relationship is still of a son and a father. "My Father in heaven will take care of me when I really need Him." The next is the Jijnasu -- one who is curious about the nature of the Supreme. All scientists actually fall in that category, because they're trying to find that God equation, the equation which will reveal the nature of the Creator who created this universe. Out of curiosity about the nature of the *self*, the supreme, the ultimate reality, they are developing a relationship with Him.

Then the third, Bhagavan says, is the Artharthi. The entire wealth on this planet is created by the Supreme Being, and therefore He is the owner. When I need wealth to support myself, my family, my community, my nation, I seek His help.

On our dollar bill it says, "In God we trust." That Bhakta seeking wealth is an Artharthi. And the last one is the Jnani -- one who has developed this relationship with the Supreme by understanding His real nature, shifting identification from the limited *self* to the higher *Self*.

The higher *Self* is my true *self*; this limited *self* is just a reflection of it. Bhagavan said the Jnani is the one closest to Him. Udarah sarva evaite jnani tu atma eva me matam. All my devotees are noble people. They're people doing good deeds.

They are on the right path. I may start developing a relationship with Bhagavan because I feel distressed, but eventually I will progress to where I understand His true nature. It's like knowing somebody -- just knowing a little bit, we start liking them more. The closer we come, the more we know them in detail. Ultimately, we know that person almost in totality.

So Bhagawan said, all these devotees of mine are noble people. However, the Jnani I consider to be my own *self*. He is no different than me. Asthitah sa hi yuktatma mam eva anuttamam gatim. By steadfastly establishing his mind in me, he comes to me.

But then he says something which discourages many of us: Bahunam janmanam ante jnanavaan mam prapadyate, Vasudevah sarvam iti sa mahatma sudurlabhah. This Jnani has not become a Jnani overnight. After going through this journey of knowing the Supreme *Self* for many, many lives, he comes to understand the nature of the Supreme. And he realizes that there is nothing in this universe --

there is nothing in this *Prakriti* which is other than Vasudeva -- Vasudeva, the supreme, all-pervading *Self*. So Bhagavan said, "I told you in the beginning that *Prakriti* is my lower nature, my manifest nature which one can experience through the senses -- I can see, I can touch, I can feel. But other than this manifest nature of mine, there is a higher nature which is unmanifest, which you have to experience."

Only then will you come to know. So after many births of trying to seek unity in diversity, such a Jnani achieves the understanding that the supreme *Self* is everywhere. Sa Mahatma sudurlabhah -- such a great soul is very rare to find. So we come to the conclusion that this is not something I can easily achieve.

But come to think of it, there's nothing in this life we achieve in any other way. We have to start somewhere and then gradually make progress one step at a time. We have learned that in elementary school somebody asked me, what do you want to become? I want to become a doctor. It does not make you become doctor the next day. It took you a long time.

From elementary school to secondary school to high school to college, then medical school, then internship. All that effort you put for many, many, many years. And then you achieved this status as doctor. Such and such people recognize you as doctor. You practice your art of medicine. All that is only possible because of the journey you started from your kindergarten which ended into your internship in some hospital.

Bhagavan says bahūnām janmanāmante, the jñānī which you see today. As a knowledgeable person. He did not achieve the *knowledge* overnight. He put his efforts into it. So Bhagawan is encouraging us. No matter where we are in our journey, we keep making progress one step at a time.

But then the caution here is we may get distracted.
snippets.reflection:
"After many births, the wise one realizes Me, understanding 'Vasudeva is all.' Such a great soul is very rare to find." This verse can either discourage or inspire. The key is understanding that every journey, no matter how long, is completed one step at a time. You did not become a professional overnight; years of education and practice were required. Similarly, spiritual maturity develops through consistent effort across time. Today, rather than lamenting how far you have to go, appreciate how far you have already come. What spiritual insights do you now hold that you did not have five or ten years ago?

Krishna then addresses those whose knowledge is stolen by desires, who worship lesser powers. This is not a condemnation of diverse worship but an observation about limitation. If I worship only the god of wealth, I limit my vision to wealth. If I worship only health, my horizon stops there. Each deity represents a facet of the one Reality. Today, notice what you functionally worship through your time, attention, and energy. Is it career success, family security, social approval, physical pleasure? These are not wrong, but are they your ultimate goal, or stepping stones toward something greater?

The beautiful teaching that Krishna strengthens the faith of every sincere seeker, regardless of the form of worship, is profoundly inclusive. Whatever path genuinely draws your heart toward the sacred, pursue it with full conviction. The caution is to eventually recognize that all paths lead to the same summit. Today's practice: If you follow a particular tradition or form of worship, honor it fully while remaining open to the truth that others who worship differently are also reaching toward the same ultimate Reality.
snippets.shortReflection: You worship what you give your attention to. Check your calendar, your screen time, your mental loops. That's your real religion, not what you say on Sunday.

snippets.title: Day 103: Finite Fruits, Infinite Self
snippets.sanskrit:
स तया श्रद्धया युक्तस्तस्याराधनमीहते |
लभते च ततः कामान्मयैव विहितान् हि तान् ||

अन्तवत्तु फलं तेषां तद्भवत्यल्पमेधसाम् |
देवान्देवयजो यान्ति मद्भक्ता यान्ति मामपि ||

अव्यक्तं व्यक्ितमापन्नं मन्यन्ते मामबुद्धयः |
परं भावमजानन्तो ममाव्ययमनुत्तमम् ||
snippets.transliteration:
sa tayā śhraddhayā yuktas tasyārādhanam īhate
labhate cha tataḥ kāmān mayaiva vihitān hi tān

antavat tu phalaṁ teṣhāṁ tad bhavatyalpa-medhasām
devān deva-yajo yānti mad-bhaktā yānti mām api

avyaktaṁ vyaktim āpannaṁ manyante mām abuddhayaḥ
paraṁ bhāvam ajānanto mamāvyayam anuttamam
verseTranslations: If he worships one form alone with real faith, then shall his desires be fulfilled through that only; for thus have I ordained.
The fruit that comes to men of limited insight is, after all, finite. They who worship the Lower Powers attain them; but those who worship Me come unto Me alone.
The ignorant think of Me, who am the Unmanifested Spirit, as if I were really in human form. They do not understand that My Superior Nature is changeless and most excellent.
snippets.commentary:
We are all seeking who we are, where we came from.

Some of us seek unconsciously and some consciously. Those who seek unconsciously obviously do not know where the answer is. Those who seek consciously are worshipping the Lord, the source of their being.

We have seen that seekers can be classified into four types. Of these four, the Gnani is so firm in his conviction that his *self* is something other than the limited self. We need to find out what that is.

But the journey from ignorance about the *self* to knowing the *self* takes its own effort. Bahunam janmanam ante jnanavaan mam prapadyate. After many years of sincere seeking, the Gnani who is sincerely seeking his own *self* finds the truth.

He comes to the conclusion: Vasudevah sarvam iti -- there is nothing other than the supreme reality. There is no separate world and there is no separate "I." All that exists is Vasudeva. Anything that I see, touch, feel, or perceive is nothing but that one supreme reality alone.

But Bhagavan said, why don't we all realize this? Kamaih taih taih hrita jnanah -- because of this desire and that desire, the *knowledge* which is inherently ours is taken away from us. And therefore we seek the fulfiller of that desire. Who do I go and meet at a party? The one I think is going to be the most beneficial to me.

Networking parties, I'm talking about. Somebody may come very lovingly and say, "Rajan!" I say, "No, no, not right now. I need to go and talk to that guy, because that's where I think my benefit lies." Even at a social party, we go say hello first to whoever we think is most important.

With this desire and that desire, our sense of who we are is looted away. And then we seek the fulfiller of that desire. That's the Devata -- the one we consider the fulfiller.

The object of our desire becomes the Devata we worship. And Bhagavan says, whatever your desire and whoever your Devata, it eventually comes from me alone. Whatever you have faith in -- that entity, that source will fulfill your desire. "I make your faith even firmer." Where does the faith come from? Faith comes from my own *attachment* and understanding.

My own consciousness, my own thinking, is only possible because the Supreme functions through me as *consciousness*. The same *consciousness* which allows me to think makes me think over and over in the same line of thinking. It makes my faith firmer and firmer the more I think in that line. "Only science can give me the answer." The more I indulge in that thought, the firmer my faith becomes. "All these sadhus and monks are nonsense." 's how he started -- "These guys are just bluffing their way." So the more we think in the same line, the firmer our faith becomes through our own *consciousness*.

Bhagawan says, "I make their faith firm." And then, the more they worship that Devata, the more they fulfill that desire sincerely. Whenever I apply myself in whatever field, the success comes from that field. Bhagavan said, wherever you apply yourself with faith, your desires will be fulfilled.

However, he said, all that comes from me alone. Sa taya shraddhaya yuktah tasya aradhanam ihate labhate cha tatah kaman *maya* eva vihitan hi tan. No matter where you think this profit came from, where you think this success came from, no matter who you think helped you -- Bhagavan said, that was your faith making you think it came from that source.

However, because I am the all-pervading Lord, everything coming to you from these different Devatas is coming from me alone. I am the only source. Those in business, you have several accounts and LLCs.

You transfer money from here and there. Eventually, whose money is it? Yours. Anytime we go out and do something, Mina asks, "How are you going to pay for this?" I say, "Oh, that's for NBJS." She thinks the money is coming from NBJS, who is paying the rent here. "Then I don't have to worry about it." As long as you don't think it's coming from me -- but eventually it all comes from me, right? At the time, I feel it didn't come from the Lord; it came from this Devata, this source.

Bhagavan says all the sources eventually merge into me. Wherever you are, whatever Devata you are worshipping, wherever the results come from, they all come from me. Apply yourself in a field of productive potential and you shall get results.

But know that all these results come from me. Antavattu phalam tesham tat bhavati alpamedhasam. But the Alpa Medhas, those with limited intellect, get finite results.

Antavattu -- which has an end. No matter how hard I try for something and get it, the joy will only last for a certain period of time. My standard example: buying a BMW.

You bought the BMW, and that joy has ended. The pursuit has its own charm. Once you reach the destination, the whole excitement of the journey has ended.

Whatever Devatas you are worshipping, certainly you will get success in that field. But the results are finite -- they have a beginning and an end. I want to see a Broadway show I have never seen in my life.

Next time I'm in New York, I want to see it. But it has a beginning and an end. The show starts and ends.

After that, I'm back to square one. Bhagawan said, these people with limited intellect think their destination lies in finite happiness. Therefore they pursue this field of finite happiness, and they get it.

Devan devayajo yanti mad bhakta yanti mam api. Those seeking small gains get small gains. The one who wants to hit the jackpot strives for that and reaches there sooner or later.

Bhagavan said, the Bhaktas of various Devatas -- all of us who have this desire and that -- continuously pursue them. And because we put in our efforts, we get them. But Bhagavan says, the one who seeks me finds me -- as simple as that.

Gandhiji could have been the most successful barrister in South Africa and could have made all that money like the other Gujaratis at the time. But he wasn't happy with that finite result. We would have never heard about Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi. "Successful barrister, practiced in Durban and died." We would have had nothing to do with him.

But he wasn't going after the small results. He was going after what he thought rightfully belongs to his countrymen. So he became immortal.

He got what he sought after. That's why I say be careful in what you think you want. You have this unlimited potential of realizing yourself.

But we are happy with small results in our life. Even in Sadhana, they say when you start meditating, Siddhis come to you, and you're pretty happy with that. A good example is *Yoga*.

In this country, *Yoga* is only for the physical. Patanjali didn't write the *Yoga* Sutras just to make your body fit. He wrote it to achieve the highest.

But we are pretty happy with the little results we get. Therefore Bhagawan says they have a limited intellect regarding where their happiness lies. They pursue fields of *action*, fields of potential gain, and they get results.

But those results have a beginning and an end. Inherently we are seeking infinite happiness, but we are applying ourselves in very small, finite fields of *action* and expecting to get infinite happiness. And therefore we oscillate between sorrow and happiness, sorrow and happiness.

Mad Bhakta Yanti Mam Api -- only my worshipper, the one who has decided that these small gains are not good enough, who needs to find the ultimate truth that gives infinite happiness. The last verse says: Avyaktam vyaktim apannam manyante mam abuddhayah. Those with no intellect to understand the truth -- all of us who have no capacity to understand it.

Because the intellect is the only instrument we use to understand things, and the intellect is a byproduct of ignorance. Ignorance creates this perception that "this limited being is me." This "me" -- the body, mind, and intellect -- is a product of Avidya, ignorance. "This mind is me, this intellect is me." That intellect is now trying to find out who the Lord is. "I'm going to figure it out by reading Bhagavad Gita, then the Bible, then the Quran. In the end, I'll tell you who the Lord is." Bhagavan said, those Abuddhayah -- they think that the Avyakta, the unmanifest, has manifested.

The Lord pervading everywhere whom we can't really see, who is the substratum without which this universe cannot exist, but who is not perceptible -- they think He manifests. And therefore we have all these Bhajans about Bhagavan coming: "Maine aapko dekha, Bhagavan." And then we have stories about Bhagavan appearing. If Bhagavan can come stand in front of me while I am also standing here and the rest of the world is also standing -- where is that unmanifest? Therefore he said, only the one without that understanding thinks the unmanifest can manifest.

The unmanifest remains unmanifest. But I am seeking that, so I say, "Oh no, this is Bhagavan." I think one of the Bal Vihar children had probably seen pictures of monks in his house. So when Dheerananda was here, the child came to our house and then went back and said, "Mom, God came to Meenanti's house!" Because to the little child, a one wearing a saffron robe is God.

The picture he has seen is Bhagavan. "God came to Meenanti's house." What does Mama say? "No, no, that's not God. That's Dheerananda." For the child, the unmanifested God has manifested. The mother said, "No, no, that's just Dheerananda." We, in our limited intellect, think that God manifests as Jesus, as Krishna.

But Bhagwan said, I remain unmanifest all the time. Param bhavam ajanantah mama avyayam anuttamam. Knowing a guru, knowing a prophet, and thinking, "This is it." said, "If that's the case, whoever went to a temple and saw the Murti would never have to find any truth -- he found Bhagavan! And anybody who found a guru would never have to do anything -- he already found the truth." He said, "No, they are just indications.

The unmanifest remains unmanifest." Our limited senses, mind, and intellect have no capacity ever to understand it.
snippets.reflection:
"The fruit that comes to men of limited insight is finite." This simple statement contains the key to understanding human dissatisfaction. We pursue finite goals expecting infinite satisfaction. The BMW brings joy, but it ends. The promotion brings pride, but it fades. The vacation provides relaxation, but we return to the same mind we left with. Today, examine your current pursuits: Are you investing tremendous energy in achieving something that, by its very nature, cannot provide lasting fulfillment? This is not to say you should abandon worldly goals, but recognize them for what they are, finite rewards from finite efforts.

Krishna distinguishes between those who worship lesser powers (devas) and those who worship Him directly: "They who worship the lesser Powers attain them; but those who worship Me come unto Me alone." The practical application is this: whatever you consistently give your attention to, you become. Worship of money makes you wealthy but not necessarily happy. Worship of fame makes you known but not necessarily at peace. Worship of the Supreme, the unchanging Reality behind all changing forms, leads to that same unchanging peace within yourself.

The verse about the ignorant thinking the Unmanifested has taken human form challenges our comfortable religious notions. If God is omnipresent, how can He be limited to any single form? This does not deny the value of divine incarnations or teachers but invites us beyond form-worship to essence-recognition. Today's contemplation: What if every person you meet is equally a manifestation of the Divine? Not just the saints and sages, but the confused, the suffering, even those who harm others? Can you glimpse the unmanifest presence wearing these countless disguises?
snippets.shortReflection: Notice how every achievement fades. The high of the promotion, the new relationship, the vacation glow—all temporary. Are you still chasing finite rewards and expecting infinite satisfaction?

snippets.title: Day 104: Hidden by Yoga Maya
snippets.sanskrit:
नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः |
मूढोऽयं नाभिजानाति लोको मामजमव्ययम् ||

वेदाहं समतीतानि वर्तमानानि चार्जुन |
भविष्याणि च भूतानि मां तु वेद न कश्चन ||
