इच्छाद्वेषसमुत्थेन द्वन्द्वमोहेन भारत |
सर्वभूतानि संमोहं सर्गे यान्ति परन्तप ||
snippets.transliteration:
nāhaṁ prakāśhaḥ sarvasya yoga-māyā-samāvṛitaḥ
mūḍho ’yaṁ nābhijānāti loko mām ajam avyayam

vedāhaṁ samatītāni vartamānāni chārjuna
bhaviṣhyāṇi cha bhūtāni māṁ tu veda na kaśhchana

ichchhā-dveṣha-samutthena dvandva-mohena bhārata
sarva-bhūtāni sammohaṁ sarge yānti parantapa
verseTranslations: I am not visible to all, for I am enveloped by the illusion of Phenomenon. This deluded world does not know Me as the Unborn and the Imperishable.
I know, O Arjuna, all beings in the past, the present and the future; but they do not know Me.
O brave Arjuna! Man lives in a fairy world, deceived by the glamour of opposite sensations, infatuated by desire and aversion.
snippets.commentary:
In this chapter, from verses 4 through 7, Bhagavan gave a thumbnail sketch of who the Lord is and what to meditate upon. First, he said his manifest Prakriti is Eightfold, available to us for perception through our senses -- everything we can think of, see, touch, and feel.

All experiences of body, mind, and intellect are part of His manifested Prakriti. But then he said there is also His higher Prakriti, the para *Prakriti*. In other words, that which is not available to us for cognition through our senses.

Therefore it's called unmanifest -- not available to thinking through my mind, thinking through my intellect, or perceiving through my senses. The lower *Prakriti* is what I can interact with. The higher I cannot perceive.

But that higher is the basis of all manifestation, without which the world which you and I know will not exist. If I'm not conscious about my world, does the world exist? It only exists because I'm aware of it. The known only exists when the Knower is there.

Because the Knower is there, the world of known things and beings exists. So therefore Bhagavan said, my Higher *Prakriti* is the one which is stringing all these manifestations together. What you perceive, what I perceive, what he perceives, what she perceives -- when you put all perception together, it is a world of beings.

That's His real nature. So from verses 4 through 7, we've seen the identity of the Lord, the Supreme, our *Self*, and how to contemplate on it. And then Bhagavan said you can perceive Him through anything which is the essence of anything.

Brilliance in the brilliant. Used to say, "I am the kick in whiskey." What is whiskey if there is no kick in it? It may look like whiskey, it may taste like whiskey, but if there is no kick, it's not whiskey. That which makes things and beings what they are -- that is who I am.

Then he said that people who have no discriminating intellect to pursue this will never pursue it, never want to think about it. But there are people who are pursuing an understanding of the very nature of the *self* and trying to get over their limitations. We have seen four types of devotees: Artah, Jijnasu, Artharthi, and Gnani.

The Gnani is very close to me. He has come close to understanding what the *self* is all about. To Arjuna: therefore, become a Gnani.

Therefore, pursue the path of *knowledge* which makes you realize who you are. And then he also said that in our delusion, we sometimes think the unmanifest comes into manifestation. But the unmanifest never manifests -- we only feel it has.

Bhagavan Vedvyasa makes this point very clear here, because we have all this fighting about different religions. We say, "Our Bhagavan manifested as Krishna. Yours manifested as Christ, but mine is greater than yours." The very first ignorance is thinking the unmanifest comes into manifest.

The unmanifest will never come into manifestation. Anyone who has used his intellect knows: every religion says God is omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent. Then how can your God be different than mine? If my God is omnipresent, there is no room for another God.

Knowing this, why are we fighting about whose God is greater? Abuddhayah -- without using my intellect, I think the unmanifest God comes into manifestation as an incarnation, a prophet, a sage. Param bhavam ajanantah. They are not aware of my real nature.

My real nature is Avyayam -- immutable. Bhagavan created this world out of His own *self* because He has no other material available. Did He ever mutate into this world? He never mutated into this world.

Therefore, one who does not know that His nature is immutable -- he is the one who is fighting about it. There is nothing higher than that. There is nothing beyond His existence.

If you take Him out, nothing remains. If you put everything together, there is nothing but Him alone. But see, that's not available to all of us.

To perceive my own *self* is what I'm trying to understand. How can it be that difficult? It is difficult because: Na aham prakasah sarvasya yogamaya samavritah. I am not available to all because my real nature is veiled by Yoga Maya.

This *Yoga* Maya, which creates the world of plurality out of these three *gunas*, confuses us so we can't see His real nature. Mudho ayam na abhijanati loko mam ajam avyayam. Deluded by that *Yoga* Maya, I do not recognize its very nature, which is unborn and immutable.

That is where our whole problem starts -- our sorrows and limitations. This Yoga *Maya* is the power with which He created this universe. The perception of plurality is because of this Yoga Maya.

It is like when I'm dreaming: out of my own mental power, I create my own world and delude myself. I create my own world, but I -- the waker -- remain immutable. In that dream, the waking *self* remains unchanged.

I remain Ajah in my dream. I never take birth as Bill Gates, but I feel in my dream that I'm Bill Gates. So he said, that is not available to all.

Nobody will ever know it. But this is not a statement to discourage us -- it is a statement for us to contemplate on. He said it is available to those who contemplate His real nature and cross over this *Maya*, who see beyond it -- therefore the word Divya Drishti.

I have one perspective about this world right now, and I can change my perspective when I get greater *knowledge*. Before I came to Richmond, I had one perspective. I thought, "Oh, Richmond is a very conservative southern town." An old-boy network type of town.

It seemed so far away in the south from Washington D.C. Where I used to live -- it's only 100 miles, but I thought it was way down in the deep south. My company kept telling me, "You need to move to Richmond." Until I came here and recognized this is a pretty cosmopolitan town.

The more *knowledge* I get, the better my perspective becomes. It becomes more encompassing. So Bhagavan said, one who does not have this perspective will not know my nature.

We will need a Divya Drishti to see His real nature in totality. Mudha means one who has not yet developed that perspective -- who doesn't yet see the totality of the Lord's nature. Therefore, we learned from verses 4 through 7 how to see Him in totality.

There is nothing separate from anything else. We are not islands by ourselves. We are connected in a way that we can never separate ourselves from each other.

You can't have this class without any one of you. We need all of you, including myself, to have this class. But if I miss that perspective, I am a Mudha.

A father cannot be a father without a son or daughter. A daughter cannot be a daughter without father and mother. This interdependence we have right from birth is what we miss because of our *ego*.

Then we say, "I am a *self-made* man." You couldn't even breathe on your own. So Bhagavan said: Vedaham samatitani vartamanani cha Arjuna bhavishyani cha bhutani. "I know all beings of past, present, and future." But mam tu veda na kashchana -- "no one knows me." It's a real hide-and-seek game. The one at the top, with a greater perspective, sees everything, but we can't see Him.

He knows everyone. It's like Krishna saying, "I know all beings in the past, present, and future, but no one knows me." It's like the space in Henrico County claiming tomorrow, "I know all the buildings in Henrico County past, present, and future." Because no building is possible without the inherent ingredient of space in it. From space's perspective, no building is unknown.

From a building's perspective, I only know the conditioned space. Therefore I think I'm limited. I have birth, I have death.

I don't know what is the real nature of the space. I think the nature of the space is the room. So all of us, as soon as we take this identification, we forget the real nature of ourselves and take the identification of the conditioning.

But from the perspective of *consciousness* -- the same *consciousness* in me as in you, as in him, as was in my father, my grandfather, my ancestors 5,000 years ago -- the same *consciousness*. Therefore, from consciousness's perspective, it knew all beings in the past, present, and future. Because it never changed; it remained what it is.

Beings and their conditioning came and went and will come and go, but the inherent ingredient, the entity which makes it all possible, remains the same. So we know God is omnipresent. None of us somehow doubt it.

That which is omnipresent, by its very nature, becomes omniscient. If I am all-pervading in this space, I know everything about it. So Bhagavan is omnipresent and therefore omniscient.

But from a narrow perspective, if I try to understand Bhagavan, it will never be possible. Therefore He says, Mam tu veda na kashchana. Because we try to personify Him as a limited entity.

Therefore, North Indian Rama looks North Indian and South Indian Rama looks South Indian. The artist paints it in his imagination. We see Bhagavan in our imagination.

We put all our conditioning on Him. Therefore Bhagavan says, "No one knows me." We have to cross over these limitations of our mind and intellect. Therefore it's called transcendental meditation.

Iccha dvesha samutthena dvandva mohena Bharata. What creates this confusion? Iccha and Dvesha -- likes and dislikes. Sarvabhutani sammoham sarge yanti parantapa.

All beings are deluded from the very moment of birth by likes and dislikes. Right from birth, the little baby knows what is comfortable and what is not. As soon as something is not comfortable -- the diaper is wet -- it starts crying.

It has already taken on that conditioning. Per our scriptures, that baby has taken its conditioning -- because of past Vasanas, that body is taken. I take this particular state of existence -- that's what I wanted to experience.

Why do I go to concerts and not to boxing matches? That's what I want to experience. That's why I go to concerts, not wrestling matches. The one who goes to wrestling matches -- tell him to go to the opera! So you have taken on your conditioning based on what you like.

Now you divide your world into the world you like and the world you don't like -- the world of your physical existence and the world of your emotions involved with your thinking.
snippets.reflection:
"I am not visible to all, for I am enveloped by the illusion of Yoga-Maya." This verse reveals why the spiritual search feels like hide-and-seek. The Divine is not hiding from us; we are veiled from seeing what is already everywhere present. Like someone searching for their glasses while wearing them, we seek what we already are. Today, instead of trying to "find" God or truth, try relaxing the very effort to seek. In moments of pure presence, without agenda or grasping, what remains?

"I know all beings in the past, the present and the future; but they do not know Me." From the perspective of space, all rooms are known because space pervades all rooms. But from the perspective of a single room, space seems confined to those four walls. Your consciousness, which seems limited to your body and mind, is actually the same universal consciousness that pervades all beings across all time. Today's exercise: When you meet someone, briefly consider that the awareness looking out from their eyes is the same awareness looking out from yours. Only the conditioning, the "room," is different.

The root cause of delusion is revealed: "Iccha-dvesha-samutthena," born of likes and dislikes. From the moment of birth, we divide the world into what we want and what we reject. This fundamental duality creates all suffering. Today, notice your automatic reactions of attraction and aversion. The morning coffee you crave, the traffic you despise, the praise you seek, the criticism you avoid. Can you observe these preferences without being completely controlled by them? Even brief moments of equanimity, accepting what is without demanding it be different, give a taste of freedom from the dvandvas (pairs of opposites).
snippets.shortReflection: You're searching for something you're already experiencing. The awareness reading these words right now—that's what you've been looking for. Stop seeking and start noticing.

snippets.title: Day 105: Freedom from Delusion
snippets.sanskrit:
येषां त्वन्तगतं पापं जनानां पुण्यकर्मणाम् |
ते द्वन्द्वमोहनिर्मुक्ता भजन्ते मां दृढव्रताः ||

जरामरणमोक्षाय मामाश्रित्य यतन्ति ये |
ते ब्रह्म तद्विदुः कृत्स्नमध्यात्मं कर्म चाखिलम् ||

साधिभूताधिदैवं मां साधियज्ञं च ये विदुः |
प्रयाणकालेऽपि च मां ते विदुर्युक्तचेतसः ||
snippets.transliteration:
yeṣhāṁ tvanta-gataṁ pāpaṁ janānāṁ puṇya-karmaṇām
te dvandva-moha-nirmuktā bhajante māṁ dṛiḍha-vratāḥ

jarā-maraṇa-mokṣhāya mām āśhritya yatanti ye
te brahma tadviduḥ kṛitsnam adhyātmaṁ karma chākhilam

sādhibhūtādhidaivaṁ māṁ sādhiyajñaṁ cha ye viduḥ
prayāṇa-kāle ’pi cha māṁ te vidur yukta-chetasaḥ
verseTranslations: But those who act righteously, in whom sin has been destroyed, who are free from the infatuation of the conflicting emotions, they worship Me with firm resolution.
Those who make Me their refuge, who strive for liberation from decay and Death, they realise the Supreme Spirit, which is their own real Self, and in which all action finds its consummation.
Those who see Me in the life of the world, in the universal sacrifice, and as pure Divinity, keeping their minds steady, they live in Me, even in the crucial hour of death.
snippets.commentary:
In the first segment, we learned all about ourselves. The second chapter gave us a summary of who we are.

What we remember from the second chapter is that the *self* is immutable, imperishable. The "myself" which I consider "me" is immutable, imperishable. But we never fully grasped what that really means. Okay, someone who realizes that -- how would he act? How would he behave in this world? Will he be completely different from us?

We saw the characteristics of a Gnani, but that didn't show us anything different from what we do. So the next few chapters gave us how to analyze our actions and ourselves, and then recalibrate our actions to become more productive and effective. That first segment ended with Chapter 6 on meditation. Meditation is the means given to us to recalibrate this instrument called mind, body, and intellect.

Then this next segment of six chapters, from 7 to 12, is all about what that imperishable *self* is which we talked about in Chapter 2. That's why the first chapter of this segment, Chapter 7 -- Gnana Vignana *Yoga* -- is about having this knowledge of the Lord, that immutable *self* we learned about in Chapter 2.

But how can we make it Vishishta *Gnana* that we can apply? Therefore Chapter 7 describes in detail the Lord's nature and why we can't realize it in our day-to-day life. Bhagavan said, "I manifest in this world as the Eightfold *Prakriti*." That's something you and I can see -- "that's nothing but my own manifestation." Then he says, "There is nothing in this world which does not come out of me. Anything you can see, feel, touch, and perceive has come out of me and will dissolve in me."

And all this world of plurality, as we see it, is strung together. Nothing is independent, like an island in this universe -- which is hinting at us, because we think we are the island of the universe as "me" and everything else revolves around me. He said, "No, everything is strung like pearls in a necklace. I am that common thread. I pervade through this universe as the Eightfold *Prakriti*."

You are part of that *Prakriti*. The unmanifest is the common thread among all the manifestations which apparently look different from each other. "Why then are we not seeing that?" "Because you are under the spell of my divine Maya, which creates plurality out of singularity. As long as you are under that spell, you see yourself as different from this world." This Maya has three *Gunas* -- Sattva, Rajas, and *Tamas* -- and through their permutation and combination, it creates the infinite varieties of things and beings.

But as long as I can't overcome that *Maya*, I can't see the truth. In the last set of verses we saw: Iccha dvesha samutthena dvandva mohena Bharata. Because of this desire or that desire, I have divided this world into two -- the world I like and the world I don't like. Right from birth, I'm deluded about myself.

That immutable, imperishable *self* talked about in Chapter 2 -- I'm not recognizing it because of the duality my mind has created. My mind says, "This is me and everything else is the world." As long as I can't get out of that concept, Bhagavan said, I won't be able to realize the truth.

However, in the last three verses he says that those Gnanis who have erased this wrong notion of who they are -- their papas are all erased by this new line of thinking. Yesham tu antagatam papam jananam punya karmanam.

So there is hope. Bhagavan said this is not just a philosophical discussion. He's not just telling us, "You will never realize it." No, let's figure out what the problem was in the beginning. The problem was my wrong line of thinking: that I am different from this world. This notion that I am this limited being, and therefore I have all these problems.

Once I undo the thinking that I am this limited being, the limitation will be gone. Yesham tu antagatam papam -- those whose papas have come to an end. The classic definition of Papa is: a thought or impression which takes me away from myself, takes me away from my understanding that I am that immutable, imperishable *self*, and creates division between "I" and the world. As long as I am driven by the desires of the flesh, my thinking will be focused on how to fulfill those desires.

When I start thinking in the same line, it creates deep channels in my mind which guide subsequent thoughts into the same channel. This habit of following the same line of thinking to fulfill desires creates Papa -- because I just can't get out of the thinking that "this will make me happy." Last time I had a cup of coffee and it made me happy. This time it should do the same thing, and I continue. Bhagavan said, that creates your own notion of who you are.

How do I come out of it? He said, more and more I become introverted through the technique given in the previous chapter -- the meditation that "No, this is not me. The one who is getting happy with the Starbucks coffee is not me; it is someone other than myself." That line of thinking erases those channels created by my attempt to satisfy all the desires that body, mind, and intellect have created. The more I fulfill desires, the more new experiences create new channels of thinking, which create new Vasanas.

These Vasanas, the tendencies, create the same line of thinking and the same line of actions. I need to stop doing actions driven by the same line of thinking that is not giving me happiness. Even though I figured out last time that investing in the stock market was not good -- because everybody says, "Don't miss this cycle," I'm back again. You need to get out of that line of thinking.

Once you start meditating on what really makes you happy -- if I analyze my experience, was it the experience that made me happy, or something else? -- you come to the conclusion that no desire makes me happy. When I'm completely at ease, when I don't want anything -- I've already eaten my lunch, I don't have anywhere to go, and I can just sit down -- at least I still have a desire to watch TV, but even if I drop that, I'll probably be completely happy.

This new line of thinking creates the undoing of all those wrong channels in my mind. Now I have removed all the Papas. Papas are just the wrong line of thinking, the wrong Vasanas.

Yesham tu antagatam papam jananam punya karmanam. The method we learned in the first six chapters is *Karma* *Yoga* -- selfless actions. When I act in a manner that erases the thinking that "working to fulfill my desires makes me happy," I also realize the real happiness comes when I do something for others -- the true happiness we get when we do something for our children, our parents, our relatives, our friends.

Jananam punya karmanam -- they have changed their line of actions, therefore changed their line of thinking, therefore changed their tendencies. Now they are in a completely different realm of actions and thinking. Their Papas are all erased.

Te dvandva moha nirmuktah -- now they are out of this duality. "I'm not just working for me; I'm working for the whole of humanity, my town, my family." I keep expanding my identity until there is no duality between "I" and the world. Te dvandva moha nirmuktah -- this Dvandva is nothing but a delusion that you and I are different from each other.

That this world and I are two different entities is nothing but a delusion. Those who, by acting in the right manner, erase those lines of thinking which create delusion -- now Bhajante mam dridha vratah. Worshipping, we have seen, is an act of love. That love for the divine becomes so firm that I am firmly established in the thought that "I" and the world are nothing but part of the same all-pervading entity.

The next verse says Jara marana mokshaya -- and why am I doing all of this? Because the two things I'm afraid of in life are Jara (old age) and Marana (death). We had a Valentine's Day party yesterday, and you know what the topic was -- because we were all probably above 50 there.

"How do we get out of this problem of dying? The 10 tubes going through you..." Because we are afraid of Jara, old age -- when I will not be in control. I was reading about Ronald Reagan, when he was taking a walk and people said, "Good morning, Mr. President." He wouldn't recognize why people were calling him president. He didn't know he was a president. He just thought, "This guy is nice; he's greeting me."

That's all he could think. The thought that a person can reach that level, where he can't even recognize who he is -- it's pretty scary for all of us. Because all our life we took pride in being in control. I take care of myself. I take care of my family. I take care of my business.

"I take care of..." -- "I am in charge" is what makes me who I am. The very thought that I will not be in control is very, very disturbing. We want to get out of that. I want to exist, and death wipes me out. It just doesn't seem right.

Jara Marana Mokshaya -- for *liberation* from this thought of old age and death. Mam ashritya -- taking complete refuge in me means not Lord Krishna or Rama or Jesus, but in that immutable *self*. Taking complete refuge in identification with my immutable *self*. Just as I'm in complete control in a barber's chair -- the hair I let go and the hair I keep, I'm in complete control. The hair I let go, I don't get attached to.

"Please, please pack it up for me!" No -- I say, "Wipe it out clean as quickly as possible."
snippets.reflection:
"Those who act righteously, in whom sin has been destroyed, who are free from the infatuation of conflicting emotions, they worship Me with firm resolution." Sin (papa) here is defined not as breaking commandments but as any thought or action that reinforces the illusion of separation between self and the Divine. Each time you act from ego, from the belief that you are a separate, isolated being fighting against the world, you deepen those grooves of wrong thinking. Each time you act from dharma, recognizing your connection to the whole, those grooves begin to fill in. Today, before each significant action, ask: "Does this reinforce my sense of separation, or does it align me with something greater?"

The chapter concludes with the profound motivation for spiritual seeking: "liberation from decay and death" (jara-marana-mokshaya). This is not morbid but urgently practical. We all fear aging and death because our identity is bound to the body. The one who knows the Self as distinct from the body has nothing to fear, like someone in a barber's chair watching hair fall away without grief. Today, contemplate: What in you is actually subject to decay? Your body certainly. Your opinions and preferences, yes. Your memories and personality, these too change. But the awareness that witnesses all these changes, has that ever aged?

The final verses point to the culmination: knowing the Divine in all aspects of existence, as Adhibhuta (in all beings), Adhidaiva (as the cosmic principle), and Adhiyajna (as the sacred offering in every action). The promise is extraordinary: "Those who know Me thus, even at the hour of death, remain united with Me." Today, practice the recognition that every action, however mundane, can be a sacred offering. Washing dishes, answering emails, driving to work, when done with awareness of the Divine presence pervading all, these become Yajna, sacrifice, paths to liberation.
snippets.shortReflection: Before your next significant action, pause and ask: Does this deepen my sense of being separate and alone, or does it connect me to something larger?

snippets.title: Day 106: The Imperishable
snippets.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच |
किं तद्ब्रह्म किमध्यात्मं किं कर्म पुरुषोत्तम |
अधिभूतं च किं प्रोक्तमधिदैवं किमुच्यते ||

अधियज्ञः कथं कोऽत्र देहेऽस्मिन्मधुसूदन |
प्रयाणकाले च कथं ज्ञेयोऽसि नियतात्मभिः ||

श्री भगवानुवाच |
अक्षरं ब्रह्म परमं स्वभावोऽध्यात्ममुच्यते |
भूतभावोद्भवकरो विसर्गः कर्मसंज्ञितः ||
snippets.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kiṁ tad brahma kim adhyātmaṁ kiṁ karma puruṣhottama
adhibhūtaṁ cha kiṁ proktam adhidaivaṁ kim uchyate

adhiyajñaḥ kathaṁ ko ’tra dehe ’smin madhusūdana
prayāṇa-kāle cha kathaṁ jñeyo ’si niyatātmabhiḥ

śhrī bhagavān uvācha
akṣharaṁ brahma paramaṁ svabhāvo ’dhyātmam uchyate
bhūta-bhāvodbhava-karo visargaḥ karma-sanjñitaḥ
verseTranslations: Who is it who rules the spirit sacrifice in many; and at the time of death how may those who have learned self-control come to the knowledge of Thee?

The Lord Shri Krishna replied: The Supreme Spirit is the Highest Imperishable Self, and Its Nature is spiritual consciousness. The worlds have been created and are supported by an emanation from the Spirit which is called the Law.
The perishable nature of beings is called Adhibhuta; the divine Self is called Adhidaiva; and I alone, dwelling in this body, am called Adhiyajna, the Lord of all sacrifices.
snippets.commentary:
Starting from chapter one, we have seen our own situation, the condition we are in.

We are fighting this battle of life, but we get confused about what is right *action* -- whether this is right or that is right, should I do this or should I do that? Constantly I'm waffling between this or that and can't come to the right conclusion. So in chapter one, Arjuna kept arguing intellectually, but could not come to any conclusion. In chapter two, in the beginning he surrenders himself to Lord Krishna.

Then comes the guidance. So the guidance comes as the revelation about the true nature of our *self*. So in chapter two, we learned that all that which I have thought about myself was erroneous.

Myself is immortal being. And therefore once I realign my understanding about who I am, everything else will fall in place in a very new pattern. Just like when we are traveling and encounter a new road pattern, we have to adjust to it.

Unless you pay attention, you go back to the old way, and if you keep traveling the old road, you are going to run into some construction. So if I change the old way of thinking about who I am to the new way of thinking about who I am, then how I act will change completely. In chapter three, we learned the nature of actions, what actions are all about.

Actions are binding, but not the ones which are performed in the spirit of Yajna. So the escape hatch is that all my actions should be performed in the spirit of Yajna for the greater good, for the common good, which is *Karma* Yoga. So we learned that Karma Yoga is the way to act in this world.

And then what is *Karma* Yoga was defined? If you give up the anxiety for the fruits of actions, that's Karma *Yoga*. So now my goal is: I have to act in this world, but I want to renounce actions. So chapter four talked about how to renounce actions in *knowledge*.

Knowing that I'm not the doer, I'll be able to renounce my actions. That renunciation of the sense of agency is sannyasa. In chapter five, we learned what Sannyasa is. *Renouncing* the anxiety of actions is Karma Yoga.

Performing Karma *Yoga*, I become a Yogi -- I become so efficient in my actions that I realize I am not the doer at all. And that is *sannyasa*. Once I renounce this sense of agency, then I have to identify with my true self.

So in chapter six we learn the techniques of meditation -- how to give up the identity with the limited self, the conditioned *self* which I currently consider to be me, and how to align with the true self that we learned about in chapter two. That alignment is chapter six: the techniques of meditation on the *self*. But now, how to meditate on the *self*? What is the subject of my meditation? We learnt that in chapter seven.

There we learned that the nature of the true supreme self is twofold. One is Lower *Prakriti* and one is higher *Prakriti*. The lower is the one which I can experience, perceive, feel, touch and cognize and say this is it.

So the reality which I can perceive through my senses is the manifest world. The Bhagavan says that's my Lower *Prakriti*. Everything that you see, touch, feel is made up of my own *self*.

The Asthatha *Prakriti*. That's his Eightfold which is Bhumi, Apaha, Kham, Analah, Vayuhu, Mana, Buddhi and Ahankar. All five great elements.

Mind, intellect and Ahankal, *Ego*. So there is nothing left. You take any entity in this world, and it will fall somewhere in this combination of eight -- start recognizing my Saguna Prakriti.

This Prakriti has names and forms. But he says there is a higher *Prakriti* which is beyond this Saguna Prakriti -- the Nirguna *Prakriti*, which has no names, no forms, no colors, no attributes, no entity, no being. He said that's my Higher *Prakriti*.

That *Prakriti* is what I'm now trying to align myself with in my meditation, because I can already identify with the Saguna *Prakriti*. So we started our journey from "me" -- being the most selfish person, only thinking about "this is me." Then we expand our horizon and say, I'm a little better than that; I identify with my family. I expand my horizon even more and say, no, no -- my community is also me, not just my family.

Then I expand a little further and say, no, no, my nation is also me. Then I go even further -- Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam -- this planet is my home. And then I say I'm going to go beyond that.

And this cosmos is me. This gradually expanding my identification from this limited me to cosmic me. From a Saguna perspective is which I can do with my open eyes meditation.

But then I have to go to the higher *Prakriti* that is beyond all the names and forms. Bhagawan says that's my imperishable nature. That's Akshara Brahma.

So chapter eight now attempts to explain what that higher nature is. In the last chapter, in the ending two verses, Bhagavan said that one who knows myself in its totality -- Adhibutam, Adhi Daivam and Adhiyagnam -- even at the time of death, even that becomes a glimpse. At the last minute this complete picture becomes clear to me: what is Saguna *Prakriti*? What is Nirguna *Prakriti*? And what is this creation is all about? So now Arjuna obviously wants to know all the technical terms he heard in last chapter.

So the chapter eight start with Arjuna's question. And as we have seen, he asked Bhagavan to define seven terms he has heard in his discourse. What is that *Brahman* which you are talking about? Then what is Adhyatma Kim? We talked about actions we know.

Without *action* I cannot even survive. I cannot maintain my body. Then what is Adhibhuta? You talked about Adhibhuta in the last chapter.

Kim Proktam Adhi Daivam -- and what is called Adhidaivam? What is it that we call Adhi Daivam? Adi Yagna Katham Ko ata Katham -- what is Yajna and how does it work? Adi Yajna is Dehe asmin Madhusudhana. We have discussed Madhu Sudhana, the slayer of Madhu. Madhu was a demon in our life -- that which feels very good is my enemy.

I learned that in old age, the only taste that survives is sweet. I was talking to one of our friends who said, "I don't know why, but I never liked sweets in my life." "And now in my old age I like nothing but sweets." Isn't it very simple? All your taste buds die as you grow older. The only ones that survive are the sweet taste buds.

So the only thing I really taste is sweetness. Everything else is not very enchanting anymore. The slayer of Madhu is Madhu Sudhana.

O Madhu Sudhana, Prayana kale cha Katham Gneyo asi Niyatatma Bihi -- in the last verse of the last chapter, he said that even at the last moment, if you know this, know myself as Adhi Bhuta, Adhi Deva, Adi Yajna. How do I know even at the last minute? You tell me, how should I know? And how do I make sure that I will know? How do I live a *self-controlled* life? Niyatatma Bhi -- *self-control* so that I will know you at the last minute. He recognized that at least there is some exercise I have to do.

Not just relying on luck or chance that I will remember him at the last minute just because I named my son after him. In fact, he may distract me -- because "Rama, Rama, O Rama" went away from here to Austin, Texas. I'm glad that I have only one son, and his name is not after any Devta.

Niraj! So Arjuna says, just let me know. All other six questions were relatively less important. What he really wanted to know about was the last minute -- that was the real question.

How do I live a *self-controlled* life so that even at the last minute I will know your real *self*? And why is the last minute so important here? That's a milestone. When I decide that I'm going to take a vacation, that's a change -- from here I'm going there. Till that time, it doesn't matter; I'm here.

Mawlik moving from here to Dallas, Texas. The day he moves is a milestone. Till that, he is just Mawlik.

So Prayana Kale Apicha -- because I know that I will have the transition from this *self* to that existence, how do I make sure that I go to the right place, to know you? The answer comes in the next two verses, which actually, if we wanted to discuss fully, could take six months. We'll do it in the next 10 minutes. Aksharam Brahma Paramam.

Very simple. *Brahman* is Akshara -- that which is imperishable is Brahman. Everything that I know in this world is perishable. *Brahman* is imperishable. That means anything which I can assign a beginning and end is not *Brahman*.

Aksha Ra, that Akshay. That which makes "I" revel in that form is Akshara. That's why the letters are called Akshara -- because they become real to us.

So Saguna, from that perspective, is Akshara. But Paramam -- Aksaram Brahma Paramam -- that which is higher than Akshara is *Brahman*. So from that definition, that which is greater than Saguna, different than Saguna is *Brahman*.

So now I have to negate everything that I know and go beyond my *knowledge*. Therefore it is transcendental -- it cannot be learned through intellect, cannot be experienced through my mind. It is transcendental.

Svabhava Adhyatma Uchyate. They ask, what is Adhyatma? It is Svabhava -- the nature of your own *self*. That which makes me who I am is my Svabhava.

Bhagavan Sankaracharya says that that which makes me who I am is Paramatma. When he resides in me, he is Pratyagatma. And when that Pratyagatma identifies with this body, mind, and intellect, it becomes the Jiva.

It is something between the Jivatma as I know myself and the all-pervading Paramatma. The part of him which is me is Pratyagatma. That is my svabhava; without that I cannot do anything.

Therefore he says, when I know my own *self*, that is Adhyatma. Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara Visargaha *Karma* Sanginitam -- this is a very revolutionary definition of *Karma*. From that perspective, *Karma* was always considered a ritualistic performance.

When you perform any rituals, they were considered Karma. From our Vedic literature, Bhagavana defines Karma as Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara. That which brings forth beings and things into existence is *Karma*.

So any creative endeavor is Karma. When I create something, it is *Karma*. When I improve something, it's *karma*.

So anything else you do is just labor. Therefore nobody congratulates me in the morning when I brush my teeth -- unless you are a two or three year old child. Because it's not *karma* unless I assign value to it and say I am doing it for the betterment of my teeth.

Then it's *karma* -- Bhuta Bhava Kara. That which creates improvement and brings things and beings into existence is *Karma*. So Bhagavan's Karma is that he creates this universe out of his self as Ishvara.

He takes the help of his *Maya*, becomes Ishwara, becomes Hiranyagarbha, and creates this universe. From our perspective, anything we do to create something, improve something, improve myself, improve the lives of others -- that is Karma. That which brings everything down is Papa, not *Karma*.
snippets.reflection:
Arjuna's seven questions in these verses reveal a fundamental human longing: to understand the ultimate nature of reality and our place within it. Before we can embark on any meaningful spiritual journey, we must first ask the right questions. Take time today to examine your own burning questions about existence. What is it that you truly want to know?

Krishna defines Karma here not as mere ritual, but as "Bhuta Bhava Udbhavakara"—that which creates improvement and brings beings into existence. This revolutionary definition transforms how we view our daily activities. Ask yourself: Are my actions today merely labor, or are they true Karma—creative endeavors that contribute to the betterment of myself and others?

The teaching that Brahman is "Akshara" (imperishable) while everything we can perceive is perishable invites deep contemplation. Consider making a list of what you cling to most tightly—possessions, relationships, achievements, identity. Recognize that all these fall within the realm of the perishable Lower Prakriti. This is not meant to create despair, but clarity. The practice is to hold these things lightly while turning your attention toward that which cannot be destroyed. In meditation today, try to shift your identification from the Saguna (with attributes) to the Nirguna (without attributes)—from the room space of your conditioned self to the infinite space of pure awareness. What would it feel like to expand your identification beyond "me" to family, community, nation, planet, and ultimately, the cosmos itself?
snippets.shortReflection: List what you're gripping tightly—your job title, your relationship status, your bank balance, your body's appearance. Everything on that list will change or disappear. Now, what remains?

snippets.title: Day 107: Remembrance at Death
snippets.sanskrit:
अधिभूतं क्षरो भावः पुरुषश्चाधिदैवतम् |
अधियज्ञोऽहमेवात्र देहे देहभृतां वर ||

अन्तकाले च मामेव स्मरन्मुक्त्वा कलेवरम् |
यः प्रयाति स मद्भावं याति नास्त्यत्र संशयः ||

यं यं वापि स्मरन्भावं त्यजत्यन्ते कलेवरम् |
तं तमेवैति कौन्तेय सदा तद्भावभावितः ||
snippets.transliteration:
adhibhūtaṁ kṣharo bhāvaḥ puruṣhaśh chādhidaivatam
adhiyajño ’ham evātra dehe deha-bhṛitāṁ vara

anta-kāle cha mām eva smaran muktvā kalevaram
yaḥ prayāti sa mad-bhāvaṁ yāti nāstyatra sanśhayaḥ

yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajatyante kalevaram
taṁ tam evaiti kaunteya sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ
verseTranslations: Matter consists of the forms that perish; Divinity is the Supreme Self; and He who inspires the spirit of sacrifice in man, O noblest of thy race, is I Myself, Who now stand in human form before thee.
Whosoever at the time of death thinks only of Me, and thinking thus leaves the body and goes forth, assuredly he will know Me.
On whatever sphere of being the mind of a man may be intent at the time of death, thither he will go.
snippets.commentary:
That was a statement.

So Arjuna starts the chapter with question about defining these terms. Adhibhuta, Adhi Deva and Adiyajna. What are those terms? What do they indicate? But he added three more terms, Brahma, *Karma* and Adyat also to be defined.

So what we have seen in the first four verses are the definitions of these terms. And we come to the last question, how the one with the steadfast mind at the end should come to know you. So what we have seen so far is the definition of Purusha and *Prakriti* -- that which is time-bound and that which is timeless.

The *self* as you consider it right now is time-bound. Therefore there is a death. Death is a milestone in your existence.

So as we have discussed last time, that these verses in the entire chapter only make sense if you take the concept of reincarnation in its essence as valid principle. But that's also not really the case because it is about the existence. That which you are talking about, the existence which I consider right now is limited existence.

Will there be any existence after I die? That's a burning question in everyone's mind. Knowingly or unknowingly, consciously or unconsciously, we ask this question -- whether you believe in reincarnation or not. No culture, no religion has ever questioned existence itself.

Every religion talks about existence after death. We have difficulty accepting the idea of reincarnation because we live in a culture bound by science and technology. Unless you are one of those who do not believe in evolution and climate change, we all seek approval from science and technology.

Therefore I don't question whether my cell phone working is the magic. We know it is supported by science and technology. Reincarnation is currently not proven from our scientific perspective.

So even when this topic came up last time, Ram had to bring university research to convince some of us that this also can be researched. But what here is indicated is the existence. That we will exist is not a question in anybody's mind.

Therefore, the incentive for terrorists to become a bomber is what? What would you do with virgins after you die? You believe you won't be existing, yet you believe you will exist and will have time to enjoy. So the existence is never questioned anywhere. In any religion, in any culture, in any thought, in any philosophy, existence is considered permanent.

There was an existence before my birth and there will be existence after my birth. But what is now important is what kind of existence I would have. So our culture has put great emphasis on planning for long-term existence.

What about short-term planning? Companies who plan for the long term make progress. Like Warren Buffett does his investment in a long term basis. Some people do investment on quarter to quarter basis.

So what we do in our life is short-term planning. We plan to have a better life in this life. One life to live is the philosophy, right? There is only one life to live.

Oh, Sastra said, no, not true. You have infinite lives to live. You have innumerable lives to live.

And therefore plan wisely so that your future existence would be happier. So these verses now try to define how to plan for a long term existence versus short term existence. See, the first thing we learn is Adi Bhuta is perishable.

That which I see has been created. Therefore the term *Karma* is defined. Bhuta Bhava udbhavakara idhi *Karma*.

That which creates Bhuta Bhava -- a being or a thing -- is *karma*. So anything which is created will be perishable. Anything which comes into existence is perishable.

So when I'm planning within the realm of objects, it is temporary. So if I want to really plan for a real long term, I want to plan beyond the realm of perishable things and beings. That is what they call it.

You will come to me, Me, the supreme Me, the imperishable. Because there are two existence which we have known through our discussion. One is imperishable, never perishes, never changes, never have any mutation.

And the one which is constantly changing. I clearly identify with the one with changes. Because I identify with this, the body, this mind, this intellect.

I clearly know that this body is perishable. I have learned through my experiences in life, this body is perishable. And also I have observed from My inferred *knowledge* that people die and people bury them or burn them, cremate them, so my body will go through the same fate.

So we have come to the clear understanding that this body is perishable. What we have not yet understood is the mind and intellect. A lot of this research which we hear is all about brain, not the mind.

Talking to psychiatrists, they say we don't understand mind. We don't know how these medications work. We just know that it works and therefore it is good enough to prescribe.

But what mind is is very much a mystery. So it is possible that our ancestors did not know much about the physical senses, but they knew a little more about mind than what we know today. So they have come to the conclusion that this mind and intellect has a life of its own, beyond this body's life.

So Prayana Kale Api -- at the time of the journey, that mind and intellect, remaining intact, is going to make a move. Bhagavan Veda Vyasa here basically reaffirms the basic principles of Hinduism or Vedantic philosophy: this body is the only thing that dies at the time of death. The jiva, the one identified with this limited mind and intellect, remains intact and seeks another state of existence to exhaust the remaining vasanas.

So Bhagavan in verse 5 gives the same answer which he gave as a statement at the end of chapter 7. Antakale Chamameva Smaranam uktvakalevaram yaha prayati samad bhavam yati na asti atra sansayaha. Only thing he does is he gives a guarantee.

Last time he made a statement, this time he gives a guarantee. I'm selling somebody something, but I don't have means to support all my claims about my product. I guarantee you that if it doesn't work, you can return it to me.

I'll return all the money. So guarantee is one way of making the student or the buyer feel more comfortable. He already said, one who knows me in totality will come to me.

So he said, even at the last moment, because we have considered this life to be the only life for me to make any progress. And if I think I wasted most of my life, what am I going to do now? This is more like my music teacher made a statement to me when I went to him when I was in my 40s. Subhas, do you know that I'm 47? He said, "So what? You're not 67 yet." So now if I go to him, he will say, "Subhas, I'm 67." And there's still time.

Even at the time of your death, if you come to realize what is truth, thou shall achieve truth. That's the guarantee. Bhagawan says Antakaale chamame vas maran muktvakale varan.

One who leaves this body at the time of death Antakaala. At the end of this body, he leaves this body. So something is leaving.

Somebody is making a journey. That means the one who is identified with the *ego* has not died yet. That *ego* is making its own journey now.

From this body to somewhere else. From this existence to some other existence. Existence is not questioned.

It is the state of existence which is questioned here. Whether will I remain in the same state of existence that I am? Will I retain my wisdom or will I retain my stupidity is the question. One who even at the last minute recognizes the truth.

He will come to know me. He will come to become one with me. There is no question about it.

So he guarantees that you have plenty of time till you die to churn over this idea of what is truth. Even the last moment, if you have eureka moment that oh that's what it is. Bhagawan says that's good enough.

Will come to recognize me and realize me. But you still have to make a supportive argument, because we are not born into guarantees. That's why we go on social networks and say, "What are the comments other people have made?" You know, Meena and I always struggle about exercise.

So Meena came across something called a seat and cycle. As usual, I said don't worry about it. But once we ordered, we realized there are five more payments to be made.

It was never revealed on that Facebook page -- see, there are five more payments! I said, if you want to go ahead, go. But by the time she had already pressed that button. So then she started reading all the opinions and the comments.

They're all pretty bad. This is not a product for elderly. You can fall down also.

It took me three times it broke down. We said cancel that order as quickly as you can. Because they didn't guarantee anything.

They only offered a free trial for 30 days. Bhagwan gave the guarantee. But realize that you will be looking for some support, watching some comments from other users.

So he makes his supporting argument. Yam yam vapi smaran Bhavam tyajatyante kalevaram tamtam eva Ithi kaunteya sada tad bhava bhavitaha. A statement of fact: whosoever you are thinking of at the time of leaving your body, that and that person alone you shall go to.

Looking at our own context of life -- who do we meet in life? The people whom we think about most. We constantly think about a person. Then we obviously make a plan to meet.

When my mother was alive, I was thinking about her the most. Every two years I was making a plan to go and see her. Now I really have not.

Even though I have my brothers and my nephews and nieces, it's not that much of a pressure on me to go to India anymore. Because I was thinking about my mother all the time. I was feeling guilty that I have left my mother at the age of 17 or 18.

Never went home, never took care of her. So constantly was thinking about her. And therefore my plans will be no other vacation.

Go to India, stay with her for a few days. So Bhagavan said that it is a given: whatever is my constant thought becomes the last thought at the time of my journey. Where will you go for vacation? Not to a place you have never thought about.

The vacation you are planning for the last six months -- you have checked all the brochures, checked out all the prices, checked out all the hotel accommodations available, researched all the places to visit. Then, at the time of your journey to take a vacation -- That's the ticket you buy and that's the place you end up going. Bhagavan says, one who is constantly thinking about me is the only one who will be thinking about me at the time of death to come to me.

Therefore the next verse says, tasmat sarveshu kaleshu -- therefore at all times, mam anusmara, think about me. And then he says, Yudhyacha this half sloka, if misunderstood, can bring down the entire generation.
snippets.reflection:
Krishna's guarantee in verse 5 is remarkable: "Whosoever at the time of death thinks only of Me... assuredly he will know Me." This is not about luck at the final moment, but about the power of lifelong habits of thought. The teaching "Yam yam vapi smaran bhavam" reveals a profound psychological truth—we become what we consistently think about. Examine your mental habits today: Where does your mind naturally drift when it is unoccupied? What do you think about first thing in the morning and last thing at night? These habitual thought patterns are shaping your inner trajectory. Just as you naturally plan vacations to places you have been researching for months, your consciousness will move toward whatever you have been contemplating most deeply.

The verse distinguishes between Adhibhuta (the perishable realm of matter) and the imperishable Self that Krishna represents. This is an invitation to shift your planning horizon. Most of our planning is short-term—this life, this career, this relationship. But these verses invite us to consider: What if you planned for your long-term existence across many lives? This week, practice the "mother meditation"—think of someone you love deeply, as the teacher spoke of thinking constantly about his mother. Notice how that consistent thought naturally creates action (visiting, caring, connecting). Now apply this same principle to your spiritual aspiration. What would it mean to think about the Supreme Self with that same consistency and devotion? Begin simply: set three reminders on your phone each day to pause and remember your true imperishable nature.
snippets.shortReflection: Where does your mind go when it's idle? In traffic, before sleep, between tasks. Those automatic thoughts are building the highway your consciousness will travel when everything else falls away.

snippets.title: Day 108: The Two Paths
snippets.sanskrit:

mayyarpita-mano-buddhir mām evaiṣhyasyasanśhayam

abhyāsa-yoga-yuktena chetasā nānya-gāminā
paramaṁ puruṣhaṁ divyaṁ yāti pārthānuchintayan

verseTranslations: Therefore meditate always on Me, and fight; if thy mind and thy reason be fixed on Me, to Me shalt thou surely come.
He whose mind does not wander, and who is engaged in constant meditation, attains the Supreme Spirit.
Whoso meditates on the Omniscient, the Ancient, more minute than the atom, yet the Ruler and Upholder of all, Unimaginable, Brilliant like the Sun, Beyond the reach of darkness;
snippets.commentary:
That was a statement.

So Arjuna starts the chapter with question about defining these terms. Adhibhuta, Adhi Deva and Adiyajna. What are those terms? What do they indicate? But he added three more terms, Brahma, *Karma* and Adyat also to be defined.

So what we have seen in the first four verses are the definitions of these terms. And we come to the last question, how the one with the steadfast mind at the end should come to know you. So what we have seen so far is the definition of Purusha and *Prakriti* -- that which is time-bound and that which is timeless.

The *self* as you consider it right now is time-bound. Therefore there is a death. Death is a milestone in your existence.

So as we have discussed last time, that these verses in the entire chapter only make sense if you take the concept of reincarnation in its essence as valid principle. But that's also not really the case because it is about the existence. That which you are talking about, the existence which I consider right now is limited existence.

Will there be any existence after I die? That's a burning question in everyone's mind. Knowingly or unknowingly, consciously or unconsciously, we ask this question -- whether you believe in reincarnation or not. No culture, no religion has ever questioned existence itself.

Every religion talks about existence after death. We have difficulty accepting the idea of reincarnation because we live in a culture bound by science and technology. Unless you are one of those who do not believe in evolution and climate change, we all seek approval from science and technology.

Therefore I don't question whether my cell phone working is the magic. We know it is supported by science and technology. Reincarnation is currently not proven from our scientific perspective.

So even when this topic came up last time, Ram had to bring university research to convince some of us that this also can be researched. But what here is indicated is the existence. That we will exist is not a question in anybody's mind.

Therefore, the incentive for terrorists to become a bomber is what? What would you do with virgins after you die? You believe you won't be existing, yet you believe you will exist and will have time to enjoy. So the existence is never questioned anywhere. In any religion, in any culture, in any thought, in any philosophy, existence is considered permanent.

There was an existence before my birth and there will be existence after my birth. But what is now important is what kind of existence I would have. So our culture has put great emphasis on planning for long-term existence.

What about short-term planning? Companies who plan for the long term make progress. Like Warren Buffett does his investment in a long term basis. Some people do investment on quarter to quarter basis.

So what we do in our life is short-term planning. We plan to have a better life in this life. One life to live is the philosophy, right? There is only one life to live.

Oh, Sastra said, no, not true. You have infinite lives to live. You have innumerable lives to live.

And therefore plan wisely so that your future existence would be happier. So these verses now try to define how to plan for a long term existence versus short term existence. See, the first thing we learn is Adi Bhuta is perishable.

That which I see has been created. Therefore the term *Karma* is defined. Bhuta Bhava udbhavakara idhi *Karma*.

That which creates Bhuta Bhava -- a being or a thing -- is *karma*. So anything which is created will be perishable. Anything which comes into existence is perishable.

So when I'm planning within the realm of objects, it is temporary. So if I want to really plan for a real long term, I want to plan beyond the realm of perishable things and beings. That is what they call it.

You will come to me, Me, the supreme Me, the imperishable. Because there are two existence which we have known through our discussion. One is imperishable, never perishes, never changes, never have any mutation.

And the one which is constantly changing. I clearly identify with the one with changes. Because I identify with this, the body, this mind, this intellect.

I clearly know that this body is perishable. I have learned through my experiences in life, this body is perishable. And also I have observed from My inferred *knowledge* that people die and people bury them or burn them, cremate them, so my body will go through the same fate.

So we have come to the clear understanding that this body is perishable. What we have not yet understood is the mind and intellect. A lot of this research which we hear is all about brain, not the mind.

Talking to psychiatrists, they say we don't understand mind. We don't know how these medications work. We just know that it works and therefore it is good enough to prescribe.

But what mind is is very much a mystery. So it is possible that our ancestors did not know much about the physical senses, but they knew a little more about mind than what we know today. So they have come to the conclusion that this mind and intellect has a life of its own, beyond this body's life.

So Prayana Kale Api -- at the time of the journey, that mind and intellect, remaining intact, is going to make a move. Bhagavan Veda Vyasa here basically reaffirms the basic principles of Hinduism or Vedantic philosophy: this body is the only thing that dies at the time of death. The jiva, the one identified with this limited mind and intellect, remains intact and seeks another state of existence to exhaust the remaining vasanas.

So Bhagavan in verse 5 gives the same answer which he gave as a statement at the end of chapter 7. Antakale Chamameva Smaranam uktvakalevaram yaha prayati samad bhavam yati na asti atra sansayaha. Only thing he does is he gives a guarantee.

Last time he made a statement, this time he gives a guarantee. I'm selling somebody something, but I don't have means to support all my claims about my product. I guarantee you that if it doesn't work, you can return it to me.

I'll return all the money. So guarantee is one way of making the student or the buyer feel more comfortable. He already said, one who knows me in totality will come to me.

So he said, even at the last moment, because we have considered this life to be the only life for me to make any progress. And if I think I wasted most of my life, what am I going to do now? This is more like my music teacher made a statement to me when I went to him when I was in my 40s. Subhas, do you know that I'm 47? He said, "So what? You're not 67 yet." So now if I go to him, he will say, "Subhas, I'm 67." And there's still time.

Even at the time of your death, if you come to realize what is truth, thou shall achieve truth. That's the guarantee. Bhagawan says Antakaale chamame vas maran muktvakale varan.

One who leaves this body at the time of death Antakaala. At the end of this body, he leaves this body. So something is leaving.

Somebody is making a journey. That means the one who is identified with the *ego* has not died yet. That *ego* is making its own journey now.

From this body to somewhere else. From this existence to some other existence. Existence is not questioned.

It is the state of existence which is questioned here. Whether will I remain in the same state of existence that I am? Will I retain my wisdom or will I retain my stupidity is the question. One who even at the last minute recognizes the truth.

He will come to know me. He will come to become one with me. There is no question about it.

So he guarantees that you have plenty of time till you die to churn over this idea of what is truth. Even the last moment, if you have eureka moment that oh that's what it is. Bhagawan says that's good enough.

Will come to recognize me and realize me. But you still have to make a supportive argument, because we are not born into guarantees. That's why we go on social networks and say, "What are the comments other people have made?" You know, Meena and I always struggle about exercise.

So Meena came across something called a seat and cycle. As usual, I said don't worry about it. But once we ordered, we realized there are five more payments to be made.

It was never revealed on that Facebook page -- see, there are five more payments! I said, if you want to go ahead, go. But by the time she had already pressed that button. So then she started reading all the opinions and the comments.

They're all pretty bad. This is not a product for elderly. You can fall down also.

It took me three times it broke down. We said cancel that order as quickly as you can. Because they didn't guarantee anything.

They only offered a free trial for 30 days. Bhagwan gave the guarantee. But realize that you will be looking for some support, watching some comments from other users.

So he makes his supporting argument. Yam yam vapi smaran Bhavam tyajatyante kalevaram tamtam eva Ithi kaunteya sada tad bhava bhavitaha. A statement of fact: whosoever you are thinking of at the time of leaving your body, that and that person alone you shall go to.

Looking at our own context of life -- who do we meet in life? The people whom we think about most. We constantly think about a person. Then we obviously make a plan to meet.

When my mother was alive, I was thinking about her the most. Every two years I was making a plan to go and see her. Now I really have not.

Even though I have my brothers and my nephews and nieces, it's not that much of a pressure on me to go to India anymore. Because I was thinking about my mother all the time. I was feeling guilty that I have left my mother at the age of 17 or 18.

Never went home, never took care of her. So constantly was thinking about her. And therefore my plans will be no other vacation.

Go to India, stay with her for a few days. So Bhagavan said that it is a given: whatever is my constant thought becomes the last thought at the time of my journey. Where will you go for vacation? Not to a place you have never thought about.

The vacation you are planning for the last six months -- you have checked all the brochures, checked out all the prices, checked out all the hotel accommodations available, researched all the places to visit. Then, at the time of your journey to take a vacation -- That's the ticket you buy and that's the place you end up going. Bhagavan says, one who is constantly thinking about me is the only one who will be thinking about me at the time of death to come to me.

Therefore the next verse says, tasmat sarveshu kaleshu -- therefore at all times, mam anusmara, think about me. And then he says, Yudhyacha this half sloka, if misunderstood, can bring down the entire generation.
snippets.reflection:
"Tasmat sarveshu kaleshu mam anusmara yudhya cha"—"Therefore meditate always on Me, and fight." warns that this half-verse, if misunderstood, can bring down an entire generation. The key insight is that Krishna is not asking us to abandon our duties to sit in constant prayer. Rather, He asks us to fight the battle of life while maintaining remembrance of our true nature. This is the integration of action and awareness.

 Today, experiment with this teaching: Choose one routine activity—washing dishes, commuting, exercising—and practice holding a background awareness of your deeper Self while fully engaging in the task. Notice how this dual awareness affects both the quality of your work and your inner state.

 Verse 9 offers a powerful word-picture for meditation on the Supreme: "Kavim Puranam Anusasitaram"—the Omniscient, the Ancient, the Ruler of all; "Anor aniyamsam"—subtler than the subtlest atom; "Aditya varnam tamasa parastat"—brilliant like the sun, beyond all darkness. This is not a form to visualize, but qualities to contemplate. The Supreme is self-effulgent—it does not need anything else to reveal itself, just as your own awareness needs nothing external to be known to you.

 In your meditation this week, rather than trying to picture a form, rest in the quality of awareness itself. Notice that you are aware. That awareness is self-revealing. Can you find where that awareness ends? Can you locate its boundaries? This pathless investigation is the meditation Krishna recommends for those who would attain "the Supreme Purusha, the Resplendent One."
snippets.shortReflection: Pick one mundane task today—dishes, email, commuting. Can you stay fully present in the activity while also aware of the awareness doing it? This split attention is the practice.

snippets.title: Day 109: Reaching the Supreme
snippets.sanskrit:
प्रयाणकाले मनसाऽचलेन भक्त्या युक्तो योगबलेन चैव |
भ्रुवोर्मध्ये प्राणमावेश्य सम्यक् स तं परं पुरुषमुपैति दिव्यम् ||

यदक्षरं वेदविदो वदन्ति विशन्ति यद्यतयो वीतरागाः |
यदिच्छन्तो ब्रह्मचर्यं चरन्ति तत्ते पदं संग्रहेण प्रवक्ष्ये ||

सर्वद्वाराणि संयम्य मनो हृदि निरुध्य च |

snippets.transliteration:
prayāṇa-kāle manasāchalena
bhaktyā yukto yoga-balena chaiva
bhruvor madhye prāṇam āveśhya samyak
sa taṁ paraṁ puruṣham upaiti divyam

yad akṣharaṁ veda-vido vadanti
viśhanti yad yatayo vīta-rāgāḥ
yad ichchhanto brahmacharyaṁ charanti
tat te padaṁ saṅgraheṇa pravakṣhye
