verseTranslations: He who leaves the body with mind unmoved and filled with devotion, by the power of his meditation gathering between his eyebrows his whole vital energy, attains the Supreme.

Now I will speak briefly of the imperishable goal, proclaimed by those versed in the scriptures, which the mystic attains when free from passion, and for which he is content to undergo the vow of continence.
Closing the gates of the body, drawing the forces of his mind into the heart and by the power of meditation concentrating his vital energy in the brain;
snippets.commentary:
As we have seen so far, the first four verses gave us the nature of the Brahman, the immanence and transcendence of *Brahman*, that everything they can think about, Shara and Akshara is all Brahman. It's all his manifestation. And then in the next few verses we have seen that how at the time of death, death of the state of existence, death of this thought, death of ego, how one can recognize that permanence of the self. And last few verses, Bhagawan had been giving us the word picture of that imperishable *Brahman*. So we have seen the Kavim Puranam Anusasitharam that he is omniscient, he is ancient and he is having the lordship over everything.

But that picture also doesn't give us the complete picture. He is minuter than minute. It is not something we can paint a picture in our head or formulate a form in our head. So anything we can formulate a form is not him. It is beyond capacity of our intellect. And Sarvasya Dhaataram Achinte Rupam.

He is a supporter of all and it cannot be thought of. Aditya Varanam tama Sahaprasthat. He is *self* effulgent. It does not require any other means to know him. By its very nature he reveals himself. *Awareness* itself is him.

I need to be aware of an object. For an object to be known, I have to be aware of it. So my *awareness* is necessary to make that object revealed to myself. But my *awareness* itself does not require anything to be known to me. *Awareness* itself makes itself available. So the next few verses talked about the Pryanakala.

We have seen the difference between Antakaala and Pryanakala. Priyanakala is the time of departure. I may be coming back. My departure may be for going now and coming back again. Antikala is the last end of it. I'm not going anywhere.

Once I go there, I'm not coming back. So the one who at the time of departure focus on the nature of the *self*, he will also achieve that realization of the impermanence. So the whole goal we have seen so far is gaining the experience of something which we have not experienced before. We have been striving all our life -- knowingly or unknowingly.

We have been trying to find a state of existence where there is no sorrow, no imperfection, no unhappiness. That state we're constantly struggling to achieve by all the means available to us through our equipment of body, mind, and intellect. We try and employ all three of them to achieve the state of perfection -- where there is no unhappiness, no sorrow, no disease.

And as Bhagavan Buddha found out, there is nothing like that in this world. So there got to be a place or state because otherwise we won't be striving for it. If health is not my nature, I won't be striving for health. I'll be very happy, be unhealthy. But that's not my natural state of my existence. Therefore as soon as something happens, I run to the doctor, fix it.

So unhappiness also cannot be a natural thing to me. However, I'm constantly unhappy. So what should I be doing to achieve that? What we have seen last is Yat Aksaram Veda Vido Vadanti -- that imperishable state which the knowers of the Vedas talk about. There is a state where all that you are seeking is available.

Vishyanti Yat Yoho Vit Ragaha. People give up everything in life to achieve that state. Brahmacharyam Charanti. By desiring that people practice *Brahmacharya*. Last time as we have seen Brahma Acharya Brahmachari. One who is reveling or pursuing the path of *Brahman* is Brahmachari.

One who is following the path of *action* is a Karmachari. In Hindi, as we have discussed last time, the clerks are called Karmacharis. But you know, one who is their boss is called Adyaksha. One who keeps eye on them is Adyaksha. So we are Karmachari in all our day to day life. Because we constantly see what is next.

I have done this, I've been there. Somebody says, "Take a cruise" -- I have done it. Tell me something else which I can do. Because we are constantly asking, what is next, what will be our next *action*? *Brahmacharya* is constantly seeking how to become one with *Brahman* -- that is a Brahmachari. And who is the Adyaksha?

In this case, our *consciousness* is keeping an eye on what's happening. Tatte padam sangrahena pravakshye -- I'm going to tell you about that state of existence which you have been seeking all your life, which you have tried everything to achieve so far but have not attained. I'm going to tell you in a summary.

Now Bhagavan explains how that state can be achieved. So the next verse says sarvadvarani samyamya mano ruddin irudhyyacha murdni adhay atmanah pranam astito yogadharana. This is obviously explaining the technique of meditation. We want to experience that state. I cannot be experiencing in our day to day life, but at least I can have a glimpse in my meditation. In meditation what I get is a glimpse of that state where there is no unhappiness, there is no sorrow.

But that cannot be just 20 minutes a day or 30 minutes a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. It has to be a continuous state of existence. I am not seeking temporary happiness; I'm seeking permanent happiness. It says Sarva dwarani samyamya. So far, everything that has caused me unhappiness is because of my sense perception. When I see that the temperature outside is not conducive to my liking, because I feel it, then I feel unhappy.

So senses are telling me whether it's conducive or not. If that information is not available to me, then I will not know. Just as in my deep sleep, I'm not aware what temperature the room is, whether Donald Trump is winning or Hillary Clinton is ahead. None of that exists in my deep sleep. So the first thing we notice is that these senses are causing agitation in my mind. Sarva dwarani samyamya -- let's experience what happens when I close all the gates of information.

You know, people who take retreats these days -- it's very difficult to take a true retreat. Ten or twenty years ago when we used to take retreats, they would say, you can't take a radio with you, you cannot take anything with you. Don't listen to radio, don't listen to television. But now people take their phone -- and everything, television included, is on your phone. The idea of a retreat was that you are constantly bombarded with information which distracts you, so at least for that week,

You are cut off from the world outside. What's happening politically, what's happening in a profession, all that you're not listening. So this takes that idea to an extreme and say close all your senses when you sit down in meditation. Sarva dwarani Samyami. Controlling all your gates. Manohrudi Nirudhyacha.

Placing your mind in your heart. In a sense, placing your mind -- which was running outside in day-to-day life -- inward. The mind's job is to go outside and get information, like the clerk who is gathering all the data from outside and reporting it to the intellect, the adyaksha, to decipher the data. Now, make that mind turn inward.

Hriddi means inward -- basically, focus on yourself. Your thoughts should be one and one alone: What is my real *self*? That's the thought, one single thought. Murdni Adhaya Atmanah -- having your pranas in your head. Now this looks like very high-level yogic exercise.

Now it can be but you can look at it in many different ways. At our level, this is a technique of a meditation when at least for those 20 minutes you're trying to cut off yourself from this world. You cut off yourself from your senses, cut off all your mind from running out and turn inward. Then say Murdni a day *atman*. Focus all your pranas into your head. Now sit down for meditation.

See where you feel any life. At that time, all your focus will be on your head. Therefore in the technical meditation chapter six we said focus your mind between your two eyebrows. Because you're not aware of rest of the body, you're dropping all your *awareness* about the rest of your body. You're focusing only the one thing, one thing alone. Your computer which is functioning at that time in your head.

They said, placing your pranas -- all the physiological activities happening in your body -- you're only aware of what's happening in your mind, at the head, at that time. Therefore pranayama helps, because first you focus on the breathing. Right now I'm focusing on everything that is happening in my body: my legs are moving, my hands are moving, my lips are moving. When doing meditation you stop thinking about your legs and hands and mouth and you only start thinking about what's happening in your mind. So when you first start focusing only on your breath, you are not focusing on anything else which is going on in your body. That puts you in a state where mind will calm down. And then you can just focus on who I am.

So only one thought and one thought alone. Pranam astitha Yogadharanam. One who has been practicing this over and over and over again can achieve the state of meditation very easily. And the next verse says Omiti ek aksaram Brahma -- this is truly a technique of meditation we have learned in chapter six. He's putting it again in a very succinct manner for you to understand.

What is the goal of meditation? The goal of meditation is to give us a glimpse of that state where there is no limitation, no unhappiness, no sorrow -- just bliss. So once you have now controlled your senses and your mind and your pranas: Omiti ek aksaram Brahma vyaharan mam anusmaran -- chant the one syllable Om, which is the sound symbol of God. God can be pictured in many different ways, but the simplest and most non-distracting form is the word Om. And we have seen before --

The Om represents the creation, sustenance and destruction or the past, present and future. But that one word contains everything that needs to be known about the *self*. So Vyaharan Mam Anusmaran -- while uttering that one syllable Om, remember Me. Don't just get focused on the sound alone. I'm thinking about that *self* which is all-pervading, and the Om is representing it.

First you can start chanting out loud, then gradually lower your pitch, and then just chant in your mind -- constantly thinking about that one *self* and that one *self* alone, which pervades everywhere -- while chanting Aum. Yah prayati tyajan Deham -- one who leaves this body, you can consider that as your death. That is the time of death. All this which we have learned in these last two verses, we all have known. Looking at people who have died in front of your eyes, it is not possible to meditate at the time of death. You are not there to meditate.

You have no control over what's happening. So this verse is actually about the death in your meditation -- the death of your identification with your body, mind and intellect. Yaha prayati tyajan Deham. The complete *detachment* from the identification with this body. In my meditation Sa yati paramam gatima he experiences that supreme state of existence.

If you perfect your meditation to a point that I can Control all my senses.
snippets.reflection:
These verses reveal a practical meditation technique: "Sarva dvarani samyamya"—close all the gates of the senses; "Mano hridi nirudhya"—draw the mind inward to the heart; "Murdhni adhaya atmanah pranam"—focus the vital energy in the head. This is not esoteric instruction reserved for advanced yogis—it describes what happens naturally when we truly withdraw attention from external stimulation. Consider how retreats work: by removing radio, television, and now phones, we close the gates of information that constantly agitate the mind. This week, create a mini-retreat for yourself. Set aside 20 minutes where you consciously close all "gates"—no phone, no conversation, no reading. Notice how when external input stops, awareness naturally turns inward and begins to settle in the "heart"—the center of your being.

The teaching about focusing pranas in the head during meditation has a practical interpretation for daily practice. When you sit for meditation, begin by noticing where you feel "alive" in your body—this is prana. Through breath awareness, gradually let go of awareness of your limbs, your torso, and gather your sense of aliveness into your head, particularly between your eyebrows. This is not about straining; it is about selective attention. Just as you can choose to feel the sensation in your left thumb right now, you can choose to center your awareness. The goal, as verse 11 states, is to glimpse "that imperishable state which the knowers of the Vedas speak of"—a state without limitation, without sorrow, of pure bliss. Your 20-minute meditation becomes a dress rehearsal for the ultimate letting go. What are you practicing? What are you becoming skilled at releasing?
snippets.shortReflection: Set a timer for 20 minutes. Turn off everything. No phone, no music, no task. Just sit with yourself. If this feels unbearable, you've found exactly where the work needs to happen.

snippets.title: Day 110: The Sacred Syllable Om
snippets.sanskrit:
ओमित्येकाक्षरं ब्रह्म व्याहरन्मामनुस्मरन् |
यः प्रयाति त्यजन्देहं स याति परमां गतिम् ||

अनन्यचेताः सततं यो मां स्मरति नित्यशः |
तस्याहं सुलभः पार्थ नित्ययुक्तस्य योगिनः ||

मामुपेत्य पुनर्जन्म दुःखालयमशाश्वतम् |
नाप्नुवन्ति महात्मानः संसिद्धिं परमां गताः ||
snippets.transliteration:
oṁ ityekākṣharaṁ brahma vyāharan mām anusmaran
yaḥ prayāti tyajan dehaṁ sa yāti paramāṁ gatim

ananya-chetāḥ satataṁ yo māṁ smarati nityaśhaḥ
tasyāhaṁ sulabhaḥ pārtha nitya-yuktasya yoginaḥ

mām upetya punar janma duḥkhālayam aśhāśhvatam
nāpnuvanti mahātmānaḥ sansiddhiṁ paramāṁ gatāḥ
verseTranslations: Repeating Om, the Symbol of Eternity, holding Me always in remembrance, he who thus leaves his body and goes forth reaches the Spirit Supreme.
To him who thinks constantly of Me, and of nothing else, to such an ever-faithful devotee, O Arjuna, am I ever accessible.
Coming thus unto Me, these great souls go no more to the misery and death of earthly life, for they have gained perfection.
snippets.commentary:
As we have seen so far, the first four verses gave us the nature of the Brahman, the immanence and transcendence of *Brahman*, that everything they can think about, Shara and Akshara is all Brahman. It's all his manifestation. And then in the next few verses we have seen that how at the time of death, death of the state of existence, death of this thought, death of ego, how one can recognize that permanence of the self. And last few verses, Bhagawan had been giving us the word picture of that imperishable *Brahman*. So we have seen the Kavim Puranam Anusasitharam that he is omniscient, he is ancient and he is having the lordship over everything.

But that picture also doesn't give us the complete picture. He is minuter than minute. It is not something we can paint a picture in our head or formulate a form in our head. So anything we can formulate a form is not him. It is beyond capacity of our intellect. And Sarvasya Dhaataram Achinte Rupam.

He is a supporter of all and it cannot be thought of. Aditya Varanam tama Sahaprasthat. He is *self* effulgent. It does not require any other means to know him. By its very nature he reveals himself. *Awareness* itself is him.

I need to be aware of an object. For an object to be known, I have to be aware of it. So my *awareness* is necessary to make that object revealed to myself. But my *awareness* itself does not require anything to be known to me. *Awareness* itself makes itself available. So the next few verses talked about the Pryanakala.

We have seen the difference between Antakaala and Pryanakala. Priyanakala is the time of departure. I may be coming back. My departure may be for going now and coming back again. Antikala is the last end of it. I'm not going anywhere.

Once I go there, I'm not coming back. So the one who at the time of departure focus on the nature of the *self*, he will also achieve that realization of the impermanence. So the whole goal we have seen so far is gaining the experience of something which we have not experienced before. We have been striving all our life -- knowingly or unknowingly.

We have been trying to find a state of existence where there is no sorrow, no imperfection, no unhappiness. That state we're constantly struggling to achieve by all the means available to us through our equipment of body, mind, and intellect. We try and employ all three of them to achieve the state of perfection -- where there is no unhappiness, no sorrow, no disease.

And as Bhagavan Buddha found out, there is nothing like that in this world. So there got to be a place or state because otherwise we won't be striving for it. If health is not my nature, I won't be striving for health. I'll be very happy, be unhealthy. But that's not my natural state of my existence. Therefore as soon as something happens, I run to the doctor, fix it.

So unhappiness also cannot be a natural thing to me. However, I'm constantly unhappy. So what should I be doing to achieve that? What we have seen last is Yat Aksaram Veda Vido Vadanti -- that imperishable state which the knowers of the Vedas talk about. There is a state where all that you are seeking is available.

Vishyanti Yat Yoho Vit Ragaha. People give up everything in life to achieve that state. Brahmacharyam Charanti. By desiring that people practice *Brahmacharya*. Last time as we have seen Brahma Acharya Brahmachari. One who is reveling or pursuing the path of *Brahman* is Brahmachari.

One who is following the path of *action* is a Karmachari. In Hindi, as we have discussed last time, the clerks are called Karmacharis. But you know, one who is their boss is called Adyaksha. One who keeps eye on them is Adyaksha. So we are Karmachari in all our day to day life. Because we constantly see what is next.

I have done this, I've been there. Somebody says, "Take a cruise" -- I have done it. Tell me something else which I can do. Because we are constantly asking, what is next, what will be our next *action*? *Brahmacharya* is constantly seeking how to become one with *Brahman* -- that is a Brahmachari. And who is the Adyaksha?

In this case, our *consciousness* is keeping an eye on what's happening. Tatte padam sangrahena pravakshye -- I'm going to tell you about that state of existence which you have been seeking all your life, which you have tried everything to achieve so far but have not attained. I'm going to tell you in a summary.

Now Bhagavan explains how that state can be achieved. So the next verse says sarvadvarani samyamya mano ruddin irudhyyacha murdni adhay atmanah pranam astito yogadharana. This is obviously explaining the technique of meditation. We want to experience that state. I cannot be experiencing in our day to day life, but at least I can have a glimpse in my meditation. In meditation what I get is a glimpse of that state where there is no unhappiness, there is no sorrow.

But that cannot be just 20 minutes a day or 30 minutes a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. It has to be a continuous state of existence. I am not seeking temporary happiness; I'm seeking permanent happiness. It says Sarva dwarani samyamya. So far, everything that has caused me unhappiness is because of my sense perception. When I see that the temperature outside is not conducive to my liking, because I feel it, then I feel unhappy.

So senses are telling me whether it's conducive or not. If that information is not available to me, then I will not know. Just as in my deep sleep, I'm not aware what temperature the room is, whether Donald Trump is winning or Hillary Clinton is ahead. None of that exists in my deep sleep. So the first thing we notice is that these senses are causing agitation in my mind. Sarva dwarani samyamya -- let's experience what happens when I close all the gates of information.

You know, people who take retreats these days -- it's very difficult to take a true retreat. Ten or twenty years ago when we used to take retreats, they would say, you can't take a radio with you, you cannot take anything with you. Don't listen to radio, don't listen to television. But now people take their phone -- and everything, television included, is on your phone. The idea of a retreat was that you are constantly bombarded with information which distracts you, so at least for that week,

You are cut off from the world outside. What's happening politically, what's happening in a profession, all that you're not listening. So this takes that idea to an extreme and say close all your senses when you sit down in meditation. Sarva dwarani Samyami. Controlling all your gates. Manohrudi Nirudhyacha.

Placing your mind in your heart. In a sense, placing your mind -- which was running outside in day-to-day life -- inward. The mind's job is to go outside and get information, like the clerk who is gathering all the data from outside and reporting it to the intellect, the adyaksha, to decipher the data. Now, make that mind turn inward.

Hriddi means inward -- basically, focus on yourself. Your thoughts should be one and one alone: What is my real *self*? That's the thought, one single thought. Murdni Adhaya Atmanah -- having your pranas in your head. Now this looks like very high-level yogic exercise.

Now it can be but you can look at it in many different ways. At our level, this is a technique of a meditation when at least for those 20 minutes you're trying to cut off yourself from this world. You cut off yourself from your senses, cut off all your mind from running out and turn inward. Then say Murdni a day *atman*. Focus all your pranas into your head. Now sit down for meditation.

See where you feel any life. At that time, all your focus will be on your head. Therefore in the technical meditation chapter six we said focus your mind between your two eyebrows. Because you're not aware of rest of the body, you're dropping all your *awareness* about the rest of your body. You're focusing only the one thing, one thing alone. Your computer which is functioning at that time in your head.

They said, placing your pranas -- all the physiological activities happening in your body -- you're only aware of what's happening in your mind, at the head, at that time. Therefore pranayama helps, because first you focus on the breathing. Right now I'm focusing on everything that is happening in my body: my legs are moving, my hands are moving, my lips are moving. When doing meditation you stop thinking about your legs and hands and mouth and you only start thinking about what's happening in your mind. So when you first start focusing only on your breath, you are not focusing on anything else which is going on in your body. That puts you in a state where mind will calm down. And then you can just focus on who I am.

So only one thought and one thought alone. Pranam astitha Yogadharanam. One who has been practicing this over and over and over again can achieve the state of meditation very easily. And the next verse says Omiti ek aksaram Brahma -- this is truly a technique of meditation we have learned in chapter six. He's putting it again in a very succinct manner for you to understand.

What is the goal of meditation? The goal of meditation is to give us a glimpse of that state where there is no limitation, no unhappiness, no sorrow -- just bliss. So once you have now controlled your senses and your mind and your pranas: Omiti ek aksaram Brahma vyaharan mam anusmaran -- chant the one syllable Om, which is the sound symbol of God. God can be pictured in many different ways, but the simplest and most non-distracting form is the word Om. And we have seen before --

The Om represents the creation, sustenance and destruction or the past, present and future. But that one word contains everything that needs to be known about the *self*. So Vyaharan Mam Anusmaran -- while uttering that one syllable Om, remember Me. Don't just get focused on the sound alone. I'm thinking about that *self* which is all-pervading, and the Om is representing it.

First you can start chanting out loud, then gradually lower your pitch, and then just chant in your mind -- constantly thinking about that one *self* and that one *self* alone, which pervades everywhere -- while chanting Aum. Yah prayati tyajan Deham -- one who leaves this body, you can consider that as your death. That is the time of death. All this which we have learned in these last two verses, we all have known. Looking at people who have died in front of your eyes, it is not possible to meditate at the time of death. You are not there to meditate.

You have no control over what's happening. So this verse is actually about the death in your meditation -- the death of your identification with your body, mind and intellect. Yaha prayati tyajan Deham. The complete *detachment* from the identification with this body. In my meditation Sa yati paramam gatima he experiences that supreme state of existence.

If you perfect your meditation to a point that I can Control all my senses.
snippets.reflection:
"Om iti ekaksharam Brahma"—Om, the single syllable, is Brahman. This verse introduces the most practical tool for meditation: the sacred syllable Om. Unlike complex visualizations or elaborate rituals, Om is simple, portable, and universally accessible. It represents all of creation, sustenance, and dissolution—past, present, and future—compressed into one sound. This week, practice the progression described: begin chanting Om aloud, then gradually soften it to a whisper, then to a mental repetition, then let even that dissolve into silent awareness. Notice how the sound carries your attention inward naturally. The instruction "Mam anusmaran"—"remembering Me"—reminds us that Om is not just a sound to repeat mechanically, but a symbol pointing to the all-pervading Self.

Verse 14 offers an extraordinary promise: "Ananya chetah satatam yo mam smarati nityashah, tasya aham sulabhah"—"To one who thinks of Me constantly with undivided mind, I am easy to attain." The word "sulabhah" (easy to attain) is striking. Usually we think of God-realization as the most difficult achievement. Krishna reverses this: for the devoted practitioner with one-pointed focus, it is natural and easy. The difficulty lies only in our divided attention. Examine your attention today: How many competing loyalties divide your mind? How many contradictory desires pull you in different directions? Verse 15 reveals the ultimate result: those who reach the Supreme "go no more to the misery and death of earthly life." This is not about escaping the world, but about completing the curriculum. Once perfection is gained, there is no need to return to the school of suffering. What would it mean to approach each day as if you were completing your final semester?
snippets.shortReflection: Try this: do something kind that no one will ever know about. Not your partner, not your journal, no one. Notice how differently your mind responds when there's zero possibility of recognition.

snippets.title: Day 111: The Imperishable Substratum
snippets.sanskrit:
आब्रह्मभुवनाल्लोकाः पुनरावर्तिनोऽर्जुन |
मामुपेत्य तु कौन्तेय पुनर्जन्म न विद्यते ||

सहस्रयुगपर्यन्तमहर्यद्ब्रह्मणो विदुः |
रात्रिं युगसहस्रान्तां तेऽहोरात्रविदो जनाः ||

अव्यक्ताद्व्यक्तयः सर्वाः प्रभवन्त्यहरागमे |
रात्र्यागमे प्रलीयन्ते तत्रैवाव्यक्तसंज्ञके ||
snippets.transliteration:
ā-brahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar āvartino ’rjuna
mām upetya tu kaunteya punar janma na vidyate

sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ
rātriṁ yuga-sahasrāntāṁ te ’ho-rātra-vido janāḥ

avyaktād vyaktayaḥ sarvāḥ prabhavantyahar-āgame
rātryāgame pralīyante tatraivāvyakta-sanjñake
verseTranslations: The worlds, with the whole realm of creation, come and go; but, O Arjuna, whoso comes to Me, for him there is no rebirth.
Those who understand the cosmic day and cosmic night know that one day of creation is a thousand cycles, and that the night is of equal length.
At the dawning of that day all objects in manifestation stream forth from the Unmanifest, and when evening falls they are dissolved into It again.
snippets.commentary:
Things have their production date or date of creation and will also have a date of destruction. Beings have their birth dates and will also have their death dates.

Nothing in this world remains permanently. Everything is perishable, exists for a limited period in both time and space. But this ever changing reality which I experience as the world cannot exist unless there is an imperishable substratum.

And Bhagavan said in this chapter that *Brahman* is that imperishable reality. *Brahman* is the truth which makes all other relative truths possible. For example, I can say this room exists. That's a statement of truth.

But it only exists because the another universal truth exists. That is the room space existed before this room was built. It is right now here as room space and will remain space when this room will be destroyed.

So based on that universal reality which I call space, the relative reality, what I call room space can exist. Bhagavan says the *Brahman* in a similar way exists. As Bhagawan Shankaracharya says, the principle that graces all bodies is their essential self.

Any being will not be aware of his own *self* unless that principle, imperishable immortal principle is residing in that body. With that *consciousness* I become aware of my conditioning which I call my body, mind and intellect. And then I'm aware of myself.

So it is the *self-knowing* reality -- the very nature of Brahman -- which makes me aware of myself as that conditioned *self*. Right now I'm not aware of my supreme self that is imperishable, deathless, and birthless. But I'm aware of myself as this limited body, limited mind, limited intellect -- as Nil Bhatt -- because of that *consciousness* which is functioning through me.

So Bhagavan says that that *consciousness* is now making you aware of your own limitations and also making you aware of the existence of this world of perishable nature. As long as I am conditioned and identified with this body, mind, and intellect, I will have all the limitations of this body, mind, and intellect. And therefore the sorrows, therefore unhappiness.

And therefore I feel bound by these limitations. My goal is to liberate myself from my limitations, my unhappiness, my sorrows and attain a state of bliss where there never will be any sorrow, never will be any limitations and never will be any unhappiness. Bhagavan said, that can only happen when you identify with me, the imperishable, and not with the one who is conditioned by your body, mind, and intellect.

As long as I remain aware of the limitations of the room, I will only be seeing the space as room space. But if I want to see this space as immortal -- If I never want to get this space destroyed, I'll be always afraid of what happens if someone destroys this building. If earthquake happens or a meteor falls on my property, well, it will be destroyed.

Is the room space getting destroyed? But right now I'm more identified with the conditioning than the space itself. And therefore that fear of destruction. If my identification was not with the conditioning, just the space.

This is my land and this is my space, and I want to own this thing forever. But here's the thing: nothing can destroy the space itself. The only thing that can be destroyed is whatever you have built on that land.

The space will never be destroyed. But as long as my identification is with that building on that land, I'll be afraid. When my identification goes beyond that, then I will not be afraid of the destruction of the building.

So Bhagavan said, one who identifies with me will come to attain me. Antakale cha mam eva kalevaram ya prayati sa mad bhavam yati na asti atra sansayah. There is no doubt that one who gives up this identification with body, mind, and intellect -- treating the leaving of this identification as the death -- and thinking about me alone, will come to me.

There is no doubt about that. So the advice we have seen so far says: therefore, tasmat sarveshu kaleshu mam anusmara yudhya cha -- engage in this battle of life constantly remembering me as your true *self*. Not this conditioned *self* as your true *self*, but me, the imperishable, who is making it possible for you to function.

Fight this battle of life with that in mind, and you shall be liberated from these limitations. You will come to be one with me, and once you become one with me, after that there is no coming and going again. Mam upetya punar janma dukhalayam ashashvatam na apnuvanti.

Having attained me, there is no coming and going back to this house of pain we call this world. But now Bhagavan says, in a stark contrast to the ones who have identified with me and one who has become one with me. If you're striving to achieve that *liberation* but haven't reached that prerequisite qualification, then you will constantly come back and forth.

So the next verse 16 says, A Brahma Bhuvanat lokah punaravartino Arjuna Mam upetya tu Kaunteya punarjanma na vidyate -- all the worlds up to the world of Brahmaji, Brahmaloka, are subject to birth and rebirth. Punara vartina -- constantly coming again and again, coming back to the same cycle. One who reaches me, there is no rebirth for him.

So what does that mean, reaching up to the world of Brahmaji? Brahmaji is the creator. As we know in our Hindu Trinity, Brahma is the creator, Vishnu is the sustainer and Shiva is the destroyer. This creation, sustenance, and destruction is constantly going on in this world.

Brahma is the ultimate creator of this entire universe. In our concept of Hiranyagarbha in Vedanta, Brahma represents the ultimate creator -- the total mind and total intellect. I am the creator of my own world.

You are the creator of your world, and she is the creator of her world. We create our world through our mind and intellect, depending on our desires and vasanas. Now, if I take this group and look at it as one -- individually we have our vasanas and desires, but we also have group vasanas and desires.

So we'll say, well, when are we going to have the Janmastami next? So everybody will say, well, I would like to have it on such and such and let's do this and let's do that. These common thoughts put together what we call it a planning, a group planning will have group activity. So that's a mind which is expanded from my mind to a group's mind.

You can continue to expand this mind and intellect, including more and more people and beings into it. When you reach the ultimate limit of all the beings and things, all the minds and intellects put together -- that is Brahmaji, Brahma the creator. When my identification rises from me to my family, to my neighborhood, to my community, I'm expanding my identity and including them as my own *self*.

So I may be making progress in my spiritual evolution by expanding my identity, but until I reach that pre-qualifying limit, I still have to come back over and over again. Well, it is something like this. If you are taking any licensing examination -- for those of you who are professionals who have to take the licensing exam, you probably know all about it.

I took mine in this country when I came here in 1984, and I knew that it was going to be difficult because I had barely come here, had no experience in this country, and people had already warned me: it's going to take you a long time to get this license, simply because there were nine parts to the exam and you have to clear all nine parts to get a license. So the firm I had joined initially a large firm, and there were at least about a couple of hundred people, at least at any given year, there are about 60 to 80 people taking exams. So they told me, "Take it easy, Rajan.

You just came to this country; it's going to take you eight to ten years before you can pass this exam." And I said, "What do you mean by that? I don't understand what you're saying. Why should it take so long?" They said, "Well, here is how it works." "You'll take the exams and probably pass maybe two parts out of nine. Then you will come back next year and may pass another couple of parts, then come back the year after and may pass one or two." People who experienced this had formulated an average: it takes about six to ten years for somebody to get licensed as an architect in this country after graduating from architecture school.

Because until you pass all nine parts -- and if you fail any one subject more than three times, you take all nine parts all over again. There were some people I knew who had already given up taking these licensing exams. I said, "Well, all you have to do is pass all nine parts and it will be fine." They said, "Yeah, that sounds easy, but it is not." That was obviously their perception.

So they go, take the exam, come back, take the exam and come back -- till you reach a point when the ninth part is cleared, then you get a license. And even after passing all nine parts and getting a license, you still have to maintain your continuing education to remain effective as an architect. This is something like our spiritual journey.

Bhagavan said that we are all pursuing our spiritual evolution as seekers, reaching from the level we are at right now to the next level as we make more progress. But at the time of death, if my evolution has not risen to the level where I can be liberated, I'll have to come back -- just as with the exams. If I haven't cleared all nine parts, I have to come back next year to clear whatever parts are left.

Same way, in our spiritual journey, things we have learned and things yet to be learned will decide how many times I have to come back. This is driven by my desires and vasanas. My desires will make me come back to that state, that stage where I feel comfortable that I can make progress from here.

After I pass my high school graduation, I go to undergraduate school. I cannot just say, "After my high school graduation, leave me alone -- my education is finished." To get to a doctorate level, I have to make my own efforts. So up to the world of Brahmaji.

In the world of Brahmaji, you have the identification with this entire creation. And in the concept of gradual *liberation*, Karma Mukti, which is accepted in Vedanta, it basically says that *karma* with Upasana can lead you to the realm of Brahmaji. If you do your karma diligently with *devotion* to the Lord, you will reach a state of identification where you will feel the whole world is your own being and you reach the world of Brahmaji.

Once reaching that, there is no coming back. From that, you will just merge into the supreme *Brahman*.
snippets.reflection:
"A Brahma bhuvana lokah punar avartino Arjuna"—even up to the world of Brahma, all realms are subject to return. This teaching shatters any notion of a permanent heavenly destination short of complete liberation. The analogy of professional licensing examinations is illuminating: just as you must pass all nine parts to become a licensed architect, you must complete your entire spiritual curriculum to achieve liberation. Failing any part means returning to retake it. Consider your own spiritual "exam results": What subjects have you mastered? What areas still need work? Patience, forgiveness, non-attachment, selfless service—which of these do you still struggle with? Each challenge in life is an examination. Each failure is simply an invitation to return and try again until mastery is achieved.

The cosmic scale presented here—one day of Brahma equals a thousand yugas, approximately 4.32 billion years—puts our earthly concerns in perspective. Your current frustrations, achievements, and dramas are occurring within a cosmic blink. Verse 18 describes how all beings stream forth at the dawn of Brahma's day and dissolve back into the unmanifest at cosmic night. Your individual existence is part of this vast breathing rhythm of the universe. This week, practice holding this expanded perspective when you encounter stress or conflict. Ask yourself: "In the scale of Brahma's day, how significant is this problem?" This is not to dismiss your real concerns, but to loosen the grip of identification. The teaching points to the one place beyond this cosmic rhythm: "Mam upetya tu Kaunteya punar janma na vidyate"—reaching Me, there is no rebirth. What would it mean to identify with the eternal witness of this cosmic dance rather than being swept along as a participant?
snippets.shortReflection: Name one habit you've fully mastered—maybe patience with your kids, or staying calm in traffic. Now name one you're still failing at repeatedly. That unmastered lesson is why you're still here, in class.

snippets.title: Day 112: Creation and Dissolution
snippets.sanskrit:
भूतग्रामः स एवायं भूत्वा भूत्वा प्रलीयते |
रात्र्यागमेऽवशः पार्थ प्रभवत्यहरागमे ||

परस्तस्मात्तु भावोऽन्योऽव्यक्तोऽव्यक्तात्सनातनः |
यः स सर्वेषु भूतेषु नश्यत्सु न विनश्यति ||

अव्यक्तोऽक्षर इत्युक्तस्तमाहुः परमां गतिम् |
यं प्राप्य न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम ||
snippets.transliteration:
bhūta-grāmaḥ sa evāyaṁ bhūtvā bhūtvā pralīyate
rātryāgame ’vaśhaḥ pārtha prabhavatyahar-āgame

paras tasmāt tu bhāvo ’nyo ’vyakto ’vyaktāt sanātanaḥ
yaḥ sa sarveṣhu bhūteṣhu naśhyatsu na vinaśhyati

avyakto ’kṣhara ityuktas tam āhuḥ paramāṁ gatim
yaṁ prāpya na nivartante tad dhāma paramaṁ mama
verseTranslations: The same multitude of beings, which have lived on earth so often, all are dissolved as the night of the universe approaches, to issue forth anew when morning breaks. Thus is it ordained.
In truth, therefore, there is the Eternal Unmanifest, which is beyond and above the Unmanifest Spirit of Creation, which is never destroyed when all these beings perish.
The wise say that the Unmanifest and Indestructible is the highest goal of all; when once That is reached, there is no return. That is My Blessed Home.
snippets.commentary:
In the beginning, we heard from Bhagavan that Brahman is imperishable, immutable, and *self-knowledge* is its nature. What is the nature of Brahman? It is self-knowledge. It does not require any other aid to understand it. It is *self-effulgent*.

It's very nature is *self* knowledge. With its creative force, it works to create things and beings. What his work is that which creates these things and beings. That Brahman which is imperishable, its nature is *self* knowledge. With its own creative force, it works to create things and beings. Then what is nature of the things and beings that *Brahman* has created?

*Brahman* is imperishable, but anything that is created by its creative force is perishable. That because the very act of creation gives it a birth date, it's now created. Something is created, therefore it will have its own life. Then it will get destroyed. It will have a limited shelf life as we call it, no matter how long. That is what makes those things and beings function as they are.

The Daivam is that same *Brahman* remaining within each created entity -- that Daivam makes the thing or being possible as a creation. And when these things and beings are reacting with each other, it's only possible because *Brahman* remains present as the Yajnam in all the activities -- that Supreme Being is present in every *action*. Therefore all activities are possible in this world of created beings. The analogy we have heard before is like my dream. I as the conscious being have experiences in my waking world.

The same experiences at night gets all jumbled up. My mind creates its own world. Out of my own mind, I create my own world. That mind by itself creates various entities, things and beings in My dream. Those entities are acting in the dream because I am in and through available to project the dream. But when I wake up, all those entities, things and beings are now unmanifest.

Till next time I go to sleep again and dream again. So this is what we have seen is how the overall cosmos is functioning at the level of *Brahman*. Him remaining supreme, unchangeable with his self knowledge, with his own creative force, he works to create these things and beings. These things and beings, their Gunana *Dharma*. I studied chemistry in Gujarati -- because I studied all throughout my school days and college days in Gujarati medium. In chemistry they used to ask us, "Padarthana Gunadharmanu Varnan karo" -- describe the characteristics and nature of this substance. So there are two things every substance has: Guna and *Dharma*.

*Guna* is the basic characteristics of that substance or a thing or a being. And Dharma is the nature of that substance depending on guna. So what is my Dharma is depending on my gunas. The *gunas* which I have as an entity creates my Dharma. So Guna and Dharma are related to each other. So *Brahman* creating things and beings.

Each thing and being has its own *Dharma*, Guna and Dharma. This Guna and *Dharma* continues to change as we acquire more impressions. So my guna before I went to architecture school has nothing to do with architecture. In fact, I was not even aware of what architecture is all about. So at that point my Dharma had nothing to do with architectural knowledge or practice. More I acquired the architectural *knowledge*.

My *gunas* changed, so my Dharma changed. So now I practice architecture. So Guna *Dharma* is constantly changing this evolutionary path a thing or being takes in the creation itself. So Bhagavan said that this creation is now guided by its own laws, where each thing and being is driven by their own Guna and Dharma. What will be my next state of existence? It depends on the *gunas* which I am creating through my experiences -- as a practicing architect or as a Bhagavad Gita student.

So my next state of existence can only be evolution from a present state. It cannot completely change overnight from where I am today. So that's the evolutionary path each thing and being in the creation takes. So from some stardust, my original evolution started and then that keeps changing. Gunanayana *Dharma* came to this level where I am today. I read in some one of these popular science books that our atoms in the body continues to change.

They are not the same atoms, because our body's cells change every few years. And they said it is possible that the atoms which existed in Shakespeare's body or Rama's body or Krishna's body have passed through my body at one point -- because there is a finite amount of energy, a finite amount of matter, and all things and beings are created out of that. The nature of this cosmos is that one thing changes into the shape and form of another and continues.

So where I am today is the product of my past -- from that stardust to who I am today. My future would be the product of my present plus my past. The advice then given to us is this: if you want to accelerate this evolution and not go through this gradual path of changing *Guna* and *Dharma*, you can directly relate to the Source. We have seen that *Brahman* is imperishable, immutable, and created this universe out of his own creative force as the efficient cause.

Material cause was the only thing available to *Brahman*, which is his own self. He created this universe out of his own *self*. And each creation has limited life. Creation remains perishable, but the underlying material which creates this universe remains imperishable. So either I can identify with my Guna and a *Dharma* today and then take a step next forward in the same path of my evolution, or I can short circuit this whole cycle and go straight to my source where I started. So that's the advice in this chapter.

At the time of death -- death is the end of this state of existence. The death of today will create tomorrow. At the time of this transition, whatever I think would be my next state of existence, that's what I will become. Bhagawan said, you can focus directly on the Source and become the Source. Up to Brahma Loka, the world of Brahma, everything has coming and going. As long as we are within the realm of this *Prakriti* -- which is made up of nothing but the total things and beings in this world -- I will keep recycling from one state of existence to another.

And we have said how long this will continue -- as long as Brahma is creating and dissolving. We see our own day and night in our day-to-day activities. Day is the active part of my life. Night is the inactive part of my life. Superimposing the same concept on Brahmaji, the total creator:

I am the creator of my world. You are the creator of your world. She is the creator of her world. When you put all things and beings together, all the ideas and vasanas and thoughts together create cosmic mind. The cosmic mind has the latency to create this cosmos. And that's called Hiranyagarpa, the golden embryo, which is all the possibilities of creating everything that is in this cosmos that continues to be go in the cycles of activity and inactivity.

When Brahma is actively creating, it's his day. When he takes rest and is inactive, it's night for him. We superimpose our experience: my day is activity, my night is inactivity. It's not so different now with nightlife, but 5,000 years ago they probably didn't have nightlife. So what is Brahma's day? Brahma's day is a thousand eons. So for thousand eons this activity of creation continues. Things changing from one thing to another to another. And then Brahmaji takes rest. All the things which he has created now goes into dormant state. Not destroyed, but in a dormant state.

Just as I, the architect, goes into dormant state from Friday to Sunday. But that doesn't mean the architect in me has died. Architect in me will wake up on Monday morning and start all over again. So all the ideas and thoughts and vasanas in this total mind go into hibernation, into a dormant state. How long does that last? Another thousand eons.

So we did some calculation the other day: 4.32 billion years is one day. A thousand of these makes 4.32 billion years, and you take two of them -- day and night -- that's 8.6-something billion years, one complete cycle. So when you think about your journey, this is what continues from day to night, day and night, from one state of existence to another. And if you as the entity are not really happy about it, then there is an escape hatch: take refuge in me, identify with the Source.

As long as I'm watching David Copperfield performing magic, it's wonderful to watch and get enchanted by it and then keep thinking, how does he do it? Till one day I show up when he is preparing for his show and say, I want to be your apprentice, sir. And he takes me and then he shows me and then I see how all these tricks are done and then all magic is gone. Now I'm not confused. Now when he's cutting the lady in half, I know exactly what he's doing. Till that time, I have to keep coming back. Till I reach Brahma Loka, the Creator's own world, I will be coming back into the same cycle. But then when I reach there and identify with the source, I will become one with that. So it gives us a scale. My quest in life to achieve happiness is not a short-term thing, even though I put it in short-term goals and long-term goals. But in the end I want happiness. If you just extend that quest to Brahma's day and night and work towards your goal, the only way to achieve that is to identify with the source. Avyakta d vyaktayaha Sarvaha prabhavanti aha Agame. So all those things in beings with all their *guna* and *Dharma* are in dormant state. When Brahmaj is inactive, which we consider as a dissolution. Pralaya, Vishnu, lying in a Kshira, Shira, Samudra, milky ocean.

There are no vasanas, pure *Sattva*, then there is no activity. If it is pure Sattva, there is no activity. *Rajas* and Tamas has to be there. So when you are in a pure state of *Sattva*, there is no activity. But all other things in being there in dormant state. All the other thoughts are in dormant state.

Just as when I go to sleep, all my thoughts about what I'm going to be doing next week are in dormant state. Not that I've forgotten anything about it. I'm just in dormant state. As soon as I wake up on Monday morning, we all come into being and becomes my work and my activity and my creation. Avyakta, vyaktaha, sarvaha prabhavanti ahaha made the arrival of the day. All those who were unmanifest now becomes manifest in all those who are manifest during the day.
snippets.reflection:
These verses introduce the concept of Guna and Dharma—the characteristics that define who we are and the duties that arise from them. The teaching that "where I am today is the product of my past" and "my future would be the product of my present" offers both responsibility and hope. You are not trapped by your current limitations; you are simply at one point on an evolutionary journey that stretches across lifetimes. The fascinating scientific observation that our atoms are constantly recycling—that atoms once in Shakespeare's or Krishna's body may have passed through yours—points to the material interconnectedness of all existence. This week, reflect on your own Guna-Dharma evolution: What qualities did you have ten years ago that have now transformed? What new capacities have emerged? What qualities are you currently cultivating that will shape your future self?

Verse 20 reveals there is something beyond even the unmanifest Prakriti from which creation emerges: "Paras tasmat tu bhavo anyo avyakto avyaktat sanatanah"—"Beyond this unmanifest is another Unmanifest, eternal, which does not perish when all beings perish." This is the ultimate goal—not just a better position within the cycle, but transcendence of the cycle itself. The analogy of watching a magician perform is apt: as long as you sit in the audience, you are enchanted by the illusion. But when you become the magician's apprentice and learn how the tricks work, the magic dissolves into understanding. Verse 21 promises: "Yam prapya na nivartante"—having reached this, one does not return. This is not a distant goal. The teaching offers a "short circuit": rather than evolving slowly through countless incarnations, you can go directly to the Source through knowledge and devotion. Today, ask yourself: Am I content to improve my position within the dream, or am I ready to wake up?
snippets.shortReflection: Look back ten years. What qualities did you have then that you've since outgrown? What new capacities have emerged? You're not fixed. You're a work in progress across a timeline much longer than this life.

snippets.title: Day 113: The Path of No Return
snippets.sanskrit:

snippets.transliteration:
puruṣhaḥ sa paraḥ pārtha bhaktyā labhyas tvananyayā
yasyāntaḥ-sthāni bhūtāni yena sarvam idaṁ tatam

yatra kāle tvanāvṛittim āvṛittiṁ chaiva yoginaḥ
prayātā yānti taṁ kālaṁ vakṣhyāmi bharatarṣhabha

verseTranslations: *Now I will tell thee, O Arjuna, of the times at which, if the mystics go forth, they do not return, and at which they go forth only to return.

If knowing the Supreme Spirit the sage goes forth with fire and light, in the daytime, in the fortnight of the waxing moon and in the six months before the Northern summer solstice, he will attain the Supreme.
Fire, light, daytime, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice — departing by this path, the knowers of God go to God.
snippets.commentary:
We are coming to the last concluding verses of this chapter. In chapter seven, we learned about the nature of the supreme as the Higher Prakriti and the Lower Prakriti.

He said, my Lower Prakriti is Eightfold Prakriti which is manifest. My Higher *Prakriti* which supports this lower Prakriti. So that higher Prakriti is the imperishable Brahman, which is the substratum for this Lower *Prakriti*.

That which is manifest is supported by that which is Unmanifest. That Unmanifest is the Supreme *Brahman*, the Imperishable. So chapter eight is our quest to understand the imperishable Brahman.

We've been discussing the nature of the Imperishable *Brahman*. In the beginning we have learned that the nature of that supreme reality is imperishable. He is *self* knowing and in his work is to create these things and beings.

That same supreme reality creates these things and beings as *Prakriti* -- the Lower Prakriti, out of his own self. So the world which we see is the manifest world, but it is supported by the Unmanifest. The Unmanifest is imperishable, but the world which it creates is perishable.

Prakriti is infinite, just as *Brahman* is infinite. Prakriti is ever-existing, just as Brahman is ever-existing. But the creations within *Prakriti* are perishable, because the same entity which creates these things and beings will keep creating and destroying.

Brahma, the Creator, while he is working -- that's his day. When he's not working, that's his night. And we have seen that how long the Brahma's day is compared to hours.

Then in the end we have talked about how can the individual *ego*, the individual entity which finds itself to be limited by these limitations of mind and intellectual, can rise above this limitations and reach the Supreme. Why I'm suffering through my limitations. And therefore there are Sorrows.

If I was having no limitation, there will not be any sorrow. So my quest in life is to get over all my limitations. So when I transit from one existence to another, my goal is always to get to a stage which has less limitations or no limitations.

So we talked about the one who dies with that thought of imperishable in mind will lead the imperishable. One who dies with the goal of achieving something will get to that state of achievement. Those who worship Devas will go to Devas.

Those who worship *Brahman* will go to *Brahman*. Then we elaborately discussed how to get to that point where we can think about that goal. Verse 21, which was the last one we discussed, says: Avyakto Akshara iti uktah tam ahuh paramam gatim.

That which is considered the unmanifest, imperishable -- that is your highest goal. They who reach it never again return. Yam prapya na nivartante.

Everyone else has to come back because of some goal or other. Some desire or other which is unfulfilled. And I want to fulfill it.

I want to achieve their capabilities and then achieve that goal. So to achieve that, now I'm in a pursuit of happiness. Because my happiness is somewhere else.

I have to come back to pursue my happiness. But one who wants to achieve that happiness which is supreme, then he doesn't have to come back. And therefore it says that your goal is to achieve that unmanifest and imperishable that is considered the highest goal.

They who reach it never again return. Bhagwan says, that is my highest abode. That's what my my abode is.

All this time we had been discussing and thinking about what is the nature of the Lord and where does he reside. He says, that is my abode and that's my nature. My nature is supreme, imperishable, unmanifest.

My abode is that state of *awareness* -- that's where you will find me. So the next seven verses, which are the concluding verses, say: Purushah sa parah partha bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya. Is it ever possible to achieve that state of oneness with the imperishable *Brahman*? Right now I can achieve oneness with my own limitations -- "this is me." I can also relate to other things in the world and achieve oneness.

But it is unthinkable right now to achieve oneness with the supreme imperishable *Brahman*. Bhagavan gives a guarantee here: it is achievable by Bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya -- by single-pointed *devotion*. Single-pointed identification with that imperishable *Brahman*.

As long as I'm identified with something else, I cannot be identifying with that. As long as I'm identified with my body, my intellect there is no way that I can identify with him. So Bhagavan said, it is possible for *Purusha*, any person to achieve that by single pointed *devotion*.

That's the only path. Yasyantahasthani Bhutani. That single pointed *devotion* for what? That which is the indwelling for all beings.

I am trying to achieve understanding about myself. But in that inward journey I have to realize that myself is not just limited to my limited *self* but it is the *self* of all the beings. Yesyanta sthani Bhutani.

That's the dwelling place for all beings. Yena sarvam idam tatam -- everything is pervaded by it. That entity with which I want to identify is the dwelling place for all beings and things.

With single-pointed *devotion*, I'm identifying with that. We can very easily identify with people and things similar to us. We have difficulty identifying with people who are a little different from us.

They speak different language, they look different. It's a way I can overcome that. But then I have to identify with entire Jagat and it goes even beyond that and says there is nothing in this universe cosmos where the *self* is not pervaded.

In my inward journey of meditation I have to understand and identify with that entity which does not leave anything out. If I say I love this, but I hate this, well, I have limited him. I created limitation for him and therefore my journey is incomplete.

So now Bhagavan said that I will explain to you how to reach there. And he said there are two paths. Yatra kale to anavrutyam avruttim chevayogina.

Well, first qualification. You should be a Yogi. You are the one who is striving to achieve this *liberation* that's given.

But the striving alone will not guarantee that you will achieve *liberation*. Because the path you may take. He said he will explain the time and path while parting from this state of existence: one which is the path of return, and one which is the path of no return.

We have been trying -- people have been trying -- but we continue to come back to the same world of sorrow. Prayatha Yanti Tamkalam Vakyami Bharata Sabah. So I will let you know what path will lead you to no return.

I also let you know what the path of return. So that's basically just an introduction to the next two verses. Next is Agnihi Jyotihi Ahaha, Shuklaha Shanmasa, Uttarayanam Tatra, Prayahata, Gachanti, Brahma, Brahma Vidojanaha.

These two mantas are very, very difficult to understand because from a superficial translation it makes no sense whatsoever. It says Agni, Jyoti, Ahaha -- fire, light, daytime -- Shuklaha, the bright fortnight, in six months of Uttarayanam. Tatra Prayata Gachanti Brahma, Brahma Vidojanaha -- one who goes through that path, they go to *Brahman*, the path of no return.

The Yogi who knows *Brahman* goes through this path of light. So now, if we take this literally, that means people who die during these six months have a chance to get liberated, and the other six months have no chance. December 22 to June 21 you get *liberation*, and after June 22 to December 21 people have to return.

That obviously makes no sense. You have to remember the Gita is the essence of Upanishads. Sarva Upanishado Gavo, Dugdham Gopala Nandanam -- all Upanishads are cows, and Gopala Nandana (Krishna) has collected the milk and given it to you.

He is the one who collected all the ideas and concepts from the Upanishads and put them in the Bhagavad Gita. You have to study the Upanishads to understand these concepts. These particular two verses about the path of Uttarayana and Dakshinayana are directly taken from the Prashna Upanishad.

The Prashna Upanishad elaborately explains the path of Uttarayana and Dakshinayana. It starts with explaining the creation of this universe -- that Prajapati himself became the sun and the moon. The sun represents energy; the moon represents matter.

Then it also explains how the year is created, how a month is created, how a day is created -- one represents energy, the other matter. Anything during the day represents energy. We know that daytime is the domain of the sun -- sunlight, energy, activity.

Nighttime is presided over by the moon -- its inactivity. Darkness -- that's the path of the Moon. So the two paths were thought of as the path of energy and the path of matter; the path of the Sun.

With Krama Mukti, the gradual *liberation* through Upasana and Karmas, you reach through the path of the sun to the Brahmaloka. We also know that we can gradually improve ourselves. So the good actions are necessary.

But we also know that doing good is not good enough. It has to be associated with *knowledge*. So that is the difference between the two parts.

One who is doing good but with a goal of getting something good out of it -- that is the path of return. One who is doing good but without seeking anything in return, seeking only to liberate himself -- those selfless actions are the path of no return. These two are symbolically described in Upanishadic language as the Path of Uttarayana and the Path of Dakshinayana.

Another way to look at it: when we face the sun in the morning, we are facing east. On your right side is south, and your left side is north. So the path of Dakshinayana is the sun rising from the east, going through the south, and setting in the west.

The path of the north is the path of the rising sun. And the path of the south is the path of the setting sun. So we are going from the rising sun to daytime, from the setting sun to nighttime.

If we associate *knowledge* and the sacred with the path of the rising sun, that is the path of Uttarayana; the path of the setting sun is the path of Dakshinayana. Both describe the mental makeup of a yogi -- one who is seeking *liberation* versus one who will come back to enjoy. If you listen to political conventions, if you just look at how the nominee is described, it looks like they're sages.

They're only driven by the common good. They just wanted to do nothing but help people. So if that is true, then he's a sage.

But if you take that and see that they are not only doing good, but they also have their own good in mind. They want to achieve something out of it. At the path of return, you're constantly coming back to do good so that you can get something out of it.

Bhagawan said it is exactly the same for the yogi. The Prashna Upanishad describes in detail that those who want to gain something out of their good actions are on the path of return. And we have seen in earlier verses that during Brahma's night, all beings are in a dormant state, and when creation starts, they emerge from whatever unfulfilled desires remain and come back into this universe again.
snippets.reflection:
"Bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya"—the Supreme is attainable through single-pointed devotion alone. This verse addresses a common concern: Is liberation actually possible for ordinary people like us? Krishna answers emphatically: yes, but the key is "ananya"—undivided, exclusive devotion. This does not mean abandoning responsibilities; it means having only one ultimate allegiance while performing all duties. Examine your divided loyalties today. We easily identify with people similar to us but struggle with those who appear different. Yet the teaching says we must identify with "that in which all beings abide and which pervades the entire universe." This week, practice expanding your circle of identification. When you meet someone who seems very different from you, look for the common awareness that animates both of you. That shared consciousness is the Supreme Self dwelling equally in all.

Verses 23-24 introduce the symbolic paths of Uttarayana (northern course) and Dakshinayana (southern course). Rather than being literal astronomical timings for death, these represent mental and spiritual states. The path of "fire, light, daytime, bright fortnight" symbolizes the illuminated mind filled with knowledge. The opposite path represents the mind clouded with ignorance and attachment. The practical question becomes: What path is your mind currently traveling? Is it moving toward greater light, clarity, and selflessness (Uttarayana)? Or toward greater attachment, confusion, and self-centeredness (Dakshinayana)? The good news is that unlike the literal sun's path, your mental path can be changed at any moment through conscious choice. Today, notice moments when your mind moves toward darkness—worry, resentment, craving—and gently redirect it toward light. Each redirection is a practice run for the ultimate journey.
snippets.shortReflection: When you meet someone who seems totally different from you—different politics, lifestyle, background—look for the one thing you share: the fact that you're both aware, both conscious. That shared awareness is the only thing that's real.

snippets.title: Day 114: The Unmanifest Beyond
