verseTranslations: But if he departs in gloom, at night, during the fortnight of the waning moon and in the six months before the Southern solstice, then he reaches but lunar light and he will be born again.
These bright and dark paths out of the world have always existed. Whoso takes the former, returns not; he who chooses the latter, returns.*
O Arjuna! The saint knowing these paths is not confused. Therefore meditate perpetually.
snippets.commentary:
Akshara Brahma *Yoga*, Yoga of Imperishable Brahman. So let's see what we have seen so far in Bhagavad Gita. We are almost at the midpoint of Bhagavad Gita. The teachings in Bhagavad Gita are basically telling us that you are not this limited *self*; your real nature is the supreme Self. The journey from this limited self to the supreme *self* is the quest of human life.

So Bhagavan has indicated in chapter one what this limited life is like using Arjuna's situation, that the life is not clearly divided between good and evil, or situations which are black and white, but they come in various shades of gray. And to learn to deal with it is the wisdom. So Bhagawan gave Arjuna the guidance and encapsulated that guidance in Bhagavad Gita for the generations to come, so that we can use the same guidance given to Arjuna for our own lives. So Bhagavan had given Arjuna in the second chapter, a clear indication of what is reality and what is superimposition on the reality. Bhagawan said, we consider ourselves to be mortal beings, but we are immortal beings identified with mortal bodies. This identification is creating all the confusion.

So the goal of life is to get rid of this ignorance about the supreme *Self*. He defined a man of wisdom, Sthita Prajna -- the one who has balanced his mind and can see the situation clearly without getting tainted by it. Bhagawan gave that wisdom in a nutshell to Arjuna. We learned that what we consider ourselves to be is not really ourselves. We are not limited beings. We are immortal beings identified with mortal bodies. Bhagavan described a man of wisdom -- a Sthita Prajna who sees this clearly because of the purification of his internal instrument. He understands that the self is different than this body, mind and intellect, and the one who is not attached, who is desireless, will achieve this wisdom. The path was then given in the following chapters: how to act in this world without desires or *attachment*. Chapter three gave us Karma *Yoga*, with the simple indication that we have no control over the results of our actions, but we do have the right to act.

I have right to act, but I cannot anticipate a particular result. Therefore I should act without any anticipation or expectation -- that's the simple first step. The second step, in chapter four: Bhagavan said you should come to the understanding that the *self* is not the doer. The *self* that you call "I" is not participating in any activity. Activities are performed by the body, mind, and intellect -- matter reacting with matter. But the *self* is not involved.

Therefore in chapter five he says, you should give up the sense of agency -- "I am the doer." Everything is happening at the body level, at the mind level, at the intellect level, but "I" is not involved. I am not doing anything; "I" is not participating in any of these activities. Chapter six then culminated in Dhyana *Yoga*, the *Yoga* of Meditation.

How can I contemplate on the real *self*? Thoughts of the same species, of the same type, when directed towards the goal -- that is called meditation. Meditation is to constantly think about the Supreme *Self* that I am. My Atma is none other than the Paramatma; that thought held constantly is meditation. Bhagawan defined meditation, the path of meditation, and the techniques of meditation in chapter six.

The second segment of Bhagavad Gita, as we have discussed many times, is about the Supreme *Self*. The first segment was about Tvam, the "you" part of Tattvamasi. The next six chapters are all about Tat, that Supreme. We defined Tvam, which is right now identified as the little *ego*.

Tat is the Supreme *Self*. And if I have to contemplate on that, I need to understand the nature of the supreme self. So in seventh chapter we learned the two aspects of that supreme reality. One is the lower Prakriti, made of the Eightfold manifestation -- Bhumi, Apah, Analah, Vayu, Kham -- that which we can perceive through our senses is the representation of that lower Prakriti. Beyond this lower Prakriti is the Higher *Prakriti*, which becomes the knower of this lower Prakriti; the self in us becomes the knower, the unmanifest aspect of that self. Bhagavan said, my real nature is beyond these two, and that is veiled by *Maya*.

That real nature is not available to all of us because it is veiled by *Maya*. Bhagawan defined Maya as the total conditioning of Ishwara. When that *Maya* operates at my individual level, it becomes ignorance -- Avidya. This Avidya is not letting me cross Maya itself. So in chapter 8, Bhagavan has given us the means to overcome this *Maya*.

So we have started this chapter 8 with clear definitions of all these terms we come across. So we have learned that the supreme reality is veiled by *Maya*. And this projection of the multitude of beings and multitude of realities in physical world is projected through Maya. In the very first verse, Arjuna asked question which basically defines all these terms for us. These terms -- Adhi Yajna and others -- we want clarified for our understanding. If you want to contemplate on the supreme *Self*, then we need to understand the differentiation between Adhi Bhuta, Adhi Daiva, and Brahman. *Brahman* is the supreme reality, one without a second. Adhibhuta is the perishable nature of the reality which we experience.

And Adhi Daivam is my own Swabhava. When it operates through me, it becomes Adhi Devam. And Bhagawan in the end said that I alone am the Adhi Yajnam. All the experiences which you have at an individual level are experienced by none other than the supreme *self* -- because the Self is real. Everything else is nothing but superimposition on it. Therefore Bhagawan says you must identify with this supreme *Self* to get over this *Maya*, this superimposition. In the discussion of what happens at the time of departure from this level of existence, we have seen two terms: Antakala and Prayanakala. Antakala is my preparation time -- I have to prepare for this journey. This existence is limited, which is a given, but there will be another existence right after that.

So if I was not really satisfied with my current existence, then I'm obviously looking for a better existence next time. Bhagawan says, that better existence is dependent on how you prepare and how you end this existence. Whatever you are thinking at the time of your departure, that's the destination you will reach. So Bhagawan said, therefore think about me all the time -- that destination which holds the ultimate happiness that you are seeking.

That world without sorrow, without any limitations, without any conditioning. And we have seen that that world is only at the level of *Brahman*. All the lokas up to Brahma's world are subject to repeated return -- that's called the path of repeated return. We have seen that Maya has three aspects: Tamas, *Rajas*, and Sattva. Any existence is nothing but a permutation and combination of these three *Gunas*.

If I am at a level where *Tamas* is predominant, then I am at the level of complete ignorance. When I rise from that level to the next level, then obviously the Rajas increases and then Tamas reduces. If I rise even further, then the Sattva increases, Rajas diminishes and Tamas diminishes. I can go all the way up to the level of pure *Sattva*. But as long as I am in Rajas and Tamas, I have to come back to a level of existence which has beginning and end -- that is the path of repeated return. But there is also a path of no return: you have to cross this Prakriti, this Maya. When you cross this *Prakriti*, there is no coming back to mortal existence. That is the path of no return.

Those two paths are described in the last few verses. The confusion obviously was: is there a particular time, a particular moment, a particular method in which one can depart and not return, or return? Those two paths we have been discussing: Agnihi Jyotihi Ahah Shuklaha Shanmasa Uttarayanam Tatra Prayata Gachanti Brahma Brahma Vido Janaha. This path is called Devayana, the Divine path -- the path which leads to no return. The path of fire, light, daytime, bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice. Following this path, men who know *Brahman* go to *Brahman* -- the wise people who acquired this *knowledge*.

Therefore we are going through *Gnana*, Vignana, Yoga. *Knowledge* about my supreme self is *Gnana*. And applying it in my life to get over these limitations is Vignana. So Brahma says, the one who has applied this, he is following the bright path. And these are probably symbolically indicated in Upanishads or how our mind sees this world. So when our mind is cheerful, we associate with the bright and sunny atmosphere.

So there is a climate outside and a climate inside my mind. Those two are related to each other but not really connected. The climate outside may be very bright and sunny, but my mind inside may be very gloomy -- that will not let me enjoy the world outside. But if I can synchronize the two, then my mind is feeling the same bright atmosphere inside as is outside. And maybe that's what was indicated here.

I can keep my mind in the same bright atmosphere of *knowledge* and then leave this existence. Then I will achieve the state of Brahman, Brahma, Vidojanaha. People who know *Brahman* will always be following this bright path. And one who knows Brahman, he obviously is not going to desire for anything less than *Brahman*. If I have known that I own a billion dollar trust fund somewhere, obviously I want to achieve that and not go for a smaller gain in life. So we have known this ultimate goal of achieving that state of imperishableness.

They will follow the path of *Brahman* so that the path was identified Uttarayanam or Devayanam. In the contrast to that, the path which we typically associate with is labeled as Dakshinayanam or Pitrayanam. So the path of ancestors or the southern path. That path, in contrast to the previous one, is followed by people who are not aware of the nature of *Brahman*, who have not realized that there is an existence without any conditioning. As we have said, the conditioning at my individual level is Avidya. Ignorance about myself has created this conditioning through identification with body, mind, and intellect.

Identifying with walls, floor, and ceiling creates room space. I, the *self*, identifying with this body, mind, and intellect, create this Jiva as a limited entity existing in this pluralistic world. When I leave this body, this existence, with only the understanding that I'm a limited being trying to achieve a higher standard of living, then I'll reach that stage. But when I exhaust my Punya, I'll come back to start working at it again. That's basically the path of return -- I have to work for 50 weeks for two weeks of vacation. Once the two weeks vacation is over, I have to start working for another 50 weeks for two more weeks of vacation.
snippets.reflection:
The contrast between Shukla (bright) and Krishna (dark) paths in verse 26 is not about external circumstances but internal orientation. The Devayana (divine path) is followed by those who know Brahman—their actions arise from knowledge and selflessness. The Pitrayana (ancestral path) is followed by those doing good with the expectation of reward. Both paths involve good actions, but the motivation differs completely. This is a crucial distinction for daily practice: When you perform a kind act today, notice your subtle expectations. Do you anticipate gratitude, recognition, or future benefit? That expectation, however reasonable it seems, keeps you on the path of return. Practice performing at least one completely anonymous act of kindness each day—something no one will ever know about, not even your closest confidant. This trains the mind in truly selfless action.

Verse 27 delivers the chapter's practical conclusion: "Tasmat sarveshu kaleshu yoga-yukto bhava Arjuna"—"Therefore, at all times, be established in yoga." The saint who understands these two paths is never confused about priorities. He knows that doing good for personal gain, while not wrong, is simply insufficient for liberation. This week, audit your spiritual activities: Are you studying scripture to become more knowledgeable (ego enhancement) or to dissolve ignorance (liberation)? Are you meditating to feel calm (personal benefit) or to realize your true nature (transcendence)? Are you serving others to be recognized as a good person (reputation) or because you see the Divine in them (devotion)? There is nothing wrong with the first motivation in each pair, but it leads to the path of return. Only the second orientation leads to the path of no return. The teaching invites us to examine not just what we do, but why we do it.
snippets.shortReflection: Next time you do something good, check your subtle scorecard. Are you expecting cosmic credits, good karma points, divine favor? That expectation is a chain. Try acting with no account balance in mind.

snippets.reflection:
This concluding verse of Chapter 8 makes a revolutionary claim: the sage who truly understands these teachings "passes beyond all merit that comes from the study of scriptures, from sacrifice, from austerities, and from charity." This does not mean these practices are worthless—they are essential stepping stones. But knowledge of the imperishable Brahman transcends all accumulated merit. Merit (Punya) keeps you on the wheel; it earns you better circumstances for future births. But the goal is to step off the wheel entirely. Reflect on your spiritual resume: How much of your practice is oriented toward accumulating spiritual merit (better rebirth, divine favor, inner peace) versus dissolving the very illusion of a separate self that could accumulate anything?

The "Supreme Primeval Abode" mentioned in this verse is not a location in space but a state of awareness—the recognition that you have always been and will always be the imperishable Brahman wearing the temporary costume of your current identity. Chapter 8 has offered a complete teaching: from Arjuna's seven questions about ultimate reality, through the meditation techniques for realizing it, to the cosmic context of creation and dissolution, to the two paths of return and no-return. The chapter ends where it began—with the imperishable. As you conclude this study, ask yourself: What has genuinely shifted in my understanding? What am I now willing to let go of that I was clinging to before? What does it mean that my true Self—the awareness reading these words right now—is "Akshara," imperishable, and has been present before this body was born and will remain after it dissolves? Let this question accompany you not just in formal meditation, but through every moment of daily life.
snippets.shortReflection: Your spiritual practices—meditation, prayer, study, service—are they making you feel like a better person, or dissolving your need to be anyone at all? One path improves the character. The other ends the movie.

snippets.title: Day 116: Royal Knowledge
snippets.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच |
इदं तु ते गुह्यतमं प्रवक्ष्याम्यनसूयवे |
ज्ञानं विज्ञानसहितं यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् ||

राजविद्या राजगुह्यं पवित्रमिदमुत्तमम् |
प्रत्यक्षावगमं धर्म्यं सुसुखं कर्तुमव्ययम् ||

अश्रद्दधानाः पुरुषा धर्मस्यास्य परन्तप |
अप्राप्य मां निवर्तन्ते मृत्युसंसारवर्त्मनि ||
snippets.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
idaṁ tu te guhyatamaṁ pravakṣhyāmyanasūyave
jñānaṁ vijñāna-sahitaṁ yaj jñātvā mokṣhyase ’śhubhāt

rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyaṁ pavitram idam uttamam
pratyakṣhāvagamaṁ dharmyaṁ su-sukhaṁ kartum avyayam

aśhraddadhānāḥ puruṣhā dharmasyāsya parantapa
aprāpya māṁ nivartante mṛityu-samsāra-vartmani
verseTranslations: Lord Shri Krishna said: I will now reveal to thee, since thou doubtest not, that profound mysticism, which when followed by experience, shall liberate thee from sin.
This is the Premier Science, the Sovereign Secret, the Purest and Best; intuitional, righteous; and to him who practiseth it pleasant beyond measure.
They who have no faith in this teaching cannot find Me, but remain lost in the purlieus of this perishable world.
snippets.commentary:
This is in continuation of what we have discussed in the last two chapters, 7 and 8. In chapter 7 we have seen Gnana Vignana Yoga, *Yoga* of Knowledge, and Visishtha Gnana, which is applied knowledge -- or what we call wisdom. Wisdom is something we have gained through our own experience. As the saying goes, "Look at my gray hair. I didn't get this gray hair standing in the sun outside -- all this is experience. " In other words, what I have learned through my experience became my own *knowledge*.

Somebody told me something that remained at the information level, then I applied it and it became my own *knowledge*. That's why in science college you have theoretical classes and then you go to the lab. The same thing you learned there -- that H2O makes water -- you go and experiment with it yourself, and you realize that's what happens. So the first thing we did after finishing the first six chapters was talk about who we are and how we purify our internal instrument by meditation, by all these sadhanas, selfless actions. Now the question is: what are we meditating upon? That is what we need to know. So from chapter seven onward, we started talking about self-knowledge -- *knowledge* about my own *self*, removing this paradox where I think "this is me" and still worry about what happens to me after death and what happened before my birth.

So the *self-knowledge*, the *Gnana* Vignana *Yoga*, tells us what is the nature of the Lord and how people approach it. In chapter seven we learned about the Chaturvida Bhakta -- the four types of devotees. Everyone wants to achieve that state of perfect happiness where there is no sorrow, no imperfection in my life. In four ways we approach that. Our quest for that perfectness is described as Aartha, Jijnasu, Artharthi, and Gnani. One is approaching him out of distress.

One is approaching because he wants to gain something. One is approaching out of curiosity -- is there a state of perfectness? And the last one approaches because out of his own intuition, he knows there is a state of perfectness. Then in the last chapter we discussed the imperishable *Brahman*. Yes, there is a state which is infinite, imperishable. At that state of existence, we call it *Brahman* -- that which pervades everywhere and everything.

My world right now is pervaded by my thoughts, you know, and my thoughts are right now limited. So my world is limited. I can think about the things only which I have experienced in the past, you know, or I heard about it from others or something which I have known from reading the books. But my thoughts are limited to that. Therefore my world is also limited to that. Beyond this world, I'm always afraid or curious.

What is beyond my thoughts? Before my birth, I can think about my life as far back as my childhood. I can think about my life in the future as far as I can think. So I had this guy trying to sell me an annuity, and he said this thing gives you lifetime income from whenever you start. I said, when can I start?

He said, you can start at age 70. I said, my lifetime may not be more than five or six years after that, so your lifetime income doesn't do much for me. He said, why do you say that? I said, by statistical data -- how many people in my family have lived beyond that?

So I know my future by observing what has happened in my family. So what is beyond that? That's where I get lost. So Bhagavan said that imperishable *Brahman* is the state of yourself. So in chapter eight we have discussed about the nature of that imperishable *Brahman* and how I as this limited being fit into that.

That as long as I identify with this limited intellect in mind, this instrument of *ego*, I constantly come back and forth because I'm hanging on to that identity. This me is where I am as long as I have that *ego*. Bhagavan says in the part of your *Prakriti*, he'll come back again and again taking another instrument of transaction with this world continuing in the same argument. Now chapter nine says, now we'll talk about the royal secret. Why is it a royal secret? Because it is already obvious to you, but you are not aware of it.

It's right there, but I can't see it. Therefore it's a secret. And it's a royal science, because "Royal" -- Rajan, Raja -- connotes supremacy. In a kingdom there is nothing higher than a king. In our case we have the president as the highest authority.

But he has many people to question him and tell him what he is not doing right. In those kingdoms, the Raja was never questioned. Even though he is not wearing clothes, nobody says the king is not wearing clothes. There was a supreme status. They say this Vidya is a Raja Vidya, the supreme *knowledge*.

Beyond that there is nothing to be known. That is *self-knowledge*. I know physics, I know chemistry, I know all these things, I know all the *knowledge* about arts and everything else. But Bhagavan says there is only one thing you need to know -- about yourself.

And there is nothing more to be known. Therefore it is the supreme *knowledge* in the *self* *knowledge*. So the first verse of this chapter starts with Bhagavan's profound statement: Idam tu te guhyatamam pravakshyami anasuya ve. I am going to tell you this. Gnanam Vignana sahitam yad Gnatva mokshyase asubhat.

I'm going to tell you this *knowledge* along with Visishtagnam -- along with its wisdom, its application. Knowing that, you will be freed from what? From Ashubha and Shubha. Shubha is auspicious, that which is good. Ashubha is not good for me.

Anything in your life which you consider not good, you'll be liberated from that. And we say, well, that's exactly what I was looking for all my life. Get rid of all the problems I have, Bhagavan, then I'll be doing your *bhakti* forever. Because right now I don't have time -- I'm just fixing my problems.

My total attention will be yours after that. Bhagavan says, idam tu te guhyatamam. This *knowledge* which is the deepest, most profound secret. Guhyatamam -- guhya means secret, tamam means most. I'm going to tell you. You know what is the supreme secret?

It's something nobody can figure out. That's a supreme secret. Other secrets you can figure out by asking someone, but this secret is right in front of you, yet you can't figure it out. Like a person in disguise walking around in a party you see in a movie.

Everybody sees him but nobody figures out who he is. And he said, I'm going to tell you this because you're anasuya ve. We have heard last time, you're a person who does not cavil or carp, who does not raise petty arguments or petty objections. Sometimes people come to a lecture to find out how smart the speaker is, to see whether he knows anything. Then they will find fault in it.

See, if you give an example and say, our life is short, but the sun is there forever, suddenly somebody says, well that's not true, the sun is not there forever. I can tell you how it works. But that was not the intention of the speaker in giving that analogy -- to give you a relationship. But because your purpose is only to see what the speaker does not know.

So you are carping at him, raising petty objections, pointing out petty faults and errors. Because you are not truly, genuinely interested in understanding. The person who is like that is obviously not going to learn, because his mind is not in learning things -- his mind is in finding out where the faults lie. So therefore he says, I'm going to tell you the deepest of secrets, the most profound secret. Because so far you have proved that you are a genuine seeker of this *knowledge*. You really want to find out how to get rid of sorrows from your life, how to readjust your thinking pattern so you can function right in this world. Having known the Gnanam vignana sahitam yad gnatva mokshyase asubhat -- after that you will get rid of all that is ashubha, sorrowful, not conducive in your life.

Bhagavan, that's what I've been looking for! If you can tell me, then after this, once I know: every time I buy a lottery, I'll be the winner. Every time I submit a proposal, I'll be the winner. Every time I put a contract on a property, I'll be the winner -- because you told me that after knowing this, there will not be any sorrow in your life.

You'll be just a winner. You'll never be a loser. Bhagavan said, that's not what it means. What it means is that after knowing this, you will not see anything happening in your life as inherently good or bad. Right now, my definition of good and bad is defined by what I want and what I want to reject. Everything which I want to reject is Ashubha. Everything I want is Shubha.

There is a story of a father who goes to visit his two daughters. One was married to a pot maker, another was married to a farmer. He went to the daughter married to the farmer and said, "What's happening?" She said, "Oh, this was a wonderful season, a lot of rains, and we are doing very well. Oh Lord, keep continuing doing that!" Then he goes to the other daughter's house, the one married to the pot maker. "So how are things going?" She said, "Pretty bad this year. There was no sun. It was raining all the time. We couldn't really bake any pots, so we are really not doing well. Hope the Lord does something and stops this rain." So the father thinks, "Oh Lord, please stop this rain so that my daughter will be happy." But what can a father do? Same situation -- one sees it as Shubha, the other sees it as Ashubha.

The Shubha and Ashubha, as we are saying, are projections of our mind. We create this Shubha and Ashubha in our life. Once I fix my perception of how to see the world, I may not find anything Ashubha in it.

There's this story in the Mahabharata. Yudhishthir and Duryodhan were both under the same teacher. The teacher said, "I have one test for both of you." He calls Yudhishthir first and says, "Go and find one bad person from this town." Yudhishthir goes off. Then he called Duryodhan and said, "Go and find one good person from this town." After a while, Yudhishthir comes back. The teacher asks, "Where is the bad person I asked you to bring?" He said, "I'm so sorry, but I couldn't find anybody bad in this town." Then Duryodhan comes back. "Where is the good person I asked you to bring?" He said, "I'm so sorry, but I couldn't find any good person in this town." Both have a different way of looking at the world.

One cannot find anything bad in this world other cannot find anything good in this world. I right now have divided my world into good and bad because of my *attachment*, my desires, my aspirations of what I want to achieve. When I achieve that, great. When I don't achieve that, the world is falling apart. Bhagavan said, having known this *knowledge*, there will not be Ashubha in your life.
snippets.reflection:
Krishna promises to reveal the "most profound mysticism" (guhyatamam) - knowledge combined with direct experience (jnana with vijnana) that liberates us from all that is inauspicious (ashubha). But this royal secret is only accessible to those who approach without caviling or carping (anasuya) - without petty objections or the desire to find fault. Today, examine your relationship with spiritual teachings: Do you approach them as a genuine seeker, or do you sometimes listen just to critique? The mind that seeks faults in the teaching never receives its nectar.

The chapter opens with a powerful reframe: what we label as "good" and "bad" (shubha and ashubha) are merely projections of our desires. Like the story of Yudhishthira who could find no bad person, and Duryodhana who could find no good person - each saw the world through the lens of their own nature. This week, when something "bad" happens, pause and ask: "Is this truly ashubha, or have I simply labeled it so because it conflicts with what I want?" Krishna says that knowing this knowledge removes all ashubha - not because circumstances change, but because our perception transforms.

Practice exercise: Each morning, set an intention to receive the day's teachings - from people, situations, and challenges - without immediately judging them as favorable or unfavorable. Notice how much mental energy is freed when you stop sorting experiences into "good for me" and "bad for me."
snippets.shortReflection: Notice your first response when hearing a teaching you disagree with. Do you immediately look for flaws, or do you sit with the discomfort and ask what it might be revealing about your own resistance?

snippets.title: Day 117: The Divine Secret
snippets.sanskrit:
मया ततमिदं सर्वं जगदव्यक्तमूर्तिना |
मत्स्थानि सर्वभूतानि न चाहं तेष्ववस्थितः ||

न च मत्स्थानि भूतानि पश्य मे योगमैश्वरम् |
भूतभृन्न च भूतस्थो ममात्मा भूतभावनः ||

यथाऽऽकाशस्थितो नित्यं वायुः सर्वत्रगो महान् |
तथा सर्वाणि भूतानि मत्स्थानीत्युपधारय ||
snippets.transliteration:
mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad avyakta-mūrtinā
mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na chāhaṁ teṣhvavasthitaḥ

na cha mat-sthāni bhūtāni paśhya me yogam aiśhwaram
bhūta-bhṛin na cha bhūta-stho mamātmā bhūta-bhāvanaḥ

yathākāśha-sthito nityaṁ vāyuḥ sarvatra-go mahān
tathā sarvāṇi bhūtāni mat-sthānītyupadhāraya
verseTranslations: The whole world is pervaded by Me, yet My form is not seen. All living things have their being in Me, yet I am not limited by them.
Nevertheless, they do not consciously abide in Me. Such is My Divine Sovereignty that though I, the Supreme Self, am the cause and upholder of all, yet I remain outside.
As the mighty wind, though moving everywhere, has no resting place but space, so have all these beings no home but Me.
snippets.commentary:
In the royal knowledge, we have seen up to chapter eight in which we have learned about ourselves -- who we are in this limited *self*, what is our goal, and how we can evolve out of it. Then we ask, but what do we meditate upon? What do we evolve into? We have said you have to evolve from this limited self, identifying with this limited being, to the infinite *self*, unlimited being -- and that's you.

Meditate upon whatever we want to achieve, we meditate on that. But unless I know the nature of that infinite *self* and my relationship with it, how can I meditate upon it? So in chapter eight we have seen imperishable *Brahman*, that entity which remains in existence all the time. Even when I perish or this world will perish, that substratum which creates this reality will always be there.

So now chapter nine says, what is my relationship with that imperishable *Brahman*? He is the source, he is the resting place. But what is my relationship with that? And so chapter nine says that is the royal secret. Right now I don't really see any relationship, even though I've heard through all these scriptures and books and religions.

But I personally cannot feel any relationship with him. So what is my relationship? He said that is the royal secret. You, knowing yourself, do not know what your relationship with yourself is.

That is the deepest secret -- the most secret is that it's right there. Looking for my key all the time, and it's always in my pocket. That is the biggest secret.

So that's the Raja Guhyam, and Raja Vidya. Knowing this -- knowing how to know this secret -- is the supreme *knowledge*. Once I realize my key is in my pocket that time I have the joy of my life.

Up till now I was so worried about where is my key, I'm going to be late for my meeting and all of that. Suddenly I realized that right here, that is the greatest *knowledge* I can have at that moment. Anything else, you tell me at that time and say, well let me tell you.

The E is equal to MC square. Look, I know I want my key. So when we get what we want to know is the supreme *knowledge*.

So Bhagavan said, that's what I'm going to tell you in this chapter. So in the first three verses he gave the promise. And now he says, let me tell you what that secret is.

So in verse four he says: Mayatatam idam sarvam jagat avyaktamurtina. I am pervading this Jagat. This entire Jagat, this entire cosmos, this entire universe is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form.

That which is illuminated is Jagat. That which is illuminated by my senses. My Jagat is limited to that.

That which I do not know is not part of my world. So Jagat is that which is illuminated by my senses. Your senses define your Jagat.

Her senses define her Jagat. When you put everyone's Jagat together, that is the total Jagat. Bhagavan said, I pervade this entire Jagat, whatever is illuminated by any being in this world.

I pervade that in my unmanifest form. The manifest is something I can say, oh yeah, I have seen it, I have touched it, I have been there. But the unmanifest is something beyond my perception.

So Bhagavan said, this world of your perception is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. Therefore you see the Jagat but do not see me, because I'm unmanifest. But I'm always there in anything you perceive, see, touch, or feel.

Here is my nature: your entire Jagat is pervaded by me. In my unmanifest form. That also includes myself -- I can perceive, feel, touch.

But wait, if that's part of your Jagat, then I am pervading through that. In my unmanifest form. My mind -- I can feel my thoughts.

Well then I am pervading in that also in my unmanifest form. My intellect. So then I'm also pervading in the unmanifest form.

Matsthani sarva bhutani. At least we understood that Bhagavan says he is in unmanifest form. Whatever you think of, right there, his presence is there.

As long as I can consider something as part of my Jagat, Bhagavan is right there. So now I come to the conclusion: Bhagavan resides in all of them. That's what all religions tell us.

Bhagavan resides in you. The Lord resides in your heart. So you say, well, let's not get confused here.

Okay, so what is my real nature? Matsthani, sarvabhutani, nacha aham te su avasthitaha. All these beings or things which you see, perceive, touch, and feel as your Jagat -- they reside in me, but I am not in them. See, in the first line he said that he pervades this entire Jagat of yours in his unmanifest form.

We put two and two together and said, therefore he is in all of them. But no -- "I am not in them, they are in me." My standard example: I buy a car and take it from Chesterfield County and bring it to Henrico County. What if Chesterfield County claims that the space in Mr.

Batue's car was Chesterfield County space? "Henrico County, you can't keep it there. Now you have extra space. Please return the extra space -- he took it with his car from Chesterfield County." Can I return that space in my car to Chesterfield County? What happened to the space which was in my car when the car was in Chesterfield County? It remained in Chesterfield County.

When the car came to Henrico County, the space in the car changed from Chesterfield to Henrico. The car moved through the space. So the conundrum is: is the space in the car, or is the car in the space? Obviously, if I cannot return the space from Henrico to Chesterfield -- "Oh, here is the extra space I brought with me" -- then obviously the car was moving in the space, not the other way around.

So now the space can say, "All the cars are in me." But it also says, "I am not in them." Now you have the puzzle -- there is no separate space "in" my car. So Bhagavan says, Matsthani Sarva Bhutani -- all the things and beings you can think of are in me. Your Jagat is whatever you can perceive, feel, think, and touch.

Now everything I see, Bhagavan says he pervades in unmanifest form. In other words, he is not limited to your Jagat. If I only say that Bhagavan pervades the entire Jagat, I know the Jagat in manifest form, and Bhagavan is in unmanifest form.

The law of conservation says, in this world there is always the same amount of energy and matter. Whether it's in a form of a matter, form of energy. The total energy remains the same at any given time.

So I can say, okay, the Bhagavan says he is unmanifest. So if I put sum it up, all the parts of my Jagat I know the Bhagavan. I say, no, they are in me, but I am not in them.

I am something beyond that. So he said, what is that relationship then? So is that it's a relationship less relations. Just as the space in the car and the space outside.

There's really no relationship to the car. It's not because the car is here. There is a space here.

The car will move, the space will move. With is my perception that the space is in the car. Space was always here outside this door.

When I brought my car and parked it, I perceived that space is in my car. Space never moved from anywhere to anywhere. In a similar way, the classical example we learn in Vedanta is that of a snake and a rope.

The existence of snake is very real. Is part of my Jagat, my world. When I see a snake, I perceive it.

I can vouch for it that there is a snake here. And therefore it is part of my Jagat. Now Bhagavan said, in unmanifest form, the rope was existing while I was seeing the snake in it.

That snake could not have come into existence without the existence of the rope. So now the rope can say that I was always pervading through this entire snake in my unmanifest form while you were seeing the snake in me. Therefore the snake is in me.

But I as the rope am not in the snake. The rope has no relationship to the snake whatsoever. Snake cannot exist without that rope.

But it takes the support of my ignorance, my perception. My perception created snake in my Jagat in my world. Because Jagat is only limited by my perception.

That which I can illumine as world of plurality is my Jagat. Snake was part of my Jagat. Without the rope, the snake could not have existed.

And therefore rope was existing in its unmanifest form in the snake all the time. But it was never in the snake. Bhagavan said, all these beings are existing in me.

In other words, without my existence, there is no existence for anything. Therefore they are in me. But I, in my pristine nature, unlimited, formless, was never in any of these shapes and forms and colors which you see.

So the next verse takes it further -- in case you think we got it all. Nachamatsthani Bhutani, Pashya Me Yogam Aishvaram, Bhuta Bhrit Na Cha Bhutastho Mamatma Bhuta Bhavanaha. Now he says that all these beings exist in me because we have seen the snake exists in the rope.

But the rope is not existing in the snake. So now you think okay, the beings are in him. But then he adds: these beings are also not existing in me.

The beings which I am perceiving, seeing, touching, and feeling are part of my Jagat. But the *Brahman* who is pervading all this Jagat has nothing to do with that. The snake which was existing in the rope -- the rope can say, "It existed in me, but I am not in them." But now he goes further.

If we think we got it correct and say, "Okay, so the snake was always in the rope," he says, no -- Nachamatsthani Bhutani. Even though these beings are existing in me, there was never a time -- from the perspective of the one who knew the rope -- that the snake was existing in that rope. In my world there was a snake.

But the next guy standing with his torchlight, who at least knew that it's a rope -- for him, there was no snake in his Jagat. The snake was only possible because of the rope, yet from his perspective, there was no snake ever in the rope. So in reality, there is never a snake existing in the rope.

The rope remained rope all the time -- before I created the snake in it and after I realized there is no snake. Therefore Bhagavan says: in your Jagat, you create this world through your perception. You create this world of plurality -- I exist, you exist, she exists, he exists.

And now I said, I am the center of my universe. The world revolves around me. You are in the center of your universe and the world revolves around you.

So from my perspective, in my Jagat, beings exist. Because the Supreme Being exist. And that being pervades through all the beings in my Jagat.
snippets.reflection:
"All beings dwell in Me, but I do not dwell in them" (matsthani sarvabhutani na caham tesvavasthitah) - this paradox holds the key to understanding our relationship with the Divine. Like space that appears to be "in" a car but actually contains the car, we exist within the infinite consciousness, not the other way around. The space doesn't move when the car travels from one county to another - the car moves through unchanging space. Similarly, your true Self remains unchanging while the body-mind moves through experiences.

The analogy of the snake and rope illuminates this further: the snake (this world of multiplicity) cannot exist without the rope (Brahman), yet from the rope's perspective, no snake ever existed. Your limitations, your problems, your separate identity - these exist in the Divine like the snake exists in the rope. They are real to your perception but have no fundamental reality. This is the "relationless relationship" - we are intimately connected to the Divine (closer than close), yet the Divine remains untouched by our perceived limitations.

Contemplation for today: When you look at any object or person, remind yourself: "This exists in consciousness, not consciousness in this." Notice how this shifts your sense of what is fundamental and what is derivative. Where you once saw solid, separate objects, begin to sense the unmanifest presence that pervades and supports all that you perceive.
snippets.shortReflection: Pick any object you can see right now. Instead of thinking 'I am here, looking at that,' try this: 'That object is appearing in consciousness.' Consciousness isn't in your head. Your head is in consciousness.

snippets.title: Day 118: Worship and Devotion
snippets.sanskrit:
सर्वभूतानि कौन्तेय प्रकृतिं यान्ति मामिकाम् |
कल्पक्षये पुनस्तानि कल्पादौ विसृजाम्यहम् ||

प्रकृतिं स्वामवष्टभ्य विसृजामि पुनः पुनः |
भूतग्राममिमं कृत्स्नमवशं प्रकृतेर्वशात् ||

न च मां तानि कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय |
उदासीनवदासीनमसक्तं तेषु कर्मसु ||
snippets.transliteration:
sarva-bhūtāni kaunteya prakṛitiṁ yānti māmikām
kalpa-kṣhaye punas tāni kalpādau visṛijāmyaham

prakṛitiṁ svām avaṣhṭabhya visṛijāmi punaḥ punaḥ
bhūta-grāmam imaṁ kṛitsnam avaśhaṁ prakṛiter vaśhāt

na cha māṁ tāni karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanañjaya
udāsīna-vad āsīnam asaktaṁ teṣhu karmasu
verseTranslations: All beings, O Arjuna, return at the close of every cosmic cycle into the realm of Nature, which is a part of Me, and at the beginning of the next I send them forth again.
With the help of Nature, again and again I pour forth the whole multitude of beings, whether they will or no, for they are ruled by My Will.
But these acts of mine do not bind Me. I remain outside and unattached.
snippets.commentary:
That's basically the topic of this discussion that Bhagawan started. So we are aware of our relationship with the Jiva to the Jagat, that I consider myself to be independent of the Jagat, the world. So the world I consider is an object, something other than me. But we still do not have any inkling about what our relationship with the Paramatma is.

The all pervading being. So Bhagavan clarified in the first six verses that his relationship to the Jagat is a relationless relationship. First he said, I am not in them, they are in me. The first conception we have from our childhood, learning from other teachers and religions, is that Bhagavan is within me, but I do not know who that Bhagavan is. Bhagavan clarified that I am not in them, I am not in the beings. So the first paradigm shift here is Bhagavan saying I am not in them.

The next thing he says is that they are in me. I pervade this entire Jagat Jagat which I can imagine and perceive in its infinity. Bhagawan said I am that infinite Jagat and all beings are in the Jagat. I am not in it, but it is in me. So *Brahman* Paramatma is the fundamental. Everything is an emergent reality.

The Jagat is emerging out of Paramatma, Jiva is emerging out of Jagat. So he clarified this relationship that I am fundamental, Jagat and Jivas are within me. But then he clarifies further saying but in reality, even they are not in me. So first we are conceived as the wind in the space, that the space is all pervading and infinite. From our perspective, the wind is finite and moving around within the space. In the same way all other elements which we see below, space, air, fire, water, earth, they're within space.

So space is the substratum for all things and beings to be in. That's our normal perception. The space is all pervading. Everything is within the space. Now Bhagavan is saying that he is beyond space and time. The Jagat is bound by space and time.

Bhagavan says, I am beyond space and time. So the Bhagavan is fundamental, infinite, all pervading, unchanging. Jagat is bound by space and time. And therefore it is changing, but is constantly changing with time. So the conundrum is: if the Jagat and Jiva came out of *Brahman*, the supreme reality, how did Brahman change? I see the manifest Jagat -- the manifest *Prakriti* which came out of *Brahman*, which is unmanifest -- so how did the unmanifest become manifest? That is the riddle we have to solve. So Bhagavan said, even they are not in me. This makes it clear that the Jiva and Jagat are apparent reality, not the fundamental reality. They appear to be in me, but they are also actually not in me.

And therefore we use this analogy of snake and rope. So that's the only way the two things can exist in the same state of manifest and unmanifest at the same time. Rope is unmanifest to the one who is afraid of snake. But someone who is aware of the rope, for him, the snake is not there. So these two are related, but have no real relationship. Snake and rope are related because without rope, the snake cannot exist.

But snake has no real reality other than the observer is creating this reality. You remove the observer, the snake and rope dichotomy goes away. So this Jagat and Jiva, which I see as two realities -- Bhagavan said that they do not really exist. They are created by my observations. It's my mind which projects space and time. Space and time are concepts of my mind.

When I am not aware of myself, in deep sleep, neither space nor time exists. When you wake up, only then can you say, "Nice sleep." But how long did I sleep? I will have no idea unless I look at the watch or clock. I went to sleep at such and such time, woke up at such and such time.

So I infer that I slept for as many hours. But a deep sleeper has no sense of time or space. So the Bhagavan said, jiva and Jagat are the conceptions of mind. But I, in reality is pristine without any change. But then Jeevan Jagat are very real for us. How do they come into existence?

Bhagawan now explains in the following verses. Sarvabhutani, Kaunteya, Prakritim, Yanti, Mamikam, Kalpakshaye, Punasthani, Kalpadau, Visrijami Aham. At the end of the Kalpa all beings, Sarva Bhutani, come back to my original nature, *Prakriti*. *Prakriti* we discussed in chapter seven is the fundamental manifest reality, also called Hiranyagarbha, also called Ishvara.

So *Brahman* with Maya is Ishvara. Brahman is the efficient cause. Maya is the material cause. *Maya* provides this material to create this Jagat. So this Maya is the fundamental Prakriti. From that fundamental Prakriti, the *Prakriti* which I see as pluralistic manifestation comes into existence.

This plurality goes back into that singular *Prakriti* at the end of Kalpa. We learned in last chapter that Brahmaji is one day is one Kalpa. Brahmaji is one day is 1000 Maha Yugas. One Mahayuga has four Yugas, Sathya, Treta, Dwapur and Kali. And we have calculated the one Kalpa is 4.3 billion years. So here Bhagavan says there is one cycle of creation.

The another cycle of dissolution is Brahmaj's night, which is equally as long as 4.3 billion years. The Bhagawan said, I create this Jagat at the beginning of my day and all that comes back to its original state at the end of the Kalpa. So the creation goes to the evolution as we perceive in our scientific observations. In our modern day, the universe came into existence, the Big Bang. It continues to expand, it continues to evolve, and at some point of time it will go back to its original state. Bhagavad said Sarvabhutani, all beings in this Jagat, Prakrutim, Yanthi, Mamikam, Kalpakshaya.

At the end of Kalpa they all come back to me in my *Prakriti*. Punahatani, Kalpada, Visrajami Aham. I recreate them at the beginning of the next Kalpa. This is very similar to our daily experience. During the day, I have all these ideas, all these goals, my to-do list. When I go to sleep, all those ideas are folded back into my *consciousness*. When I'm in deep sleep, I don't really feel anything.

I have no to-do list, no idea what I need to become, what I need to acquire, what I already accomplished. All those ideas are in a dormant state when I'm sleeping. The next morning when I wake up, exactly those same ideas will create my new day. I went to sleep as an architect; I wake up as an architect. A doctor who went to sleep as a doctor wakes up as a doctor. My problems from yesterday, unresolved?

They're still unresolved today. So we start from where we left off last night. Bhagavan said here in the case of the Srishti, at the individual level, my world starts at the beginning of the day or ends when I go to sleep at night. At the Samasthi level. At the end of Kalpa, the whole world goes to sleep. But all those Vasanas tendencies of all the beings are in a dormant state.

The new Kalpa will start with the old Kalpa. So nothing really changes. When the new Kalpa starts, the same cycle will start all over again. And so Bhagavan said, Prakrutim swam Avastabhya Vishrujami Puna Puna. This is unending cycle. The Brahmaji wakes up one day and then goes to sleep.

And then we are done with it. Brahmaji's life is considered a hundred years. One day and one night make up two Kalpas. Now multiply that by his hundred years. That Brahma then gets *liberation*, *Moksha*. The new Brahma takes over.

The new cycle starts all over again. So this is unending creation. My world comes out of my ideas and it dissolves into my nothingness. When I go to deep sleep, when I wake up, it starts all over again. This happens all throughout my life. When I die, everything gets merged into tendencies.

I will have no memory of my experiences, but I'll carry that fragrance with me of what I have experienced in this life, which will be the beginning of my next life. At an individual level and at Brahma's level, the entire Srushti is in that state. Bhagavan said, you can visualize this entire Jagat as your own *self*, just as you're visualizing yourself right now as a limited being. Bhuta Gramam Imam Kritsnam Avasam Prakriteh Vashat.

This cycle continues perpetually, because *Brahman* is beyond time. Time does not exist for *Brahman*. Time exists because we are perceiving events in space. Time is an interval between two events. If you remove all events, there is no time.

If I don't experience anything, there is no time. But I experience one event, then a second event -- this interval becomes time. This Bhuta Gramam Kritsnam, this entire group of beings, Avasham, without any choice -- as long as I have a tendency, I'm going to manifest that tendency. If I have desire, I'll act according to that desire. Visrijami Punah Punah, Avasam Prakriteh Vashat.

Because they are under the spell of *Prakriti*, the *Maya*. Therefore they do not have any choice but to act according to their own tendencies and vasanas. All beings are propelled to act according to their swadharma, according to their makeup of their own vasanas and desires. Even when they go into dormant state, those vasanas and desires remain in dormant state. When you wake up, those vasanas and desires come back again. And this cycle continues perpetually unless you get out of this cycle of becoming and doing.

Now the question Bhagavan answers here is: does that affect *Brahman*? Because he is the propeller, the prompter, the supporter of all this activity which is happening perpetually. Creation and dissolution are continuing. They cannot happen without the presence of *Brahman*. My day, my night, and my activity cannot happen unless I'm conscious of it.

As long as my *consciousness* is there, there will be a waking state for me, a dream state for me, a deep sleep state for me. The question is: is my *consciousness* getting affected by my experiences at an individual level? At the Samashti level, does *Brahman* get affected by these happenings? Bhagavan clarifies in this verse: Na Cha Mam Tani Karmani Nibadhnanti.

These actions of creation and dissolution which is only possible because I, the Supreme *Consciousness* is supporting it by using Maya. But the *Maya* is Brahma Shraya. It is supported by *Brahman*. There is no magician. You have to have magician to create magic. So that magic is supported by magician.

This *Maya* is supported by Brahman. But *Brahman* uses that *Maya* as the material to create this Jagat. Just as in my dream state, I create the experiences of my waking state as the material to create my dreams. No matter how weird a dream is, it is never based on something which you have not experienced before. It may be jumbled up of all the experiences. But all my dreams are based on my experiences, not on anybody else's experiences.

So *Brahman* creating this *Maya* as the material, creating this Jagat and then dissolving this Jagat into *Prakriti* again remain in its pristine state, unaffected by individual actions.
snippets.reflection:
Krishna describes cosmic cycles - at the end of each Kalpa (4.3 billion years), all beings return to Prakriti, and at the beginning of the next, they are sent forth again. This mirrors our daily experience: each night when you enter deep sleep, your entire world - your to-do list, your achievements, your worries - dissolves into dormant consciousness. Each morning, you wake up exactly where you left off. The architect who sleeps wakes as an architect; your unresolved problems remain unresolved. Understanding this cycle reveals something profound: nothing is truly lost or gained; everything is a manifestation from and dissolution back into the same source.

The crucial teaching in verse 9 is: "These actions do not bind Me" (na ca mam tani karmani nibadhnanti). Though Brahman is the support of all cosmic activity - creation, preservation, dissolution - it remains utterly unaffected, like the dreamer who creates an entire dream world yet wakes unchanged. Your consciousness similarly witnesses all your experiences - joy and sorrow, success and failure - without being touched by any of it. The witness is never the witnessed.

Daily practice: Tonight, before sleep, consciously notice how your entire world - relationships, responsibilities, identity - dissolves as you drift off. In the morning, observe how it all reconstructs. Ask yourself: "What remains constant through this daily creation and dissolution?" That unchanging awareness is your true nature, unbound by the cosmic dance of manifestation.
snippets.shortReflection: Tonight before sleep, notice how your entire world dissolves—your to-do list, your worries, your identity. Tomorrow morning, notice how it all reconstructs. What remains constant through this daily death and rebirth?

snippets.transliteration:
mayādhyakṣheṇa prakṛitiḥ sūyate sa-charācharam
hetunānena kaunteya jagad viparivartate

avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣhīṁ tanum āśhritam

verseTranslations: Under my guidance, Nature produces all things movable and immovable. Thus it is, O Arjuna, that this universe revolves.
Fools disregard Me, seeing Me clad in human form. They know not that in My higher nature I am the Lord-God of all.
Their hopes are vain, their actions worthless, their knowledge futile; they are without sense, deceitful, barbarous and godless.
snippets.commentary:
I am the source and I am also the final resting place for all things. Things come out of me and they will return back into me.

There is nothing really that can exist without me. As we said in that classical example, a ghost cannot exist without the post. So from the post's point of view, the post can say the ghost came out of me.

And once you realize there is no ghost, it also goes back into me. At any given time the ghost has no modifications or it never changed into ghost. But my ignorance and my perception has created this perception of a ghost.

In a similar way, Bhagavan says from me the whole *Prakriti* comes into existence. This world of plurality as you see, is because of my existence. If I'm not there, there is no world of plurality.

This world as we know is I. And the world only exists because the fundamental basic reality is the *self*. I know I exist because of myself.

You know you exist because of yourself. She knows she exists because of herself. But we think these are different selves.

Bhagavan says it's just me, myself reflecting through all of them. But we don't recognize it because of Mogha Asha -- vain desires. I think I am the center of my universe.

The world needs to revolve around my desires. I want things to be like this, I want the world to be like this, I want the market to do this when I invest. And therefore we do the wrong actions.

Because I have now considered this limited being as me, I now have my false desires. We know we have very little power over how things work in this world. But when we act, we forget what we know.

Even buying a gallon of milk -- so many people do so many things to bring that gallon of milk to your nearest Martin's or Food Lion. Then, and only then, can you go and buy it. But I think that if I have $4 in my pocket, I'm the king and can buy that milk.

That Mogha Asha creates this false notion that I am in control. And Bhagavan says Mogha *Jnana* Vichetasaha -- because of this false knowledge that "this is me and I can change this world as I want," we create a false notion of control. Rakshasim Asuram Chaiva -- these people are of the nature of Rakshasa and Asura.

Rakshasa is one who is predominated by the Rajasic nature. We have seen in Vedanta that nothing can exist in this world of time and space if it does not have these three qualities of Sattva, *Rajas*, and Tamas -- the fundamental classifications of the basic *gunas*. For any effect to exist in time and space, you need *Sattva*, which is the awareness that this exists.

Then there is the activity -- the intense activity we see at the atomic level, subatomic level, or even at the level of our daily experience. And then *Tamas*, the inertia for the thing to remain in its state as long as it can, until another force changes it. He said that those with the most Rajasic predominance are the Rakshasas, because they consider that their activity will give them control over their world.

And the Asuras are the Tamasic ones, with the predominant quality of *Tamas*. They rely on inertia. If I don't do anything, things won't change.

Let's keep things as is, don't change it. Not realizing that the nature of this world is Samsara -- constantly changing. In that Samsara, I try to keep things inert, as is.

That is the nature of the Asura. These two qualities make us forget the real nature of the *self*. In contrast to that -- Mahatmanastumam Partha, Devim Prakritim Ashritaha.

There is another group of people who do not fall into these two categories of Rajasic and Tamasic. The Rajasic and Tamasic are constantly interested only in material existence. They see their physical existence and say, "My goal in life is to maintain this existence and have as much pleasure from this world as possible" -- not realizing that this is a temporary existence in time and space.

But my real existence is infinite, permanent, immutable -- in the nature of the *self*. The other group of people, the Mahatmas, are great souls simply because they realize the nature of the *self*. Mahatmanastumam Partha, Devim Prakritim Ashritaha -- because they have taken refuge in the divine nature of the *self*, which is to recognize *Sattva*, the truth, that eternal truth which does not change with time.

Everything in this world is relative truth. Somebody says, "What is it?" I say, "It's a day outside." Well, that's a relative truth. It was not true at 4 o'clock in the morning.

It will not be true at 8 o'clock at night. It is true only now in this time. So it's called a relative truth.

But the truth which remains constant in any period of time is called *Sattva*, which I can say it was this 150 years ago. It is now and it will be for eternity. That's the universal truth, the *Sattva*.

Those who take taken refuge into this awareness of that immutable truth which is the nature of the *self*. My *self* is not this limited being which has started its life on day one time. When I was born and I'll die is time T2.

And I want to make the most out of this life. Between this span of T1 and T2 are those Asuras and Rakshasas. But one who says, "This is just a flicker in my existence.

My existence was infinite before and will be infinite after. I want to achieve that sense back, not get bogged down with this limited being" -- those are the great souls. They identify not with the limited *self*, but with the higher *self*.

Here is the example I have used many times, because I'm an architect. The space in this room is a conditioned space. Right now my association with this space is room space conditioned by these walls, floor, and ceiling.

But I also recognize that this space is universal space. It is here and it will be here, whether this building is there or not. The one who recognizes that myself will always be here, whether his body is there, mind is there, or intellect is there or not.

They are the great souls. Therefore they have taken refuge in the Daivi *Prakriti* -- this *Sattva*, predominantly Sattvic in nature. They recognize the ultimate truth about their own *self*.

Bhajanti ananya manasaha. Therefore they devote themselves to me with a single-pointed mind. Now obviously there are word connotations that come from our own experience in life.

Bhajanti -- with that kirtan and all that, you know. Bhajanti ananya manasaha, satatam. So constantly they are doing this.

But that's not possible in the literal sense. But we know that the Vedantic connotation of the word bhajanti means love. Love for the Divine is *devotion*.

Love is nothing but identification. The more I identify with someone, the more my love increases. The more I identify with the Divine.

So ananya manasaha means without any other thought -- without any other thought that this limited being is me. I'm not an architect, I'm not a father, I'm not a son. All these are superimpositions on me.

Amitabh Bachchan never forgets when he plays the coolie that he is Amitabh Bachchan. He never forgets while doing all these roles he plays. I too play all these roles, but I forget and get identified with them.

And I get carried away with them. The Mahatma never gets carried away. So bhajantim Ananya Manasaha Gnatva Bhut adim avyam.

Knowing that I am the source of all the beings imperishable. We typically see that the source get destroyed into you take a seed and seed becomes a tree. The seed is no more there.

Now I can say, okay, now I want the seed back. That's a perishable source of the tree. Bhagavan said, but I am the source of this universe.

All the being but imperishable never get destroyed. Because the creation is a *Maya* Post never became ghost. Therefore it never had to go into any transformation into something else.

So once you see the ghost, post doesn't go away. It remains exactly what it was before. Bhagavan says, knowing that I am the immutable, imperishable source of all the beings.

These Mahatmas wants to get back to their original *self*. At the immutable, imperishable *self*. They drop the identification with the limited.

Playing this part very efficiently in this world. But always the identification is with the higher *self*. Just as Amitabh Bachchan never forgets in Amitabh Bachchan.

But he is a coolie at the time. You know, say, Satatam Kirtayantah maam Yatan taschadiravratah. So now what will be my attitude once I have recognized that this limited being is not me.

This life is just a part I am playing for the time being. Before I was born, I existed as the universal being. After that all existed as a universal being.

Before this building was built, this space was here. And I can vouch for it because I live here long enough. Long before this building was here, this space was here.

After the building is built, there's room spaces here. And someday somebody will decide we can do better use of this land. And the building will be gone, but the space will be here.

I am here, I was here and I will be here. That's the eternal truth. Bhagavan says Satatam Kirtayantah.

Having known this, so what will be my actions? Satatam constantly Kirtayantaha. I am singing the glory of that eternal *self* that I am my Lord, who functions through me as this limited being. Kirtan du Visival.

We have a bhajan, you know, next week. So that's the kirtan. That's the only time we do kirtan Bhajan and kirtan.

This singing, with equally crude and noisy instruments -- it has its own place, for that time only, to occupy the mind. Because at least at that time, my mind is focused on those songs and the verses and what they mean. At that time, I'm not thinking of anything else.

Those who do any kind of art know this -- the mind has to be occupied with something. And if it doesn't occupy, then it wanders away. One whose mind is constantly attached to that understanding that I am not this limited *self*, this universal *self* is manifesting in this world.

There is nothing that can exist in this world without Him. And therefore there is no existence for anything else other than that. If God is all pervading, where are we? If we are here, then he is limited.

He cannot be all pervading. So if he is all pervading, there is no place for anyone else. All that I see is nothing but his manifestations.

So now that constantly when I see anything in this world, the thought at the back of my mind says, that is nothing but the Lord's manifestation. Whether that is good, bad or ugly. See, we have no problem.

We see something very beautiful, nice, and divine -- "That's God's manifestation." Early morning the sun rises and we see, "O God!" But when we see darkness and evil and still see his presence in it -- that's where the real test is. Then my Kirtan, Bhagavan says, is complete, no matter what I encounter. I know he pervades the entire universe and all its happenings.

Nothing other than him can exist, and therefore there cannot be anything other than Him.
snippets.reflection:
"Fools disregard Me, seeing Me clad in human form" (avajnanti mam mudha manusim tanum asritam). The Divine pervades everything, yet we fail to recognize it because we expect something extraordinary. We look for God in temples and sacred texts while ignoring the consciousness that animates every being we meet. The Divine is not hiding - it is the most obvious reality, present in every eye that sees, every heart that beats. Our failure to perceive it comes from looking for the wrong thing in the wrong way.

Those caught in Mogasha (vain desires), Moghakarma (vain actions), and Moghajnana (vain knowledge) live as if they are the center of the universe, believing their limited efforts can secure lasting happiness. Dominated by Rajasic (restless activity) and Tamasic (inertia) tendencies, they remain blind to the Sattvic truth of their own divine nature. The Rakshasa nature says "I will acquire and control," the Asura nature says "I will resist all change" - both miss the recognition that the Self is already complete.

Self-inquiry for this week: Examine your primary operating mode. Are you driven by endless activity toward acquisition (Rajasic)? Or by resistance and avoidance (Tamasic)? Neither brings lasting peace. The alternative is to cultivate Sattva - the quality of awareness that recognizes the Divine presence in all. Today, practice seeing the same consciousness looking out from every pair of eyes you encounter. What shifts when you recognize that the one perceiving through you is perceiving through all?
snippets.shortReflection: Track yourself for one day. Are you driven by endless activity, always chasing the next thing? Or by avoidance and resistance, defending against change? Both are exhausting. Neither is peace.

snippets.title: Day 120: The Great-Souled Ones
snippets.sanskrit:
महात्मानस्तु मां पार्थ दैवीं प्रकृतिमाश्रिताः |
भजन्त्यनन्यमनसो ज्ञात्वा भूतादिमव्ययम् ||

snippets.transliteration:
mahātmānas tu māṁ pārtha daivīṁ prakṛitim āśhritāḥ
bhajantyananya-manaso jñātvā bhūtādim avyayam

satataṁ kīrtayanto māṁ yatantaśh cha dṛiḍha-vratāḥ
namasyantaśh cha māṁ bhaktyā nitya-yuktā upāsate

jñāna-yajñena chāpyanye yajanto mām upāsate
