verseTranslations: I enter this world and animate all My creatures with My vitality; and by My cool moonbeams I nourish the plants.
Becoming the fire of life, I pass into their bodies and, uniting with the vital streams of Prana and Apana, I digest the various kinds of food.
I am enthroned in the hearts of all; memory, wisdom and discrimination owe their origins to Me. I am He Who is to be realised in the scriptures; I inspire their wisdom and I know their truth.
snippets.commentary:
So far we have seen Bhagavan saying that everything that you see, everything that you can perceive, and everything that you can experience is nothing but me. In the last few verses we have seen he said: the light which is from the sun, which illumines this entire world of yours, is nothing but my light -- it comes from me alone.

The light from the moon which nourishes the plants is nothing but my own light. And the fertility in this soil which supports all the beings on this planet is nothing but me. My mind, my intellect, which is aware of this world -- That *awareness* comes from him.

And this world which I experience also comes from him. Then he says, not only that this being is supported by me, but all this functions within the sentient beings which makes them living beings. I support those functions.

Aham Vaishva Narobhatva Prani Namdha Masridha. Residing in the bodies of all the beings, I digest these four types of food. Basically, as I said, our ancestors were fond of classification, so they always have some classification.

Foods are of four types. And once you look at what the four types of foods are, there's nothing left out. So any food that a being can eat, it gets digested.

Bhagavan said, by me residing in this body as this *eternal* fire, this internal fire. So everything I see, everything I hear, everything I experience -- there is really nothing other than the Lord. And this somewhat, if you really think logically fits into the normal belief, a normal declaration in all religion that the God is omnipresent.

Once something we have taken as omnipresent, there is no room left for anything else. So if we say that God is omnipresent in this world, then there is no room for you and I as an individual other than God. As we have discussed so many times from the physics perspective, if I say I am omnipresent in my chair, there is no room for anything else or anybody else.

So now everything in this chair has to be me. Whether it's my leg, it's my hand, my torso, whatever, it's all me. So Bhagavan said, I am omnipresent.

And therefore all the experiences illumined by your *consciousness* is nothing but me alone. So we have so far seen Bhagavan is giving his identity. What is the identity of the supreme Being? That there is none other than that being exist.

So the last verse 14 we say prani nam deha masirithah prana pana samayukta Pachami annam Chaturvedam. I can see at the macro level that the Lord is everywhere. At the micro level, the Lord is also in my body.

This body, mind and intellect come from this world. This world is nothing but his expression. But the functions within me -- which I think differentiate me from the insentient world called matter -- make me consider myself as something completely different than matter.

That's why my body is so spatial. Because I don't think it's a matter. I consider that's me.

But that me from the matter to me is because of these functions which makes me a living being. These pranas and apanas, all these activities happening in my body. And Bhagawan says that also I control by living in your body.

In the next verse it says, Sarvasya chaham Hrudhisan niveshtah matthaha smriti gnanam upo hanamcha vedeshcha sarve ham eva vedyo vedantakrut veda Videva chaham. So what is my relationship to the Lord now? He said, I am residing in the hearts of all beings. How do I know? This great Lord is everywhere, and that may overwhelm my intellect.

I am a seeker seeking my experience or realization of my Lord. Now he says, the light of the sun is me, the light of the moon is me. I am the fertility in the earth.

Then we give up and say, I will never be able to reach him. Somebody says, "Rajan, if you want to do something, why don't you call up the President?" If you tell me to call a project manager, I can think about it. But make a cold call to the President of the United States, Barack Obama? That really doesn't sound like a practical thing to do.

So we say, well, if Bhagavan is so supreme, then there is no way that I'll ever be able to get connected with him. So now Bhagawan said, no, that's not the truth. The truth is I'm residing in the hearts of all beings.

Sarvasenni, Vistaha, Matthaha, Smrutihi, Gnanam and Upohanam. Because I'm residing in the hearts of all beings. And because of me they have a memory.

Because of me they have *knowledge*. And because of me they have forgetfulness or *ignorance*. Everything which I know today is because of my *consciousness*.

I'm aware of my experiences, so it becomes my memory. I'm aware of what I have learned. So my memory has become my *knowledge*.

If somebody says what month comes after January? Well, I learned in kg, it's February. That's nothing but my memory. I consider that as my *knowledge*.

But it's actually my memory. All this, Bhagavan said, comes from me. I will only remember if I'm conscious.

Without that, I won't. But more important than this *knowledge* is also forgetfulness. If I remember everything that happened, there won't be any room for me to learn anything new.

The IT guys were telling me, "Rajan, our server is really getting to capacity now." We had been in business for 12 years and we keep piling all this data on it. I think it's a time for you to change the server. It's 80% capacity you really have to have.

So I said, well, I'll tell you what. We can't really afford a new server right now. Purge all the old projects which are done five years ago.

I don't need them anymore. Purge them so I can put new projects onto my server. Forgetfulness is the gift from God to us.

If we don't forget, we will not be able to learn anything new. All the bad memories of our childhood literally get erased from us. That's why we also recall our childhood as so good.

My college days were so good. Because the bad memories are erased. What you remember is all the fun you had.

Now there are some bad memories that remain there. But most of it get erased. So I had a nice childhood when I was growing up.

Because the Bhagavan has given a gift of forgetting things which is not useful to you. Forgetting things which removes all the unnecessary *ignorance* out of your mind. So you can fill that void with new *knowledge*.

Sarvasya Chaham Rudhisa Nivestaha. I am residing in the hearts of all. So we obviously in my heart Bhagavan is here.

And obviously you and I can logically say "heart" is not that physiological organ literally pumping the blood. It is the core of my being. What I consider "me" is my heart.

What is at the heart of Richmond city? What is at the heart of this community? What I consider the core of my being. Bhagavan said, I reside there. The core of my being is my *awareness* about me.

My *awareness* about me, makes me who I am. That has these good qualities about *compassion*, charity, love. But once I decide in there, when my God is invoked then I will have this good quality manifest.

When I am in a *divine* mood, then I will have love, *compassion*, charity, all the good qualities. When I am forgetting about my Lord, my being, then I will have all the negative qualities. Because those negative qualities are the product of my *ignorance*.

I hate somebody, I'm evil to someone. All these things are because of the lack of my connection with my core of my being, my heart, my Lord who makes me who I am. So Bhagavan says, Sarvasyacham, Hrudhi Sanniveshtah.

I am residing in all the beings at the core of their heart. When I am really aware of myself, I can only manifest my *divine* qualities -- love, *compassion*, charity. Whatever the good qualities we think of.

It's only when I'm devoid of those connections that I will have jealousy, hatred. He said, Matthaha Smritih. Because of me is the memory.

Because of me is the *knowledge*. Because I'm aware of myself, I have a memory. Because I'm aware of myself, I have a *knowledge*.

And because I'm aware of myself, I have forgetfulness. I am also our *ignorance*. I am as much aware of my *knowledge* as I am aware of my ignorance. "Rajan, do you know medicine?" "No, I know nothing about it." "Do you know architecture?" "Yes, tell me all about it." I am aware of my *knowledge*.

I am also aware of my *ignorance*. Bhagavan said, it's all because of my presence in you, the *consciousness*. I reside in you as your being.

I am the Vedas and I am that needs to be known. I am the author of the Vedanta and knower of the Vedas. Now Vedas, as we have seen, they are our scriptures.

What do they represent? They represent *knowledge*. The knowledge compiled by the sages becomes Veda. This knowledge encompass everything.

Utilitarian knowledge as well as the *divine* knowledge, secular as well as sacred. Now the secular knowledge obviously also come from my *awareness*. I learn things and I use it.

I am all this *knowledge* that is out there. And I am only the one to be known. And Veda in the end says what? The only thing to be known is your own *self*.

Once you realize yourself, there is nothing more to be known. Having reached that place, we have learned that no one comes back. That's what Veda says.

That's what Vedanta said. In the end of Veda, the section which deals with the Upanishads and the *knowledge* about yourself is called Vedanta. So who gave this *knowledge* of the *self* to the Rishis? Bhagavan said, I did.

And therefore there is no authorship in our Vedas of who wrote this Vedanta. There is no authorship because it is a revealed *knowledge*. That is what is remembered.

So I can say I thought about it many times. Honestly, I can tell you, I give some examples in my lectures. And I really sometimes feel good that I really thought about really neat example.

Then I read 's commentary and I find the exact same example in it. I said, how did that happen? I thought, I thought about it. What I really forget is I'd been listening to since I was 16 years old.

So all this thing which I think, I'm thinking fresh, new is literally come from what I heard since I was 16 year old. Now, I may not have understood the time, I may not have got the gist of it at the time, but things stay with you. Then we are really churning on that idea.

Things come out and now you think, I invented this idea. And therefore in Hinduism there is no originality. The only originality is with him.

Everything else we do is just relearn. So Bhagavan says, therefore I am the author of Vedanta. Now I am the one to be known.

Everything which I can consider is the quest of my life. If Bhagavan said, is me, know that I am at the core of your being. So how difficult would it be for you to know your core of your being? Not that difficult, Bhagavan said, as long as you turn your gaze towards yourself.

So these verses are obviously very contemplative verses and not really intellectual verses, but contemplative verses. But going back to our understanding of what is real, what is unreal, what is transitory or temporary, and what is permanent.
snippets.reflection:
These verses reveal the Supreme Person as the sustainer of all existence at every level - cosmic, earthly, and personal. Krishna declares that He enters the earth and sustains all beings with His energy, becomes the moon (Soma) and nourishes all plants with life-giving essence, and as the digestive fire (Vaishvanara) within all living beings, digests the four kinds of food. This teaching dissolves the boundary between sacred and mundane. The very act of digestion happening in your body right now is a divine function. The next time you eat, consider: the fire that transforms food into energy is not merely a biological process but the Lord functioning within you through prana and apana.

Verse 15 is especially intimate: "Sarvasya chaham hridi sannivishto" - I am seated in the hearts of all beings. From Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal. This means your capacity to remember, to know, and even to forget is a divine gift. Forgetfulness, often seen as a flaw, is actually a blessing - it allows old wounds to heal and makes room for new learning. The verse concludes by stating that the Lord is what is to be known through all the Vedas, is the author of Vedanta, and the knower of the Vedas. Today, reflect: if the Supreme dwells in my heart as the source of all my knowing, how far do I need to search? Turn your attention inward, to the very awareness that makes all experience possible, and recognize that the goal of all seeking is already present as the seeker.
snippets.shortReflection: The fire that transforms your food into energy right now—that's not just biology. Next time you eat, remember: the very act of digestion is a divine function within you. If the source of all knowing dwells in your heart, how far do you really need to search?

Now Vedas, as we have seen, they are our scriptures. What do they represent? They represent *knowledge*. The knowledge compiled by the sages becomes Veda.

This knowledge encompass everything. Utilitarian knowledge as well as the *divine* knowledge, secular as well as sacred. Now the secular knowledge obviously also come from my *awareness*.

I learn things and I use it. I am all this *knowledge* that is out there. And I am only the one to be known.

And Veda in the end says what? The only thing to be known is your own *self*. Once you realize yourself, there is nothing more to be known. Having reached that place, we have learned that no one comes back.

That's what Veda says. That's what Vedanta said. In the end of Veda, the section which deals with the Upanishads and the *knowledge* about yourself is called Vedanta.

So who gave this *knowledge* of the *self* to the Rishis? Bhagavan said, I did. And therefore there is no authorship in our Vedas of who wrote this Vedanta. There is no authorship because it is a revealed *knowledge*.

That is what is remembered. So I can say I thought about it many times. Honestly, I can tell you, I give some examples in my lectures.

And I really sometimes feel good that I really thought about really neat example. Then I read 's commentary and I find the exact same example in it. I said, how did that happen? I thought, I thought about it.

What I really forget is I'd been listening to since I was 16 years old. So all this thing which I think, I'm thinking fresh, new is literally come from what I heard since I was 16 year old. Now, I may not have understood the time, I may not have got the gist of it at the time, but things stay with you.

Then we are really churning on that idea. Things come out and now you think, I invented this idea. And therefore in Hinduism there is no originality.

The only originality is with him. Everything else we do is just relearn. So Bhagavan says, therefore I am the author of Vedanta.

Now I am the one to be known. Everything which I can consider is the quest of my life. If Bhagavan said, is me, know that I am at the core of your being.

So how difficult would it be for you to know your core of your being? Not that difficult, Bhagavan said, as long as you turn your gaze towards yourself. So these verses are obviously very contemplative verses and not really intellectual verses, but contemplative verses. But going back to our understanding of what is real, what is unreal, what is transitory or temporary, and what is permanent.
snippets.reflection:
These verses introduce the crucial distinction that gives this chapter its name. There are two Purushas in the world: the perishable (kshara) comprising all beings, and the imperishable (akshara) - the unchanging witness within. But beyond both stands the Supreme Person (Purushottama), the Paramatma who pervades the three worlds and sustains them. Consider this carefully in your own experience: your body-mind complex is clearly perishable - it changes moment to moment. But there is something in you that notices these changes, that remembers being young, that fears death - this is the imperishable self, still conditioned by its association with the perishable. The Purushottama is beyond even this duality.

The analogy of space helps illuminate this: room space is imperishable relative to the walls, floor, and ceiling that define it. But remove those boundaries, and "room space" as a concept disappears into the infinite space that was always there. Similarly, when conditioning is removed, your individual self (jivatma) is recognized as the universal Self (Paramatma). Krishna declares: "Because I transcend the perishable and am higher than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Vedas as Purushottama." Today, practice observing your experience through these three lenses: what is changing (kshara), what witnesses the change (akshara), and what makes both possible - the ever-present awareness that is neither limited nor unlimited, but simply IS.
snippets.shortReflection: Your body-mind changes constantly, but something in you notices these changes. That's still not the deepest you. Practice observing through three lenses: what's changing, what witnesses the change, and what makes both possible—the awareness that simply is.

snippets.title: Day 195: The Most Secret Teaching
snippets.sanskrit:
यो मामेवमसम्मूढो जानाति पुरुषोत्तमम् |
स सर्वविद्भजति मां सर्वभावेन भारत ||

इति गुह्यतमं शास्त्रमिदमुक्तं मयाऽनघ |
एतद्बुद्ध्वा बुद्धिमान्स्यात्कृतकृत्यश्च भारत ||
snippets.transliteration:
yo mām evam asammūḍho jānāti puruṣhottamam
sa sarva-vid bhajati māṁ sarva-bhāvena bhārata

iti guhyatamaṁ śhāstram idam uktaṁ mayānagha
etad buddhvā buddhimān syāt kṛita-kṛityaśh cha bhārata
verseTranslations: He who with unclouded vision sees Me as the Lord-God, knows all there is to be known, and always shall worship Me with his whole heart.
Thus, O Sinless One, I have revealed to thee this most mystic knowledge. He who understands gains wisdom and attains the consummation of life.
snippets.commentary:
We have heard these terms before in Bhagavad Gita and Vedanta, Purusha and *Prakriti*. We understood from this discussion that the Prakriti is the manifest.

Anything that which I can see, touch, feel and vouch for its existence is Prakriti, including my thoughts, my ideas. Because other people may not be able to vouch for, I can vouch for it that they exist. Anything that exists in the realm of my perception, feeling in thoughts is a *Prakriti*.

But that which supports this *Prakriti* or awareness is the Purusha. I am aware of this *Prakriti* because I am alive. If I am not alive, this body cannot perceive whether it is day or night.

So that conscious principle in me is a Purusha. That's what we understood. The *Prakriti* is changing every minute, every second.

At a micro level, my body. My body has been changing every minute. I may not realize it till I see my pictures from five years ago.

One good thing about these pictures on a website, we never change it. So I have a picture which was taken in 2003 on my website and anywhere else. So when the people come in contact with you in person, they get shocked.

Rajan, you know, look a little different. Well, I never realized it. But other people who say it or when we see our picture, we realize this is constantly changing.

What it was yesterday is not today. So that falls into the category of a perishable things and beings. This body is perishable.

But this body is supported by something which remains constant. This change I'm noticing in my body because something remains constant. That constant factor is gauging the change.

I used to look like this. I used to have all dark hair, all my beard was dark. That one who notices the change remains constant.

That the support for this change. Change can only takes place if there is something constant. So in my life, I, the *consciousness*, I, the *awareness* is constant.

So when we remember Our childhood memories we don't think that that was something a different person. I remember this happened to me I remember that I remain constant. Everything else about me keeps changing.

So at my micro level, there are two Purushas, two "me." One is perishable, which is the body, mind and intellect. One is *imperishable*, which is the one who is aware of these changes -- the one who is afraid of death. Otherwise, why would I be afraid if there is not someone watching and saying, "Looks like this body is going to go out"? People ask me all the time now, "Rajan, what's your plan?" I said, "What do you mean, what's my plan?" He said, "We're talking about retirement." I said, "I have no plan, because I feel the way I felt when I started NBG Architecture the very first day.

I'm the same person." "You're going to be qualified for Medicare in a couple of months, so I'm sure you have some plan." And at that time I started thinking, oh, is that so? Statistically, Indians don't really last longer than somewhere about the early 70s. That's 65 -- I probably have less than 10 years. If I have less than 10 years, I haven't even planned what I'm going to do.

Because I never feel old. That "I" at my level is always *imperishable*. We started out this chapter by saying that when I think about myself, it seems like my source is somewhere unknown up above, but my life is all here, spread all around.

The same way, now I look at it: when Bhagavan talked about the nature of the Supreme Being, everything that you see, perceive and feel is nothing but my expression. Right now I'm only worried about me. I'm not worried about whether you're going to retire or she is going to retire or he's going to retire -- what am I going to do? I'm also not worried about whether you people will be around when I die.

After I die, I'm only worried about what will happen to me. So at my level, Bhagavan said, in this Loka, Dvau Purushau -- there are two Purushas in this world. In my world there are two Purushas.

One which is perishable, that I see. Bhagavan said, nothing that you see is other than me. I only exist and pervade everywhere.

Everything you see, touch, feel and perceive is nothing but my expression -- including the perception of my own body, mind and intellect, which is deteriorating. I can't remember even my employee who has just left me three days ago. "She used to work here." Because the memory is not now as good as it used to be. So I see this perishable me, which is also the *Purusha*.

And I also see the imperishable one who doesn't think about retirement even now. Dvau Imau Purushau -- in this loka of mine, in this world of mine, there are two Purushas. One is perishable, one is *imperishable*.

Does the world end here for me? Beyond these two, there is a supreme *Purusha*. Right now that supreme *Purusha* I really have no connection with. So therefore I'm only worried about this Purusha.

The one I feel is imperishable. Whatever I feel is still as young as when I used to be a little child. Bhagawan said that beyond these two there is a *Purusha* which transcends both the imperishable and perishable.

And the example which we have seen is this room space is *imperishable*. Room, walls, floor and ceiling is perishable. We are doing some renovation next door.

So we say I'll move this wall here and do this because that's perishable. But we know that the space itself is *imperishable*. In relationship to the wall, floor and ceiling, this space is *imperishable*.

But if we remove this walls, floor and ceiling out of the equation, what happens to this *imperishable* space? It's not even *imperishable* anymore. If there is no perishable things in this world, the word *imperishable* means nothing, right? Because it is *imperishable* compared to perishable thing. Long-lasting battery, short-lasting battery.

Lifetime warranty -- but whose lifetime? The battery's life, or the manufacturer's life? Or that company's life? All of our contractors, we ask them we need 10 year warranty or 15 year warranty. 20 years warranty guy gladly give. 5 years from now you'll try to call him and say we have problem, we need you to. The phone number is out of service. So the lifetime warranty we get is not your lifetime, it's the lifetime of the company.

As long as companies, the warranty is good. But all these things are relative. But if you take the relationship out, what remains is absolute which you cannot really compare in this world.

So this *Purusha*, one is perishable, this body one is imperishable. Which is conditioned by this body, mind and intellectual. But if you remove the conditioning, what remains is absolute *Purusha* which is neither perishable nor *imperishable* but ever existing.

And that Bhagavan said is by nature. So he said Uttamahapuru Sahatu Annyaha Paramatma ITI Udahrutah. We heard the word Paramatma.

What does paramatma means? My atma is *imperishable* compared to my *self*. The body, mind, intellect. But if I don't have this body, mind, intellect, that atma is absolute.

Therefore it is param Atma. Not in reference to this. Our idea is that *imperishable*.

Bhagavad Gita said that I'm *imperishable*. Even if I die, I'll be nil bhatt somewhere. Bhagavan said Paramatma, it will be part of the infinite.

Therefore that supreme being which forms this being as me is a paramatma. Gives a very nice example. Even within a room space there is a pot space.

The space in the coffee cup is room space. The space remains in the room. But when I even remove the room, the whole room space becomes so.

When we take these layers out of identification, this is my mind, this is my body, this is my intellectual. They have their own identity and then I have my identity. The I which is my mind, my body, my intellect.

When you remove in this I, what remains is just an absolute *self*. My atma, not conditioned by my limitations is Paramatma. Your lokatriyam Avishya Bibhartya via Ishvaraha.

That Paramatma is supporting the three worlds I live in my three worlds. Waking dream and deep sleep. My waking world is different.

My dream world is different and my deep sleep world is different. I, the conditioned *self* is going through all these three experiences in my life. But the condition *self* is supported by whom? This room space is bigger, smaller, depending on where I put the walls here.

But supported by what? By the universal space. This is a part of that universal space. Yasmaat Aksharam Atito Aham Aksarat Apicho Uttamah.

Therefore Bhagavan's Yasmat Aksharam Adith. This *self* is even beyond imperishable. This *self* in me is much greater than this perishable Me.

That's what we take some solace in learning Bhagavad Gita that even if I die, I will not die. Bhagavan said, but that *self* is even beyond Aksharaha. Beyond this imperishableness. *Imperishable* as we have seen is only reference to the perishable.

So let's say my life is hundred years. But there are things here which are 5000 years old. Compared to me, that thing has existing forever.

But this time frame, when we completely remove the scale from our mind, what remains is absolute existence. No past, no present, no future. So Bhagavan said, Yasmat Aksharam Atitah -- beyond *imperishable* and perishable.

I am even supreme beyond this perishable and *imperishable*. Atah Asmi Loke Cha Vede Cha Prathitah Purushottamah. We had been hearing this word Purushottama.

What is that Purushottama? He said, because my real nature -- I the Lord, the Ishvara -- and I say Lordship is that which supports my existence. That is my Lord. That's when we call King a Lord.

Because my existence as the commoner is because of his *grace*. He allows me to do that. That's why he's the Lord.

In this case my Lord is him. Because my existence is because of him. Therefore in this world I am called Purushottama in the Vedas.

Purushottama is described in Vedas as the one which is beyond perishable and *imperishable*. And also the scholars and poets in this world has sung its glory as something beyond perishable and imperishable. And therefore Bhagavan said, I am called Purushottama.

Therefore this chapter was called Purushottama *Yoga*. *Yoga* of Purushottama. Right now I am completely yoked with this perishable and *imperishable* *Purusha*. I am very aware this is perishable me.

I also know this body is going to die. But I have complete identification with it. I also have some solace because I had been learning Bhagavad Gita for many, many, many years.

That something within me is *imperishable*. Bhagavan said, but I am Purushottama. I am beyond this perishable and *imperishable*.

Therefore I am called Purushottama. My own self, when it drops its relationship with this body, mind and intellect, this world, this perception, this feeling, these thoughts -- it becomes Purushottama. Yo Mam Evam Asammudhah Janati Purushottamam -- who knows his *self* as Purushottama? One who is Asammudhah, one who is undeluded.

We, whether we like it or not, are deluded -- fooled by the *illusion* that you are different from me and she is different from he. No matter how hard we try, this conditioning is so complete that we will not be able to get out of it. R.

Bhagavan said there is a state for a Gyani to go beyond this *illusion* or *delusion* that he sees all the time that his relationship is with the Purushottama and not with this *Purusha*. Sarva Vid Bhajati Maam Sarva Bhavena Bharata.
snippets.reflection:
The chapter concludes with both a promise and a proclamation. "Yo mam evam asammudho janati purushottamam" - whoever knows Me thus, without delusion, as the Supreme Person, knows all there is to be known. This is not intellectual knowledge but direct recognition. The word "asammudha" (undeluded) is key - our usual state is one of delusion, convinced that we are separate individuals competing with other separate individuals. The sage who sees through this illusion recognizes that the same Purushottama that animates his being animates all beings. Such a person, says Krishna, worships Me with his whole being (sarva-bhavena). This is not partial devotion squeezed between other activities, but total orientation of life.

Verse 20 calls this teaching "guhyatamam shastram" - the most secret of all scriptures. Why secret? Not because it is hidden, but because it can only be understood by a prepared mind. Krishna promises that one who truly understands this becomes wise (buddhiman) and has accomplished all that needs to be accomplished (kritakritya). Imagine that - nothing more to achieve, nothing more to become. This is the consummation of human life. Today, carry this question: What if my deepest identity is not the struggling person I take myself to be, but the Purushottama itself, temporarily playing the role of this individual? How would that change what I pursue, what I fear, and how I treat others who are equally expressions of that same Supreme Person?
snippets.shortReflection: What if your deepest identity isn't the struggling person you think you are, but something playing that role temporarily? How would that change what you pursue, what you fear, and how you treat others who are equally expressions of that same presence?

snippets.title: Day 196: Divine Qualities
snippets.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच |
अभयं सत्त्वसंशुद्धिः ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थितिः |
दानं दमश्च यज्ञश्च स्वाध्यायस्तप आर्जवम् ||

अहिंसा सत्यमक्रोधस्त्यागः शान्तिरपैशुनम् |
दया भूतेष्वलोलुप्त्वं मार्दवं ह्रीरचापलम् ||

तेजः क्षमा धृतिः शौचमद्रोहो नातिमानिता |
भवन्ति सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातस्य भारत ||
snippets.transliteration:
śhrī-bhagavān uvācha
abhayaṁ sattva-sanśhuddhir jñāna-yoga-vyavasthitiḥ
dānaṁ damaśh cha yajñaśh cha svādhyāyas tapa ārjavam

ahinsā satyam akrodhas tyāgaḥ śhāntir apaiśhunam
dayā bhūteṣhv aloluptvaṁ mārdavaṁ hrīr achāpalam

tejaḥ kṣhamā dhṛitiḥ śhaucham adroho nāti-mānitā
bhavanti sampadaṁ daivīm abhijātasya bhārata
verseTranslations: Lord Shri Krishna continued: Fearlessness, clean living, unceasing concentration on wisdom, readiness to give, self-control, a spirit of sacrifice, regular study of the scriptures, austerities, candour,
harmlessness, truth, absence of wrath, renunciation, contentment, straightforwardness, compassion towards all, uncovetousness, courtesy, modesty, constancy,
Valour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, freedom from hate and vanity; these are his who possesses the Godly Qualities, O Arjuna!
snippets.commentary:
So far in Bhagavad Gita, we have seen in the first six chapters who we are as the limited beings. Then the next six chapters we have seen, what is the nature of of the Lord, the one, the Bhagavan which I'm seeking? In the last three chapters, which is chapter 13, 14 and 15, we had been seeing how to differentiate the two and how to go from one to the other, from manhood to godhood. So the first thing we have learned in chapter 13 is how to differentiate between the field and its knower. Because right now we have a confusion about what is field and what is knower.

I, the knower, think the world is the field. Even your body, mind and intellect which you consider you, is actually part of the field. One that knows this field is the Knower. So you've seen the differentiation between the knower and the field. We also come to the conclusion in that chapter. The knower is only one.

Whether it knows to you, knows through me, knows through him, knows through her, Knower is only one. The field has many expressions, which we call *Prakriti*. The variety of manifestations in the Prakriti creates individuality. The same knower, functioning through these different manifestations, creates the individuality we call ego. Each ego thinks he or she is the Knower, while the knower remains one. So now the question arises for a seeker who is sincere: if the Knower is one, why is my *knowledge* different from your knowledge, and your knowledge different from his *knowledge*?

In the last chapters we have seen the qualities of the *Prakriti* -- the 3 Gunas. The Prakriti has these three qualities: Sattva, *Rajas* and Tamas. Depending on the permutation and combination of these three gunas in that particular individual, and as the light of consciousness shines through that equipment, the result will be according to the nature of that equipment. So these three *gunas* create various perception of the reality. Reality Remaining the same, you see differently and I see it differently. Something which is quite obvious to you becomes soul intriguing for me. And something so intriguing to you becomes so obvious to me.

That's because of the nature of our equipment. So to reach that transcendental *self* which we have seen in chapter 15, the Purushottama -- we've seen there are three levels of recognizing the all-pervading *self*. The first level is the perishable one which we can identify as myself, yourself, this world, my children, your children, my family, your family. We see that as a perishable world -- they come into being and will go away. But because we have come to the conclusion that there is only one entity which exists, which is the omnipresent Lord, even these transitory manifestations are also nothing but his *self*.

And therefore we call it the perishable *Purusha*, Kshara Brahman. Next, the Akshara -- the one who knows these changes are happening in me, in you, in him, in her -- is the imperishable *self*. So I know that my body is decaying, my mind is losing its grip, my intellect is fading. But the one who knows these changes are happening is the imperishable in me. Therefore we call it the conditioned imperishable *self*. This body is the outward expression, which is perishable.

One who knows this body is decaying is the *imperishable* self. But we learnt in the last chapter that the Supreme Being transcends both the perishable and imperishable. And therefore he is called Purushottama -- Supreme Purusha, Supreme Being. Because the qualifications of perishable and *imperishable* are invalid at that point. Knowledge is only in reference to ignorance. I can say my knowledge of the English language started when I was in fifth standard, because in reference to that *knowledge*, I was ignorant. Before my fifth standard, I was ignorant about English.

But if there is no *ignorance* ever, the knowledge has no meaning. Or if there is no knowledge to be known, the ignorance has no meaning. *Ignorance* about my own tail has no meaning because I don't have a tail. So when you remove the both perishable imperishable, what remains is the Supreme Being, the Purushottama. Having understood this intellectually, we have a difficulty grasping these ideas. So now the chapter 16 starts with the qualifications required to purify your mind and intellect to reach the level of clarity so that the knowledge of the supreme *self* shines through automatically.

It also talks about what is right now stopping this *knowledge* -- what are the impurities which are veiling this truth from me. My own *self* is not very evident to me right now. My own *self*, I'm seeing through my colored glasses of identification with my body, mind and intellect. I do recognize I exist. I do recognize that no one else has to come and convince me that I exist. But that existence I can only perceive in terms of my body, mind and intellect.

Just as I know the space exists, and I can perceive this space as room space. But only as long as the walls, floor and ceilings are there can I perceive room space. You remove all objects from this world -- perception of space is very difficult. So right now I do recognize myself, but in the context of my body, mind and intellect. I want to transcend this relationship.

How do I transcend? By purifying my internal instrument -- Antahkarana, mind and intellect. Antahkarana Shuddhi, purity of mind and intellect. So in Vedanta, the whole of mankind is divided into three categories. People who are *divine* -- those who have developed the *divine* qualities of mind and intellect -- are called Devas. Those who have demonic qualities, which bring you down to this world and bind you to this world, are called Asuras. Then there are the completely ignorant, completely indifferent about what is good and bad, called Rakshasas. And the goal of Bhagavad Gita is to help everyone.

So the goal of Bhagavad Gita is just like our president said: "I'm not only the president of the 51% who voted for me. I'm also the president of the 49% who did not vote for me. I'm the president of 100% of Americans. My goal as president is to help each and every American, whether they voted for me or not." So Bhagavad Gita is like that. See, normally we say Bhagavan will only help you if you pray to him.

Bhagavan will only help if you do good things. But Bhagavan says, my goal is to help all of you -- whether you are *divine*, you are Asura (demonic), or you are Rakshasa. Now, the completely ignorant ones -- there is no help readily available for them.

They have to go through the adversity of nature to destroy this mold in which their mind and intellect is right now imprisoned -- to break that mold so they can get out of it. So that's why we say about some criminal, we can understand why they did this. But then the law of society, the law of nature, or the law of some *divine* force will break their mold for them. There is no advice given in this chapter for them, but the rest of us either fall into demonic or *divine* qualities. This chapter gives us guidance.

So the purpose of this chapter is the topics we have already discussed before. We have indication in chapter seven and chapter nine about people who have the *knowledge* will understand this, but people with the deluded intellect will not understand that. Now we have a chance to elaborate on them and see what are the qualities I can introspect in myself which I need to cultivate more and one which I need to negate. So the chapter starts with Sri Bhagavan Oacha Bhagavan directly comes out and gives this knowledge without any introduction to it. Abhayam Sattva Sansuddhi *Gnana* Yoga, Vivasthidhi Dhanam Damasta Yagnascha Swadhyayavam. We have seen this in first three verses that 26 *divine* qualities are enumerated for you and I to use it as the litmus test.

How many of these do I have? Now, most of us write it off: well, these are for saintly people, not for me. However, if you carefully look at it, all of these are in you. You practice all 26 of them in your daily life at some level. But now it is our turn to look at these qualities. And what we have latently is our ability to cultivate them, so that they become my own personality.

So the first one I say is Abhayam -- fearlessness. Now we know where fear comes from. Out of *ignorance* -- when I am not comfortable about a situation, I am fearful. One time I took the Chamberlain exit. Somehow I thought I'm going towards VCU. I ended up on the other side.

And as I drove further I started getting more and more nervous about how can I take a short turn. Why I never been to that neighborhood ever before. Getting lost in West End is no big deal. I get lost in West End sometime, try to take a shortcut and then can't find a way out of that neighborhood. But I'm comfortable because I know this neighborhood, other side of Chamberlain Avenue. I did not know, so I was fearful.

Fear comes from *ignorance*. Therefore when someone who doesn't look like me, doesn't talks like me, does not dress like me, I am fearful of him. So Bhagavan says Abhayam, the first quality to be developed is Abhayam. And Abhayam comes from that basic understanding that no matter what the outward expression of the thing or being is, it is Lord's expression. So how far that expression is from me, as far as I am from my own *self*, there is nothing to fear in this world. So Bhagawan said Abhayam is the first quality a seeker develops.

We have heard that Alexander, going back, wanted to take a saint with him and said, "Well, you come with me. Are you not afraid of me? I can kill you!" The saint replied, "You can't take anything from me and you can't do anything to me. So I'm not afraid of you, no matter who you are." He had nothing to lose. If I have no fear of losing anything, nobody can make me afraid of him or her.

So Bhagavan said, Abhayam -- the first quality a seeker develops is fearlessness, and that comes naturally to me if I have purity of my mind and intellect. *Sattva* Samshuddhi -- purity of heart. As we had heard before, these qualities are obviously linked to each other. One cannot be developed without others being developed. Without the purity of heart, fearlessness does not come. If I don't have purity of heart, I'll always be fearful of others -- that they will take advantage of me.

People are going to walk over me if I don't behave this way. They will misunderstand me. All this fear is actually my own inbuilt fear of how incomplete I am. The more I know I'm incomplete, the more fearful I become. The more fearful I become, the more arrogant I will become. Therefore we see that people who have achieved a lot become more and more humble.

One of my friends had an encounter with Amitabh Bachchan. A whole group of actors were stranded at a New Jersey airport. Amitabh Bachchan was one of them, and he was telling me -- now this is obviously what I heard from him -- he said all these guys are jumping up and down about why they were stuck. He said Bachchan was peacefully sitting on one side. They were saying, "Well, put me in a five-star hotel" and all that.

Bachchan ended up in my friend's motel in a comfort suite. And he said he was so happy and peaceful.
snippets.reflection:
These opening verses present twenty-six divine qualities beginning with abhayam (fearlessness) and sattva-samshuddhi (purity of heart). Krishna teaches that fear arises from ignorance - when we do not understand a situation or person, we become fearful. True fearlessness emerges when we recognize that all beings, regardless of outward appearance, are expressions of the same divine presence. As the teaching illustrates, the more we know ourselves as unlimited, the less we have to lose, and the less we fear. Consider: What situations or people trigger fear in you? Can you trace that fear back to ignorance or unfamiliarity? Today, when fear arises, pause and remind yourself that nothing external can diminish your true Self.

The qualities listed here - ahimsa (non-injury), satya (truthfulness), daya (compassion), kshama (forgiveness), and others - are not exotic virtues reserved for saints. They already exist within you at some level; the work is to consciously cultivate them so they become your natural personality. Choose one quality from these verses to practice intentionally today. If you select arjavam (straightforwardness), notice moments when you are tempted to be indirect or manipulative, and choose honesty instead. If you select mardavam (gentleness), observe how you speak to those around you and soften your tone. Write down at the end of the day: How did practicing this quality change my interactions? What resistance did I encounter within myself?
snippets.shortReflection: What situations trigger fear in you? Trace it back—it's usually unfamiliarity or ignorance. The more you know yourself as unlimited, the less you have to lose. Choose one quality from today's reading and practice it intentionally. Notice what resistance arises within you.

snippets.title: Day 197: Demonic Qualities
snippets.sanskrit:
दम्भो दर्पोऽभिमानश्च क्रोधः पारुष्यमेव च |
अज्ञानं चाभिजातस्य पार्थ सम्पदमासुरीम् ||

दैवी सम्पद्विमोक्षाय निबन्धायासुरी मता |

द्वौ भूतसर्गौ लोकेऽस्मिन् दैव आसुर एव च |
दैवो विस्तरशः प्रोक्त आसुरं पार्थ मे श्रृणु ||
snippets.transliteration:
dambho darpo ’bhimānaśh cha krodhaḥ pāruṣhyam eva cha
ajñānaṁ chābhijātasya pārtha sampadam āsurīm

daivī sampad vimokṣhāya nibandhāyāsurī matā
mā śhuchaḥ sampadaṁ daivīm abhijāto ’si pāṇḍava

verseTranslations: Hypocrisy, pride, insolence, cruelty, ignorance belong to him who is born of the godless qualities.
Godly qualities lead to liberation; godless to bondage. Do not be anxious, Prince! Thou hast the Godly qualities.
All beings are of two classes: Godly and godless. The Godly I have described; I will now describe the other.
snippets.commentary:
We are all hung up on "estate" these days, because the Republicans want the highest value of the estate you can pass on to your children without any taxes. That's because we consider this estate as something which I have acquired and accumulated. Something which is rightfully acquired becomes mine, and everything associated with it I consider to be my estate. Now this estate I want to preserve, because I want to pass it on to my children even after I die. Therefore, I don't want the government to take it away.

Bhagavad Gita says that the only estate you will take with you is the quality of your mind and intellect. We have seen in previous chapters and in Vedanta in general that death is only for the body. The mind and intellect remain intact, identifying as an individuality by their own conditioning. The only goal in life, scriptures tell us, is to uncondition myself from this conditioning, so that Mama Atma -- myself, which I consider "me" -- is without any conditioning and becomes the Paramatma, the supreme *self*. The only difference between myself and the supreme *self* right now is that myself is conditioned by these limitations -- my body, my mind, my intellect. The body, I know, has its own limitations.

It was born at a time T1 and will die at time T2. That I consider my death. What I do not know about is the nature of my mind and intellect -- when it was born, when will it die? Our scriptures tell us that the death of the body is not the death of the mind and intellect. And therefore, to uncondition this mind and intellect is the goal of my life.

Therefore the scriptures say the only responsibility a seeker has is to purify his antahkarana. This Antahkarana Shuddhi is the goal of all the practices, all the learnings that we have. So this antahkarana is my mind and intellect. The nature of my mind and intellect will decide what kind of wealth I have accumulated over my existence as this mind and intellect. And this wealth is nothing but my experiences and my tendencies. So that the experiences are good and I have developed the good qualities. My experience was bad and I developed bad qualities that became my estate.

So the nature of this estate is now defined into two categories. First, that which brings me closer to my supreme *self*, the Paramatma. The qualities which take me closer to my unconditioned self are called *divine* estate. Second, the qualities which bind me to this world -- to these limitations and therefore to the sorrows and unhappiness associated with limitations -- are considered devilish estates. *Divine* is something which is beyond my conditioning.

Devilish is something which is tying to my conditioning. So this chapter defines those two estates which I have. And all of us have some *divine* and some devilish estates. You know, just like viz. How about your portfolio? There are some good stocks in my portfolio.

But then there are some really, really bad ones. Same way my mind and intellect has some *divine* tendencies and some devilish tendencies. But therefore we have heard that the Mahabharata war is a war in my mind and intellect. Few good thoughts are fighting too many bad thoughts, but few good thoughts. If they are aligned with the *self*, the Paramatma, the Sri Krishna, then the war will be won between these good and bad tendencies in my heart. Now what can I do proactively is to introspect regularly and constantly and see what is the nature of my mind and intellect.

Am I more on a *divine* side or am I on the devilish side? Am I gathering more divine qualities or am I gathering more devilish qualities? I will be only able to do that if I understand what is divine and what is devilish. Now it has nothing to do obviously with Hinduism or any particular scripture or any particular faith. These *divine* qualities are universal qualities no matter which faith I belong to or which scripture I study. Because this divine quality is Thou shall not kill non injury, *compassion*.

All that we have learned is nothing which I need to be taught. It is something that comes to me naturally. Even as cave people, human beings knew that something which I have gathered with my efforts, nobody should take away from me. And therefore a good person will not do the same to others. If I don't want somebody to take away from my efforts, I also shouldn't be taking away from somebody else's efforts. So that became one virtue for a good person.

Then there are all the others which I don't want others to do to me. I don't want somebody to hurt me. I don't want somebody to kill Me, I don't want somebody to cheat me. So now my good virtues are. I will not cheat anybody. I will not kill anybody.

I will not hurt anybody. One of the criteria of a good seeker is defined in Vedanta as: just as, even in my sleep, I can never think about hurting myself -- even when I am completely deluded, I can't think about hurting myself -- a true seeker, even while in his conscious state, will never think about hurting anybody else.

So the good virtues are nothing so sacred or exotic to us. Good virtues are universal -- accepted by all cultures, all faiths, and people of all caliber of intellectual levels. But we need to remind ourselves time and again so that we can introspect. So the first three verses which we had seen in chapter 16 define those 26 virtues which are *divine*.

In other words, if I develop those 26 in my internal instrument, mind and intellectual. I will get closer to my supreme *self*. My mind and intellect's true nature is pristine. That it has an ability to see the reality as is. It is what I have acquired and superimposed on it as my estates have clouded that ability. Therefore, we consider the little children are *divine*.

Little children are the reflection of God, because they see reality as it is. They don't really have biases. I never had a chance to see a little baby growing, because as I told you, I have only one son, and for up to three years I didn't even know how he was growing up -- he was with my in-laws.

But now my granddaughter has given me a chance to see that how a little baby grows from time of her birth to where she is right now, 15 months old. And I could say that gradually she's developing personality. She's developing likes and dislikes. Things which she consider is good for her and things not good for her. Previous to this, her stage is 15 months. She was completely oblivious about.

She knows what is good and what is bad, and that's about it. So our mind and intellect, its very nature, is pristine -- it can see through to the reality as it is. But this coloring of my likes and dislikes, which I have acquired, has created this veil or tint on it. So now I'm seeing this world through my tinted glass.

So which tint is good and which tint is not good -- that is what we had been discussing. The first 26 virtues which we have seen are universal virtues which, once developed, will purify the mind and intellect, bringing them to their own pristine nature. So I can see the reality of myself as it is. I start seeing that this *Self* is nothing

But the Paramatma is the supreme *self*, just conditioned by my own limitations. Then the next three verses talks about which qualities which are really binding me to these limitations. So the verse four says Dhambah, Darpah, Abhimanaha, Chakrodah, Parushyam. You assume the good virtues. Now what are the vices? What are the bad qualities I can develop by my likes and dislikes which can be harmful?

First is Dhambha hypocrisy to some respect. If you really introspect, we all do some kind of a Dhamba, something which I am not. I am trying to show enhancing your resume, Rajan, is absolutely necessary in this world. You have to say how great you are. You fake it till you make it. So when I came to this country, I obviously came from Africa and in somewhat of a trained by British system where an architect cannot write his name larger than 2 inches anywhere in the world.

So our sign boards cannot have the names more than 2 inches tall. You cannot market, you cannot go and advertise. People are supposed to come to me for design and I'm not supposed to go to them. So I was in Houston, I obviously did not have a job. And one of the person who had a contracting company, he was trying to help me. So he gave me a little project, tiny little project.

He said, but Rajan, we need a building permit and you don't know the system here, so I'll come with you to the Houston City hall and help you out. So we were standing in a line for the building permit application, and just before me is a Hispanic lady who wanted to extend her house. She was asking this guy and said, but I want a building permit to add this bedroom to my house. And the guy said, do you have plans? No, I don't have plans. Do you have an architect?

Well, you need to get the plans drawn so that we can give you a building permit. My friend standing next to me said, Rajan, tell her that you're an architect. Rajan, tell her that you're an architect. You can draw that plan for her. And I tell her, but how can I do that? She doesn't know me unless somebody introduce her to me.

I can go and tell her that I'm an architect, that's okay. And he'll just go and give you a card. I don't have a card, you know, and he got so mad at me. You're never going to make it in this country. He said, this country, you need to walk as if you're the only architect ever walked on this earth there is nobody as great as you are. That was my first lesson in American marketing.

Now we would consider a Dhamba. I know in my heart there are a lot of good architects. Much better than I am. At least I know where I am. But if I make that as my obsession to show the people it becomes a negative quality. First devilish quality.

Is Dhambha showing something other than who I am. Nobody as good as I am. That's an arrogance which is obviously over estimation of my own capabilities or evaluation of myself. Then nobody can cheat me. And that's the guy who gets cheated very easily. I kept telling him this is not right for you.

And he kept saying oh no, no. I've done so many businesses. I keep telling you you're going to get hurt on this project if you don't listen to me. He certainly was the easiest target to get hurt by others. Abhimanaha, these are the qualities even though I consider the helpful to me are actually most hurtful to me. Even when we are watching television or a movie only characters we like in them are one.

Who are the nice guys? We don't like the villains. All the people who are very arrogant and pompous. So how can we like in real life if we are like that? How can we expect other people? And in the end, in all the movies and television who get hurt, those villains get hurt.
snippets.reflection:
Verse 4 names six demonic qualities: dambha (hypocrisy), darpa (arrogance), abhimana (self-conceit), krodha (anger), parushyam (harshness), and ajnana (ignorance). Notice how these qualities are interconnected - when I feel incomplete within myself, I become arrogant to compensate; when I project something I am not, I live in hypocrisy; when my inflated self-image is challenged, I respond with anger and harshness. The teaching reminds us that the person who has achieved much often becomes more humble, while the one who feels lacking becomes more defensive. Today, honestly examine: Where do I project qualities I do not actually possess? Where does my self-conceit create friction with others? When someone questions my competence, how do I react?

Krishna offers Arjuna reassurance in verse 5: "Do not grieve, O Pandava, you are born with divine qualities." This same assurance extends to anyone sincerely engaged in self-inquiry. The very fact that you are studying these teachings, examining your own nature, and seeking liberation indicates the presence of divine tendencies within you. Yet verse 6 reminds us that both divine and demonic qualities exist in varying degrees within everyone. Rather than labeling yourself or others as wholly good or bad, use this teaching as a mirror. Ask yourself each evening: Did my actions today move me toward liberation (freedom from limitation and sorrow) or toward bondage (deeper identification with my limited ego)? Keep a simple tally and watch the pattern over a week.
snippets.shortReflection: When someone questions your competence, how do you react? Where do you project qualities you don't possess? The very fact you're examining yourself indicates something genuine within you. Ask each evening: Did today's actions move me toward freedom or deeper ego-identification?

snippets.sanskrit:

न शौचं नापि चाचारो न सत्यं तेषु विद्यते ||

snippets.transliteration:

verseTranslations: The godless do not know how to act or how to renounce. They have neither purity nor truth. They do not understand the right principles of conduct.
They say the universe is an accident with no purpose and no God. Life is created by sexual union, a product of lust and nothing else.
Thinking thus, these degraded souls, these enemies of mankind - whose intelligence is negligible and whose deeds are monstrous - come into the world only to destroy.
snippets.commentary:
As per some of the commentators, this chapter from 16 onwards, except 16, 17, 18 are elaboration on the ideas which are already discussed in Bhagavad Gita previously. But now we are elaborating on those ideas so that we can understand and apply in our daily life.

The idea which we have seen earlier in the Bhagavad Gita is that the soul is divine, your self is *divine*. But the imposition on the self by all the layers which you have acquired through interactions with the Prakriti is hiding that self from you. I can't recognize myself right now because of all the layering on this pristine *self*.

So we have talked about who I, the individual, am. We talked about who the pristine *self* is. Now we are talking about what created this layering.

In chapter 15 we talked about the Supreme *Purusha*. The Purushottama is beyond perishable and *imperishable*. This body is perishable.

The *self* is imperishable. The equipment which I have to transact with this world, this body, this mind, this intellectual are perishable. But the one who is supporting this equipment using this equipment is imperishable.

Then Bhagawan said that I am even higher than them both the conditioned self in me which I consider my soul, my *self* is imperishable and perishable self that I condition myself, my body, my intellect are the two perishable me and imperishable me. Beyond this is the Supreme Me which transcends both Me the perishable and Me the *imperishable*. Those are the ideas we have seen in chapter 15.

And then in chapter 15 we also learned how that all pervading, *imperishable* became an individual soul. It's a portion of mine which is as eternal as my real *self*. When associated with this world of Prakriti then acquires five senses in mind then it enjoys the world of objects through those five senses and then gathering those experiences it creates its own personality.

Now, while interacting with this *Prakriti*, I gain both types of experiences -- experiences which are conducive and experiences which are non-conducive. The tendencies which I acquire become my wealth. So when we say "my wealth" in our day-to-day life, it is all that I earned and acquired.

Now that has become my estate, it's my portfolio. So this chapter says I as the individual going through the variety of experiences from the day my soul started as an individual till today has acquired lots of impressions and built its own personality which has become my wealth, my estate. That estate has *divine* qualities but also some devilish qualities.

And as these verses now will describe, what are the differences between the two? So the chapter opens with the first three verses which defines all the *divine* qualities or 26 qualities we have seen in first three verses. These are similar to the verses we have seen before where the Kshetra Gna was described by 20 qualities. Kshetra was defined very elaborately in that chapter where Kshatragna was just given the qualities Amanittam oddam bitvam ahinsaakshantihi arjavam acharya upasana.

Because the *divine* can only be expressed through its own expressions. Outside my physical appearance can be described by my mind, can only be read through my actions. Expressions of my mind, through my speech, my actions.

So the *divine* is defined only by its expressions. And expressions we have seen in Kshatragna the Amani tum vadu. Their similar qualities are here now described as *divine* qualities of a being, a person.

The my estate then rest of the chapter now focuses on the devilish qualities or demoniac qualities. The reason for that is for us to know that the unique thing about ourselves is: it's very easy for me to detect *divine* qualities in me. Also, it is very easy for me to detect devilish qualities in others.

My own devilish qualities I'm either completely unaware of, or even if I'm aware of them, I have justification for them. But my *divine* qualities I'm very aware of and I can detect very easily. Well, I'm a very honest person.

I'm a straightforward person. All that I others see me other way around. So you ask Meena, my opinion about myself is very different than my opinion about myself.

We constantly see the demonic qualities in other but *divine* qualities in us. On the other hand, when I have to judge myself -- am I a *divine* being or a demonic being? -- I'll always say, maybe, I'm not sure, I'm not *divine*. So we are completely confused about what our real nature is all about.

So now Bhagavan clearly defines these qualities. *Divine*, as we said, is very easy to identify. But demonic is difficult when it comes to me. It's very easy for me to say that's not a good quality in others.

But the same behavior when I do, I will have a justification for it. So Bhagavan now goes into elaboration of why these qualities should be detected within yourself, how to detect them, and then how to avoid them. Verse 4 gave us in brief the devilish qualities.

He said: Dambhah Darpah Abhimanah Cha Krodhah Parushyam Eva Cha Agnanam Cha Abhijatasya Partha Sampadam Asurim. These qualities are born out of your Asuric Sampat. What you have acquired is not your real nature.

This Sampat is not your real nature. So as most of us at my age say, "We came from India with $8 in our pocket. Everything I have here, I acquired from the United States by working here." So we were born with pristine nature, the *self* without any quality.

And we acquired all these qualities -- of what? So, Dambha -- hypocrisy; Darpa -- arrogance. Now there are subtle differences between them, even though we feel they all basically fall into the same behavior pattern. Dambha, hypocrisy: something which I am not, but I'm projecting.

I'm not a very religious person, but outwardly I try to come across as a religious person. Darpa -- arrogance, I don't care. Abhimana -- *self-conceit*, a greater opinion about oneself.

Abhimana. Krodha -- anger. Then Parushyam -- harshness, whether physical harshness or mental harshness.

Agnanam -- *ignorance*. Bhagavan says, the more I associate with this world of materialistic *Prakriti*, the more I lose my identity with my true *self*. Agnanam -- they are Abhijatasya Partha Sampadam Asurim.

They are born out of your devilish estate. The qualities which you acquire from this world by attaching yourself to the materialistic values. So in simple obviously it is defined as *divine* qualities are one which are spiritual and devilish quality ones which are materialistic.

So ed that the whole humankind can be divided into two those who are more *divine* and those who are more demonic. And then he also goes into the third kind called Raksasis. Now obviously Sid is here so you have to be careful in defining this in historical terms.

But Asuras and Raxasas were probably tribes at one point of time or Asura is actually one of the gods. Then there was a split. So people who followed Asura went to Iran, and those who remained stayed here.

But as far as the ideas here: there are people who have more *divine* qualities or predominant sattvic qualities, who are closer to their real *self*. Those with more materialistic tendencies, who give more emphasis to enjoying the material pleasures, they are called Asuras. And Rakshasas are considered those who are completely ignorant about either.

They are at the animalistic level, left on the lap of Mother Nature. They don't have *self* efforts to improve themselves. So Bhagawan said here that these are the qualities which are considered demonic.

Dhamba, Darpa, Abhimana, Krodha, Parushyam and Agnanam. And then rest of the chapter elaborates on the behavior and the verse 5 says Devi Sampadvi Mokshaya. Why should I be focusing on the *divine*? Because it will liberate you from your *bondage*. *Bondage* with the identification with your limited self.

Right now I consider myself to be the limited being. The limitedness is creating all the sorrows in my life. I'm not powerful enough, I'm not tall enough, I'm not strong enough.

All those things which is stopping me to enjoy the unbroken happiness is because of my *bondage* to this limitedness. Once it is Devi Sampath Vimokshaya is for liberating you from your *bondage*. Nibandhaya Asuri Mata Asuri is considered to be binding you to this limitedness.

Masuchaha Sampadam daibim Abhijato Asi Bandava. But O Pandav, you don't worry, O Arjuna, don't worry. You are born with *divine* qualities.

And last time we had discussion about whether Bhagavan said that because you are a royal prince. It does not say anything about royal prince here. It simply says you are born with *divine* qualities.

Bhagavan just assured him that just the behavior you have exhibited in your life. I assure you that you are born in divine qualities. We all can be assured that we have *divine* qualities.

The very fact that on a Sunday morning you are learning Bhagavad Gita because of the *divine* quality. Giving assurance to seekers that if you are sincere about Liberating yourself, you need to have some courage. As I said, we have easy detection of a *divine* quality.

But when it comes to our judgment, we are not sure whether we are divine or not. So here is an assurance that because you are exhibiting *divine* qualities that you are divine. So the Master Chaha, do not worry.

I look back on my life and I see a lot of mistakes I made and now I am worried about whether this is my exhibition of my devilish qualities. The very fact that you're interested in liberating yourself tells you that you are exhibiting the *divine* quality. Continue in a path of your journey for seeking your *liberation*.

Now start making statements. Dvav Bhuta Sargo Loki Asmin Deva Asura Evacha Devo Vistarasahaprakhtaha Asuram Partha Meshrunaho. There are two types of beings in this world, Divine and demonic. *Divine* we have talked about at length in the previous chapters in Bhagavad Gita we have been talking about these *divine* qualities of the Supreme Being manifesting through all beings.

We have been describing in detail. Bhagawan said, so now I'll just focus on Asuri. I'm going to tell you Asuri in detail now.

So rest of the chapter now focus on the behavior of Asuri. *Prakriti* Pravritimcha Nivruttimcha Janana Vidhu Asuraha. Very first manifestation of demonic qualities. I do not know what should be done and what should not be done, what is the right thing to do, what is not right thing to do, what I should be engaging into and what I should refrain from, what I should stay away from if I can decide that Bhagavan said, this is the first quality of your demonic estate.

No Saucam, there is no purity. Purity at the physical level, mental level, intellectual. Now Socham na cha API acharaha na satyam tesu vidyate.

Those people with demonic qualities, they do not know what to do, what not to do. They neither have purity nor right conduct. They do not know the truth.

All these things are the manifestation of demonic qualities. So now we can start looking at ourselves and say, is that something I should be detecting in myself and correcting? And with that, I'll stop here because the rest is a continuation of this discussion. We are discussing chapter 16, Deva Asura Sampath Vibhaga *Yoga* -- *Yoga* of *Divine* and Devilish Qualities, or Estate, or Wealth.

We have started learning Bhagavad Gita from Lord Krishna, where he first gave us this scenario of Arjuna -- that Arjuna is a broken-down hero, a person who has all the strength, all the valor, all the training to fight his situations.
snippets.reflection:
Verse 7 identifies the first sign of demonic tendency: not knowing pravritti (what to engage in) and nivritti (what to refrain from). This confusion about right action was precisely Arjuna's condition in Chapter 1. The teaching clarifies that such confusion is not a personal failing but the natural result of an impure mind - one lacking saucha (cleanliness), achara (right conduct), and satya (truth). When you find yourself unable to decide what is right, recognize this as a signal to purify your inner instrument through study, reflection, and disciplined practice. Ask yourself today: In what areas of my life am I genuinely confused about right action? What impurities - desires, fears, attachments - might be clouding my discrimination?

Verses 8-9 describe those who believe the universe has no underlying truth (asatya), no foundation (apratishtha), and no governing intelligence (anishvara) - that everything arose by chance from the union of opposites. Krishna calls such people alpa-buddhayah (of small intellect) and ugra-karmanah (of fierce actions). This is not condemnation but diagnosis: when I see no sacred purpose in existence, I treat life - mine and others' - as expendable. Notice how your worldview shapes your behavior. When you act as if only material success matters, what becomes of your compassion, patience, and honesty? Today, consciously affirm: "There is a deeper order to existence. My actions have consequences beyond what I can immediately see." Observe how this shift in perspective changes your choices, even in small matters.
snippets.shortReflection: When you're genuinely confused about what's right, recognize this as a signal that your inner instrument needs cleaning. Your worldview shapes everything. When you act as if only material success matters, what happens to your compassion, patience, and honesty?
