verseTranslations: Giving themselves up to insatiable passions, hypocritical, self-sufficient and arrogant, cherishing false conception founded on delusion, they work only to carry out their own unholy purposes.
Poring anxiously over evil resolutions, which only end in death; seeking only the gratification of desire as the highest goal; seeing nothing beyond;
Caught in the toils of a hundred vain hopes, the slaves of passion and wrath, they accumulate hoards of unjust wealth, only to pander to their sensual desire.
snippets.commentary:
We have started learning Bhagavad Gita from Lord Krishna, where he first gave us this scenario of Arjuna -- a broken-down hero, a person who has all the strength, all the valor, all the training to fight his situations. But under the burden of the circumstances, he broke down and did not know what to do and what not to do.

So Bhagavan told him that the only cure for your condition is to correct your understanding about what is right and what is wrong, what is permanent and what is impermanent. Since the second chapter, it clearly says that your mistake is that you are identifying with your limited *self* and looking at all the other people through their limited equipment. But they are *imperishable* when it comes to the soul.

Their real being is imperishable, just as yours. So that was the correction Bhagavan wanted Arjuna to make the identification from this limited to unlimited. In Bhagavad Gita, the journey is to change your identification from the limited being that I think I am to the unlimited soul that I actually am.

Everything we have discussed so far in Bhagavad Gita is towards that goal -- changing my identification from the limited *self* to the unlimited *self*. So entire Bhagavad Gita up to chapter 15 has described that unlimited *self* and how to identify with that. And in chapter 16 now we are discussing what is that which is binding me to their limited self.

So as we have discussed, the first three verses told us about the qualities of the *divine* being or the *divine* estate. As we transact in this world, we are going to acquire wealth, we also accumulate other wealth. Respect, recognition, appreciation, and on the other side, disgust, criticism, all that also we accumulate along with accumulating the wealth which is generally our normal endeavor in life.

So these become our estate. Some are *divine* and some are devilish. Something which are acquired is pure and something we are called impure.

So Bhagavan gave us the first 26 qualities of the *divine* estate. And then in the fourth verse he gave another six qualities of the devilish estate. So he said, the *divine* is quite obvious.

Most of us recognize divinity when we see it. And as we have discussed last time, it is easier for us to find divinity in us. For my mind to detect good quality in me is easy, very difficult for my mind to detect the negative tendencies in me, but it is very easy for my mind to see negative tendencies in others.

That person is very hypocritical. Well, he is doing it for *ego* only. We can very clearly recognize it, but it is very difficult for us to recognize in ourselves.

So this chapter takes upon itself to describe in detail what would be the behavior of a person who is predominated by negative tendencies, which in this case we call asuric tendencies. So when we see this behavior in others, it is easier to detect. But when I do something similar, I consider that as well very, very minor or well, this is the way the life works.

If I don't do it, then people will trample over me, I'll be a doormat. So my behavior I can justify saying that's how you survive in this world. But Bhagavan makes it very clear that if you detect this type of behavior, this behavior is very negative for your evolution, for your goal of *liberation*.

So he said there are two types of one helps you to liberate yourself from the limitation. Other will be binding you to this limitation. The more you try to satisfy your desires to get happiness through material goals, the more you will be binding yourself to these limitations.

Pravrittim nivrittim cha janah na viduh asurah. The first indication is that the person does not know what to get engaged in and what to stay away from. I do not know what to do and what not to do -- which is what Arjuna's situation was in the very first chapter.

He did not know what is right for him. Bhagawan is not saying the Arjuna is asura, but the behavior he exhibited was clearly of asuric tendency. So something in him which was not allowing him to decide what is right and what is wrong.

But once I know that that's a negative tendency Pravrittimcha nivruttimcha janahanna vidhu asuraha those who have the predominant qualities, they will not know what to do, what not to do. Na saucam, na apiyacharah na satyam teshu vidyate they will not have purity, cleanliness also na satyam teshu vidyate. They will not be able to tell the truth.

And it is not to put them down that Bhagavan is saying this. It's actually somewhat of a pity for them that they're incapable of doing so. They're incapable of living an honest life, incapable of telling the truth.

Because they're so afraid that telling truth will put them in trouble. In our daily life we call it white lie. Because you know, telling truth is going to put me in trouble.

Well, you really don't want to say what you really think about. They will say generally around looks good. So that basically is my incapacity to tell the truth.

These people, when look at overall life, they are just not capable of telling truth because of their *desire* to protect what they consider is giving them happiness. And then he continues. Asatyam a pratishtam te jagat ahuhu Anishwaram.

This statement relates to what we have learned so far in Bhagavad Gita. In Bhagavad Gita we have learned that the nature of the *self* is Sat chit in Ananda that Sat is ever existing. We also learned that Sat truth is something which is consistent in all three periods of time.

In the past, in the present and future. Something which was true in past has to be true today and will also be true tomorrow. So that is considered Sathya.

But that which is not consistent, something which was true yesterday, which is not true today. At some point it was true. Everybody agreed with each other.

Other will all fall down at the edge of the earth. But now we know that that's not true. So that was not true.

Now what we know was true then even though we did not know it. It is true today and will remain true tomorrow. The people with asuric tendencies, they think that this world is asat.

In a sense it is impermanent. It came in existence by chance and will perish. That means it's not permanent or pratish.

It just by chance occurring. It happened Te jagat ahuhu an ishwaram. And there is no controller.

There is no central authority who govern the laws of nature. Their view is it all came about by an accident. Will remain in this situation for a while and will disappear.

There is no basis for this world to exist. There is no fundamental substratum which supports this universe. Universe came in Existence by accident will get destroyed by accident, basically.

Or pratishtham te jagat ahu Anishwam. This is the worldview, a person is a materialistic view. When I try to analyze the truth in this nature through pure physical science, only then obviously the only thing I can find is these two came together by some accident.

These elements came together by accident and then it happened this. Then other things happened by accident and then this happened this. So starting from the Big Bang, we can say Big Bang occurred.

Why it occurred we don't know. But it's an accident. It occurred and after that it started expanding and then hydrogen became helium.

And all this is just an accident without any basis. Anishwaram There is no controller who is controlling the laws of nature. Aparaha paraha sambhutam.

By coming together two opposites. Kim annyat kaama haithu kam. So the progeny or the continuing of this life on this planet came out by just accident.

By coming two together and for the only purpose fulfilling *desire*. There was no master plan, there is no underlying truth, there is no substratum. But it just all chance occurring.

This is the view of the materialistic atheistic people. They have no *faith* in any underlying reality for this world. Etam drastim avastabya nastaatmanaha alpa buddhayaha.

Obviously this is a direct criticism from the Gitacharya that these people are wrong. They are seeing this from a very narrow perspective because they are viewing this world from a very narrow perspective. So when I see my life as a living being and I just analyze from a chemical perspective, electrical perspective, this is just a pure machine.

It came together and it is pumping blood through the pumping *action*. And I can define everything in a mechanical term, in a physical term, in a chemical term, and say this is me. But what is it that keeping all the systems together, I really don't have an answer.

Simply saying it's just all working together. Physics came together, science came together. So basically you can see this life either as something *divine* which is supporting it, or simply say this is all just chance occurring.

There is a book I have read called Brief History of Almost Everything. It's a fantastic book. It explains right from the Big Bang to where we are today in a very succinct manner.

His conclusion is that we as human beings existing on this planet is almost a chance. That one in a million odds that happen thing and it happened and continue happening and we are still existing. But anything could have gone wrong and we wouldn't have been here.

So basically you're saying that maybe just a chance that we have become who we are. So here Bhagavan is saying that these people are looking at the world from a material perspective, analyzing what's happening from a material perspective. They're coming to the conclusion it's just chance occurring.

Why I am not tall enough and other guy 7ft tall is just a chance occurring. So Bhagavan said that having such view Nast Atmanah they are destroying their own *self* because they are negating their own *self*. They are not even recognizing that there is underlying reality.

Called myself Alpa Buddhaya. They have intellect they are obviously analyzing. They are using all the faculties to understand this world.

But from a very narrow perspective. Alpam Buddha Fools it basically says very narrow perspective. Prabhavanti Ugrakarmanah Shayaya Jagato Ahitah.

So the actions are very harsh because they are not recognizing the underlying unity of our things and being. You can take example of vegetarianism. The one underlying theme of vegetarianism is that every life has right to survive and live.

So you have to inflict as little harm to a life to support yourself. But if I don't have that view, then obviously killing other animals may be justified. So Bhagawan said that because they have a narrow perspective, their actions are harsh.

Shaya Jagato Ahithaha because of the misunderstanding of how this universe work, they are the enemies of the world for its destruction. You can relate to our green movement about saving the planet. Now obviously there are a lot of people coming out saying all this thing is a hoax.

We really don't need to preserve anything. This planet will preserve itself. In fact, I just read that somebody written a book that actually the global warming will be very good for farming.

There are more warmer weather and it will make people rich. So you can look at it from any perspective and your perspective will decide how you're going to act in this world.
snippets.reflection:
Verse 10 describes those driven by dushpuram kamam - insatiable desires. The key word is "insatiable." A natural desire (I am thirsty, I drink water) is fulfilled and ends. But obsessive craving (I must have more, bigger, better) can never be satisfied because it arises from an inner emptiness that no external object can fill. The verse also mentions asuchi-vratah - impure resolves, actions taken without consideration of their ethical consequences. Examine your desires today: Which are simple needs that can be met and released? Which are obsessions that keep growing regardless of what you acquire? Choose one insatiable desire and ask: What inner lack am I trying to fill with this external pursuit?

Verses 11-12 paint a vivid picture: those bound by hundreds of ropes of hope (asha-pasha-shataih baddhah), slaves to desire and anger (kama-krodha-parayanah), accumulating wealth through unjust means (anyayena artha-sanchayan). Notice the progression - endless hoping leads to attachment, attachment to frustration, frustration to unethical action. The teaching uses the powerful image of being "bound by hundreds of ropes." Each unfulfilled desire is another rope. Each resentment is another knot. Today, identify one "rope" that binds you - perhaps an expectation about how someone should treat you, or an attachment to a particular outcome. Practice releasing it, not through suppression but through understanding: "This hope is creating my bondage. I can act appropriately without being imprisoned by the result."
snippets.shortReflection: Examine your desires: Which are simple needs that can be met and released? Which are obsessions that keep growing no matter what you acquire? Each unfulfilled expectation is a rope binding you. Identify one today and practice releasing it—not through suppression, but through understanding.

verseTranslations: This I have gained today; tomorrow I will gratify another desire; this wealth is mine now, the rest shall be mine ere long;
I have slain one enemy, I will slay the others also; I am worthy to enjoy, I am the Almighty, I am perfect, powerful and happy;
I am rich, I am well-bred; who is there to compare with me? I will sacrifice, I will give, I will pay - and I will enjoy. Thus blinded by Ignorance,
snippets.commentary:
We have seen that these are the qualities of my mind. Even though it seems like it is describing two sets of different people, one are *divine* and one are devilish.

And as if we are dividing this world again into divine and devilish. The purpose of these qualities to be described in Bhagavad Gita is to understand our own mind. Our own mind has this both qualities, the *divine* and devilish, depending on which one we promote, either we'll be liberated or will be bound more and more into this world of limitations.

So the last verse we had seen last time says Asa Pasas Satayi Baddhaha, the person who is not knowledgeable enough about what will liberate him and what will bind him by depending on this notion that the sense enjoyment is the only purpose of life. By hook or crook, I should achieve what I want. They will be more and more bound by unlimited *desire*, Asha Pasa, bound by this *bondage* of desires.

You know, satay, that means innumerable desires. And therefore they will do anything which is either appropriate or inappropriate. They will try to achieve, acquire, hoard things which they think will give them the happiness by even illegal means.

Inappropriate means continuing in the same dialogue as we have seen, Bhagavan now describes what will be the tendency or the thinking of these people. There's not really much to elaborate on it. Just as we have seen that the first three verses which describe the *divine* quality, there is not really much to be discussed about.

These are universal qualities. Even cavemen knew what is right and wrong. Somebody should not take the food which I have acquired with my labor.

Therefore, if I do that to others, it will be wrong. I don't want somebody to kill me, and therefore killing somebody is bad. These are universal values which every human being from the dawn of the civilization know.

In the same way, the tendencies and thinking of a devilish mind that we are going to be discussing also don't require much explanation. Why? Because we all have experienced this at some point or other, at some level or other. Except that at that time, I did not know that my thinking was going to create more unhappiness for me.

When I was thinking about that, I was thinking I'm doing this to get more happiness, for financial security. I put more and more money into the stock market, and as it grows I get the statement every month -- it made 8%, then next month 10%. Feeling pretty good.

Except when it collapsed. Didn't have the courage to open up your statement. But while I was doing that, I thought, I'll get this and then I'll also get this, and therefore I'll be completely secured.

We didn't think it through -- we work all our lives so hard. I have not come across a single person who says, "I really need to work hard in my life, but I'm enjoying it." Everybody thinks the same thing. What I was thinking all the time was: Idam Adya *Maya* Labdham -- I have gained this today.

Today I can say I have this. I reconcile my statement of what my assets are at the end of the year, for taxes or whatever. "Boy, that's pretty good." Or, "Well, at least I have this." And then what is my next thought? Imam Prapsye Manoratham -- I have this, but I will also get this. What if the financial planner says, "Okay, well you need to have this to retire at the age of such and such.

This many times your current income -- you will need this, and therefore you need to do the following." So you start planning. The first time a financial planner, a friend of ours coming to Chinmaya Mission in Dallas -- I was pretty young at the time. I was like 30 something.

And he looked at them and said you need million something dollar to retire. I don't think I'll ever have a million dollar. At the time I was probably making like $35,000 a year and the guy was trying to tell me I need million dollar to retire.

You forget about it, okay? I'm going to work till I die. No planning required. Because when you see that I have this, I need to achieve this or work hard.

Rajan, you have to have at least this much when you retire. I have this right now. This is a common thinking.

Nobody will label that as devilish. Bhagavan says that's the quality which binds you to this world of constant changes and disappoints you more times than you think it will. Idham asti idam API me bhavishyati punardhanam.

And this wealth shall also be mine in the future. It's simple planning. I acquired this, and I'll work a little hard and do this project, then invest here, and then I'll get that.

Bhagavan says that may be okay for planning purposes, but when that becomes your obsession, then it has a sure capacity for failure. You should be planning. I can never forget this thing in my life.

I bought my first house in Dallas, Texas in 1984, just before the election. I guess it was the Reagan second election. And they told me that after the election the prices will go so out of control that you won't be able to buy.

So you should buy before the election. Says, okay, you buy this house, $150,000 minimum, it will have 5% appreciation. You have compounded 5% for 10 years.

The value of this thing will be this. Oh boy, that's pretty good. They say that's guaranteed 3 to 5%.

It may go up and it's guaranteed. I sold that house, the one which I bought in 1984, in 2000. Now you apply that formula, 150,000.

Should have been at least $350,000, right? I sold it for $10,000 more than what I bought in 1984. And as if I have not learned the lesson yet, I bought a house in Northern Virginia where they say it was Dallas. You know, that's an oil dependent economy.

It goes down or it goes up. We are federal government dependent economy. Guaranteed 20% appreciation every year.

You can look at it last five years and you will see it. I bought a house again in 1988, Northern Virginia, in Fairfax. And again I said, well, they say 20%.

I'm going to be on 5%. Okay, at least I'm safe. I projected in about 10 years, eight years, five years.

I bought it in 1988, sold it in 1996 for exactly $6,000 more than what I had bought for. I made $6,000 after eight years owning that house in Fairfax, Virginia. We plan, but what will come out of my actions is not guaranteed.

Bhagavan said, there's nothing wrong in planning. That's not in a devilish pursuit. What devilish pursuit is, if this doesn't happen by hook or crook, I will make somebody a Scapegoat and get my money.

So therefore it says Idamasti Idham Apimi Bhavishati Punardhanam. This is mine and this will also be mine. That which I have projected at a 5% appreciation that shall also be mine in 10 years.

I can say this is what I have. This is its value today. What will happen 10 years from now only he knows.

And whoever after 10 years has to buy this house knows. So it is the attitude of my mind makes the same thing either *divine* or devilish. I took care of this competition.

Obviously in those days they were enemies and they were killing each other. But in a normal day to day even they say I never have killed anybody. So I never said I killed this person.

But we do mentally all the time. I killed this competition. He was trying to be the VP of the company.

But I really manipulated. I went around and talked to all the other bosses and I really pushed him down. And now I got the promotion as vp.

That's I who killed him for that purpose. So Asaomaya Hataha Satrahu who was my enemy who is in the path of my happiness. My enemy is the one who is obstructing me to be united with my happiness.

I killed this person, initiator Aparanape and the others who I think will be on my way, I will kill them too. It always gives me a kick. Anytime I read this Rasi Bhavishya we get this South Carolina Sati magazine and only thing I read is honestly the horoscope.

Because I have nothing to do with all these businesses in South Carolina. Only thing I can relate to is that last page which says your monthly horoscope. And this guy constantly warns me.

At least the Aries who I am, you know, born in that sign. Be careful about the people around you. They may be planning to harm you.

Now what do you think? My thinking would be well look at Meena, Pourvi, Neeraj, little Medha. They must be all planning something against me or my employees or my friends. This is just insecurity.

We bank on people's insecurities. Because if you don't take these annuities the market may go down. You will have no security when you are retiring.

You need a guaranteed income. Annuities will give you this guaranteed income. He fails to tell you that those annuities cost lot more than any other investment you would do.

They are making money in your insecurities. What will happen when I return If I don't have money they say okay we'll take care of it. But we'll take part of your money and put it in our pocket and make you feel good that you will have the guaranteed income.

I took care of this computation, this enemy, even the others I'll take care of them too. Therefore I will be secured. When I'm doing this, my state of my mind is I am the Lord of my being.

I take care of myself. Not only I take care of myself, I take care of all people around me. What would happen to them had I not been doing what I am doing.

All these people are dependent on me. Bhogihi and I'm enjoying it. All these efforts which I'm putting and gaining this I have got that I'll be getting.

I'm the Lord of lord is on whom my existence is dependent on. So in the feudal system whether you live or die, the way you live is dependent on the Lord. He decides how much money there was no unions and nobody decides how much to give it to the workers.

He decides whatever he has to give. So therefore he's the Lord and you're the commoner. Ishwara Same he decides how this world is going to function.

So when I decide that I am the Lord of my Sansar I decide in old Indian system the head of the house will tell how everyone should leave in that house. I think that I control everybody and everything. Bhogi and I'm enjoying the fruits of my actions.

I'm a successful one. What you have accomplished in your profession and it's admirable and what you accomplished in your wealth and it's all admirable. Guy doesn't know the other side of the story.

What I not accomplished and where I have failed. It is okay for others to think about that. When I start thinking about my own accomplishments that's where the problem starts.

It's perfectly okay for us to admire the people who accomplished some great things such as Isaac Newton or Bill Gates or Steve Jobs.
snippets.reflection:
These verses expose the inner monologue of the ego-driven mind: "This I have gained today; tomorrow I will get more. This wealth is mine; more shall be mine soon. I have defeated this enemy; I will defeat others. I am the lord, the enjoyer, successful, powerful, happy. I am rich and well-born - who is equal to me?" Read these statements slowly and notice which ones resonate uncomfortably with your own thought patterns. This is not about shame but honest recognition. When we reconcile our assets, review our accomplishments, or compare ourselves favorably to others, we are walking the edge of this mindset. The teaching does not condemn planning or achievement - it warns against the intoxication that comes when success inflates the ego rather than humbling it.

Verse 15 reveals the final delusion: "I will sacrifice, I will give, I will enjoy" - even spiritual and charitable acts become corrupted when performed for ego-gratification. The person described here makes donations to see their name on plaques, performs rituals to impress others, and serves the community for recognition. Examine your own generous acts: Do you give anonymously, or do you need acknowledgment? Do you serve quietly, or do you need others to notice? Today, perform one act of kindness or generosity that no one will ever know about. Notice what resistance arises when your ego cannot claim credit. This practice reveals how deeply ajnana (ignorance) has penetrated even our noblest intentions.
snippets.shortReflection: Read these slowly: 'I've achieved this. I'll achieve more. I'm successful, powerful, happy. I'm rich and well-born—who compares?' Which statements make you uncomfortable? That's not shame—it's recognition. Today, do one generous act that no one will know about. Notice the resistance when your ego can't claim credit.

verseTranslations: Perplexed by discordant thoughts, entangled in the snares of desire, infatuated by passion, they sink into the horrors of hell.
Self-conceited, stubborn, rich, proud and insolent, they make a display of their patronage, disregarding the rules of decency.
Puffed up by power and inordinate conceit, swayed by lust and wrath, these wicked people hate Me Who am within them, as I am within all.
snippets.commentary:
The divine and devilish qualities are the estates. This is the only estate you and I will carry with us when we die. All other estates will remain. But these qualities or tendencies of my mind, which are both as some *divine* tendencies and some devilish tendencies, I will carry that as my estates and I'll start from there. You've seen so far that this *divine* tendencies will liberate me from my limitations.

The veilings on my mind which is right now is not letting me see the reality as is that myself and the supreme *self* is one and the same. On the other hand, the devilish qualities or the aspheric tendencies which in reality all it means is it binds me to this manifest world and therefore I will be more covered with ignorance from my own *self*. And therefore it is very important for me to understand what are these qualities. So in the beginning we have learnt about all the *divine* qualities and they are universal as we have said. So therefore there is not really much explanation needed. I should treat others just as I would like others to treat me.

Such *divine* qualities in if I practice it will liberate me from my limitations. But more and more I get bound to this world of manifestation. This is me and this is the world. This I want and this I want to avoid. It binds me more and more to this world. And therefore it is very important to understand how this thing works.

So we have seen so far that asuric tendencies make people believe that there is nothing more to this world than enjoy the sense gratification or satisfying the desires that I have, the lust that I have, and who knows, because I cannot see what was before my birth and I cannot see what was after my birth. Well, let's just consider this life is the only life that I have. And therefore let's make the most out of this life by by hook or crook. So I have now come to the conclusion that hoarding more and more wealth will make me happy. I will achieve that by any means, any unjust means. Even though I know this is not right, I will go ahead and do it anyway.

And once I get into that mode of mind, my situation would be that I will be constantly worried. Chintama Aparimayamcha AP I'll be overwhelmed by the worries. I'm always worried about things which I don't have. Once I acquire it, I'll be always worried about how to safeguard it. Because just as I took it away from somebody, somebody will take it away from me. So this mode of mind will be constantly be engulfed by these worries.

But then at the same token my *ego* will start rising into its power and start thinking look, I have acquired this. These are the natural tendencies of my *ego*. Once I accomplish something, I start thinking nobody else could have done it but I did. The last few verses which we have seen describe this mode of mind. Even success is something that is very difficult to digest or to become worthy of, because success can intoxicate you with wrong thoughts.

Instead of getting you to a higher level by whatever you learned or achieved, it sometimes brings you down. And if you fall into that category, what happens is what we have seen in the last few verses, which basically says: Adhyah Abhijanavan Asmi -- "I am rich." Once I have acquired wealth because I thought that's my security, that will give me happiness, I now forget why I acquired this wealth. It starts giving my *ego* a boost -- "Look, I am rich." So now I'm associating myself with my riches.

I start thinking I am my car, my car is me. I expand my identity not just to me as the body, mind and intellect, but now to all the possessions that I have. So my identity is incomplete without my possessions. Me minus my possessions is nothing. Now therefore I think: "I am rich." Abhijanavan Asmi -- "I am well-born." And Konyo Asti Sadrusho *Maya* -- "Who is there who is like me?"

These are the side effects of success. Success is something obviously very necessary for you to do what you need to do. But if that success only associate with why I wanted to achieve this then it's not really that big of a problem. But when I start associating with my *ego* then all these side effects will kick in. So now what I'm doing, even the thing which I'm doing good instead of giving me good results give me actually wrong results. So Yakshe Dashyami Modishya I am making the *sacrifice*.

*Sacrifice* is something you make so that you become more humble. But now I'm making sacrifice which makes me more arrogant. That look I am making *sacrifice*. Other people are not doing it. I am giving this donation. Donation is something is for you to get rid of more of your *ego*.

But it actually gives you boost your *ego* more that I am making donation. So the things which are supposed to be giving you the right results now start giving you the wrong results. Bhagavan said that this Asurik Sampath is. You need to be very careful in understanding that what are its evil effect on your mind and yourself. Once you are deluded. They get these wrong results even from the right actions.

Anek Chitta Vibranta Mohajal Samavrataha. Why all these things happening to them? Because they are Anek Chitta Vibhranta. They are bewildered by many fancy. They have all different kinds of fancies about what they are going to achieve, what their capabilities are. And I can also do that.

I tell all the time that if you are in one profession you always like to start thinking that something associated with it also I can do it. Most architects start getting into development and investment and real estate and all that. Because everybody comes to ask me how to do this. Why don't I do myself and also make money? In the end every architect who has tried has failed. Because that's not your really expertise or nature.

You're good at something -- that's why you became something. But this fancy of mine which says, "I can do this, I can also do this. I have achieved this, I can also accomplish this." Moha Jala Samavritah.

Because they are entangled into the snare of Moha *delusion*. This moha is simply my mind just cannot see the value of things and being as they are. So I start associating more and more values where they don't belong. Including on my own *self*, my own abilities. So I'm completely entangled into it. Prasaktaha kama Bhageso.

We know how the addiction works. Once I get something, I want to get it again and again. My Starbucks example, first time I had the Starbucks coffee. It's not an addiction. The second time and a third time and after that, how can you live without it? Prasaktaha kama Bhagesha.

Once I start enjoying the sense gratification more and more I get addicted to it. Patanti Naraki Ashucha. These unclean minds, people with the unclean intentions, they fall into the Naraka hell. When things don't go right for us and we start worrying about it and start losing sleep over that. It's falling into hell. Other people may think you are doing very well but you ask yourself how you are doing.

"Are you enjoying, Rajan?" Because 18 things are going right in my life, but these two are not letting me enjoy those 18 things which are going right for me. So where am I living? Not in heaven, but in hell. From an outsider's perspective, I may be doing very well. Therefore you read these stories about people like the hedge fund manager.

There'd be billions, not even millions and still they are suffering through. He is under investigation, going to jail. If money was the only object which was going to make him happy, he wouldn't be living in this situation. Patanti Naraki Asuchao with that unclean intentions, pursuing the goals of satisfying their desires instead of giving them joy which they were seeking from those endeavors, they fall into this hell. Atma Sambhavitah Stabdaha. Now other people can see, but I think he's doing wrong.

He's going to get hurt by this thing. But I don't see myself. I'm suffering but I'm still continuing. In Gujarat there is a saying, a gambler who is losing, he puts double the stake. He thinks the next time I can make it up. And this is really true.

Stock market, forget about gambling. Stock market people put money, the stocks go down. He think, oh now this is the time to get in. He puts more money into it. There was a company I was designing a headquarter in Charlottesville called Value America. I don't know any of you remember, but 2000, it was a rising company.

Internet bubble at the peak. And they hired me to design their headquarter in like June or July. And they had 600 people. And then they told me that by December we had thousand people. So they were designed with 1000 people. This building has to be completed by end of next year or so.

We are rushing to do that. And then just before the end of the year in December, I get a call and say, Rajan, send your invoice as quickly as possible because tomorrow the company may not be there. So anyway, the company was in a stock market. And then by the time I got involved, 15. And then when they called me it was about like $4 and say, got to be this good. No matter how much $4 will at least put $4,000.

I put thousand shares at $4, I said, I have seen that all the setup and those computers and all that is more than what they are saying. Well, the $4, then it eventually became 20 cents and eventually become zero. Even though I knew things are going down, I thought there's got to be a better deal. That's because we're atma Sambhavidah. We're overconfident about our own ability to think what reality is. Atma sambhavitah tab dhaha stubborn.

Everybody else says, I understand this thing better than you. Sabdaha dhanamanam adhan vitaha. Filled with pride and intoxication by their own achievement. No matter what the other people see what I'm doing, which is dangerous, I don't say it myself. Yajante nama yagnehi te dambena Avidhi purvakam. I want to do right things.

I have done this thing because I think this will help me doing right thing. But I got completely distracted by my *ego*. It has affected my Ahankar so much that now when I am doing the right thing, as I said the *sacrifice*, I'm doing it just in the name of it. It's not truly a *sacrifice* anymore. And I'm doing everything else. Giving a donation, showing off what I'm doing right for the community, services, all that.

I'm doing it for the namesake only. "If you don't put my name in this, I'm not interested. I will be making a donation as long as you make me a board member." So my thinking has now gone completely in the wrong direction. I understood before, when I didn't have all this wealth, that all these yajnas and daan and *sacrifice* and services are for my own good -- to purify my own *self*.

But with all this achievement of my wealth, I have started thinking other way around. And therefore now I'm doing all the things avidhi purvakam not in a right manner.
snippets.reflection:
Verse 16 describes the state of being aneka-chitta-vibhrantah (bewildered by many fancies) and moha-jala-samavritah (entangled in the net of delusion). This is the scattered mind that chases multiple desires simultaneously, convinced that each new acquisition will finally bring fulfillment. The verse warns that such minds, addicted to sense pleasures (prasaktah kama-bhogashu), fall into naraka - not a place but a state of constant anxiety, dissatisfaction, and inner torment. Reflect honestly: How many "fancies" are you currently pursuing? How scattered is your mental energy? The teaching suggests that even worldly success, when pursued obsessively, becomes its own hell. Today, practice simplification: identify one desire you can release, one pursuit you can let go of, to reduce the chaos of competing wants.

Verse 17 reveals how even sacred acts become corrupted: the wealthy and proud (dhana-mana-madanvitah) perform sacrifices in name only (nama-yajnaih), motivated by ostentation (dambhena) and without proper understanding (avidhi-purvakam). Verse 18 identifies those who, filled with ego, power, arrogance, lust, and anger, actually hate the divine presence within themselves and others (mam atma-para-deheshu pradvisantah). This hatred of the Self manifests as disregard for one's own conscience and dismissal of others' good intentions. Ask yourself: When has success made me more arrogant rather than more grateful? When have I ignored my inner voice because it conflicted with my desires? When have I dismissed good advice because it came from someone I felt superior to? These are the subtle ways we "hate" the divine within.
snippets.shortReflection: Think of the last time success went to your head. Did achievement make you more grateful or more entitled? When we confuse our accomplishments with our identity, even doing good becomes a trap. Notice how your ego inflates when praised and deflates when criticized—that's the sign you're still bound by results, not liberated by action.

snippets.title: Day 202: Lust, Anger, and Greed

क्षिपाम्यजस्रमशुभानासुरीष्वेव योनिषु ||

snippets.transliteration:
tān ahaṁ dviṣhataḥ krūrān sansāreṣhu narādhamān
kṣhipāmy ajasram aśhubhān āsurīṣhv eva yoniṣhu

āsurīṁ yonim āpannā mūḍhā janmani janmani

verseTranslations: Those who thus hate Me, who are cruel, the dregs of mankind, I condemn them to a continuous, miserable and godless rebirth.
So reborn, they spend life after life, enveloped in delusion. And they never reach Me, O Prince, but degenerate into still lower forms of life.
The gates of hell are three: lust, wrath and avarice. They destroy the Self. Avoid them.
snippets.commentary:
*Yoga* of Differentiation between the *divine* and Devilish Estates. These are the two types of qualities we have acquired in this world, going through the various experiences throughout our life. And when we look at it from our perspective, for many lives, we've been going through many different experiences. These experiences leave impressions on my mind. Those impressions create tendencies.

Those tendencies which I have is my wealth. That's all I carry around from one life to another. All other wealth which I consider my wealth right now is temporary and I have to leave behind. But this wealth which my tendencies I carry with me. So that's my permanent wealth, my permanent portfolio. So Bhagavan said that in that portfolio you may have *divine* qualities or *divine* tendencies and also devilish tendencies.

Put simply: positive tendencies and negative tendencies. Positive, as we always know, is helpful. Negative, as we always know, is harmful. So these *divine* tendencies which I have are liberating. Bhagavan said in the beginning of the chapter, these are liberating tendencies. These tendencies will lead me to act in a manner which will liberate me from my limitations.

Limitations are the ones which are binding me to sorrows and unhappiness. If I were powerful enough to own every piece of real estate in this town, then obviously I won't be competing for buying a house in Twin Hickory because I own everything. But because I am never infinite, this limitedness creates competitions and failures, and that creates sorrows and unhappiness. So we're going to say that these *divine* tendencies which you have acquired through your experiences, which align you more with your own self, are liberating from this bondage -- the *bondage* of identification with this body, mind and intellect, this limited self which I have right now considered to be my true *self*. On the other hand, there is the devilish tendency.

Now in this case, even though the word devilish or diabolical sounds too negative, but they are basically tendencies born out of my *ignorance*. What is the truth about my own *Self*. So I come to the conclusion that there is no higher *self*. There is no one to control anything. Whatever I can do, I am by myself. Whatever I need, I need to do to get happiness.

That type of belief will lead me to do things which are only for the sense gratification. These creates the negative tendencies and binds me more and more to this limited *self*. Bhagawan said these tendencies are binding which are in our normal term. We call it a materialistic view of the world and materialistic approach to life. That this material will give me happiness. The things which I acquire from this world, things which I accomplish in this world will make me happy is the materialistic viewpoint.

The spiritual viewpoint is: if I can be happy by myself, then I really don't need anything external to make me happy. Everything else may be just to fulfill my needs, but not wants. So the *desire* to sustain myself is not unhealthy. But when that *desire* becomes an obsession for something, then it becomes unhealthy. As we know, everything in moderation is good. Even obsession to not do something can become very dangerous sometimes.

So Bhagavan described these tendencies and said that these are the tendencies you should avoid. These are tendencies you should try to cultivate in yourself. And then he came to the last topic. He initially said that we have talked about *divine* qualities a lot. "We'll talk about these devilish qualities in detail. That's what we need to pay attention to." As I said in the beginning, our mind has a tendency to only see the *divine* in us.

*Divine* qualities in us. Devilish qualities in others. Very easy to see what other people are doing wrong. Very difficult to see what I am doing wrong. We always enhance our resumes. We ask somebody to do his own *self* evaluation in the end of the year.

If you see his *self-evaluation*, there is no negative in it, period. His supervisor will find negatives in it. It is very important that we develop the discipline to introspect and find what is not right within my own thinking and negate them. Bhagavan says, these tendencies -- you must know these devilish tendencies. When you detect them in you, remove them so that you can move forward in your life.

Your goal is to be happy. These tendencies will never make you happy. Even though it may seem that they will make me happy, they eventually make you unhappy -- and therefore avoid them. So you have seen that Bhagavan described what an asuric person looks like: Ahankaram Balam Darpam Kamam Krodham Cha Samshritah.

They are full of *ego*, power, *self-conceit*, lust and anger. Now we all have all of that in some degree. But if all of them together are powerful, then you become an Asura. If all five of them are at full capacity, then you become an Asura. Mam Atma Para Deheshu Pradvisanto Abhyasuyakah -- they hate my presence in them and in others. In other words, they have no value for life.

They will have no value of life, of their own or others. They will have no value for any noble act or have no *desire* or to appreciate other people. So they have no *knowledge* about what is *divine* in them or their own conscience. They will suppress their own conscience when it is trying to guide them for a right actions. And they will also not recognize the good intentions of others around them when others are trying to help them. These people will hate me in their own body and also in the others.

Tan Aham Dvishatah Kruran Samsareshu Naradhaman Kshipami Ajasram Ashubhan. To these cruel doers, the lowest of men -- as I said, when you are qualified for this distinction, when all five of those qualities are fully developed in you, there is no room for any *divine* tendency. Then Bhagavan says, I send them to the lowest of the yonis. And we have discussed last time: it is not that Bhagavan is punishing.

So Bhagavan is not sitting there and punishing people. Because you are not doing this right, your own actions will lead you towards the lower and lower state of existence. Whatever the tendency you develop, that is the environment you will feel comfortable. My tendency is to come to Gita class. I will feel comfortable here and somebody may be comfortable doing something else. Because their tendencies.

If your tendency leads you down to this path of the Hankara, Balam, Darpam, Kamam Krudam, you will be born into the same environment again. If you consider this sense gratification is the only goal of life then obviously you will be only seeking that environment. And Bhagawan said, I, as the lawgiver and law enforcement forcer in this world put them into the lowest yoni again and again. Asurim Yonim Apanna Muda Janmani Janmani. Birth after birth, having born in the demonic wombs. Because that's the path I have chosen.

Whatever path I take, I become good at that. So you start your career in engineering or architecture, medicine. You do the first project and the second project and in a short time you'll have a huge portfolio of work you do. And suddenly, whether you like it or not, you become an expert in that. And other people say, but you are only expert in this. We can give you work in this field because you only do this.

That's how we become all experts in something. Because we continue to do the same thing over and over again in the same line of work or same line of actions. So these people are now becoming expert in asuric existence. Ashram yuni mapanna by taking birth in Ashram yuni again and again. Mama aprapyevakantoya tatoyati Adhamam gatim. They continue their existing without attaining me, Attaining me.

By not recognizing their own *self*. They continue their existence from one life to another without recognizing what is *divine* in them, without recognizing the sanctity of life. And yantim adamam gatim. And they continue to go lower and lower and lower. Because that's the path they are pursuing, they are progressing into. Then he says, trivedam naraka sidham dwaram.

So up till now we have just discussed what the *divine* qualities are, what the devilish qualities are, who are *divine*, who are devilish. But what is the cause? This verse gives us the cause and also the prescription for how to avoid them. Trividham Narakasya Idam Dvaram Nashanam Atmanah. These three are the gates of hell, which are the destroyers of the *self*. Kamah, Krodhah, Tatha Lobhah -- lust, anger and greed.

These are the only three things which you have to avoid, Bhagawan. Now knowing this, we fall prey to these three. Because how the *karma* works is once you start thinking about some object. When you constantly think about any object, you develop *attachment* to it. Then you create a *desire* for that. If you don't get that object, you're a krodha.

So you created *attachment*. That *attachment* became lust. Lust in a sense, I ought to have it. Without that, life is not worth living. So that becomes a kamaha. A normal *desire* to buy a car is not a kamah because I need it for transportation.

But it becomes obsessed and I have to have BMW and then BMW, BMW, BMW. Then it's a problem if I don't get it. Because I said I can buy BMW in $50,000. And then by the time I accumulate 50,000, the car has gone to 60,000 or 70,000. It almost is slightly above my pay grade. And that will make me angry.

So Bhagawan said, that's the mechanism of lust. A normal *desire* is Innocent. I'm thirsty, I need water. I have a *desire* to drink water. I'll get up, get a glass of water and I'm done with it. But a constant obsession about something becomes *karma*.

When that obsession is obstructed by this world for me to attain that I become angry. So that Krodha, we all learned in chapter two the anger. It shuts down my buddhi. Because we have this safety mechanism just like the breaker trips and electricity that to protect integrity of your mind and intellect. The intellect will shut off so it doesn't overburden. So you have no access to your buddhi.

Your memory bank is completely out of your reach. So you cannot access your *wisdom* when you're angry. Therefore people say, well I, I did it because I was angry. That means it's not appropriate. But I did it because I was angry. So all my actions within the state of anger are actually not really good for me.

We all know that Bhagawan said so avoid *karma* so you don't have to get angry with Crowther. That's the second gate of and now what happens is if I have a lust for something or *karma* for something and I achieve that object easily then become greedy. I have the one time I've got it done. I buy a lotto for the first time and I get a hundred dollar prize. Well, looks like this is an easy pass. So I do it again and again.

Maybe I can win a jackpot. So that success actually became problem for me. Because I now crave to get that experience again and again and again. When I fail at that, I'll be angry again. So at the end of the day I was nothing but angry. If I get what I want, I still will be angry.

And if I don't get what I want, I still will be angry. So I live in the hell all the time.
snippets.reflection:
Verses 19-20 describe the consequence of persistent demonic tendencies: birth after birth in environments that reinforce those same qualities. This is not divine punishment but natural law - whatever tendencies we cultivate, we become expert in; whatever path we follow, we continue along. Just as a person who builds a career in one field becomes increasingly specialized in that domain, someone who practices cruelty, hatred, and delusion becomes increasingly skilled at those patterns. The teaching warns that such souls, never recognizing their divine nature (mam aprapya), sink to lower and lower states (adhamam gatim). Examine your own "expertise": What patterns have you become increasingly skilled at through repetition? Are they patterns that liberate or bind? Today, consciously interrupt one negative pattern before it runs its usual course.

Verse 21 offers the most practical guidance in this chapter: "Trividham narakasya idam dvaram" - there are three gates to hell: kama (lust/obsessive desire), krodha (anger), and lobha (greed). These three are the root destroyers of the Self. Notice how they interconnect: desire, when obstructed, becomes anger; desire, when fulfilled, becomes greed for more. The cycle is self-perpetuating. Krishna's prescription is simple: "tasmad etat trayam tyajet" - therefore, abandon these three. Today, keep a mental note each time you feel the pull of obsessive wanting, the heat of anger, or the grasping of greed. Do not judge yourself - simply observe. At day's end, review: Which gate did I approach most often? What triggered it? What would it mean to turn away from that gate rather than enter?
snippets.shortReflection: You've built patterns through repetition—some serve you, most don't. Every time you chase the same comfort, avoid the same discomfort, or replay the same resentment, you're becoming an expert in that loop. What are you practicing daily? Generosity or bitterness? Presence or distraction? You're getting better at something—make sure it's what you actually want.

As I said in the beginning, our mind has a tendency to only see the *divine* in us.

*Divine* qualities in us. Devilish qualities in others. Very easy to see what other people are doing wrong. Very difficult to see what I am doing wrong. We always enhance our resumes. We ask somebody to do his own *self* evaluation in the end of the year.

If you see his *self-evaluation*, there is no negative in it, period. His supervisor will find negatives in it. It is very important that we develop the discipline to introspect and find what is not right within my own thinking and negate them. Bhagavan says, these tendencies -- you must know these devilish tendencies. When you detect them in you, remove them so that you can move forward in your life.

Your goal is to be happy. These tendencies will never make you happy. Even though it may seem that they will make me happy, they eventually make you unhappy -- and therefore avoid them. So you have seen that Bhagavan described what an asuric person looks like: Ahankaram Balam Darpam Kamam Krodham Cha Samshritah.

They are full of *ego*, power, *self-conceit*, lust and anger. Now we all have all of that in some degree. But if all of them together are powerful, then you become an Asura. If all five of them are at full capacity, then you become an Asura. Mam Atma Para Deheshu Pradvisanto Abhyasuyakah -- they hate my presence in them and in others. In other words, they have no value for life.

They will have no value of life, of their own or others. They will have no value for any noble act or have no *desire* or to appreciate other people. So they have no *knowledge* about what is *divine* in them or their own conscience. They will suppress their own conscience when it is trying to guide them for a right actions. And they will also not recognize the good intentions of others around them when others are trying to help them. These people will hate me in their own body and also in the others.

Tan Aham Dvishatah Kruran Samsareshu Naradhaman Kshipami Ajasram Ashubhan. To these cruel doers, the lowest of men -- as I said, when you are qualified for this distinction, when all five of those qualities are fully developed in you, there is no room for any *divine* tendency. Then Bhagavan says, I send them to the lowest of the yonis. And we have discussed last time: it is not that Bhagavan is punishing.

So Bhagavan is not sitting there and punishing people. Because you are not doing this right, your own actions will lead you towards the lower and lower state of existence. Whatever the tendency you develop, that is the environment you will feel comfortable. My tendency is to come to Gita class. I will feel comfortable here and somebody may be comfortable doing something else. Because their tendencies.

If your tendency leads you down to this path of the Hankara, Balam, Darpam, Kamam Krudam, you will be born into the same environment again. If you consider this sense gratification is the only goal of life then obviously you will be only seeking that environment. And Bhagawan said, I, as the lawgiver and law enforcement forcer in this world put them into the lowest yoni again and again. Asurim Yonim Apanna Muda Janmani Janmani. Birth after birth, having born in the demonic wombs. Because that's the path I have chosen.

Whatever path I take, I become good at that. So you start your career in engineering or architecture, medicine. You do the first project and the second project and in a short time you'll have a huge portfolio of work you do. And suddenly, whether you like it or not, you become an expert in that. And other people say, but you are only expert in this. We can give you work in this field because you only do this.

That's how we become all experts in something. Because we continue to do the same thing over and over again in the same line of work or same line of actions. So these people are now becoming expert in asuric existence. Ashram yuni mapanna by taking birth in Ashram yuni again and again. Mama aprapyevakantoya tatoyati Adhamam gatim. They continue their existing without attaining me, Attaining me.

By not recognizing their own *self*. They continue their existence from one life to another without recognizing what is *divine* in them, without recognizing the sanctity of life. And yantim adamam gatim. And they continue to go lower and lower and lower. Because that's the path they are pursuing, they are progressing into. Then he says, trivedam naraka sidham dwaram.

Up till now we have discussed what the *divine* qualities are, what the devilish qualities are, who are *divine*, and who are devilish. But what is the root cause of these devilish qualities? This verse gives us the cause and also the prescription for how to avoid them. Trividham Narakasya Idam Dvaram Nashanam Atmanah. These three are the gates of hell, which are the destroyers of the *self*. Kamah, Krodhah, Tatha Lobhah -- lust, anger and greed.

These are the only three things which you have to avoid, Bhagawan. Now knowing this, we fall prey to these three. Because how the *karma* works is once you start thinking about some object. When you constantly think about any object, you develop *attachment* to it. Then you create a *desire* for that. If you don't get that object, you're a krodha.

So you created *attachment*. That *attachment* became lust. Lust in a sense, I ought to have it. Without that, life is not worth living. So that becomes a kamaha. A normal *desire* to buy a car is not a kamah because I need it for transportation.

But it becomes obsessed and I have to have BMW and then BMW, BMW, BMW. Then it's a problem if I don't get it. Because I said I can buy BMW in $50,000. And then by the time I accumulate 50,000, the car has gone to 60,000 or 70,000. It almost is slightly above my pay grade. And that will make me angry.

So Bhagavan said, that's the mechanism of lust. A normal *desire* is innocent. I'm thirsty, I need water. I have a *desire* to drink water. I get up, get a glass of water, and I'm done with it. But a constant obsession about something becomes kama.

When that obsession is obstructed and I cannot attain what I want, I become angry. So that Krodha, we all learned in chapter two the anger. It shuts down my buddhi. Because we have this safety mechanism just like the breaker trips and electricity that to protect integrity of your mind and intellect. The intellect will shut off so it doesn't overburden. So you have no access to your buddhi.

Your memory bank is completely out of your reach. So you cannot access your *wisdom* when you're angry. Therefore people say, well I, I did it because I was angry. That means it's not appropriate. But I did it because I was angry. So all my actions within the state of anger are actually not really good for me.

We all know that Bhagawan said so avoid *karma* so you don't have to get angry with Crowther. That's the second gate of and now what happens is if I have a lust for something or *karma* for something and I achieve that object easily then become greedy. I have the one time I've got it done. I buy a lotto for the first time and I get a hundred dollar prize. Well, looks like this is an easy pass. So I do it again and again.

Maybe I can win a jackpot. So that success actually became problem for me. Because I now crave to get that experience again and again and again. When I fail at that, I'll be angry again. So at the end of the day I was nothing but angry. If I get what I want, I still will be angry.

And if I don't get what I want, I still will be angry. So I live in the hell all the time.
snippets.reflection:
Verse 22 offers the positive counterpart to the previous warning: one who is freed from the three gates of darkness - lust, anger, and greed - naturally acts for their own highest good (acharaty atmanah shreyah) and attains the supreme goal (param gatim). This is liberation not as escape from the world but as freedom within it - the ability to act wisely without being driven by compulsion. Notice that Krishna does not say such a person has no desires, never feels irritation, or wants nothing. Rather, they are vimuktah - freed from being controlled by these forces. Today, practice this freedom in one small area: when desire arises, acknowledge it without acting on impulse; when irritation surfaces, feel it without speaking harshly; when greed whispers "more," recognize the voice without obeying. This is the beginning of liberation.

Verse 23-24 establish scripture (shastra) as the guide for determining what should and should not be done (karya-akarya-vyavasthitau). When we act merely from desire (kama-karatah), we achieve neither perfection (siddhi), nor happiness (sukham), nor the supreme goal. This teaching acknowledges our tendency to rationalize - "I know what is right for me" - while being driven by hidden motives. Scripture serves as an objective standard, a wisdom accumulated over millennia, that can check our self-deception. Practically, this means: before major decisions, consult the teachings; when confused about right action, return to the principles you have studied. Ask yourself today: In what area of life am I acting purely from personal desire while convincing myself it is right? What would the scriptural wisdom - non-injury, truthfulness, non-attachment - counsel in that situation? Let this chapter's teaching be your compass when your own judgment is clouded.
snippets.shortReflection: Before big decisions, who do you consult? Your anxious thoughts? Your peer group? Or something deeper—a principle you'd defend even when inconvenient? Most of us outsource our moral compass, then wonder why we feel lost. Pick one choice you're facing and ask: what would wisdom say, not what would comfort or approval say?

verseTranslations: Arjuna asked: My Lord! Those who do acts of sacrifice, not according to the scriptures but nevertheless with implicit faith, what is their condition? Is it one of Purity, of Passion or of Ignorance?
Lord Shri Krishna replied: Man has an inherent faith in one or another of the Qualities -Purity, Passion and Ignorance. Now listen.
The faith of every man conforms to his nature. By nature he is full of faith. He is in fact what his faith makes him.
snippets.commentary:
The Gita opens with Dhritarashtra. Dhritarashtra, as we have discussed, is our state of mind.

Right now we live in the Dhritarashtra state. We are blind to our reality, the supreme reality, the real reality. We are blind to the truth that I am part of that supreme being, and instead we live in the world of Mamakaha -- I and mine.

So that's basically how the Bhagavad Gita started: this is our problem. All our problems start with that one misunderstanding that I am this limited being, that Mamakaha is my world, I and mine is my world. And then I separate the rest of the world as something other than me.

The next few verses focus on Duryodhana -- the Duryodhana in us. This Duryodhana represents the thief in us -- the part that wants to take away something which belongs to somebody else and make it mine. I want it so badly that I will use any means to get it.

All over our day-to-day life we see inequality in our society, because obviously there is wealth which is common to all, given by God, natural. Yet somebody hoards so much and doesn't leave enough for the others. So the Duryodhana in us wants this thing so badly.

He knows it's not his, but he wants it. And therefore he is always very anxious, because he has decided: I need to have it. I know it is not mine, but I need to have it for my own happiness, to make myself complete.

This sense of incompleteness started with our state of Dhritarashtra. Because we are blind to our reality, we make ourselves limited to this *self*, and that I-and-mine creates incompleteness. That incompleteness has created a thief in us -- I want to take away from others and make it mine so that I will feel complete.

That's what Duryodhana felt all his life: I need all this kingdom for myself. He was already given half the kingdom after the first match of chess, and now he wants all of it. So his mental state is that of any thief who is trying to steal something away from somebody else.

One, he is insecure -- when you are trying to steal something, you wonder: is somebody watching me? So there is insecurity, and then fear. Obviously you are fearful, you are insecure. That's why you want to make sure you get what you want by any means.

So there are three things in that mentality: I want this so badly that I'll be willing to do anything; I'm insecure; and I'm fearful. The next few verses we have seen are just describing this. The first six verses said: Look at the Pandava's army -- it looks pretty well protected.

Great warriors on their side. He is basically going to Drona and saying, these are all your Shishyas. Arjun, son of Drupada, Drishtadharamna, who is now commanding the army.

So I'm not sure that we are totally protected having somebody like Drona with us, because his shishyas are on the other side. That's a fear in him. So he describes all that he feels are the weak points from looking at the other side.

And now he realizes that he may have gone overboard. When somebody is in that state, he wants to cover both bases. On one side he feels insecure.

On the other side he feels very powerful -- I have all the shrewdness and smartness and strength to do it. So first he looked at his insecurity and his weaknesses, seeing the other side as powerful. Now he's looking at it differently: no, no, I can do it.

So from verse 7 onwards, he now looks at his strength. Asmakamtu Visishtaye Tani Bauda Dwijottama. Obviously he's addressing Drona, and he said Dvijottama.

We have discussed before: Dwijottama, Dwija, Brahmin. Brahmin is considered twice born. One is a physical birth, and the second is a birth in this *knowledge* of who you are, which starts at the time of Upanayam when the Guru gives a mantra in his ear.

Then he goes to the Gurukul to get that education and becomes established in this *knowledge*. That's why it's called Dwij -- because the first is just a physical birth for a limited being, and the second birth is where he takes birth as a wise person. So therefore they are called Dwijaha.

Drona, being a Brahmin, is Dwijaha. But he said Dwijottama -- you are the best among the Brahmins. Now this could have been the best compliment in a normal situation.

But in this situation it is not because we know or at least the society knew at the time. Brahmins are soft hearted. They are not fighting type.

They are not war mongerers. They are not the ones who can be in the situation. They want to avoid this type of conflict.

We have seen that that's how Karna was caught by Parasuram. Karna went to Parasuram because he realized that other than Drona, Parasuram could teach him what the other Pandavas were learning. Parasuram had taken a vow that he would not teach any Kshatriya, because he wanted to eliminate Kshatriyas from this planet.

He would not teach this art of warfare to any Kshatriya. So Karna goes there as a Dvija, as a Brahmin. He disguises himself as a Brahmin -- lies that he is a Brahmin.

And then obviously he was a good student. One day, the teacher was sleeping with his head in Karna's lap. A bumblebee comes and sits on Karna's thigh.

He realizes that if he moves, his Guru will be disturbed, and he does not want to make his Guru uncomfortable at all. The Guru is in a deep sleep. This bumblebee bores through his flesh and blood is oozing out of that wound.

He tolerates all that pain but does not move a muscle, so that his Guru won't be disturbed in his sleep. The blood comes running down his thigh, under the Guru's head. The Guru wakes up because of the warm blood he feels.

He sees what's happening, realizes what has occurred, and Karna says, I'm fine. But the Guru was angry. He said: you lied to me.

You are not a Brahmin. A Brahmin would not have been capable of tolerating this kind of pain. You are a Kshatriya who lied to me.

And then obviously, as the story goes, Karna asked for forgiveness and all of that. But Parasuram said: you will have this *knowledge*, but it will not come handy to you when you really need it in the battlefield. You will lose this *knowledge*.

The relevance here is that Dvija is not a positive compliment when you are in a war. So Duryodhana reminds Drona: look, I know you are a great teacher and a great archer and a great warrior, but in the end you are a Dvija -- so don't be soft-hearted here. It's actually his fear that maybe this guy will go soft-hearted and will not fight this battle.

Sangartam tan bravi mi te -- therefore I am going to now describe to you who are the great warriors on our side. Don't go soft-hearted on me. We have also great people on our side.

You don't need to worry about it. You just do your job. Bhavan Bismast Chakranastha starting with you Bhavan, you who are on our side so that we feel that we are protected.

Bhavan, you Bisma, Karna, Krupastha, Samitin, Jaya and Krupacharya who are victorious. All these people have good track record of resume of winning battle. Asvathama, Vikranscha, Somadatt, Tatha, Evacharya and then all others like Asvathrama.

Last time we have seen Kurupacharya is Dronacharya's brother in law and Aswathrama is Dronacharya's son. So or we can't have in one family all this bravery and valor. So he's obviously making it up a little more than what he should be.

But whatever it is, these are all great warriors. Swathama was more like Duryodhana. He was Duryodhana's best friend and was basically looking for this: if he stays with Duryodhana and Duryodhana wins the war, then he will have a kingdom of his own.

Drona and Drupada were friends and they probably learned together at some Guru's place. Drona goes to Drupada asking for some favor to make him a Raja somewhere, and Drupada insults him. That's where their animosity started.

So the long story all weaved into it. But in the end basically Duryodhana said these are all people, the great people on our side and not only the main characters but Anyeche, Baha, Bahasuraha, Madharte, Tyakta, Jeevitaha and there are many others on our side who are ready to give up their life for me. Many, many brave people are on our side.

In other words, they're committed to fight this war. Yudwijotama, I'm not sure about you but I'm sure about everybody else. They are committed to fight.

So let's do the right thing here. Nana Sastra Praharanaha, Sarve, Yuddha, Visharadaha. Not only they are ready to fight for me but they are equipped with various types of weapons.

So we are well equipped. We have a human capital, we have technology. So let's not worry about it.

Yudda Visaradaha they are expert in warfare. This verse obviously confuses everybody -- why "Apar Yaptam," insufficient? Now every translation I have seen does say "insufficient," even though it seems that "unlimited" is more appropriate here. I had asked once:, all this translation, where does that come from? And we don't get involved in this because you need a Sanskrit pandit to translate this.

He says there are Sanskrit pandits in Kashi who have translated the Bhagavad Gita after thorough discussion, and that's the translation we use. So even well-known translations do not really come from individual teachers -- they actually came from Pandits who decided on the translation. So we have to take it as it is and say Apar Yaptam in our vernacular languages.

Apariyapta is insufficient. He's saying it's insufficient. Now remember, his mentality is that of a thief.

He always feels that he is incomplete. No matter how much that person has, he will always feel there is something more he should have. And therefore his vision about what we have is never that we are sufficient.

We have plenty, so why even be fighting this battle? But even the army he sees as insufficient. All these people who went on Pandava's side -- they actually should have been on my side, and then it would have been much better. And my army is protected by Bheeshma, because he knew that Bheeshma has taken a vow that as long as he lives, he will guard the throne of Hastinapur.

Whoever is in Hastinapur, he will be protecting him. He also knows that Bheeshma has Ichamrityu -- he will only die if he wants to die. As long as Bheeshma is alive, he is protected.

So on one hand, he knows that as long as Bheeshma is on his side, he obviously does not have to worry. But at the same token he thinks: if I had more, then I would have felt a little better about it. So he said: Apariyaptam Tadasnakam Balam Vishna Bhirakshitam -- our strength protected by Bhishma still feels a little insufficient.

Whereas on the other side, Pariyaptam twidam Etesham Balam Bhima Bhirakshitam -- they are protected by Bhima. And then last time, Sid or somebody pointed out that this is not correct. Bhima was not the commander; the commander was changing every day in this army.

If you read the Mahabharata -- and I have never read it, so I'm not an authority on this.
snippets.reflection:
These opening verses reveal a profound truth: "As is the faith, so is the person" (yo yacchraddhaḥ sa eva saḥ). Krishna teaches that our faith is not merely what we intellectually believe, but the deep orientation of our entire being - it arises from our svabhava, our inherent nature shaped by past experiences and tendencies. This faith, whether sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic, colors everything we perceive and pursue. When Arjuna asks about those who worship with faith but set aside scriptural guidance, Krishna does not condemn them. Instead, he reveals that faith itself is the defining factor of who we become.

Take time today to honestly examine: What do you truly have faith in? Not what you think you should believe, but what actually drives your decisions when no one is watching. When faced with a difficult choice, what conviction do you fall back on? Consider keeping a "faith journal" this week - note the moments when your deepest convictions reveal themselves, whether in moments of stress, temptation, or quiet reflection. Ask yourself: Does my faith lead me toward light and clarity (sattva), toward restless ambition (rajas), or toward confusion and inertia (tamas)? Remember, awareness of our current state is the first step toward transformation.
snippets.shortReflection: What do you truly have faith in—not what you say, but where your actions point? Track your time and money this week. That's your real theology. If your faith is in control, you'll be anxious when things feel uncertain. If it's in appearances, you'll be exhausted by performance. Faith isn't belief; it's where you rest when you're afraid.
