verseTranslations: The Pure worship the true God; the Passionate, the powers of wealth and magic; the Ignorant, the spirits of the dead and of the lower orders of nature.
Those who practise austerities not commanded by scripture, who are slaves to hypocrisy and egotism, who are carried away by the fury of desire and passion,
They are ignorant. They torment the organs of the body; and they harass Me also, Who lives within. Know that they are devoted to evil.
snippets.commentary:
That's a simple question, simply because in the last chapter, the clear advice by Krishna is to follow the prescriptions of the Sastras in deciding what to do and what not to do. And as we have seen, Sastras literally means the collective *wisdom* of your culture, your society, your ancestors.

So unless I really rely on the *wisdom* of my ancestors, I will have no foundation to decide what is right and wrong. Any profession, any science -- you build on what has already been tried and true and proven in the labs or in workshops, and then say, now where do I go from here? So the clear prescription was not to ignore the *wisdom* of your ancestors, your civilization, your culture, and then decide what is right and wrong for you. It's not saying that you don't think yourself, but think based on the tried and true wisdom.

When we go to high school and learn chemistry and the teacher says H2O makes water, well, you have to have some faith in him. Unless you have faith, you will not learn, because you have *faith* in the teacher that you will accept that and then you will prove yourself going to the lab. So the prescription was follow the Sastras and decide what to do and not to do.

Arjuna's question is, if someone completely sets aside the prescription in Sastras for lack of knowledge or lack of faith in the Sastras, but he has a faith in something he believes in, does that *faith* to be classified as Sattvik Rajasik or Tamasic? Because as we have seen, everything can be classified Sattvik, Rajasik, or Tamasic. Bhagavan said: I'll tell you, it's not a one-label-fits-all type of answer. Your *faith* will be as you are.

My *faith* will be as per my experiences. Every time I walk into the airport, I'm absolutely sure the plane will be on time -- if the last few times I went there the plane was on time, I'll say it will be on time. But if the last few times I'd been going there it was always late, what will be my *faith*? Chances are my flight will be delayed.

So anytime I'm going to India, what I do is I leave about six hours of gap between when I go from Richmond to New Jersey airport and New Jersey to Mumbai. We have no *faith* that the flight from Richmond to New Jersey will take me in time. They say, keep a two-hour gap.

No, no -- six hours gap. You don't want to miss an international flight. That's my *faith* in our airline based on my experience.

And then the other people may have other things. So Bhagavan said that your faith is *Sattva* Anurupa. It in accordance with your own self, your own core of your being, core of your mind.

So my *faith* will be what my experiences are. *Faith* is something that comes intuitively to you, more like a tendency. Why do I like music? I don't know -- that's my tendency. But the more I follow my tendency, the more I will be following that path.

The more I have *faith* in the Gita, the more Gita I will read; the more I read the Gita, the more *faith* I have in it. So the two are wedded together. The more *faith* I have, the more I will pursue that path.

The more I pursue that path, the more my *faith* increases. So Bhagavan said, it is the individual who decides whether he will have *faith* which is Sattvik, Rajasic, or Tamasic, depending on the tendencies of his mind. Yajante Sattvika Devan -- so if the overall makeup of my mind is Sattvik, what will I do? Well, I will follow Sattvic beings.

I will strive to pursue or worship *divine* beings. My role models depend on my tendencies. If I am pursuing wealth, my role model is Bill Gates.

If I want to be a great leader, my role model will be Mahatma Gandhi. If I want to be spiritual, my role model will be a great sage or teacher. Depending on my *faith*, my role model would be different.

That's as simple as that. So Bhagavan said: Sattvika Yajante Devan -- one whose makeup is Sattvik, predominantly Sattvik. These are not exclusive qualities of one person, one thing, or one being.

Everything is made up of some combination of Sattvik, Rajasik, and Tamasic. But if my mental makeup is predominantly Sattvik, I will be pursuing the Deva, the *divine* beings, Yaksa, Rakshansi, Rajasaha, those who are Rajasik will pursue or worship Yakshas and Rakshasas. From the Puranas we have the descriptions of Devas and Yakshas and Rakshasas, but it's simply told here is Sattvik will follow the *divine* beings, Rajasik will follow the one which has wealth and power.

Yaksas are supposed to be wealthy beings. There is a story in Mahabharata 1 where Yudhishthir goes to this lake when he wants to drink water. That lake was controlled by a Yaksha.

Yaksha said, you can't drink water till you answer all my questions. If you answer all my questions, I'll let you take water. In other words, he was the controller of that lake.

He was wealthy enough to control his lake. These days people own islands because they're wealthy. So the Yaksa that the wealthy beings, and here in Purana, I say they're Kubera's brothers or cousins.

So they're wealthy beings or Rakshasa's immense power. There are stories in Puranas about Rakshasas' immense power. In other words, even in society there will be people who are Sattvic and people who are wealthy and powerful.

So if my tendency is Rajasic, then I will be pursuing the wealthy and powerful. If my quality is Sattvik, I'll pursue the *divine* being. Preta Bhuta Ganas -- the others who have Tamasic qualities will pursue the Preta and Bhuta.

We obviously know from our vernacular languages that Preta and Bhuta are the dead spirits. Now in this society, if there are three people pursuing the same goal of making a million, the one with a Sattvik tendency will say: let's find some creative way which will help the society and at the same time create the wealth -- and that's how I'll make my million. The Rajasik will say: let's destroy my competition or take over someone else, and I'll get my million.

And the last one will say: let's pursue the lottery, buy the Mega Millions. All three have the same goal, but all three have a different avenue to reach there. Now all three are working hard to achieve the same goal -- making a million.

The Sattvic person is working very hard to achieve his goal creatively. The Rajasic is working just as hard but competitively. The Tamasic is also working hard but relying on chance.

Their means are different, depending on where their *faith* is. The one who's pursuing the lottery has complete *faith* that he cannot get a million in any other way -- this is the only way he can make a million. The one who wants to employ himself in a business has complete *faith* he can succeed that way.

And the Sattvic person has complete faith that if he creates something good for society, he will also benefit from it. Depending on your own experiences, your mental makeup is made. That mental makeup now defines where I have the *faith* in.

That *faith* will lead me into my actions. So Bhagavan said these faiths cannot be labeled simply because someone is not following Sastra. He may not know the Sastras but has Sattvic tendencies -- he will follow *Sattva*.

He may not know Sastras but has Rajasic tendencies -- he is following Rajasik. And he may not know Sastras because he's Tamasic -- he's following *Tamas*. So Preta and Bhuta are the dead spirits.

In other words, normal society will consider that to be a non-starter. Somebody says, well Rajan, why don't you buy a lottery? I never won anything in my life. Let's not waste my dollar.

At least I have a dollar. After that I won't have a dollar. But somebody has the *faith* and says, well, I have $10, I'll put nine of them in the lottery.

I'm pretty much against the lottery, by the way, because we're taxing the people who can afford the least in the society. They say lottery is good for education, it will reduce your taxes. No -- it's a tax on the people who cannot afford that tax.

Most lottery tickets are bought by people who can least afford it. But they are following their *faith*. Asastra vihitam ghoram tapyante ye tapo janaha.

Now I have my *faith* that this is how I can pursue my goal. My *faith* is dependent on my experiences. So now I'm pursuing my goal vigorously because I'm as sincere as anybody else.

But I'm pursuing it in a field which I think is the most conducive for me to achieve that -- not knowing what is right or wrong because I did not take time to find out. I'm working very hard. As I said last time, I want to go to New Jersey, but I'm driving as fast as I can on I-95 south just because I didn't take time to figure out whether New Jersey is north or south, without knowing what is right or wrong from the tried and true *wisdom* of my society.

If I had just taken the directions from AAA or a GPS, it would tell me New Jersey is to the north. But I didn't take it. I didn't want to take that time.

They're working very hard. They are pursuing these austerities vigorously. Dambha ahankara sanyuktaha -- because they're filled with dambha, hypocrisy.

And ahankara, *ego* -- nobody knows better than I do. So who are they to tell me that New Jersey is to the north? I know it's got to be this way. Ahankara sanyuktaha, Kama raga balanvitaha -- they are propelled to do this by what? Kama, *desire*, and raga, *attachment*.

Kama and raga are propelling my actions, and I think my happiness lies there. My goal is to achieve happiness, just as everybody else's is. But I think my happiness lies in these actions, where others are saying no -- that's where you have the danger that you probably will be unhappy.

We tell our kids: don't do that. But at that time the child does not think he is going to get hurt. But if he listens to you -- you as an elder person have learned from your own experience that jumping from that second floor is going to get you in trouble.

A young person, at the age of 8 or 9 or 10, thinks he can do anything he wants. Propelled by that *desire* and attachment, he wants to show off to his friend that he can jump from the second story. We have seen that in our childhood.

Hypocrisy and arrogance, the *ego* filled with that and propelled by attachment and *desire*. And they are putting vigorous actions in the fields which they consider appropriate for them. Karshayantaha Sarirastham bhutagramam a Chaitasaha.

This is a description of someone who has completely ignored the advice from the Sastras. We read the Bhagavad Gita every Sunday -- what do we do after that? The Bhagavad Gita says one thing, but that's not really what we follow. So now we fall into this category.

Knowing fully well, we set aside the prescription in the Shastra. We are propelled by our *desire* and our attachments, and also we are dambha ahankara sanyukta.
snippets.reflection:
These verses present a sobering warning about misguided worship and extreme practices. Krishna describes those who, driven by hypocrisy (dambha), ego (ahankara), desire (kama), and attachment (raga), perform harsh austerities not prescribed by scriptures. Most striking is the statement that such people "torment the organs of the body" and "harass Me also, Who lives within" - revealing that when we abuse our body-mind complex through extreme or misguided practices, we are actually disrespecting the Divine that dwells within us. The sattvic worship Devas (divine beings representing light and wisdom), the rajasic pursue Yakshas and Rakshasas (representing wealth and power), while the tamasic follow spirits of the dead.

Examine your own spiritual practices and the role models you follow. Who are your "Devas" - the ideals and beings you worship through your attention and energy? If you seek wealth above all, your role model might be a billionaire; if wisdom, perhaps a sage; if power, perhaps a political figure. Today, notice when ego or the desire to show off enters your spiritual practice. Do you meditate to genuinely purify the mind, or partly to feel superior to others? Do you practice austerities that honor the body as a temple, or do you engage in extreme behaviors driven by pride or self-punishment? Ask yourself: Are my practices nourishing the Divine within, or harassing it?
snippets.shortReflection: Look at the way you eat when no one's watching. Rushed? Mindless? Punishing or indulgent? Your relationship with food mirrors your relationship with life. Are you eating to live or living to eat? One small shift: before your next meal, pause and ask yourself what you're actually hungry for.

snippets.title: Day 206: Austerity
snippets.sanskrit:
आहारस्त्वपि सर्वस्य त्रिविधो भवति प्रियः |
यज्ञस्तपस्तथा दानं तेषां भेदमिमं श्रृणु ||

snippets.transliteration:
āhāras tv api sarvasya tri-vidho bhavati priyaḥ
yajñas tapas tathā dānaṁ teṣhāṁ bhedam imaṁ śhṛiṇu

āyuḥ-sattva-balārogya-sukha-prīti-vivardhanāḥ
rasyāḥ snigdhāḥ sthirā hṛidyā āhārāḥ sāttvika-priyāḥ

verseTranslations: The food which men enjoy is also threefold, like the ways of sacrifice, austerity and almsgiving. Listen to the distinction.
The foods that prolong life and increase purity, vigour, health, cheerfulness and happiness are those that are delicious, soothing, substantial and agreeable. These are loved by the Pure.
Those in whom Passion is dominant like foods that are bitter, sour, salty, over-hot, pungent, dry and burning. These produce unhappiness, repentance and disease.
snippets.commentary:
We have seen in the last chapter, when Bhagavan ended the chapter, he gave the advice to Arjuna: do everything in life according to the advice given in the scriptures or by the sages. That's how you will acquire more divine qualities. And these *divine* qualities are liberating -- they will liberate you from your limitations which are creating sorrows in life.

If you do not follow that, you may incur more negative tendencies which will be more binding. They bind you to this material world. So Bhagavan said that follow the scriptural advice when you decide what to do and what not to do in this world. So obvious question Arjuna had was that what about the people who never had a chance to refer to scriptures? Either by their own choice, that they didn't think it was important, or they never had an opportunity to learn scriptures. And we can imagine in that society, probably the larger mass of people were not allowed to even learn scripture.

Arjuna had a very logical doubt: what happens to all those people? They are working in this world with *faith*. They have a *faith* that this is the right way to live life, which will give them happiness. Because at the end of the day, as we have discussed, the goal of life is to be happy. No matter who we are, our goal in life is very simple.

We all want to be happy. If I look at my entire life, it is divided into two pursuits: one is to achieve happiness, and the other is to avoid unhappiness. Bhagavan said we are all working toward the same goal. But those who do not listen to the advice in the scriptures, the books of *knowledge*, teachers, wise people, ancestors -- they suffer by developing wrong tendencies. Those who follow the advice from the wise people, because they've gone through that and come to the conclusion this is the right way to act, will benefit from that and acquire the *divine*, liberating tendencies.

Arjuna said: the people in this world, working in their field, in their life, with *faith* but having no *knowledge* of what is prescribed in the scriptures -- as I said, either by choice (they decided it's not worth it) or they never had a chance. So what is the nature of their sraddha? They have sraddha too -- that this is where I'll get my happiness in life. Is it Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic? Because if it is just out of my *ignorance*, one would say that is tamasic. Bhagavan said it is all of the above.

It can be any of the three. If you have not referred to the scriptures but still have *faith*, your faith can be of any of these three, and at any given time it can be one or another. It is predominantly whatever my personality is -- my *faith* will be according to my personality. As the faith, so is the person. As the person, so is the *faith*.

So it's a symbiotic relationship. Whichever field I choose to work in, I eventually become an expert in that. I go to architecture school, work in architecture field. More I work in that field, more I get *knowledge*. More my tendencies become to work in that field. And after about 30 years you become an expert in that field.

At that point somebody says, you made a mistake, Rajan, you should have gone to medical school -- you would have made lots of money. Yeah, I'd want to switch overnight but can't do it because my tendencies are now firmly established in the field I've been working in all my life. Bhagavan says the same thing happens with your shraddha. Whatever shraddha you have, you will continue to pursue that path and have similar experiences. And it will make your shraddha even firmer.

The firmer your shraddha becomes, the more it becomes your nature, your personality. That's how you can identify or label a person as a Sattvic person, a Rajasic person, or a Tamasic person, depending on the predominant nature of their personality. Bhagavan said their *faith* can be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. And then he said that depending on their personality, everything they do will be guided by that *faith*. The food they eat, the disciplines they practice, the charities they do -- all will be guided by their personality, whether Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic.

And therefore he said, now we'll discuss in detail what these are. So we have seen the verse: Ahara Tu Api Sarvasya Trividho Bhavati Priyaha. We have to pay attention to the words. Here all he's saying is that ahara, the food, also becomes dear to these people in three different ways. Depending on your personality, your *faith*, your tendencies, you will like one type of food or another. He did not say that these foods are inherently Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic.

These qualities depend on the mood of your mind. We all know that there are times you like to eat some chatpata, spicy food. And times you really want to stay away from it. Early morning somebody says have idli dosa for breakfast. But we went to the South and there, early morning, the breakfast comes -- idli dosa. And I said, are you serious that you want me to eat idli dosa at this hour?

I thought it's lunchtime. No, in the breakfast also idli dosa. So depending on my mood, I like one type of food or another. Yajna, tapah, tatha danam -- not only food is driven by the mood of my mind. These sattvic, rajasic and tamasic qualities are not inherent in the things we see in this world.

They're actually the qualities of my mind -- the moods of my mind. That mind will decide whether something is sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. So depending on my mood, I will decide what I like. Bhagavan said even the food you like will be dependent on the mood of your mind. Whether sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic. Even the efforts you make.

Yajna -- traditionally we call that havan, which we do with fire and put offerings in it. Basically all your life you're doing yajna by putting your efforts, *offering* your actions in this yajna of your life. That will also be determined by the mood of your mind. The disciplines which you follow -- tapas, austerities -- not just sitting with folded legs. Everything you do to discipline yourself is basically tapas.

If you have to run a marathon, you have to do tapas for that, right? You have to train for that. That's your tapas. That will be determined by the mood of your mind -- whether sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic.

Where do I make charities when I give something back to society? He says that will also depend on the mood of my mind. Some people will donate toward hospitals and health care. Some toward a sports complex. Whatever you think is dear to your heart, that's where you are going to make charities. Bhagavan said everything in your life will be driven by your *faith*, your conviction -- whether it is sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic.

Your life will be driven by that. And therefore he said, let's talk about how that affects you. Ayuh *sattva* bala arogya sukha priti vivardhanah rasyah snigdhah sthira hrdya aharah sattvikapriyah. You really have to be very careful in reading this verse. First of all, it says that if the mood of my mind is sattvic, what do I want to get out of my life? My sattvic mood will say that I want Ayuh -- I want to prolong my life through my efforts.

I want to live a pure life, a long life. Bala, strength -- doesn't mean I want to be like Hercules, but means I don't have to be dependent on others for help. Arogya, health. Health is my real nature. I don't wake up any morning and say, I don't know why I'm feeling so good -- let me call my doctor, there's got to be something wrong. Because that's my nature, my real nature. I take it for granted. My health is my nature.

It's when I'm not healthy that I notice. Whatever it is, let's take care of it, because it's not my real nature. So Bhagavan said sukha, priti -- I want to be comfortable. Nobody wants to be uncomfortable.

I want to choose the food which will make me comfortable. Priti doesn't mean falling in love with somebody. Priti means something that makes me feel good. So I decide what my goal is in eating food first. My goal in eating food is to have ayuh, *sattva*, bala, arogya, sukha, and priti.

And I want to eat the food which promotes this kind of health. So that's the mood of my sattvic mind. And therefore the food he or she chooses would be rasyah, snigdhah, sthira, hrdya. Snigdhah doesn't mean oily with lots of calories. It means fresh, substantial, has nutritional value. Hrdya means agreeable, which works with my system, which I can digest.

Rasyah, snigdhah, sthira, hrdya. So either I'm living to eat, or eating to live, is the question. Here he says the sattvic person will first decide what they want to get out of food. This is the purpose of eating: I want to increase my ayuh, *sattva*, my purity, my strength, my health, my comfort and my mood. So let's find out which food will be agreeable for me to do that.

And we find that rasyah, snigdhah, sthira, hrdya -- the fresh foods, pure food, healthy food -- are the ones which will give me that. Therefore sattvic people like this type of food. That's all Bhagavan said here. He did not say eat this or don't eat this, or that people who eat other foods are not good. He said because your goal of life is to increase these types of qualities, you will choose that type of food.

In the next verse he says katva amla lavana atyushna tikshna ruksha vidahinah, ahara rajasasya ishta duhkha shoka amaya pradah. This type of food rajasic people like -- bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, dry, burning. But in the end he says the result would be this. See, in the first verse he said what the sattvic goal is. The sattvic person decided what their goal is first, then chose the food. The rajasic person decided the food I like, that's why I'm going to eat it.

Then Bhagavan said the result would be duhkha, shoka, amaya pradah. This food gives you duhkha, discomfort. Anybody who went to a party, had a good dose of hors d'oeuvres, and then dinner at 10:30 -- tell me, was that the best night you had? It was uncomfortable. I'll tell you what, I didn't sleep well that night.

I wish I had controlled myself. Shoka, grief, and amaya, disease. Katva, amla, lavana, atyushna, tikshna, ruksha, vidahinah -- bitter, sour, salty, extremely hot, pungent, dry, burning. Now Bhagavan didn't say this food is bad. He also did not say don't eat this food.

He said the result of this food will be duhkha, shoka, amaya pradah. These foods will result in discomfort, grief and disease. But he said when I'm in a rajasic mood, I don't really have time to think about my food. So whatever is tasty, I will eat that. In a rajasic mode, it's not that one group of people only eat this and another group only eat that. When I am in a sattvic mood I'll be very careful about what I'm eating. When I'm in a rajasic mood I'll say I don't really care -- I'm on a one-day trip, whatever.
snippets.reflection:
These verses introduce a fascinating principle: even something as basic as food preference reveals the texture of our mind. Krishna describes how sattvic foods are "rasyah snigdhah sthira hrdya" - juicy, wholesome, substantial, and pleasing to the heart - and they promote longevity, purity, strength, health, and cheerfulness. Rajasic foods are bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, and dry, leading to discomfort, grief, and disease. Notice that Bhagavan does not command "eat this, not that" - rather, he reveals that our food preferences mirror our mental state, and our food choices reinforce that state.

This week, practice mindful eating as a spiritual discipline. Before each meal, pause and ask: "Am I eating to live, or living to eat?" Notice your cravings - are you reaching for fresh, nourishing foods that promote vitality (sattvic), or for stimulating "comfort foods" loaded with spices and calories (rajasic)? When in a hurry, do you grab whatever is available without thought (tamasic)? The teaching here is not about rigid dietary rules, but about using food as a mirror for self-knowledge. Try one meal this week eaten in complete silence, savoring each bite, noticing how different foods affect your energy and mental clarity. Remember: your body is the vehicle for spiritual growth, and how you fuel it reflects - and shapes - your inner state.
snippets.shortReflection: You're more careful with your words in public than in private. But your inner monologue shapes everything. Is your self-talk harsh or kind? Cynical or hopeful? That voice becomes your reality. Mental discipline isn't about forced positivity—it's about not letting every passing thought rent space in your head.

snippets.transliteration:
yāta-yāmaṁ gata-rasaṁ pūti paryuṣhitaṁ cha yat
uchchhiṣhṭam api chāmedhyaṁ bhojanaṁ tāmasa-priyam

verseTranslations: The Ignorant love food which is stale, not nourishing, putrid and corrupt, the leavings of others and unclean.
Sacrifice is Pure when it is offered by one who does not covet the fruit thereof, when it is done according to the commands of scripture, and with implicit faith that the sacrifice is a duty.
Sacrifice which is performed for the sake of its results, or for self-glorification - that, O best of Aryans, is the product of Passion.
snippets.commentary:
Culturally we are obsessed with classifications, so we classify everything. In this case, Arjuna asked the question: if somebody does not have any guidance from the Sastras -- either voluntarily rejected or not available -- but he still has faith and is working, propelled by his faith, what type of *faith* is that? Bhagavan says: as the man, so is his faith; also, as the *faith*, so is the man. Both have a very synergistic relationship.

My *faith* and who I am are basically very closely related to each other. And therefore this chapter is all about explaining the types of faith one can develop. If I have a goal to be one type of a person or other, I should examine what type of faith do I have? Or I should at least see that what type of faith will lead me to the goal which I want to achieve. So therefore the whole discussion about the three types of faith, and obviously it was quite anticipated after learning 16 chapters of Bhagavad Gita, that these three types of *faith* correspond with the three qualities of Maya, Sattva, Rajas and *Tamas*. Everything can be the Sattvik, Rajasik or Tamasic.

Once again we have to remember that nothing we have discussed ever said that one quality can be exclusive of other two. The one quality always comes with the little shades of the other two. But it is the predominance of my personality or my *faith* makes me who I am. The worship people do are also depending on their faith. Sattvicas will worship the Devas -- in other words, to get the *illumination* of their mind. They want the light of *knowledge* in their internal instruments. The Rajasic wants to achieve wealth, prosperity, something they think will give them infinite happiness. But we know it is transitory.

The goal is the same for all of us: *liberation* from our sorrows and unhappiness. We should examine whether my path is the one which will lead me to that goal. And therefore the discussion. Even the likes and dislikes of people depend on their personality, their *faith*. The type of food I like depends on which mood my mind is in.

So when I'm in a sattvic mode, the type of food I like will be what we discussed. Sighnaha rasaha, that which promotes health. When I'm in rajasik mood, something which tastes good and when I'm tamasik mood, whatever is available now, this mood continues to change in our day to day life. Also, at times I would love to listen to Jagjit Singh's ghazal. But there are times I shut him off -- this is not the time.

I'm sometimes driving for like a couple of hours. You normally think that I'll be putting Jagjit Singh ghazal or two hours. I never listen to it. I want to listen to Bloomberg or CNBC or something which keeps my mind alert about this world. Because I'm not in a mood of listening to music. So mood of my mind determines what I like and dislike.

This mood continues to change. But my goal is to make sure the predominance of my mind is in the one or the other which I am currently convinced that which gives me the *liberation* from my sorrow. And therefore this elaborate discussion about these three faiths: aphalakankshi bhih yajnaha. We have seen what they worship, what types of likes and dislikes they have and therefore what they receive, the ahara, what they eat, what they receive through their senses. Type of music I like. All that is depending on the mood of my mind.

So now it says what type of yajna, the actions. Yajna basically is a *sacrifice*. When we sacrifice something we are offering to someone. Every action of mine in this world is my Yajna, my *offering* to this world. But whether I'm offering with expectations or no expectations is what makes that action either a yajna or a normal *action*.

So Aphalakankshi bhih Yajnah Vidhidrishtah ya ijyate Yastavyam eveti manah samadhaya sa Sattvikah. That yajna or *sacrifice* which is offered without *desire* for fruits and performed as per the ordinance -- in other words, done methodically. I can do something haphazardly or I can do something methodically. Both will have different results. You know, when I first went to architecture school, the first thing they teach you -- well, they don't teach you, actually, you have to learn on your own.

In those days we used to have drawing boards. You put a paper on it and then you have T-squares and set squares -- those of you in engineering understand. For the first two months, I never understood how to do that, because nobody ever tells you how to align this paper. So you haphazardly start something and it never really comes out right. One day I had to ask my seniors. One of my friends, who was a senior student -- I said: you know, Gupta, this never comes out right. All my borders are always off.

He said: Rajan, let me tell you how to do it. First thing, you set your board correctly. Then make sure your seat is comfortable so you can reach everything. Then align your paper to your T-square, not to your board. And that was like an eye-opener to me -- oh, that's why his drawing comes out better than mine.

Because when I was putting the effort before, without Vidhi Purvakam, I had never tried to find out what is the right method, or at least had no *knowledge* of it. Once I found out the right method, then I realized why it is so important. Before you start, make sure everything is correct -- drawing board is stable, my seat is stable, nothing is falling apart, everything is aligned. Now things work out much better than before.

So Bhagavan said, one who is doing Vidhi Purvakam -- Vidhi Drishtah, Yastavyam Eveti Manah Samadhaya Sa Sattvikah -- with the firm *faith* that sacrifice is a duty. Why am I doing it? snippets.reflection:
These verses complete the teaching on food and introduce the three types of yajna (sacrifice or action). Tamasic food is described as "yatayamam gatarasam puti paryusitam" - stale, tasteless, putrid, and leftover - reflecting a careless, inert approach to life. But the heart of this section lies in understanding sattvic versus rajasic action. The sattvic yajna is performed "aphalakankibhih" (without desire for fruits), following proper method (vidhi-drsta), with the firm conviction that "this is my duty" (yastavyam eva). The rajasic yajna, by contrast, is performed "abhisandhaya tu phalam dambhartham" - with expectation of results and for the sake of showing off.

Reflect on your motivations at work and in service. When you take on a project, do you first calculate "what's in it for me?" (rajasic) or do you recognize it as your duty and trust that appropriate results will follow (sattvic)? Krishna's teaching here connects to the law of karma: if you have faith that your worth will be recognized - if not by this employer, then by another - you can focus entirely on excellence rather than anxiety about rewards. This week, choose one task and approach it purely as duty, without mental bargaining about recognition or reward. Notice how this shifts your energy and the quality of your work. Ask yourself: "Am I performing this action to show off my abilities, or because it genuinely needs to be done?"
snippets.shortReflection: Notice how the pursuit of 'more' has contaminated even your good actions. You meditate to feel calmer. You give to feel generous. You help others to feel worthy. Every transaction keeps the ego alive. Try this: do something kind today with zero expectation of how it'll make you feel. Watch what happens when you stop measuring.

snippets.reflection:
These verses describe tamasic sacrifice and introduce the beautiful teaching on threefold tapas (austerity). Tamasic yajna is "vidhihinam" (without proper method), "mantrahinam" (without sacred intention), "adaksinam" (without appropriate offering), and most importantly, "shraddha-virahitam" (devoid of faith) - it is mere ritual going through the motions. But then Krishna reveals three levels of genuine tapas: physical (sharira tapa) includes worship of the Divine, respect for teachers and the wise, purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence. Verbal tapas (vak tapa) is speech that is "anudvegakaram" (non-agitating), true, pleasant, beneficial, and includes study of scriptures.

The teaching on speech is particularly practical: your words should be truthful AND pleasant AND beneficial - not just one or two of these qualities. Many pride themselves on "brutal honesty" while causing harm, or speak sweetly but without truth. This week, before speaking, especially in difficult conversations, pause and ask: "Is what I am about to say true? Is it pleasant (or at least not agitating)? Is it beneficial to the listener?" Practice the discipline of svadhyaya (self-study) by reading even a few verses of sacred text daily. Also examine your physical tapas: Do you show genuine respect to teachers and elders, or is it merely formal? Is there violence in your actions, even subtle forms like impatience or carelessness with others' time and feelings?
snippets.shortReflection: Your speech reveals you. Do you speak to be heard or to connect? To assert or to understand? To wound or to heal? Before your next difficult conversation, ask: is what I'm about to say true, necessary, and kind? If it's only one or two of those, reconsider. Silence is also a choice.

snippets.title: Day 209: The Silence of the Mind
snippets.sanskrit:
मनःप्रसादः सौम्यत्वं मौनमात्मविनिग्रहः |
भावसंशुद्धिरित्येतत्तपो मानसमुच्यते ||

श्रद्धया परया तप्तं तपस्तत्ित्रविधं नरैः |

snippets.transliteration:
manaḥ-prasādaḥ saumyatvaṁ maunam ātma-vinigrahaḥ
bhāva-sanśhuddhir ity etat tapo mānasam uchyate

verseTranslations: Serenity, kindness, silence, self-control and purity - this is austerity of mind.
These threefold austerities performed with faith, and without thought of reward, may truly be accounted Pure.
Austerity coupled with hypocrisy or performed for the sake of self-glorification, popularity or vanity, comes from Passion, and its result is always doubtful and temporary.
snippets.commentary:
We are coming to the concluding portion of the Bhagavad Gita, and some of us who started from chapter one and have gone through all 16 chapters may start wondering: what about the people who never get a chance to learn the Bhagavad Gita? We are fortunate that we get a chance to learn the Bhagavad Gita one way or another. But what about the people who never thought about learning it or never had a chance? The thought does come to our mind: how do they live their life in a manner which is appropriate? A similar question Arjuna asked in the beginning of this chapter.

Arjuna says: I learned from you all this *knowledge* which you have given me, and I have Shraddha. But how about the people who have never gone through the scriptures or had the guidance from the scriptures? They also have Shraddha -- everyone has Shraddha in something, that we know. So how is their Shraddha helping them, or how do you classify their Shraddha? What kind of Shraddha is that, without any basis or guidance from any guru or scriptures?

And Bhagavan said each person has a Shraddha according to his or her mental makeup. It as simple as that. Whatever my mental makeup is that will decide what type of things I will be convinced will give me happiness. Bhavan said that there are three types of Shraddha you find in people. One is Sattvik, other is Rajasic, third is Tamasic depending on the texture of the person's mind. We know that texture of our mind changes as the circumstances change.

So depending on my circumstances and the basic nature of my mind, my mind will be either in a Sattvic mode or in a Rajasic mode or a Tamasic mode. But with practice I can control mood of my mind. Even when these circumstances are not conducive, Bhagavan said, that becomes your predominant nature. Some people, no matter what it is, get angry. Some people, no matter what situation has come, enter the room and people will be all agitated. But that is because that is your basic nature.

Your basic nature is what is predominantly the life you are living and how you are reacting to the situations. And that makes up your mental texture. And as your mental texture, so is your *faith*. And as your faith, so will be your mental texture. So we'll go back and forth between who I am, what I have *faith* in, what my *faith* in what make me who I am. So what are the three types of Shraddha?

And this Shraddha is so powerful that it will lead your life. It will guide your life. Wherever I have my conviction that this is right. This is what will give me happiness. It will pursue that path. So our life is not really divided.

What I do in one aspect of my life does not affect the other aspect of my life. Even though we think, well, I compartmentalize my life -- my professional life is different from my personal life -- in reality there is nothing like that. Who you are will permeate through the entire life that you live, whether it is personal, professional, social, or sacred.

So Bhagawan said that that's very important. That you control the texture of your mind. Because that will exhibit your qualities no matter what you are doing. And therefore he said that even to something as simple as Ahar food also you will pursue according to the mental makeup of yours. So in the beginning we had talked about three types of people. What type of food they will like.

That is, something which will give nourishment, is life-giving, promotes health. When you're Rajasic, you will like something which is tasty, feel-good food, comfort food. As soon as the word "comfort" comes, you know it's not really healthy. There is a restaurant in downtown that specializes in comfort food. I finally realized it's all loaded with calories.

That's why it's good. I don't know why Bhagavan made it that way -- why can't comfort food be healthy? I always question why fried food is not the healthiest food. So up till now people have been saying low-fat milk, skim milk, low fat.

I just read article in New York Times said the whole milk is now rising in popularity. Because now the research says the whole milk is actually healthier than your skim milk. Still he said the American association, whatever the doctors recommend that you should have the low calorie diet. But the low calorie diet is gradually losing its glitter. So Bhagavan said that the person with Sattvic mood will find something which is nourishing and health giving. Rajesh will find something which tastes good and comfort food and it's a tamasic.

Will get anything that is available. Does not matter whether it is good or bad. Then we said even the Yajna they perform in a broader sense. All my efforts are basically offered in the Yajna of my life. My life is a Yajna and I am *offering* all my efforts into it to achieve something good. Bhagawan saying the Yajna is for the greater good.

Even when I consider that I'm doing something for the greater good it will be all as per my mental makeup. Even though I may have good intentions, I may end up doing something which may not be helpful to others. The road to hell is paved with good intentions -- I think the Rolling Stones or somebody said that. So sometimes, even though I have good intentions, my mental makeup will make me put efforts in a place where I feel right. They may not be right.

Therefore he says the Sattvik will put efforts where it is. He has figured out what is the right way to put actions. With *faith*, with guidance that he will put his effort. When I buy furniture, I'm so impatient. Let's not worry about the instructions. Let's start putting it together.

Halfway I realize that I missed a couple of steps. I have to go back and undo it. Bhagavan said the sattvic person will find out the right way to do it first. Whatever he does, he'll follow the proper method. A rajasic person will say let's get it done. Right or wrong, let's just get it done.

Because I want a result instantaneously -- that which gives me a result instantaneously, that's what I want to do. You don't have patience to go through this step by step, or Vidhi Purvakam. So because we want instantaneous results, I sing a song and people who are just like me, who don't know what music is, say: great, you are doing very well. That's what I was looking for.

So that's Rajasic Yajna -- without any method but with a result, a fruit, in mind. And then the last one we have seen: Yajna where I don't even have *faith* in it, but it's supposed to be done as per society's norm, or people think I'm not doing right, so let's do it anyway. It's like a factor of safety before an exam -- go to the temple. I know that's not really going to help, but you might as well do it because there is no harm. Just as a factor of safety, maybe let's go to the temple and say: Bhagavan, take care, tomorrow I have an exam. Without *faith*, without any method, without any reason -- that Yajna, Bhagavan says, is Tamasic Yajna.

Then we came to the Tapas.

This *faith* affects ahara, yajna, tapa, and dana. So now we came to the Tapas part. Tapas, austerities, or as we loosely translate it, the disciplines which we follow. We discipline ourselves so that we can get some benefit out of it. We exercise routinely for our good health. I want to run a marathon -- I have to prepare myself.

So when we started this discussion, Bhagavan described three types of Tapas. First is at the physical level, next is Tapas at the speech level, and third is Tapas at the mental level, the thoughts level. So at the physical level:

In my activities, Bhagavan described worship of the Devas, Dwijah, Prajnah, and Guru -- deities, *divine* beings, twice born, wise people, and your guru. *Ahimsa* and Shaucham are considered Sharira Tapas. All of us, at some level or other, try to do that in our activities.

Next, speech: whatever I speak is non-agitating to others, it is truth but sweet-sounding truth, and it is beneficial to others. That's Tapas at the speech level.

And then Tapas at the mind level, where my mind is silent and not creating unnecessary noise in the background. At the thought level, my thoughts are disciplined. My thoughts are always about my highest goal, which is to achieve that oneness with God, as we call it. But in reality, what we are looking for is unbroken happiness.

When I achieve a state where my happiness remains permanent -- it's not temporary, it's not coming and going -- Bhagavan said that's at the thought level. We know that most of us try at the physical level. The majority of people will fall into a category where they are trying their Tapas at the actions level. Where we fail is at the speech level, because we think that saying something is not hurting anybody.

I'm *Ahimsa-minded*, but I say things that will hurt other people. "I'm not hitting him, I'm not hurting him -- I'm just saying things." We hear this in the media all the time these days. But Bhagavan said that's also very harmful, and therefore very important to watch. So the majority will stop at the physical level of Tapas in actions, but fail to do it at the speech level.

Then out of the remaining, there are few who try hard to be at the speech level, but most of us fail at the thought level. Because I think nobody knows what I'm thinking. Nobody has any clue what I'm thinking. Only my outward actions and my speech are the things people are noticing or judging me from. Most of our lives we're doing things for others to judge us by, right? That's why I said all marketing works very well.

Because all these people in marketing psychology figured out we never think about what this will look on me. We're only thinking about what it looks on others. So when we look at Tom Cruise wearing a suit which looks good on him, so I think it looks good on him, it should look good on me. So we try to judge ourselves by reflecting in the mirror of the society. And we think that what I am thinking in my mind nobody knows. And therefore we fail to do Tapas at the thought level.

But Bhagavan said all three, when performed together, will yield the good results. So the next verse says: Shraddhaya Paraya Taptam Tapah Trividham Naraihi Aphalakankshi Bhih Yuktaihi Sattvikam Parichakshate. A man with firm *devotion* -- Shraddhaya Paraya -- with firm faith, when a person is practicing all these three Tapas -- Trividham, all three -- and Aphalakankshi, he has no particular gain in mind. When I'm doing Tapas also, I shouldn't be expecting a particular result, because I must have complete *faith* in the *Karma* Phaladata -- that if I put my efforts, the results will be there.

So I constantly hear from my staff: Rajan, I don't think that when we come on Sunday and work, anybody is appreciating it. I said, but I don't even know that you came on Sunday. Did you put down your timesheet that you were here on Sunday?
snippets.reflection:
These verses complete the teaching on tapas by introducing the most subtle and important level: mental austerity (manasa tapa). Krishna describes it as "manah prasadah" (serenity of mind), "saumyatvam" (gentleness), "maunam" (silence or contemplation), "atma-vinigrahah" (self-control), and "bhava-samsuddhih" (purity of intention). This is the deepest discipline because, as Krishna notes, most people may discipline their actions and even their speech, but fail at the level of thought - believing that "no one knows what I'm thinking." Yet inner noise eventually corrupts both speech and action. Sattvic tapas is performed with supreme faith, without desire for reward; rajasic tapas is done for "satkaramana-pujartham" - for honor, respect, and praise - and its results are "chalam adhruvam" (unstable and temporary).

This week, practice the discipline of mental silence. Set aside even five minutes daily to simply observe your thoughts without engaging them. Notice: Is your mind predominantly serene or agitated? When you perform good actions, is there a hidden desire for recognition? The teaching reveals that rajasic tapas - discipline performed for applause - yields only temporary, unstable results. Ask yourself honestly: "Would I still practice this discipline if no one ever knew about it?" Also examine bhava-samsuddhih (purity of intention): even if your actions appear sattvic and your speech is controlled, what is the quality of your underlying motivation? True mental austerity means your inner world matches your outer presentation.
snippets.shortReflection: What do you do when no one's watching? That's your real character. Mental discipline is the hardest because no one sees it. You can fake outer composure while your thoughts spiral. But inner chaos eventually leaks out. One practice: when a harsh thought about yourself or someone else arises, notice it without feeding it. That's mental tapas.

snippets.title: Day 210: The Art of Giving
snippets.sanskrit:

parasyotsādanārthaṁ vā tat tāmasam udāhṛitam

verseTranslations: Austerity done under delusion, and accompanied with sorcery or torture to oneself or another, may be assumed to spring from Ignorance.
The gift which is given without thought of recompense, in the belief that it ought to be made, in a fit place, at an opportune time and to a deserving person - such a gift is Pure.
That which is given for the sake of the results it will produce, or with the hope of recompense, or grudgingly - that may truly be said to be the outcome of Passion.
snippets.commentary:
We had been learning in Bhagavad Gita that our goal in life is to find ultimate happiness. And one thing we have noticed in our life is that I only can feel happy when my mind is happy.

So the goal is to keep this mind in a happy mode. And for that I have to purify my mind, purify my mind and intellect, which is an internal instrument to achieve the ultimate goal of *liberation*, *liberation* from my limitations. Right now, the limitations which I have create sorrows and anxieties and regrets.

So to become ultimately happy, I need to get out of my limitations. These limitations exist right now because of my identification with this body, mind, and intellect. Mind is the tool I use to decide whether I am happy or unhappy.

So my first goal is to purify my mind, so it remains in a happy mode -- the Mana Prasadah. So we have seen in this chapter that as my mind, so is my personality, my *faith*. Bhagavan said that there is someone who has no guidance from the scriptures or from a guru, or from any wise person.

But each one of us has faith that I will achieve happiness one way or other. And then wherever my *faith* is that my happiness lies, those are the pursuit I'll pursue. So Arjuna asked Bhagavan, what kind of a faith is that? Bhagavan said, this *faith* can be of three different kinds.

This *faith* can be Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic. Depending on your mind being Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic, you will be convinced your happiness lies in those types of endeavors. So Bhagavan said: your faith, your mental texture -- as the faith, so is the person; as the person, so is the *faith*.

It is very important for me to understand what is making me unhappy, what makes my mind unhappy. And therefore this chapter helps us understand how Sattva, Rajas, and *Tamas* affect my life. So the first thing we have seen: Bhagavan said that everything you do in life will be controlled by your mental makeup -- the type of food you like, the type of food you will take, the yajnas which you perform, all the effort you put for the greater good.

But that greater good also include myself. So therefore, all my actions which I perform are basically to achieve their ultimate goal of becoming happy. So those actions which I offer as my *sacrifice* to get my happiness is my yajna.

See, those yajnas will be also of three different types. Sattvik, rajasik and tamasic. So we have seen that the ahara, the sattvik people will eat what is good for them.

And nutritious. Rajasic people will eat whatever is pleasant, whatever feels good. And Tamasic will take whatever is available.

Yajnas -- Sattvic people will perform without any expectations for the fruits; the Rajasic will have a goal in mind, what they want to get out of these efforts; and the Tamasic just doesn't care. Then we talked about tapas, austerities -- but in our life we call it discipline. I have to discipline myself to do this.

I was just reading this morning. Now, the new research says that not doing exercise is as bad as smoking cigarettes every day. I better be careful because I'm the one who obviously does not get motivated for exercise that easily.

So now I say, oh, I need to exercise. That's something I'm telling myself. I need to perform to be in a good shape.

I want to be in good shape because I want to be healthy. I want to be healthy because that makes me happy. So ultimately, all the tapas which we do, all the disciplines which we practice, are for my happiness.

Bhagavan said Tapas is performed at three different levels: you perform at your physical level in your actions, you perform at your speech level, And you perform at the mental level. So the actions level, My actions should be helping others and not harming others. All my activities, I keep in mind that my actions are for the greater good.

Once I take care of the greater good, I am already included in it. Because any *action* performed by any one person in this universe affects the entire universe. We know that we are all connected with each other.

If one person in family is unhappy, it makes the whole family unhappy. So we know that that why I should be performing this for greater good. Because it ultimately will affect me if someone is suffering.

That suffering will eventually come down to me. The bhagavan said that the tapas are performed at three different levels. My activities should be such that it is for the greater good, then at the speech level, my speech should be such that it is truth but pleasant sounding truth.

All we husbands have a good idea of this. When your wife says, how do I look -- do you really want to be truthful? You can be truthful, but it has to be pleasant-sounding. Satyam Vada, Priyam Vada.

Bhagavan said your speech should be not only truthful and pleasant, but also beneficial. If I tell somebody a truth, it has to be for his or her benefit, not just because I want to be *Satya* Vadi Harishchandra. So that's at the speech level.

And then at the mental level -- I may be acting in a manner that looks so Sattvic, I may be speaking so softly and nicely, but if there is noise in my mind which is completely different from my actions and my speech, it will eventually affect my speech and my actions. Therefore, at the mental level, this tapas is what Bhagavan is describing. Now when I'm performing, it can also be the same three categories of Sattvik, rajasic and tamasic.

Again, my tapas is for not for getting anything out of it, but it is something I need to do. So that's the purification of your internal instrument. My tapas is to purify my internal instrument so that I can experience that happiness in my mind.

And the last thing we are seeing is the Dana. Charity is our general idea is it is to help others. In reality, charity is to help yourself.

Therefore, Vivekananda said: if you find somebody who is worthy of helping, when you help, thank him for giving you the opportunity to help -- so that you can help yourself. Dhanam is for me to purify my mind and control my *ego*. Dana gives me the opportunity to purify my mind by giving away things which are in abundance with me.

Dana is also a social phenomenon to keep the equilibrium in society. We know that in any given society there will be income inequality. People are not born with the same resources and therefore there will be inequality.

And if I happen to be the one who is fortunate enough to have more than what I need, it becomes my *duty* and it becomes my means to purify my mind by doing charities. So charities are strictly for me and not for others. So when the I perform charities, I must be very clear why I'm performing these charities.

So there Bhagavan said that these charities can be seen as three types. Again, Sattvik Rajasik or Tamarsic. The first one says Datavyam.

The very first requirement for appropriate Sattvic Dana, which will give you the most result of what you're looking for. What you're looking for in your life is to purify your mind to a point that it is always in a sunny, bright mood and you're always happy. You do not want to be grouchy and unhappy, complaining and regretful.

So to keep my mind in that mode, I'm performing all of this -- I'm eating the right food, doing the right yajna, doing the right tapas. When I do also, I have to keep in mind I'm doing it for me and therefore I should know how to make these charities. So the first requirement is Datavyam Iti -- I see a cause and realize there is no other way but for me to help.

You are going on a road and you see a little child just about to get hit by a car. You don't sit down and say: is this going to be a Sattvic act or Rajasic? Is it going to be Tamasic? At that point you have no other thought than I need to help that child get him or her out of the harm's way. So when you do a charity and you have that attitude, it has to be done, it has to be done then that's the right charity.

And when you give, you are not obliging that person -- actually, you should thank him: you are obliging me by giving me a chance. If there's no one to help, who are you going to help? When we were at the old temple, we were having this annadhanam, because every Sunday people would come there. But if you are feeding people who are already fed, that is not Annadhanam -- it is just a party you are having.

Every week we all get together. When a person needs food and you give him food, that's Annadhanam. If a person is already fed, you can't give him food and call it charity.

Deshe kale cha patre cha ta danam sattvikam smrutam -- when it is given at the right time, at the right place, to the right person. So if I want to help somebody and that person is sitting in a group of his friends, and I go and say: you told me that you need help -- Here is my hundred dollars which you asked for. You are insulting him in front of his friends and family.

He didn't want other people to know his problems. He came to you to ask for help, and now you're helping him at the wrong place. Wrong place, wrong time.

You should also not help somebody who you know does not need any help. Sometimes people say: I don't get a chance to do all this social work. I want to do social work, but people are not making me president of this organization.

You shouldn't worry about it. Bhagavan says Patra -- only help someone who really needs help and is seeking help. When you find that opportunity, take that opportunity that is God's given to you.

Consider that as God's blessing that you came across this opportunity to help that person and therefore you're helping. Bhagawan says that's a Sattvik dharam. You're not expecting anything out of it.

Just like the example of a child in a harm's way. When you help that child you're not expecting anything, not even thank you from anybody. At that point your only thought is I need to get that child out of the harm's way.

It's the exact same emotion you should have when you give somebody any help: that person needs help, and I have the means -- I need to help that person. Bhagavan says that's Sattvic Dana. Yatu pratyupakarartham phalam uddishya va punah diyate pariklistam tadanam rajasam smrutam.

In contrast to that, the gift which is given in view of receiving something in return -- phalam uddishya. I'll make this donation so I can get this tax benefit. And at least people will think that he is a good donor.

I am doing these charities so it will help my business. So all companies say "we are connected, we give back" -- all that is actually just marketing.
snippets.reflection:
These verses describe tamasic tapas and introduce the profound teaching on dana (charity). Tamasic austerity is performed "mudha-grahena" (with foolish stubbornness), involving self-torture or harming others - discipline without wisdom or proper understanding. But the verses on dana reveal a transformative truth: sattvic giving is "datavyam iti" - done with the conviction that "this must be given," to one who cannot reciprocate (anupakarine), at the right place, time, and to the right recipient. Rajasic giving, by contrast, is "pratyupakarartham" (expecting something in return) or "pariklistam" (given grudgingly). Vivekananda captured this beautifully: when you find someone worthy of help, thank them for giving you the opportunity to purify your own mind.

 Reflect deeply on your relationship with giving. When you donate or help someone, do you calculate the tax benefit or social recognition? Do you give reluctantly, feeling the pinch? The sattvic giver experiences the spontaneous urgency of "datavyam iti" - like seeing a child about to be hit by a car, where helping is not a choice but an imperative.

 This week, practice giving with complete anonymity - help someone who cannot possibly repay you, without anyone knowing. Notice how this feels different from publicized charity. Also examine: Do you give at the right time and place (not embarrassing the recipient), to those who genuinely need help (not just those who can acknowledge you)? Remember, dana purifies the giver more than it helps the receiver.
snippets.shortReflection: Check your giving. When you help someone, do you secretly wait for acknowledgment? When you donate, do you calculate the social credit? When you sacrifice, do you keep score? Real generosity leaves no trace, not even in your own memory. Give something today—money, time, attention—and practice forgetting you did it.

snippets.reflection:
These verses describe tamasic giving and introduce the sacred formula "Om Tat Sat" - the triple designation of the Eternal Spirit (Brahman). Tamasic dana is given "adesha-kale" (at the wrong place and time), "apatrebhyah" (to unworthy recipients), "asatkrtam" (without respect), and "avajnatam" (with contempt) - it demeans both giver and receiver. But then Krishna offers a powerful tool for transformation: "Om Tat Sat" - by which the Vedas, Brahmanas, and sacrifices were ordained from the beginning. Om represents the transcendental reality beyond all parts; those who understand the Spirit begin all acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity by uttering Om, remembering that all manifestation is ultimately one.

The teaching of Om is profoundly practical. Even if your faith is currently rajasic or tamasic, beginning any action with the remembrance of Om - the ultimate unity behind all diversity - can gradually purify and transform that faith toward sattva. This week, experiment with this ancient practice: before beginning any significant action (work, conversation, meal, or practice), pause and silently invoke Om, remembering that you and all beings are manifestations of one reality. Notice how this shifts your relationship to the action and to others involved. Also examine your giving: Have you ever given in a way that embarrassed the recipient or showed contempt? True giving preserves dignity and arises from respect for the Divine in the other person.
snippets.shortReflection: Most of your suffering comes from doing the right thing for the wrong reason or the wrong way. You help, but with resentment. You give, but at the wrong moment. You speak truth, but harshly. Timing, intention, and method matter as much as the act itself. Today, ask before any action: is this the right thing, in the right way, at the right time?

snippets.title: Day 212: Tat, Sat, and Asat
snippets.sanskrit:
तदित्यनभिसन्धाय फलं यज्ञतपःक्रियाः |
दानक्रियाश्च विविधाः क्रियन्ते मोक्षकाङ्क्षि ||

सद्भावे साधुभावे च सदित्येतत्प्रयुज्यते |
प्रशस्ते कर्मणि तथा सच्छब्दः पार्थ युज्यते ||

यज्ञे तपसि दाने च स्थितिः सदिति चोच्यते |
कर्म चैव तदर्थीयं सदित्येवाभिधीयते ||
snippets.transliteration:
tad ity anabhisandhāya phalaṁ yajña-tapaḥ-kriyāḥ
dāna-kriyāśh cha vividhāḥ kriyante mokṣha-kāṅkṣhibhiḥ

sad-bhāve sādhu-bhāve cha sad ity etat prayujyate
praśhaste karmaṇi tathā sach-chhabdaḥ pārtha yujyate

yajñe tapasi dāne cha sthitiḥ sad iti chochyate
karma chaiva tad-arthīyaṁ sad ity evābhidhīyate
verseTranslations: Those who desire deliverance begin their acts of sacrifice, austerity or gift with the word 'Tat' (meaning 'That'), without thought of reward.
'Sat' means Reality or the highest Good, and also, O Arjuna, it is used to mean an action of exceptional merit.
Conviction in sacrifice, in austerity and in giving is also called 'Sat.' So too an action done only for the Lord's sake.
snippets.commentary:
Thinking is driven by our convictions. And therefore who I am is all about my convictions. So who I am is depending on my *faith*. And therefore this chapter elaborates what are the types of faiths a person can have? Then we have broadly classified, just as everything else, in three categories.

*Faith* can be Sattvic, faith can be Rajasic, faith can be Tamasic, and depending on that, I may be a Sattvic person, a Rajasic person or a Tamasik person, and my understanding of that will help me how do I change my faith so that my thinking changes, so my behavior changes, my mind changes and ultimately gives me the result which I'm looking for, which is in the end is to achieve happiness. You're all looking for one and one thing alone is to get out of our limitations and sorrows. So Bhagavan has described in this chapter the three types of *faith* and how it controls our Ahara, our Yagna, our Tapa and our Dana. As we have seen last time, it is what we take from this world, how we interact and connect with this world, how we discipline ourselves for what we want and then what we give back to this world, all dependent on my faith. And therefore my goal obviously is to make my faith more Sattvic. If I detect that I have Tamasic *faith*, I want to make it more Rajasic.

If I detect I'm more Rajasya, make it Sattvik. Eventually I can get to my goal of achieving that happiness. So now our question was: well, I may or may not have that capability, and I may be all filled with Rajasic *faith* and not be able to change that. The last three verses we have seen say there is one way of mitigating that. There is a threefold indicator of that transcendental reality, the ultimate reality, the one unifying entity which binds us all, which is indicated in the Sastras as Om Tat Sat. Om is the transcendental form of the Lord that I have learned in the previous chapter. The Astadha Prakrithi, Eightfold manifest *Prakriti* of the Lord.

So everything which I see and perceive and feel is basically nothing but his manifestation. But then I come to the conclusion, maybe if I put everything together that's Lord, or if I put all the parts together, will it make a machine? The question is how you put it together. So all this part putting together does not still make the identity of the Lord. That is something beyond that. Lower *Prakriti* and higher *Prakriti*.

I have all these parts and say if I put all this together, it will be the whole. No, it has to be in a particular manner. Then only that machine functions as it's supposed to be functioning. All these parts, I have to put it together and perceive it in a way that it will reveal the Lord's identity. And that's the transcendental part, is how to see this whole in a manner that I can see Him. I see this world in its parts, but I can't put it together as his identity.

That's the Aum, a transcendental part. Om is the indicator of that. And if I can remember that -- that all that I see, perceive, and experience put together -- I will never be able to fully understand the Lord through parts alone. But Om points to that reality beyond the parts. My *faith* may be rajasic, it may be even tamasic, but remembering Om will transform it into sattvic *faith*. That's basically a way out given to us by these last three verses.

Om Tat Sat iti nirdeshah brahmanah trividhah smritah. These are the three indicators of that supreme reality. I know all the parts right now, but I can't put together the machine. I can't put together its real identity. So Aum is the one indicator. Tat we have seen is another indicator.

That is that that which I constantly keep referring to the God, the Lord, that entity other than this which I can perceive, feel, touch and vouch for it, that it exists. That which I cannot vouch for, that it exists, does exist, but beyond my perception. So that's Tat and Sat, the existence or the truth. Truth is that which exists in all periods of time. In other words, it was true yesterday, it is true today and it will be true tomorrow. That is Sat.

So these are the three indicators. And Bhagavan said that those who are Brahmavadina -- those who are completely convinced about the existence of that ultimate reality. Just like Mudivad (capitalism), Samajvad (socialism) -- because they're convinced that this is the only way to help the society. Vaad means I'm completely on the side of that.

Those who are completely convinced that *Brahman* is the only reality -- they will start all their activities by uttering Om. Utterance means remembrance. It's an indication to me that Om is the ultimate reality. I may be perceiving a difference between you and me right now, and therefore I may have developed a liking or disliking for you.

But Om is the ultimate reality which manifests as me, which manifests as you. As long as I have that thought in the beginning, whatever I do afterwards will be purified. Om Iti Udahritya Yajna Dana Tapaha Kriyaha -- we have discussed all that in the previous verses. The activities we are performing in this world:

We receive from the world, we interact with the world, we connect with this world, we prepare ourselves for how to interact with the world, and then we give back to the world. First, those who are Brahmavadina.

We see that those who are seeking *liberation* have come to the conclusion that there is no way that in my present state of limitedness the ultimate goal of infinite happiness is possible. I have come to that clear understanding that no matter how hard I try with my mind and intellect and body that unbroken happiness is not possible at all. It's only possible if I can identify with that. That which is unlimited. That which has no limitations.

That which has no sorrows, that which has no competition, that which is all-pervading. People who are seeking *moksha* -- and we are all *Moksha* Kankshi, believe it or not -- we want *liberation* from anything which we think is our limitation.

All of us who are aware of our limitations and are not happy with them -- if you're happy with your limitations, you're not a *Moksha* Kankshi. If I have some limitations but think this is good enough, then I'm not seeking *liberation*. But we all have one limitation we cannot stand: running into a situation which makes me unhappy. Therefore I'm constantly trying to avoid the things which create sorrows and want to pursue the things which give me happiness.

So at least I want to get rid of the limitations that run me into situations which give me unhappiness. Bhagavan says those *Moksha* Kankshi who want to get rid of those limitations will start all their activities -- the same yajna, tapa, dana kriyaha -- with Tat. Tat anabhisandhaya phalam yajna tapah kriyaha. They have come to the conclusion that if I remember Him as the *Karma* Phaladata, He is the giver of the fruits. So I leave the results to Him and do all my activities, trusting that He will give me the result that will lead to *liberation*.

We have learned that as *Karma* *Yoga*. The last one: sad bhave sadhu bhave cha sad iti etat prayujyate, prashaste karmani tatha sat shabdah partha yujyate. Sat is used in the sense of reality. Sat, as we have said is only that can be proven true in all three phases. In the past, in the present, in the future. Everything else is unreal. It existed one point of time in time and space, another period of time.

It has no existence whatsoever. It's completely gone. Just like a film on a screen or a hologram. It exists in my perception for a period of time. So the lamp is shut off. The word sat is used in the sense of reality and also for goodness.

Now we are coming back to the world which you and I know -- not transcendental unlimitedness, but the world of good and bad. Our world is divided by good and bad. Bhagavan said the real and the good is indicated in this world as Sat. As we say, there are values and there are universal values.

There are values may be applicable to me in this situation which may not be applicable in other situations. Well, those are transitory values. I work for a company and what are the values of the company? It only applies to me as long as I am there. But there are values which applies to me whether I'm working or not. Whether I'm working for this company or not or that company or not.

Those are universal values. Therefore we have said even before the civilization started, human beings knew what is right and what is wrong. Even before any religious were established, they knew what is good and what is bad. Those universal good and those universal truths are indicated as Sat. It is not dependent on any culture, not dependent on any beliefs -- those are the universal good and universal reality. So Bhagavan said, the word Sat is used in this sense of reality and of goodness. And also, Partha:

The word is used in the sense of auspiciousness. Anything which is good is auspicious. And therefore you start that work, same thing, yajna pohadana kriya with that word sat. Then may this be auspicious. May this act of mine be of goodness and of kindness and of reality. So you start with sat.

So obviously in the Sikh tradition, the word Sat is given the most importance: Sat Sri Akal, that Sat which is Akal, which is timeless, no beginning, no end. So that Sat is uttered: yajne tapasi dane cha sthitih sat iti uchyate. Therefore, if I am one who is clearly aware of good and bad in this world -- I divide my world into this is good and this is evil, this is good for me, this is bad for me -- then I should start all my activities with Sat. Bhagavan says yajne tapasi dane cha -- the activities remaining the same.

Whether it is my tamasic *faith*, my rajasic *faith*, or the sattvic *faith*, it is what my mind tells me is good, I'm gonna do. No matter how much I tell you this is good for you, as long as your mind does not tell you it is good, you will not be able to follow. Everybody says, do this. Okay, okay, I'll think about it. But the thinking part never comes, because I have already decided it is not worth thinking about. So Bhagavan said -- and that's what yajne tapasi dane cha sthitih means:

To be steadfast in my yajna, dana, and tapa. I do some yajnas, but only occasionally -- some *sacrifice* here and there. But occasionally I'm not steadfast. I sometimes get all excited and say, I think we should all do some charity or some kind of community service. We organize this, and then after about two weeks, everything gradually dies down.
snippets.reflection:
These verses explain "Tat" and "Sat" - completing the sacred formula. "Tat" (That) is uttered by those seeking liberation (moksha-kankibhih) who perform yajna, tapas, and dana without attachment to results (anabhisandhaya phalam). They remember that the fruits belong to "That" - the Supreme, the Karma Phaladata (giver of fruits). "Sat" signifies reality, goodness, and auspiciousness - it represents universal truth that transcends all cultures and beliefs, the values that were known even before civilizations and religions were established. Krishna teaches that steadfastness (sthiti) in yajna, tapas, and dana is itself called Sat.

The distinction between Tat and Sat offers practical wisdom. Use "Tat" when you need to surrender the fruits of action - remembering that results belong to That which is beyond your control. Use "Sat" when you need grounding in universal goodness - what is true, beneficial, and auspicious regardless of circumstance. This week, when anxious about outcomes, silently invoke "Tat" to release attachment. When uncertain about whether an action is right, invoke "Sat" and ask: "Is this aligned with universal truth and goodness?" Also examine your steadfastness: Do you enthusiastically begin charitable projects only to abandon them after initial excitement fades? Sthiti (steadfastness) in your practices is itself a form of Sat. What one practice can you commit to maintaining with unwavering consistency?
snippets.shortReflection: When anxiety about the future grips you, use two words: 'Tat' to release control of outcomes, 'Sat' to ground yourself in what's universally true and good. Not every decision requires perfect certainty. Some require surrender. Some require principle. Learning which is which is wisdom.
